vsm1.0:0.4.verse: Chapter I. Description of Virtue (Sīla-niddesa) — [I. Introductory]

vsm1.0:1.1.verse: 1. “When a wise man, established well in virtue, develops consciousness and understanding, then as a bhikkhu ardent and sagacious he succeeds in disentangling this tangle” (S I 13).

vsm1.0:1.3.verse: But why was it said? While the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, it seems, a certain deity came to him in the night, and in order to do away with his doubts, he asked this question:

vsm1.0:1.4.verse: “The inner tangle and the outer tangle—this generation is entangled in a tangle.

vsm1.0:1.5.verse: And so I ask of Gotama this question: who succeeds in disentangling this tangle?” (S I 13).

vsm1.0:1.6.verse: This was the question he asked.

vsm1.0:2.1.verse: 2. Here is the meaning in brief. Tangle is a term for the network of craving.

vsm1.0:2.2.verse: For that is a tangle in the sense of lacing together, like the tangle called network of branches in bamboo thickets, etc., because it goes on arising again and again up and down among the objects [of consciousness] beginning with what is visible. But it is called the inner tangle and the outer tangle because it arises [as craving] for one's own requisites and another's, for one's own person and another's, and for the internal and external bases [for consciousness].

vsm1.0:2.3.verse: Since it arises in this way, this generation is entangled in a tangle.

vsm1.0:2.4.verse: As the bamboos, etc., are entangled by the bamboo tangle, etc., so too this generation, in other words, this order of living beings, is all entangled by the tangle of craving—the meaning is that it is intertwined, interlaced by it.

vsm1.0:2.5.verse: And because it is entangled like this,

vsm1.0:2.6.verse: so I ask of Gotama this question, that is why I ask this.

vsm1.0:2.7.verse: He addressed the Blessed One by his clan name as Gotama.

vsm1.0:2.8.verse: Who succeeds in disentangling this tangle: who may disentangle this tangle that keeps the three kinds of existence entangled in this way?—What he asks is, who is capable of disentangling it?

vsm1.0:3.1.verse: 3. However, when questioned thus, the Blessed One, whose knowledge of all things is unimpeded, deity of deities, excelling Sakka (Ruler of Gods), excelling Brahmā, fearless in the possession of the four kinds of perfect confidence, wielder of the ten powers, all-seer with unobstructed knowledge, uttered this stanza in reply to explain the meaning:

vsm1.0:3.2.verse: “When a wise man, established well in virtue, develops consciousness and understanding,

vsm1.0:3.3.verse: then as a bhikkhu ardent and sagacious he succeeds in disentangling this tangle.”

vsm1.0:3.4.verse: This is the stanza he spoke.

vsm1.0:4.1.verse: 4. My task is now to set out the true sense, divided into virtue and the rest, of this same verse composed by the Great Sage.

vsm1.0:4.2.verse: There are here in the Victor's Dispensation seekers gone forth from home to homelessness, and who although desiring purity have no right knowledge of the sure straight way comprising virtue and the other two, right hard to find, that leads to purity—

vsm1.0:4.3.verse: who, though they strive, here gain no purity.

vsm1.0:4.4.verse: To them I shall expound the comforting Path of Purification, pure in expositions, relying on the teaching of the dwellers in the Great Monastery;

vsm1.0:4.5.verse: let all those good men who do desire purity listen intently to my exposition.

vsm1.0:5.1.verse: 5. Herein, purification should be understood as Nibbāna, which being devoid of all stains, is utterly pure.

vsm1.0:5.2.verse: The path of purification is the path to that purification;

vsm1.0:5.3.verse: it is the means of approach that is called the path.

vsm1.0:5.4.verse: The meaning is, I shall expound that path of purification.

vsm1.0:6.1.verse: 6. In some instances this path of purification is taught by insight alone, according as it is said:

vsm1.0:6.2.verse: “Formations are all impermanent: When he sees thus with understanding And turns away from what is ill, That is the path to purity” (Dhp 277).

vsm1.0:6.3.verse: And in some instances by jhāna and understanding, according as it is said: “He is near unto Nibbāna In whom are jhāna and understanding” (Dhp 372).

vsm1.0:6.4.verse: And in some instances by deeds (kamma), etc., according as it is said: “By deeds, vision and righteousness, By virtue, the sublimest life—By these are mortals purified, And not by lineage and wealth” (M III 262).

vsm1.0:6.5.verse: And in some instances by virtue, etc., according as it is said: “He who is possessed of constant virtue, Who has understanding, and is concentrated, Who is strenuous and diligent as well, Will cross the flood so difficult to cross” (S I 53).

vsm1.0:6.6.verse: And in some instances by the foundations of mindfulness, etc., according as it is said: “Bhikkhus, this path is the only way for the purification of beings … for the realization of Nibbāna, that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness” (D II 290);

vsm1.0:6.7.verse: and similarly in the case of the right efforts, and so on.

vsm1.0:6.8.verse: But in the answer to this question it is taught by virtue and the other two.

vsm1.0:7.1.verse: 7. Here is a brief commentary [on the stanza]. Established well in virtue: standing on virtue. It is only one actually fulfilling virtue who is here said to “stand on virtue.”

vsm1.0:7.2.verse: So the meaning here is this: being established well in virtue by fulfilling virtue.

vsm1.0:7.4.verse: Wise: possessing the kind of understanding that is born of kamma by means of a rebirth-linking with triple root-cause.

vsm1.0:7.5.verse: Develops consciousness and understanding: develops both concentration and insight. For it is concentration that is described here under the heading of “consciousness,”

vsm1.0:7.8.verse: For it is energy that is called “ardour” (ātāpa) in the sense of burning up and consuming (ātāpana-paritāpana) defilements.

vsm1.0:7.9.verse: He has that, thus he is ardent.

vsm1.0:7.10.verse: Sagacious: it is understanding that is called “sagacity”; possessing that, is the meaning.

vsm1.0:7.12.verse: For understanding is mentioned three times in the reply to the question.

vsm1.0:7.13.verse: Herein, the first is naïve understanding, the second is understanding consisting in insight, while the third is the protective understanding that guides all affairs.

vsm1.0:7.14.verse: He sees fear (bhayaṃ ikkhati) in the round of rebirths, thus he is a bhikkhu.

vsm1.0:7.15.verse: He succeeds in disentangling this tangle: Just as a man standing on the ground and taking up a well-sharpened knife might disentangle a great tangle of bamboos, so too, he—this bhikkhu who possesses the six things, namely, this virtue, and this concentration described under the heading of consciousness, and this threefold understanding, and this ardour—

vsm1.0:7.16.verse: standing on the ground of virtue and taking up with the hand of protective-understanding exerted by the power of energy the knife of insight-understanding well-sharpened on the stone of concentration, might disentangle, cut away and demolish all the tangle of craving that had overgrown his own life's continuity.

vsm1.0:7.17.verse: But it is at the moment of the path that he is said to be disentangling that tangle;

vsm1.0:7.18.verse: at the moment of fruition he has disentangled the tangle and is worthy of the highest offerings in the world with its deities.

vsm1.0:7.19.verse: That is why the Blessed One said: “When a wise man, established well in virtue, develops consciousness and understanding, then as a bhikkhu ardent and sagacious he succeeds in disentangling this tangle.”

vsm1.0:8.1.verse: 8. Herein there is nothing for him to do about the [naïve] understanding on account of which he is called wise;

vsm1.0:8.2.verse: for that has been established in him simply by the influence of previous kamma.

vsm1.0:8.3.verse: But the words ardent and sagacious mean that by persevering with energy of the kind here described and by acting in full awareness with understanding he should, having become well established in virtue, develop the serenity and insight that are described as concentration and understanding. This is how the Blessed One shows the path of purification under the headings of virtue, concentration, and understanding there.

vsm1.0:9.1.verse: 9. What has been shown so far is the three trainings, the dispensation that is good in three ways, the necessary condition for the threefold clear-vision, etc., the avoidance of the two extremes and the cultivation of the middle way, the means to surmounting the states of loss, etc., the abandoning of defilements in three aspects, prevention of transgression etc., purification from the three kinds of defilements, and the reason for the states of stream-entry and so on.

vsm1.0:10.1.verse: 10. Here the training of higher virtue is shown by virtue; the training of higher consciousness, by concentration; and the training of higher understanding, by understanding.

vsm1.0:10.2.verse: The dispensation's goodness in the beginning is shown by virtue. Because of the passage, “And what is the beginning of profitable things? Virtue that is quite purified” (S V 143), and because of the passage beginning, “The not doing of any evil” (Dhp 183), virtue is the beginning of the dispensation. And that is good because it brings about the special qualities of non-remorse, and so on.

vsm1.0:10.3.verse: Its goodness in the middle is shown by concentration. Because of the passage beginning, “Entering upon the profitable” (Dhp 183), concentration is the middle of the dispensation. And that is good because it brings about the special qualities of supernormal power, and so on.

vsm1.0:10.4.verse: Its goodness in the end is shown by understanding. Because of the passage, “The purifying of one's own mind—this is the Buddhas' dispensation” (Dhp 183), and because understanding is its culmination, understanding is the end of the dispensation. And that is good because it brings about equipoise with respect to the desired and the undesired.

vsm1.0:10.5.verse: For this is said: “Just as a solid massive rock Remains unshaken by the wind, So too, in face of blame and praise The wise remain immovable” (Dhp 81).

vsm1.0:11.1.verse: 11. Likewise the necessary condition for the triple clear-vision is shown by virtue. For with the support of perfected virtue one arrives at the three kinds of clear-vision, but nothing besides that.

vsm1.0:11.2.verse: The necessary condition for the six kinds of direct-knowledge is shown by concentration. For with the support of perfected concentration one arrives at the six kinds of direct-knowledge, but nothing besides that.

vsm1.0:11.3.verse: The necessary condition for the categories of discrimination is shown by understanding. For with the support of perfected understanding one arrives at the four kinds of discrimination, but not for any other reason.

vsm1.0:11.4.verse: And the avoidance of the extreme called devotion to indulgence of sense desires is shown by virtue. The avoidance of the extreme called devotion to mortification of self is shown by concentration.

vsm1.0:11.5.verse: The cultivation of the middle way is shown by understanding.

vsm1.0:12.1.verse: 12. Likewise the means for surmounting the states of loss is shown by virtue; the means for surmounting the element of sense desires, by concentration; and the means for surmounting all becoming, by understanding.

vsm1.0:12.2.verse: And the abandoning of defilements by substitution of opposites is shown by virtue; that by suppression is shown by concentration; and that by cutting off is shown by understanding.

vsm1.0:13.1.verse: 13. Likewise prevention of defilements' transgression is shown by virtue; prevention of obsession (by defilement) is shown by concentration; prevention of inherent tendencies is shown by understanding.

vsm1.0:13.2.verse: And purification from the defilement of misconduct is shown by virtue; purification from the defilement of craving, by concentration; and purification from the defilement of (false) views, by understanding.

vsm1.0:14.1.verse: 14. [6] Likewise the reason for the states of stream-entry and once-return is shown by virtue; that for the state of non-return, by concentration; that for Arahantship by understanding.

vsm1.0:14.2.verse: For the stream-enterer is called “perfected in the kinds of virtue”; and likewise the once-returner.

vsm1.0:14.3.verse: But the non-returner is called “perfected in concentration.”

vsm1.0:14.4.verse: And the Arahant is called “perfected in understanding” (see A I 233).

vsm1.0:15.1.verse: 15. So thus far these nine and other like triads of special qualities have been shown, that is, the three trainings, the dispensation that is good in three ways, the necessary condition for the threefold clear-vision, the avoidance of the two extremes and the cultivation of the middle way, the means for surmounting the states of loss, etc., the abandoning of defilements in three aspects, prevention of transgression, etc., purification from the three kinds of defilements, and the reason for the states of stream-entry, and so on.

vsm1.1:16.1.verse: However, even when this path of purification is shown in this way under the headings of virtue, concentration and understanding, each comprising various special qualities,

vsm1.1:16.2.verse: it is still only shown extremely briefly.

vsm1.1:16.3.verse: And so since that is insufficient to help all,

vsm1.1:16.4.verse: there is, in order to show it in detail, the following set of questions dealing in the first place with virtue:

vsm1.1:16.5.verse: (i) What is virtue? (ii) In what sense is it virtue?

vsm1.1:16.6.verse: (iii) What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? (iv) What are the benefits of virtue?

vsm1.1:16.7.verse: (v) How many kinds of virtue are there? (vi) What is the defiling of it? (viii) What is the cleansing of it?

vsm1.1:17.3.verse: It is the states beginning with volition present in one who abstains from killing living things, etc., or in one who fulfils the practice of the duties.

vsm1.1:17.4.verse: For this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “What is virtue? There is virtue as volition, virtue as consciousness-concomitant,

vsm1.1:17.5.verse: virtue as restraint, virtue as non-transgression” (Paṭis I 44).

vsm1.1:17.6.verse: Herein, virtue as volition is the volition present in one who abstains from killing living things, etc., or in one who fulfils the practice of the duties.

vsm1.1:17.7.verse: Virtue as consciousness-concomitant is the abstinence in one who abstains from killing living things, and so on.

vsm1.1:17.8.verse: Furthermore, virtue as volition is the seven volitions [that accompany the first seven] of the [ten] courses of action (kamma) in one who abandons the killing of living things, and so on.

vsm1.1:17.9.verse: Virtue as consciousness-concomitant is the [three remaining] states consisting of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, stated in the way beginning, “Abandoning covetousness, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness” (D I 71).

vsm1.1:18.1.verse: Virtue as restraint should be understood here as restraint in five ways: restraint by the rules of the community (pātimokkha), restraint by mindfulness,

vsm1.1:18.2.verse: restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy.

vsm1.1:18.3.verse: Herein, “restraint by the Pātimokkha” is this: “He is furnished, fully furnished, with this Pātimokkha restraint” (Vibh 246).

vsm1.1:18.4.verse: “Restraint by mindfulness” is this: “He guards the eye faculty, enters upon restraint of the eye faculty” (D I 70).

vsm1.1:18.5.verse: “Restraint by knowledge” is this: “The currents in the world that flow, Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “are stemmed by means of mindfulness; restraint of currents I proclaim, by understanding they are dammed” (Sn 1035);

vsm1.1:18.7.verse: And use of requisites is here combined with this.

vsm1.1:18.8.verse: But what is called “restraint by patience” is that given in the way beginning, “He is one who bears cold and heat” (M I 10).

vsm1.1:18.9.verse: And what is called “restraint by energy” is that given in the way beginning, “He does not endure a thought of sense desires when it arises” (M I 11);

vsm1.1:18.10.verse: purification of livelihood is here combined with this.

vsm1.1:18.11.verse: So this fivefold restraint, and the abstinence, in clansmen who dread evil, from any chance of transgression met with,

vsm1.1:18.12.verse: should all be understood to be “virtue as restraint.”

vsm1.1:18.13.verse: Virtue as non-transgression is the non-transgression, by body or speech, of precepts of virtue that have been undertaken.

vsm1.1:18.14.verse: This, in the first place, is the answer to the question, “What is virtue?”

vsm1.1:19.1.verse: Now, as to the rest— (ii) IN WHAT SENSE IS IT VIRTUE? It is virtue (sīla) in the sense of composing (sīlana).

vsm1.1:19.3.verse: It is either a coordinating (samādhāna), meaning non-inconsistency of bodily action, etc., due to virtuousness;

vsm1.1:19.4.verse: or it is an upholding (upadhāraṇa), meaning a state of basis (ādhāra) owing to its serving as foundation for profitable states.

vsm1.1:19.5.verse: For those who understand etymology admit only these two meanings.

vsm1.1:19.6.verse: Others, however, comment on the meaning here in the way beginning, “The meaning of virtue (sīla) is the meaning of head (sira), the meaning of virtue is the meaning of cool (sītala).”

vsm1.1:20.1.verse: (iii) Now, WHAT ARE ITS CHARACTERISTIC, FUNCTION, MANIFESTATION, AND PROXIMATE CAUSE? Here:

vsm1.1:20.2.verse: The characteristic of it is composing, even when analyzed in various ways, as visibility is of visible data even when analyzed in various ways.

vsm1.1:20.3.verse: Just as visibleness is the characteristic of the visible-data base even when analyzed into the various categories of blue, yellow, etc.,

vsm1.1:20.4.verse: because even when analyzed into these categories it does not exceed visible-ness,

vsm1.1:20.5.verse: so also this same composing, described above as the coordinating of bodily action, etc., and as the foundation of profitable states, is the characteristic of virtue even when analyzed into the various categories of volition, etc.,

vsm1.1:20.6.verse: because even when analyzed into these categories it does not exceed the state of coordination and foundation.

vsm1.1:21.2.verse: Its function has a double sense, as action, to stop misconduct, and as achievement, the quality of blamelessness in virtuous men.

vsm1.1:21.3.verse: So what is called virtue should be understood to have the function (nature) of stopping misconduct as its function (nature) in the sense of action,

vsm1.1:21.4.verse: and a blameless function (nature) as its function (nature) in the sense of achievement.

vsm1.1:21.5.verse: For under [these headings of] characteristic, etc., it is action (kicca) or it is achievement (sampatti) that is called “function” (rasa—nature).

vsm1.1:22.1.verse: Now, virtue, so say those who know, shows itself as purity; and for its proximate cause they tell the pair, conscience and shame, as well.

vsm1.1:22.2.verse: This virtue is manifested as the kinds of purity stated thus: “Bodily purity, verbal purity, mental purity” (A I 271);

vsm1.1:22.3.verse: it is manifested, comes to be apprehended, as a pure state.

vsm1.1:22.4.verse: But conscience and shame are said by those who know to be its proximate cause; its near reason, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:22.5.verse: For when conscience and shame are in existence, virtue arises and persists;

vsm1.1:22.6.verse: and when they are not, it neither arises nor persists.

vsm1.1:22.7.verse: This is how virtue's characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, should be understood.

vsm1.1:23.2.verse: 23. (iv) WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF VIRTUE?

vsm1.1:23.3.verse: Its benefits are the acquisition of the several special qualities beginning with non-remorse.

vsm1.1:23.4.verse: For this is said: “Ānanda, profitable habits (virtues) have non-remorse as their aim and non-remorse as their benefit” (A V 1).

vsm1.1:23.5.verse: Also it is said further: “Householder, there are these five benefits for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:23.7.verse: Here, householder, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, obtains a large fortune as a consequence of diligence;

vsm1.1:23.8.verse: this is the first benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:23.9.verse: Again, of one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, a fair name is spread abroad;

vsm1.1:23.10.verse: this is the second benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:23.11.verse: Again, whenever one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, enters an assembly, whether of khattiyas (warrior-nobles) or brahmans or householders or ascetics,

vsm1.1:23.12.verse: he does so without fear or hesitation;

vsm1.1:23.13.verse: this is the third benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:23.14.verse: Again, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, dies unconfused;

vsm1.1:23.15.verse: this is the fourth benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:23.16.verse: Again, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, on the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destiny, in the heavenly world;

vsm1.1:23.17.verse: this is the fifth benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue” (D II 86).

vsm1.1:23.18.verse: There are also the many benefits of virtue beginning with being dear and loved and ending with destruction of cankers described in the passage beginning, “If a bhikkhu should wish, ‘May I be dear to my fellows in the life of purity and loved by them, held in respect and honoured by them,’ let him perfect the virtues” (M I 33).

vsm1.1:23.19.verse: This is how virtue has as its benefits the several special qualities beginning with non-remorse.

vsm1.1:24.2.verse: Dare anyone a limit place On benefits that virtue brings, Without which virtue clansmen find No footing in the dispensation?

vsm1.1:24.3.verse: No Ganges, and no Yamunā No Sarabhū, Sarassathī, Or flowing Aciravatī, Or noble River of Mahī,

vsm1.1:24.4.verse: Is able to wash out the stain In things that breathe here in the world; For only virtue's water can Wash out the stain in living things.

vsm1.1:24.5.verse: No breezes that come bringing rain, No balm of yellow sandalwood, No necklaces beside, or gems Or soft effulgence of moonbeams,

vsm1.1:24.6.verse: Can here avail to calm and soothe Men's fevers in this world; whereas This noble, this supremely cool, Well-guarded virtue quells the flame.

vsm1.1:24.7.verse: Where is there to be found the scent That can with virtue's scent compare, And that is borne against the wind As easily as with it?

vsm1.1:24.8.verse: Where Can such another stair be found That climbs, as virtue does, to heaven? Or yet another door that gives Onto the City of Nibbāna?

vsm1.1:24.9.verse: Shine as they may, there are no kings Adorned with jewellery and pearls That shine as does a man restrained Adorned with virtue's ornament.

vsm1.1:24.10.verse: Virtue entirely does away With dread of self-blame and the like; Their virtue to the virtuous Gives gladness always by its fame.

vsm1.1:24.11.verse: From this brief sketch it may be known How virtue brings reward, and how This root of all good qualities Robs of its power every fault.

vsm1.1:25.1.verse: 25. (v) Now, here is the answer to the question, HOW MANY KINDS OF VIRTUE ARE THERE?

vsm1.1:25.2.verse: 1. Firstly all this virtue is of one kind by reason of its own characteristic of composing.

vsm1.1:25.3.verse: 2. It is of two kinds as keeping and avoiding.

vsm1.1:25.4.verse: 3. Likewise as that of good behaviour and that of the beginning of the life of purity, 4. As abstinence and non-abstinence,

vsm1.1:25.5.verse: 5. As dependent and independent, 6. As temporary and lifelong,

vsm1.1:25.6.verse: 7. As limited and unlimited, 8. As mundane and supramundane.

vsm1.1:25.7.verse: 9. It is of three kinds as inferior, medium, and superior.

vsm1.1:25.8.verse: 10. Likewise as giving precedence to self, giving precedence to the world, and giving precedence to the Dhamma, 11. As adhered to, not adhered to, and tranquillized.

vsm1.1:25.9.verse: 12. As purified, unpurified, and dubious. 13. As that of the trainer, that of the non-trainer, and that of the neither-trainer-nor-non-trainer.

vsm1.1:25.10.verse: 14. It is of four kinds as partaking of diminution, of stagnation, of distinction, of penetration.

vsm1.1:25.11.verse: 15. Likewise as that of bhikkhus, of bhikkhunīs, of the not-fully-admitted, of the laity, 16. As natural, customary, necessary, due to previous causes,

vsm1.1:25.12.verse: 17. As virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, of restraint of sense faculties, of purification of livelihood, and that concerning requisites.

vsm1.1:25.13.verse: 18. It is of five kinds as virtue consisting in limited purification, etc.;

vsm1.1:25.14.verse: for this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “Five kinds of virtue: virtue consisting in limited purification, virtue consisting in unlimited purification,

vsm1.1:25.15.verse: virtue consisting in fulfilled purification, virtue consisting in unadhered-to purification,

vsm1.1:25.16.verse: virtue consisting in tranquillized purification” (Paṭis I 42).

vsm1.1:25.17.verse: 19. Likewise as abandoning, refraining, volition, restraint, and non-transgression.

vsm1.1:26.1.verse: 26. 1. Herein, in the section dealing with that of one kind, the meaning should be understood as already stated.

vsm1.1:26.2.verse: 2. In the section dealing with that of two kinds: fulfilling a training precept announced by the Blessed One thus: “This should be done”

vsm1.1:26.4.verse: not doing what is prohibited by him thus: “This should not be done” is avoiding.

vsm1.1:26.6.verse: they keep (caranti) within that, they proceed as people who fulfil the virtues, thus it is keeping (cāritta);

vsm1.1:26.7.verse: they preserve, they protect, they avoid, thus it is avoiding.

vsm1.1:26.8.verse: Herein, keeping is accomplished by faith and energy; avoiding, by faith and mindfulness.

vsm1.1:26.9.verse: This is how it is of two kinds as keeping and avoiding.

vsm1.1:27.1.verse: 27. 3. In the second dyad good behaviour is the best kind of behaviour.

vsm1.1:27.2.verse: Good behaviour itself is that of good behaviour;

vsm1.1:27.3.verse: or what is announced for the sake of good behaviour is that of good behaviour.

vsm1.1:27.4.verse: This is a term for virtue other than that which has livelihood as eighth.

vsm1.1:27.5.verse: It is the initial stage of the life of purity consisting in the path, thus it is that of the beginning of the life of purity.

vsm1.1:27.6.verse: This is a term for the virtue that has livelihood as eighth.

vsm1.1:27.7.verse: It is the initial stage of the path because it has actually to be purified in the prior stage too.

vsm1.1:27.8.verse: Hence it is said: “But his bodily action, his verbal action, and his livelihood have already been purified earlier” (M III 289).

vsm1.1:27.9.verse: Or the training precepts called “lesser and minor” (D II 154) are that of good behaviour;

vsm1.1:27.10.verse: the rest are that of the beginning of the life of purity.

vsm1.1:27.11.verse: Or what is included in the Double Code (the bhikkhus' and bhikkhunīs' Pātimokkha) is that of the beginning of the life of purity;

vsm1.1:27.12.verse: and that included in the duties set out in the Khandhakas [of Vinaya] is that of good behaviour.

vsm1.1:27.13.verse: Through its perfection that of the beginning of the life of purity comes to be perfected.

vsm1.1:27.14.verse: Hence it is said also “that this bhikkhu shall fulfil the state consisting in the beginning of the life of purity without having fulfilled the state consisting in good behaviour—that is not possible” (A III 14–15).

vsm1.1:27.15.verse: So it is of two kinds as that of good behaviour and that of the beginning of the life of purity.

vsm1.1:28.1.verse: 28. 4. In the third dyad virtue as abstinence is simply abstention from killing living things, etc.;

vsm1.1:28.2.verse: the other kinds consisting in volition, etc., are virtue as non-abstinence.

vsm1.1:28.3.verse: So it is of two kinds as abstinence and non-abstinence.

vsm1.1:29.1.verse: 29. 5. In the fourth dyad there are two kinds of dependence: dependence through craving and dependence through [false] views.

vsm1.1:29.2.verse: Herein, that produced by one who wishes for a fortunate kind of becoming thus, “Through this virtuous conduct [rite] I shall become a [great] deity or some [minor] deity” (M I 102),

vsm1.1:29.4.verse: That produced through such [false] view about purification as “Purification is through virtuous conduct” (Vibh 374)

vsm1.1:29.6.verse: But the supramundane, and the mundane that is the prerequisite for the aforesaid supramundane,

vsm1.1:29.8.verse: So it is of two kinds as dependent and independent.

vsm1.1:30.1.verse: 30. 6. In the fifth dyad temporary virtue is that undertaken after deciding on a time limit.

vsm1.1:30.2.verse: Lifelong virtue is that practiced in the same way but undertaking it for as long as life lasts.

vsm1.1:30.3.verse: So it is of two kinds as temporary and lifelong.

vsm1.1:31.1.verse: 31. 7. In the sixth dyad the limited is that seen to be limited by gain, fame, relatives, limbs, or life.

vsm1.1:31.3.verse: And this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “What is the virtue that has a limit? There is virtue that has gain as its limit, there is virtue that has fame as its limit,

vsm1.1:31.4.verse: there is virtue that has relatives as its limit, there is virtue that has limbs as its limit,

vsm1.1:31.5.verse: there is virtue that has life as its limit.

vsm1.1:31.6.verse: What is virtue that has gain as its limit? Here someone with gain as cause, with gain as condition, with gain as reason, transgresses a training precept as undertaken:

vsm1.1:31.7.verse: that virtue has gain as its limit” (Paṭis I 43),

vsm1.1:31.8.verse: and the rest should be elaborated in the same way.

vsm1.1:31.9.verse: Also in the answer dealing with the unlimited it is said: “What is virtue that does not have gain as its limit? Here someone does not, with gain as cause, with gain as condition, with gain as reason, even arouse the thought of transgressing a training precept as undertaken,

vsm1.1:31.10.verse: how then shall he actually transgress it?

vsm1.1:31.11.verse: That virtue does not have gain as its limit” (Paṭis I 44),

vsm1.1:31.12.verse: and the rest should be elaborated in the same way.

vsm1.1:31.13.verse: So it is of two kinds as limited and unlimited.

vsm1.1:32.1.verse: 32. 8. In the seventh dyad all virtue subject to cankers is mundane;

vsm1.1:32.2.verse: that not subject to cankers is supramundane.

vsm1.1:32.3.verse: Herein, the mundane brings about improvement in future becoming and is a prerequisite for the escape from becoming,

vsm1.1:32.4.verse: according as it is said: “Discipline is for the purpose of restraint, restraint is for the purpose of non-remorse, non-remorse is for the purpose of gladdening, gladdening is for the purpose of happiness,

vsm1.1:32.5.verse: happiness is for the purpose of tranquillity, tranquillity is for the purpose of bliss, bliss is for the purpose of concentration, concentration is for the purpose of correct knowledge and vision,

vsm1.1:32.6.verse: correct knowledge and vision is for the purpose of dispassion, dispassion is for the purpose of fading away [of greed], fading away is for the purpose of deliverance,

vsm1.1:32.7.verse: deliverance is for the purpose of knowledge and vision of deliverance, knowledge and vision of deliverance is for the purpose of complete extinction [of craving, etc.] through not clinging.

vsm1.1:32.8.verse: Talk has that purpose, counsel has that purpose, support has that purpose, giving ear has that purpose, that is to say, the liberation of the mind through not clinging” (Vin V 164).

vsm1.1:32.9.verse: The supramundane brings about the escape from becoming and is the plane of reviewing knowledge.

vsm1.1:32.10.verse: So it is of two kinds as mundane and supramundane.

vsm1.1:33.1.verse: 33. 9. In the first of the triads the inferior is produced by inferior zeal, [purity of] consciousness, energy, or inquiry;

vsm1.1:33.2.verse: the medium is produced by medium zeal, etc.;

vsm1.1:33.3.verse: the superior, by superior (zeal, and so on).

vsm1.1:33.4.verse: That undertaken out of desire for fame is inferior;

vsm1.1:33.5.verse: that undertaken out of desire for the fruits of merit is medium;

vsm1.1:33.6.verse: that undertaken for the sake of the noble state thus, “This has to be done” is superior.

vsm1.1:33.7.verse: Or again, that defiled by self-praise and disparagement of others, etc., thus, “I am possessed of virtue, but these other bhikkhus are ill-conducted and evil-natured” (M I 193), is inferior;

vsm1.1:33.10.verse: Or again, that motivated by craving, the purpose of which is to enjoy continued existence, is inferior;

vsm1.1:33.11.verse: that practiced for the purpose of one's own deliverance is medium;

vsm1.1:33.12.verse: the virtue of the perfections practiced for the deliverance of all beings is superior.

vsm1.1:33.13.verse: So it is of three kinds as inferior, medium, and superior.

vsm1.1:34.1.verse: 34. 10. In the second triad that practiced out of self-regard by one who regards self and desires to abandon what is unbecoming to self

vsm1.1:34.2.verse: is virtue giving precedence to self.

vsm1.1:34.3.verse: That practiced out of regard for the world and out of desire to ward off the censure of the world

vsm1.1:34.4.verse: is virtue giving precedence to the world.

vsm1.1:34.5.verse: That practiced out of regard for the Dhamma and out of desire to honour the majesty of the Dhamma

vsm1.1:34.6.verse: is virtue giving precedence to the Dhamma.

vsm1.1:34.7.verse: So it is of three kinds as giving precedence to self, and so on.

vsm1.1:35.1.verse: 35. 11. In the third triad the virtue that in the dyads was called dependent (no. 5)

vsm1.1:35.2.verse: is adhered-to because it is adhered-to through craving and [false] view.

vsm1.1:35.3.verse: That practiced by the magnanimous ordinary man as the prerequisite of the path,

vsm1.1:35.4.verse: and that associated with the path in trainers, are not-adhered-to.

vsm1.1:35.5.verse: That associated with trainers' and non-trainers' fruition is tranquillized. So it is of three kinds as adhered-to, and so on.

vsm1.1:36.1.verse: 36. 12. In the fourth triad that fulfilled by one who has committed no offence or has made amends after committing one is pure.

vsm1.1:36.2.verse: So long as he has not made amends after committing an offence it is impure.

vsm1.1:36.3.verse: Virtue in one who is dubious about whether a thing constitutes an offence or about what grade of offence has been committed or about whether he has committed an offence

vsm1.1:36.5.verse: Herein, the meditator should purify impure virtue.

vsm1.1:36.6.verse: If dubious, he should avoid cases about which he is doubtful and should get his doubts cleared up.

vsm1.1:36.7.verse: In this way his mind will be kept at rest. So it is of three kinds as pure, and so on.

vsm1.1:37.1.verse: 37. 13. In the fifth triad the virtue associated with the four paths and with the [first] three fruitions is that of the trainer.

vsm1.1:37.2.verse: That associated with the fruition of Arahantship is that of the non-trainer.

vsm1.1:37.3.verse: The remaining kinds are that of the neither-trainer-nor-non-trainer. So it is of three kinds as that of the trainer, and so on.

vsm1.1:38.1.verse: 38. But in the world the nature of such and such beings is called their “habit” (sīla) of which they say:

vsm1.1:38.2.verse: “This one is of happy habit (sukha-sīla), this one is of unhappy habit, this one is of quarrelsome habit, this one is of dandified habit.”

vsm1.1:38.3.verse: Because of that it is said in the Paṭisambhidā figuratively: “Three kinds of virtue (habit):

vsm1.1:38.4.verse: profitable virtue, unprofitable virtue, indeterminate virtue” (Paṭis I 44).

vsm1.1:38.5.verse: So it is also called of three kinds as profitable, and so on.

vsm1.1:38.6.verse: Of these, the unprofitable is not included here since it has nothing whatever to do with the headings beginning with the characteristic, which define virtue in the sense intended in this [chapter].

vsm1.1:38.7.verse: So the threefoldness should be understood only in the way already stated.

vsm1.1:39.1.verse: 39. 14. In the first of the tetrads:

vsm1.1:39.2.verse: The unvirtuous he cultivates, He visits not the virtuous, And in his ignorance he sees No fault in a transgression here,

vsm1.1:39.3.verse: With wrong thoughts often in his mind His faculties he will not guard— Virtue in such a constitution Comes to partake of diminution.

vsm1.1:39.4.verse: But he whose mind is satisfied. With virtue that has been achieved, Who never thinks to stir himself And take a meditation subject up,

vsm1.1:39.5.verse: Contented with mere virtuousness, Nor striving for a higher state— His virtue bears the appellation Of that partaking of stagnation.

vsm1.1:39.6.verse: But who, possessed of virtue, strives With concentration for his aim— That bhikkhu's virtue in its function Is called partaking of distinction.

vsm1.1:39.7.verse: Who finds mere virtue not enough But has dispassion for his goal— His virtue through such aspiration Comes to partake of penetration.

vsm1.1:39.8.verse: So it is of four kinds as partaking of diminution, and so on.

vsm1.1:40.1.verse: 40. 15. In the second tetrad there are training precepts announced for bhikkhus to keep irrespective of what is announced for bhikkhunīs.

vsm1.1:40.2.verse: This is the virtue of bhikkhus.

vsm1.1:40.3.verse: There are training precepts announced for bhikkhunīs to keep irrespective of what is announced for bhikkhus.

vsm1.1:40.4.verse: This is the virtue of bhikkhunīs.

vsm1.1:40.5.verse: The ten precepts of virtue for male and female novices are the virtue of the not fully admitted.

vsm1.1:40.6.verse: The five training precepts—ten when possible—as a permanent undertaking and eight as the factors of the Uposatha Day, for male and female lay followers are the virtue of the laity.

vsm1.1:40.7.verse: So it is of four kinds as the virtue of bhikkhus, and so on.

vsm1.1:41.1.verse: 41. 16. In the third tetrad the non-transgression on the part of Uttarakuru human beings is natural virtue.

vsm1.1:41.2.verse: Each clan's or locality's or sect's own rules of conduct are customary virtue.

vsm1.1:41.3.verse: The virtue of the Bodhisatta's mother described thus: “It is the necessary rule, Ānanda, that when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother's womb, no thought of men that is connected with the cords of sense desire comes to her” (D II 13), is necessary virtue.

vsm1.1:41.4.verse: But the virtue of such pure beings as Mahā Kassapa, etc., and of the Bodhisatta in his various births is virtue due to previous causes.

vsm1.1:41.5.verse: So it is of four kinds as natural virtue, and so on.

vsm1.1:42.1.verse: 42. 17. In the fourth tetrad: (a) The virtue described by the Blessed One thus: “Here a bhikkhu dwells restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of the [proper] conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training, (Vibh 244)”

vsm1.1:42.3.verse: (b) That described thus: “On seeing a visible object with the eye, he apprehends neither the signs nor the particulars through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil and unprofitable states of covetousness and grief might invade him;

vsm1.1:42.4.verse: he enters upon the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

vsm1.1:42.5.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear … On smelling an odour with the nose … On tasting a flavour with the tongue … On touching a tangible object with the body …

vsm1.1:42.6.verse: On cognizing a mental object with the mind, he apprehends neither the signs nor the particulars through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil and unprofitable states of covetousness and grief might invade him; he enters upon the way of its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty (M I 180), is virtue of restraint of the sense faculties.

vsm1.1:42.7.verse: (c) Abstinence from such wrong livelihood as entails transgression of the six training precepts announced with respect to livelihood and entails the evil states beginning with “Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain” (M II 75)

vsm1.1:42.9.verse: (d) Use of the four requisites that is purified by the reflection stated in the way beginning, “Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for protection from cold” (M I 10) is called virtue concerning requisites.

vsm1.1:43.1.verse: 43. Here is an explanatory exposition together with a word commentary starting from the beginning.

vsm1.1:43.3.verse: A bhikkhu: a clansman who has gone forth out of faith and is so styled because he sees fear in the round of rebirths (saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanatā) or because he wears cloth garments that are torn and pieced together, and so on.

vsm1.1:43.4.verse: Restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint: here “Pātimokkha” (Rule of the Community) is the virtue of the training precepts;

vsm1.1:43.5.verse: for it frees (mokkheti) him who protects (pāti) it, guards it, it sets him free (mocayati) from the pains of the states of loss, etc.,

vsm1.1:43.6.verse: that is why it is called Pātimokkha.

vsm1.1:43.7.verse: “Restraint” is restraining; this is a term for bodily and verbal non-transgression.

vsm1.1:43.8.verse: The Pātimokkha itself as restraint is “Pātimokkha restraint.”

vsm1.1:43.9.verse: “Restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint” is restrained by means of the restraint consisting in that Pātimokkha;

vsm1.1:43.10.verse: he has it, possesses it, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:43.11.verse: Dwells: bears himself in one of the postures.

vsm1.1:44.1.verse: 44. The meaning of possessed of [the proper] conduct and resort, etc., should be understood in the way in which it is given in the text.

vsm1.1:44.3.verse: “Possessed of [the proper] conduct and resort: there is [proper] conduct and improper conduct.

vsm1.1:44.4.verse: Herein, what is improper conduct? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, bodily and verbal transgression—

vsm1.1:44.6.verse: Also all unvirtuousness is improper conduct.

vsm1.1:44.7.verse: Here someone makes a livelihood by gifts of bamboos, or by gifts of leaves, or by gifts of flowers, fruits, bathing powder, and tooth sticks, or by flattery,

vsm1.1:44.8.verse: or by bean-soupery, or by fondling, or by going on errands on foot,

vsm1.1:44.9.verse: or by one or other of the sorts of wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddhas—this is called improper conduct.

vsm1.1:44.10.verse: Herein, what is [proper] conduct? Bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, bodily and verbal non-transgression—

vsm1.1:44.12.verse: Also all restraint through virtue is [proper] conduct.

vsm1.1:44.13.verse: Here someone “does not make a livelihood by gifts of bamboos, or by gifts of leaves, or by gifts of flowers, fruits, bathing powder, and tooth sticks, or by flattery,

vsm1.1:44.14.verse: or by bean-soupery, or by fondling, or by going on errands on foot,

vsm1.1:44.15.verse: or by one or other of the sorts of wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddhas—this is called [proper] conduct.”

vsm1.1:45.1.verse: 45. “[Proper] resort: there is [proper] resort and improper resort.

vsm1.1:45.2.verse: Herein, what is improper resort? Here someone has prostitutes as resort, or he has widows, old maids, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, or taverns as resort;

vsm1.1:45.3.verse: or he dwells associated with kings, kings' ministers, sectarians, sectarians' disciples, in unbecoming association with laymen;

vsm1.1:45.4.verse: or he cultivates, frequents, honours, such families as are faithless, untrusting, abusive and rude, who wish harm, wish ill, wish woe, wish no surcease of bondage, for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, for male and female devotees—this is called improper resort.

vsm1.1:45.5.verse: Herein, what is [proper] resort? Here someone does not have prostitutes as resort … or taverns as resort;

vsm1.1:45.6.verse: he does not dwell associated with kings … sectarians' disciples, in unbecoming association with laymen;

vsm1.1:45.7.verse: he cultivates, frequents, honours, such families as are faithful and trusting, who are a solace, where the yellow cloth glows, where the breeze of sages blows, who wish good, wish well, wish joy, wish surcease of bondage, for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, for male and female devotees—this is called [proper] resort.

vsm1.1:45.8.verse: Thus he is furnished with, fully furnished with, provided with, fully provided with, supplied with, possessed of, endowed with, this [proper] conduct and this [proper] resort.

vsm1.1:45.9.verse: Hence it is said, ’Possessed of [the proper] conduct and resort’” (Vibh 246–47).

vsm1.1:46.1.verse: 46. Furthermore, [proper] conduct and resort should also be understood here in the following way;

vsm1.1:46.2.verse: for improper conduct is twofold as bodily and verbal.

vsm1.1:46.3.verse: Herein, what is bodily improper conduct?

vsm1.1:46.4.verse: “Here someone acts disrespectfully before the Community, and he stands jostling elder bhikkhus, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, talks standing up, talks waving his arms …

vsm1.1:46.5.verse: walks with sandals while elder bhikkhus walk without sandals, walks on a high walk while they walk on a low walk, walks on a walk while they walk on the ground …

vsm1.1:46.6.verse: stands pushing elder bhikkhus, sits pushing them, prevents new bhikkhus from getting a seat …

vsm1.1:46.7.verse: and in the bath house … without asking elder bhikkhus he puts wood on [the stove] … bolts the door …

vsm1.1:46.8.verse: and at the bathing place he enters the water jostling elder bhikkhus, enters it in front of them, bathes jostling them, bathes in front of them, comes out jostling them, comes out in front of them …

vsm1.1:46.9.verse: and entering inside a house he goes jostling elder bhikkhus, goes in front of them, pushing forward he goes in front of them …

vsm1.1:46.10.verse: and where families have inner private screened rooms in which the women of the family … the girls of the family, sit, there he enters abruptly, and he strokes a child's head” (Nidd I 228–29). This is called bodily improper conduct.

vsm1.1:47.1.verse: 47. Herein, what is verbal improper conduct?

vsm1.1:47.2.verse: “Here someone acts disrespectfully before the Community. Without asking elder bhikkhus he talks on the Dhamma, answers questions, recites the Pātimokkha, talks standing up, talks waving his arms …

vsm1.1:47.3.verse: having entered inside a house, he speaks to a woman or a girl thus: ‘You, so-and-so of such-and-such a clan, what is there?

vsm1.1:47.4.verse: Is there rice gruel? Is there cooked rice? Is there any hard food to eat? What shall we drink? What hard food shall we eat? What soft food shall we eat?

vsm1.1:47.5.verse: Or what will you give me?’—he chatters like this” (Nidd I 230). This is called verbal improper conduct.

vsm1.1:48.1.verse: 48. Proper conduct should be understood in the opposite sense to that.

vsm1.1:48.2.verse: Furthermore, a bhikkhu is respectful, deferential, possessed of conscience and shame, wears his inner robe properly, wears his upper robe properly,

vsm1.1:48.3.verse: his manner inspires confidence whether in moving forwards or backwards, looking ahead or aside, bending or stretching, his eyes are downcast, he has (a good) deportment,

vsm1.1:48.4.verse: he guards the doors of his sense faculties, knows the right measure in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, possesses mindfulness and full awareness, wants little, is contented, is strenuous, is a careful observer of good behaviour, and treats the teachers with great respect. This is called (proper) conduct.

vsm1.1:48.5.verse: This firstly is how (proper) conduct should be understood.

vsm1.1:49.1.verse: 49. (Proper) resort is of three kinds: (proper) resort as support, (proper) resort as guarding, and (proper) resort as anchoring.

vsm1.1:49.2.verse: Herein, what is (proper) resort as support? A good friend who exhibits the instances of talk,

vsm1.1:49.3.verse: in whose presence one hears what has not been heard, corrects what has been heard, gets rid of doubt, rectifies one's view, and gains confidence;

vsm1.1:49.4.verse: or by training under whom one grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity and understanding—

vsm1.1:49.5.verse: this is called (proper) resort as support.

vsm1.1:50.1.verse: 50. What is (proper) resort as guarding? Here “A bhikkhu, having entered inside a house, having gone into a street, goes with downcast eyes, seeing the length of a plough yoke, restrained,

vsm1.1:50.2.verse: not looking at an elephant, not looking at a horse, a carriage, a pedestrian, a woman, a man,

vsm1.1:50.3.verse: not looking up, not looking down, not staring this way and that” (Nidd I 474). This is called (proper) resort as guarding.

vsm1.1:51.1.verse: 51. What is (proper) resort as anchoring? It is the four foundations of mindfulness on which the mind is anchored;

vsm1.1:51.2.verse: for this is said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, what is a bhikkhu's resort, his own native place? It is these four foundations of mindfulness” (S V 148).

vsm1.1:51.3.verse: This is called (proper) resort as anchoring.

vsm1.1:51.4.verse: Being thus furnished with … endowed with, this (proper) conduct and this (proper) resort,

vsm1.1:51.5.verse: he is also on that account called “one possessed of (proper) conduct and resort.”

vsm1.1:52.1.verse: 52. Seeing fear in the slightest fault (§42):

vsm1.1:52.2.verse: one who has the habit (sīla) of seeing fear in faults of the minutest measure, of such kinds as unintentional contravening of a minor training rule of the Pātimokkha, or the arising of unprofitable thoughts.

vsm1.1:52.3.verse: He trains himself by undertaking (samādāya) the precepts of training:

vsm1.1:52.4.verse: whatever there is among the precepts of training to be trained in, in all that he trains by taking it up rightly (sammā ādāya).

vsm1.1:52.5.verse: And here, as far as the words, “one restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint,”

vsm1.1:52.6.verse: virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is shown by discourse in terms of persons.

vsm1.1:52.7.verse: But all that beginning with the words, “possessed of [proper] conduct and resort”

vsm1.1:52.8.verse: should be understood as said in order to show the way of practice that perfects that virtue in him who so practices it.

vsm1.1:53.1.verse: 53. (b) Now, as regards the virtue of restraint of faculties shown next to that in the way beginning, “on seeing a visible object with the eye,”

vsm1.1:53.2.verse: herein he is a bhikkhu established in the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint.

vsm1.1:53.3.verse: On seeing a visible object with the eye:

vsm1.1:53.4.verse: on seeing a visible object with the eye-consciousness that is capable of seeing visible objects and has borrowed the name “eye” from its instrument.

vsm1.1:53.5.verse: But the Ancients (porāṇā) said: “The eye does not see a visible object because it has no mind. The mind does not see because it has no eyes.

vsm1.1:53.6.verse: But when there is the impingement of door and object he sees by means of the consciousness that has eye-sensitivity as its physical basis. Now, (an idiom) such as this is called an ‘accessory locution’ (sasambhārakathā), like ‘He shot him with his bow,’ and so on.

vsm1.1:53.7.verse: So the meaning here is this: ‘On seeing a visible object with eye-consciousness.’”

vsm1.1:54.1.verse: 54. Apprehends neither the signs: he does not apprehend the sign of woman or man, or any sign that is a basis for defilement such as the sign of beauty, etc.;

vsm1.1:54.2.verse: he stops at what is merely seen.

vsm1.1:54.4.verse: he does not apprehend any aspect classed as hand, foot, smile, laughter, talk, looking ahead, looking aside, etc., which has acquired the name “particular” (anubyañjana) because of its particularizing (anu anu byañjanato) defilements, because of its making them manifest themselves.

vsm1.1:54.5.verse: He only apprehends what is really there.

vsm1.1:54.6.verse: Like the Elder Mahā Tissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata.

vsm1.1:55.1.verse: 55. It seems that as the elder was on his way from Cetiyapabbata to Anurādhapura for alms,

vsm1.1:55.2.verse: a certain daughter-in-law of a clan, who had quarrelled with her husband and had set out early from Anurādhapura all dressed up and tricked out like a celestial nymph to go to her relatives’ home, saw him on the road, and being low-minded, she laughed a loud laugh.

vsm1.1:55.3.verse: [Wondering] “What is that?” the elder looked up and

vsm1.1:55.4.verse: finding in the bones of her teeth the perception of foulness (ugliness), he reached Arahantship.

vsm1.1:55.5.verse: Hence it was said: “He saw the bones that were her teeth, And kept in mind his first perception; And standing on that very spot The elder became an Arahant.”

vsm1.1:55.6.verse: But her husband, who was going after her, saw the elder and asked, “Venerable sir, did you by any chance see a woman?”

vsm1.1:55.7.verse: The elder told him: “Whether it was a man or woman That went by I noticed not, But only that on this high road There goes a group of bones.”

vsm1.1:56.1.verse: 56. As to the words through which, etc., the meaning is:

vsm1.1:56.2.verse: by reason of which, because of which non-restraint of the eye faculty, if he, if that person, left the eye faculty unguarded, remained with the eye door unclosed by the door-panel of mindfulness,

vsm1.1:56.3.verse: these states of covetousness, etc., might invade, might pursue, might threaten, him.

vsm1.1:56.4.verse: He enters upon the way of its restraint: he enters upon the way of closing that eye faculty by the door-panel of mindfulness.

vsm1.1:56.5.verse: It is the same one of whom it is said he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

vsm1.1:57.1.verse: 57. Herein, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the actual eye faculty,

vsm1.1:57.2.verse: since neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness arises in dependence on eye-sensitivity.

vsm1.1:57.3.verse: On the contrary when a visible datum as object comes into the eye’s focus,

vsm1.1:57.4.verse: then, after the life-continuum has arisen twice and ceased, the functional mind-element accomplishing the function of adverting arises and ceases.

vsm1.1:57.5.verse: After that, eye-consciousness with the function of seeing; after that, resultant mind-element with the function of receiving;

vsm1.1:57.6.verse: after that, resultant root-causeless mind-consciousness-element with the function of investigating; after that, functional root-causeless mind-consciousness-element accomplishing the function of determining arises and ceases.

vsm1.1:57.8.verse: Herein, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint on the occasion of the life-continuum,

vsm1.1:57.9.verse: or on any of the occasions beginning with adverting.

vsm1.1:57.10.verse: But there is non-restraint if unvirtuousness or forgetfulness or unknowing or impatience or idleness arises at the moment of impulsion.

vsm1.1:57.11.verse: When this happens, it is called “non-restraint in the eye faculty.”

vsm1.1:58.2.verse: Because when this happens, the door is not guarded, nor are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series.

vsm1.1:58.4.verse: Just as, when a city’s four gates are not secured, although inside the city house doors, storehouses, rooms, etc., are secured,

vsm1.1:58.5.verse: yet all property inside the city is unguarded and unprotected

vsm1.1:58.6.verse: since robbers coming in by the city gates can do as they please,

vsm1.1:58.7.verse: so too, when unvirtuousness, etc., arise in impulsion in which there is no restraint, then the door too is unguarded, and so also are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.

vsm1.1:58.8.verse: But when virtue, etc., has arisen in it, then the door too is guarded

vsm1.1:58.9.verse: and so also are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.

vsm1.1:58.11.verse: Just as, when the city gates are secured, although inside the city the houses, etc., are not secured,

vsm1.1:58.12.verse: yet all property inside the city is well guarded, well protected,

vsm1.1:58.13.verse: since when the city gates are shut there is no ingress for robbers,

vsm1.1:58.14.verse: so too, when virtue, etc., have arisen in impulsion, the door too is guarded and so also are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.

vsm1.1:58.15.verse: Thus although it actually arises at the moment of impulsion, it is nevertheless called “restraint in the eye faculty.”

vsm1.1:59.1.verse: 59. So also as regards the phrases on hearing a sound with the ear and so on.

vsm1.1:59.2.verse: So it is this virtue, which in brief has the characteristic of avoiding apprehension of signs entailing defilement with respect to visible objects, etc., that should be understood as virtue of restraint of faculties.

vsm1.1:60.1.verse: 60. (c) Now, as regards the virtue of livelihood purification mentioned above next to the virtue of restraint of the faculties (§42), the words of the six precepts announced on account of livelihood mean, of the following six training precepts announced thus: “With livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes, lays claim to a higher than human state that is non-existent, not a fact,” the contravention of which is defeat (expulsion from the Order);

vsm1.1:60.2.verse: “with livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, he acts as go-between,” the contravention of which is an offence entailing a meeting of the Order;

vsm1.1:60.3.verse: “with livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, he says, ‘A bhikkhu who lives in your monastery is an Arahant,’” the contravention of which is a serious offence in one who is aware of it;

vsm1.1:60.4.verse: “with livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, a bhikkhu who is not sick eats superior food that he has ordered for his own use,” the contravention of which is an offence requiring expiation:

vsm1.1:60.5.verse: “With livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, a bhikkhunī who is not sick eats superior food that she has ordered for her own use,” the contravention of which is an offence requiring confession;

vsm1.1:60.6.verse: “with livelihood as cause, with livelihood as reason, one who is not sick eats curry or boiled rice that he has ordered for his own use,” the contravention of which is an offence of wrongdoing (Vin V 146). Of these six precepts.

vsm1.1:61.1.verse: 61. As regards scheming, etc. (§42), this is the text: “Herein, what is scheming? It is the grimacing, grimacery, scheming, schemery, schemedness, by what is called rejection of requisites or by indirect talk, or it is the disposing, posing, composing, of the deportment on the part of one bent on gain, honour and renown, of one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes—

vsm1.1:62.1.verse: 62. ”Herein, what is talking? Talking at others, talking, talking round, talking up, continual talking up, persuading, continual persuading, suggesting, continual suggesting, ingratiating chatter, flattery, bean-soupery, fondling, on the part of one bent on gain, honour and renown, of one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes—

vsm1.1:63.1.verse: 63. ”Herein, what is hinting? A sign to others, giving a sign, indication, giving indication, indirect talk, roundabout talk, on the part of one bent on gain, honour and renown, of one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes—

vsm1.1:64.1.verse: 64. ”Herein, what is belittling? Abusing of others, disparaging, reproaching, snubbing, continual snubbing, ridicule, continual ridicule, denigration, continual denigration, tale-bearing, backbiting, on the part of one bent on gain, honour and renown, of one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes—

vsm1.1:65.1.verse: 65. ”Herein, what is pursuing gain with gain? Seeking, seeking for, seeking out, going in search of, searching for, searching out material goods by means of material goods, such as carrying there goods that have been got from here, or carrying here goods that have been got from there, by one bent on gain, honour and renown, by one of evil wishes, a prey to wishes—

vsm1.1:65.2.verse: this is called pursuing gain with gain.” (Vibh 352–53)

vsm1.1:66.1.verse: 66. The meaning of this text should be understood as follows:

vsm1.1:66.2.verse: Firstly, as regards description of scheming: on the part of one bent on gain, honour and renown is on the part of one who is bent on gain, on honour, and on reputation;

vsm1.1:66.3.verse: on the part of one who longs for them, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:66.4.verse: Of one of evil wishes: of one who wants to show qualities that he has not got.

vsm1.1:66.5.verse: A prey to wishes: the meaning is, of one who is attacked by them.

vsm1.1:66.6.verse: And after this the passage beginning or by what is called rejection of requisites is given in order to show the three instances of scheming given in the Mahāniddesa as rejection of requisites, indirect talk, and that based on deportment.

vsm1.1:67.1.verse: 67. Herein, [a bhikkhu] is invited to accept robes, etc., and, precisely because he wants them, he refuses them out of evil wishes.

vsm1.1:67.2.verse: And then, since he knows that those householders believe in him implicitly when they think, “Oh, how few are our lord’s wishes! He will not accept a thing!” and they put fine robes, etc., before him by various means,

vsm1.1:67.3.verse: he then accepts, making a show that he wants to be compassionate towards them—it is this hypocrisy of his, which becomes the cause of their subsequently bringing them even by cartloads, that should be understood as the instance of scheming called rejection of requisites.

vsm1.1:68.1.verse: 68. For this is said in the Mahāniddesa: “What is the instance of scheming called rejection of requisites? Here householders invite bhikkhus [to accept] robes, alms food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.

vsm1.1:68.2.verse: One who is of evil wishes, a prey to wishes, wanting robes … alms food … resting place … the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, refuses robes … alms food … resting place … the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, because he wants more.

vsm1.1:68.3.verse: He says: ‘What has an ascetic to do with expensive robes? It is proper for an ascetic to gather rags from a charnel ground or from a rubbish heap or from a shop and make them into a patchwork cloak to wear. What has an ascetic to do with expensive alms food? It is proper for an ascetic to get his living by the dropping of lumps [of food into his bowl] while he wanders for gleanings.

vsm1.1:68.4.verse: What has an ascetic to do with an expensive resting place? It is proper for an ascetic to be a tree-root-dweller or an open-air-dweller. What has an ascetic to do with an expensive requisite of medicine as cure for the sick? It is proper for an ascetic to cure himself with putrid urine and broken gallnuts.’

vsm1.1:68.5.verse: Accordingly he wears a coarse robe, eats coarse alms food, uses a coarse resting place, uses a coarse requisite of medicine as cure for the sick. Then householders think, ‘This ascetic has few wishes, is content, is secluded, keeps aloof from company, is strenuous, is a preacher of asceticism,’ and they invite him more and more [to accept] robes, alms food, resting places, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.

vsm1.1:68.6.verse: He says: ‘With three things present a faithful clansman produces much merit: with faith present a faithful clansman produces much merit, with goods to be given present a faithful clansman produces much merit, with those worthy to receive present a faithful clansman produces much merit.

vsm1.1:68.7.verse: You have faith; the goods to be given are here; and I am here to accept. If I do not accept, then you will be deprived of the merit. That is no good to me. Rather will I accept out of compassion for you.”

vsm1.1:68.8.verse: Accordingly he accepts many robes, he accepts much alms food, he accepts many resting places, he accepts many requisites of medicine as cure for the sick. Such grimacing, grimacery, scheming, schemery, schemedness, is known as the instance of scheming called rejection of requisites’ (Nidd I 224–25).

vsm1.1:69.1.verse: 69. It is hypocrisy on the part of one of evil wishes, who gives it to be understood verbally in some way or other that he has attained a higher than human state, that should be understood as the instance of scheming called indirect talk,

vsm1.1:69.3.verse: ”What is the instance of scheming called indirect talk? Here someone of evil wishes, a prey to wishes, eager to be admired, [thinking] ‘Thus people will admire me’ speaks words about the noble state. He says, ‘He who wears such a robe is a very important ascetic.’

vsm1.1:69.4.verse: He says, ‘He who carries such a bowl, metal cup, water filler, water strainer, key, wears such a waist band, sandals, is a very important ascetic.’

vsm1.1:69.5.verse: He says, ‘He who has such a preceptor … teacher … who has the same preceptor, who has the same teacher, who has such a friend, associate, intimate, companion; he who lives in such a monastery, lean-to, mansion, villa, cave, grotto, hut, pavilion, watch tower, hall, barn, meeting hall, room, at such a tree root, is a very important ascetic.’

vsm1.1:69.6.verse: Or alternatively, all-gushing, all-grimacing, all-scheming, all-talkative, with an expression of admiration, he utters such deep, mysterious, cunning, obscure, supramundane talk suggestive of voidness as ‘This ascetic is an obtainer of peaceful abidings and attainments such as these.’

vsm1.1:69.7.verse: Such grimacing, grimacery, scheming, schemery, schemedness, is known as the instance of scheming called indirect talk” (Nidd I 226–27).

vsm1.1:70.1.verse: 70. It is hypocrisy on the part of one of evil wishes, which takes the form of deportment influenced by eagerness to be admired, that should be understood as the instance of scheming dependent on deportment, according as it is said:

vsm1.1:70.2.verse: “What is the instance of scheming called deportment? Here someone of evil wishes, a prey to wishes, eager to be admired, [thinking] ‘Thus people will admire me,’ composes his way of walking, composes his way of lying down;

vsm1.1:70.3.verse: he walks studiedly, stands studiedly, sits studiedly, lies down studiedly; he walks as though concentrated, stands, sits, lies down as though concentrated;

vsm1.1:70.4.verse: and he is one who meditates in public. Such disposing, posing, composing, of deportment, grimacing, grimacery, scheming, schemery, schemedness, is known as the instance of scheming called deportment” (Nidd I 225–26).

vsm1.1:71.1.verse: 71. Herein, the words by what is called rejection of requisites (§61) mean: by what is called thus “rejection of requisites”; or they mean: by means of the rejection of requisites that is so called.

vsm1.1:71.2.verse: By indirect talk means: by talking near to the subject.

vsm1.1:71.3.verse: Of deportment means: of the four modes of deportment (postures).

vsm1.1:71.4.verse: Disposing is initial posing, or careful posing.

vsm1.1:71.5.verse: Posing is the manner of posing.

vsm1.1:71.6.verse: Composing is prearranging; assuming a trust-inspiring attitude, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:71.7.verse: Grimacing is making grimaces by showing great intenseness; facial contraction is what is meant.

vsm1.1:71.8.verse: One who has the habit of making grimaces is a grimacer.

vsm1.1:71.11.verse: The way (āyanā) of a schemer (kuha) is schemery (kuhāyanā).

vsm1.1:71.12.verse: The state of what is schemed is schemedness.

vsm1.1:72.1.verse: 72. In the description of talking: talking at is talking thus on seeing people coming to the monastery,

vsm1.1:72.2.verse: “What have you come for, good people? What, to invite bhikkhus? If it is that, then go along and I shall come later with [my bowl],” etc.;

vsm1.1:72.3.verse: or alternatively, talking at is talking by advertising oneself thus, “I am Tissa, the king trusts me, such and such king’s ministers trust me.”

vsm1.1:72.4.verse: Talking is the same kind of talking on being asked a question.

vsm1.1:72.5.verse: Talking round is roundly talking by one who is afraid of householders’ displeasure because he has given occasion for it.

vsm1.1:72.6.verse: Talking up is talking by extolling people thus, “He is a great land-owner, a great ship-owner, a great lord of giving.”

vsm1.1:72.7.verse: Continual talking up is talking by extolling [people] in all ways.

vsm1.1:73.1.verse: 73. Persuading is progressively involving [people] thus, “Lay followers, formerly you used to give first-fruit alms at such a time; why do you not do so now?” until they say, “We shall give, venerable sir, we have had no opportunity,” etc.;

vsm1.1:73.3.verse: Or alternatively, seeing someone with sugarcane in his hand, he asks, “Where are you coming from, lay follower?”—”From the sugarcane field, venerable sir”—”Is the sugarcane sweet there?”

vsm1.1:73.4.verse: —”One can find out by eating, venerable sir”—”It is not allowed, lay follower, for bhikkhus to say ‘Give [me some] sugarcane.’”

vsm1.1:73.5.verse: Such entangling talk from such an entangler is persuading.

vsm1.1:73.6.verse: Persuading again and again in all ways is continual persuading.

vsm1.1:74.1.verse: 74. Suggesting is insinuating by specifying thus, “That family alone understands me; if there is anything to be given there, they give it to me only”;

vsm1.1:74.2.verse: pointing to, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:74.3.verse: And here the story of the oil-seller should be told.

vsm1.1:74.4.verse: Suggesting in all ways again and again is continual suggesting.

vsm1.1:75.1.verse: 75. Ingratiating chatter is endearing chatter repeated again and again without regard to whether it is in conformity with truth and Dhamma.

vsm1.1:75.2.verse: Flattery is speaking humbly, always maintaining an attitude of inferiority.

vsm1.1:75.3.verse: Bean-soupery is resemblance to bean soup; for just as when beans are being cooked only a few do not get cooked, the rest get cooked,

vsm1.1:75.4.verse: so too the person in whose speech only a little is true, the rest being false, is called a “bean soup”;

vsm1.1:76.1.verse: 76. Fondling is the state of the act of fondling. For when a man fondles children on his lap or on his shoulder like a nurse—he nurses, is the meaning—that fondler’s act is the act of fondling. The state of the act of fondling is fondling.

vsm1.1:77.1.verse: 77. In the description of hinting (nemittikatā): a sign (nimitta) is any bodily or verbal act that gets others to give requisites.

vsm1.1:77.2.verse: Giving a sign is making a sign such as “What have you got to eat?”, etc., on seeing [people] going along with food.

vsm1.1:77.3.verse: Indication is talk that alludes to requisites.

vsm1.1:77.4.verse: Giving indication: on seeing cowboys, he asks, “Are these milk cows’ calves or buttermilk cows’ calves?” and when it is said, “They are milk cows’ calves, venerable sir,” [he remarks] “They are not milk cows’ calves. If they were milk cows’ calves the bhikkhus would be getting milk,” etc.;

vsm1.1:77.5.verse: and his getting it to the knowledge of the boys’ parents in this way, and so making them give milk, is giving indication.

vsm1.1:78.1.verse: 78. Indirect talk is talk that keeps near [to the subject].

vsm1.1:78.2.verse: And here there should be told the story of the bhikkhu supported by a family.

vsm1.1:78.3.verse: And here there should be told the story of the bhikkhu supported by a family. A bhikkhu, it seems, who was supported by a family went into the house wanting to eat and sat down. The mistress of the house was unwilling to give. On seeing him she said, “There is no rice,” and she went to a neighbour’s house as though to get rice.

vsm1.1:78.4.verse: The bhikkhu went into the storeroom. Looking round, he saw sugarcane in the corner behind the door, sugar in a bowl, a string of salt fish in a basket, rice in a jar, and ghee in a pot. He came out and sat down. When the housewife came back, she said, “I did not get any rice.”

vsm1.1:78.5.verse: The bhikkhu said, “Lay follower, I saw a sign just now that alms will not be easy to get today.”—“What, venerable sir?”—

vsm1.1:78.6.verse: ”I saw a snake that was like sugarcane put in the corner behind the door; looking for something to hit it with, I saw a stone like a lump of sugar in a bowl. When the snake had been hit with the clod, it spread out a hood like a string of salt fish in a basket, and its teeth as it tried to bite the clod were like rice grains in a jar. Then the saliva mixed with poison that came out to its mouth in its fury was like ghee put in a pot.”

vsm1.1:78.7.verse: She thought, “There is no hoodwinking the shaveling,” so she gave him the sugarcane and she cooked the rice and gave it all to him with the ghee, the sugar and the fish.

vsm1.1:79.1.verse: 79. Such talk that keeps near [to the subject] should be understood as indirect talk.

vsm1.1:79.2.verse: Roundabout talk is talking round and round [the subject] as much as is allowed.

vsm1.1:80.1.verse: 80. In the description of belittling: abusing is abusing by means of the ten instances of abuse.

vsm1.1:80.3.verse: Reproaching is enumeration of faults such as “He is faithless, he is an unbeliever.”

vsm1.1:80.4.verse: Snubbing is taking up verbally thus, “Don’t say that here.”

vsm1.1:80.5.verse: Snubbing in all ways, giving grounds and reasons, is continual snubbing.

vsm1.1:80.6.verse: Or alternatively, when someone does not give, taking him up thus, “Oh, the prince of givers!” is snubbing;

vsm1.1:80.7.verse: and the thorough snubbing thus, “A mighty prince of givers!” is continual snubbing.

vsm1.1:80.8.verse: Ridicule is making fun of someone thus, “What sort of a life has this man who eats up his seed [grain]?”

vsm1.1:80.9.verse: Continual ridicule is making fun of him more thoroughly thus, “What, you say this man is not a giver

vsm1.1:80.10.verse: who always gives the words ‘There is nothing’ to everyone?”

vsm1.1:81.1.verse: 81. Denigration is denigrating someone by saying that he is not a giver, or by censuring him.

vsm1.1:81.3.verse: Tale-bearing is bearing tales from house to house, from village to village, from district to district, [thinking] “So they will give to me out of fear of my bearing tales.”

vsm1.1:81.4.verse: Backbiting is speaking censoriously behind another’s back after speaking kindly to his face;

vsm1.1:81.5.verse: for this is like biting the flesh of another’s back, when he is not looking, on the part of one who is unable to look him in the face; therefore it is called backbiting.

vsm1.1:81.6.verse: This is called belittling (nippesikatā) because it scrapes off (nippeseti), wipes off, the virtuous qualities of others as a bamboo scraper (veḷupesikā) does unguent,

vsm1.1:81.7.verse: or because it is a pursuit of gain by grinding (nippiṃsitvā) and pulverizing others’ virtuous qualities, like the pursuit of perfume by grinding perfumed substances; that is why it is called belittling.

vsm1.1:82.1.verse: 82. In the description of pursuing gain with gain: pursuing is hunting after.

vsm1.1:82.2.verse: Got from here is got from this house.

vsm1.1:82.6.verse: Seeking out is hunting after again and again.

vsm1.1:82.7.verse: The story of the bhikkhu who went round giving away the alms he had got at first to children of families here and there and in the end got milk and gruel should be told here.

vsm1.1:82.8.verse: Searching, etc., are synonyms for “seeking,” etc.,

vsm1.1:82.9.verse: and so the construction here should be understood thus: going in search of is seeking; searching for is seeking for; searching out is seeking out.

vsm1.1:82.10.verse: This is the meaning of scheming, and so on.

vsm1.1:83.1.verse: 83. Now, [as regards the words] The evil states beginning with (§42): here the words beginning with should be understood to include the many evil states given in the Brahmajāla Sutta in the way beginning, “Or just as some worthy ascetics, while eating the food given by the faithful, make a living by wrong livelihood,

vsm1.1:83.2.verse: by such low arts as these, that is to say, by palmistry, by fortune-telling, by divining omens, by interpreting dreams, marks on the body, holes gnawed by mice; by fire sacrifice, by spoon oblation …” (D I 9).

vsm1.1:84.1.verse: 84. So this wrong livelihood entails the transgression of these six training precepts announced on account of livelihood, and it entails the evil states beginning with “Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain.”

vsm1.1:84.2.verse: And so it is the abstinence from all sorts of wrong livelihood that is virtue of livelihood purification,

vsm1.1:84.3.verse: the word-meaning of which is this: on account of it they live, thus it is livelihood.

vsm1.1:84.4.verse: What is that? It is the effort consisting in the search for requisites.

vsm1.1:85.1.verse: 85. (d) As regards the next kind called virtue concerning requisites: [here is the text: “Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of concealing the private parts. Reflecting wisely, he uses alms food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the life of purity: ‘Thus I shall put a stop to old feelings and shall not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.’ Reflecting wisely, he uses the resting place only for the purpose of protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of warding off the perils of climate and enjoying retreat. Reflecting wisely, he uses the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick only for protection from arisen hurtful feelings and for complete immunity from affliction” (M I 10).] Herein, reflecting wisely is reflecting as the means and as the way; by knowing, by reviewing, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:85.2.verse: And here it is the reviewing stated in the way beginning, “For protection from cold” that should be understood as “reflecting wisely.”

vsm1.1:86.1.verse: 86. Herein, the robe is any one of those beginning with the inner cloth.

vsm1.1:86.2.verse: He uses: he employs; dresses in [as inner cloth], or puts on [as upper garment].

vsm1.1:86.3.verse: Only is a phrase signifying invariability in the definition of a limit of a purpose;

vsm1.1:86.4.verse: the purpose in the meditator’s making use of the robes is that much only, namely, protection from cold, etc., not more than that.

vsm1.1:86.5.verse: From cold: from any kind of cold arisen either through disturbance of elements internally or through change in temperature externally.

vsm1.1:86.6.verse: For protection: for the purpose of warding off;
