vsm1.1:86.7.verse: for the purpose of eliminating it so that it may not arouse affliction in the body.

vsm1.1:86.8.verse: For when the body is afflicted by cold, the distracted mind cannot be wisely exerted.

vsm1.1:86.9.verse: That is why the Blessed One permitted the robe to be used for protection from cold.

vsm1.1:86.11.verse: except that from heat means from the heat of fire, the origin of which should be understood as forest fires, and so on.

vsm1.1:87.1.verse: 87. From contact with gadflies and flies, wind and burning and creeping things: here gadflies are flies that bite;

vsm1.1:87.4.verse: Wind is distinguished as that with dust and that without dust.

vsm1.1:87.5.verse: Burning is burning of the sun.

vsm1.1:87.6.verse: Creeping things are any long creatures such as snakes and so on that move by crawling. Contact with them is of two kinds: contact by being bitten and contact by being touched.

vsm1.1:87.7.verse: And that does not worry him who sits with a robe on. So he uses it for the purpose of protection from such things.

vsm1.1:88.1.verse: 88. Only: the word is repeated in order to define a subdivision of the invariable purpose;

vsm1.1:88.2.verse: for the concealment of the private parts is an invariable purpose; the others are purposes periodically.

vsm1.1:88.3.verse: Herein, private parts are any parts of the pudendum.

vsm1.1:88.4.verse: For when a member is disclosed, conscience (hiri) is disturbed (kuppati), offended.

vsm1.1:88.5.verse: It is called “private parts” (hirikopīna) because of the disturbance of conscience (hiri-kopana).

vsm1.1:88.6.verse: For the purpose of concealing the private parts: for the purpose of the concealment of those private parts.

vsm1.1:88.7.verse: [As well as the reading “hiriko-pīna-paṭicchādanatthaṃ] there is a reading “hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ.”

vsm1.1:89.1.verse: 89. Alms food is any sort of food.

vsm1.1:89.2.verse: For any sort of nutriment is called “alms food” (piṇḍapāta—lit. “lump-dropping”) because of its having been dropped (patitattā) into a bhikkhu’s bowl during his alms round (piṇḍolya).

vsm1.1:89.3.verse: Or alms food (piṇḍapāta) is the dropping (pāta) of the lumps (piṇḍa);

vsm1.1:89.4.verse: it is the concurrence (sannipāta), the collection, of alms (bhikkhā) obtained here and there, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:89.5.verse: Neither for amusement: neither for the purpose of amusement, as with village boys, etc.; for the sake of sport, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:89.6.verse: Nor for intoxication: not for the purpose of intoxication, as with boxers, etc.;

vsm1.1:89.7.verse: for the sake of intoxication with strength and for the sake of intoxication with manhood, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:89.8.verse: Nor for smartening: not for the purpose of smartening, as with royal concubines, courtesans, etc.;

vsm1.1:89.9.verse: for the sake of plumpness in all the limbs, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:89.10.verse: Nor for embellishment: not for the purpose of embellishment, as with actors, dancers, etc.;

vsm1.1:89.11.verse: for the sake of a clear skin and complexion, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:90.1.verse: 90. And here the clause neither for amusement is stated for the purpose of abandoning support for delusion;

vsm1.1:90.2.verse: nor for intoxication is said for the purpose of abandoning support for hate;

vsm1.1:90.3.verse: nor for smartening nor for embellishment is said for the purpose of abandoning support for greed.

vsm1.1:90.4.verse: And neither for amusement nor for intoxication is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters for oneself.

vsm1.1:90.5.verse: Nor for smartening nor for embellishment is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters for another.

vsm1.1:90.6.verse: And the abandoning of both unwise practice and devotion to indulgence of sense pleasures should be understood as stated by these four.

vsm1.1:90.7.verse: Only has the meaning already stated.

vsm1.1:91.1.verse: 91. Of this body: of this material body consisting of the four great primaries.

vsm1.1:91.2.verse: For the endurance: for the purpose of continued endurance.

vsm1.1:91.3.verse: And continuance: for the purpose of not interrupting [life’s continued] occurrence,

vsm1.1:91.4.verse: or for the purpose of endurance for a long time.

vsm1.1:91.5.verse: He makes use of the alms food for the purpose of the endurance, for the purpose of the continuance, of the body, as the owner of an old house uses props for his house, and as a carter uses axle grease, not for the purpose of amusement, intoxication, smartening, and embellishment.

vsm1.1:91.6.verse: Furthermore, endurance is a term for the life faculty.

vsm1.1:91.7.verse: So what has been said as far as the words for the endurance and continuance of this body can be understood to mean: for the purpose of maintaining the occurrence of the life faculty in this body.

vsm1.1:92.1.verse: 92. For the ending of discomfort: hunger is called “discomfort” in the sense of afflicting.

vsm1.1:92.2.verse: He makes use of alms food for the purpose of ending that, like anointing a wound, like counteracting heat with cold, and so on.

vsm1.1:92.3.verse: For assisting the life of purity: for the purpose of assisting the life of purity consisting in the whole dispensation and the life of purity consisting in the path.

vsm1.1:92.4.verse: For while this [bhikkhu] is engaged in crossing the desert of existence by means of devotion to the three trainings depending on bodily strength whose necessary condition is the use of alms food, he makes use of it to assist the life of purity

vsm1.1:92.5.verse: just as those seeking to cross the desert used their child’s flesh,

vsm1.1:92.6.verse: just as those seeking to cross a river use a raft, and just as those seeking to cross the ocean use a ship.

vsm1.1:93.1.verse: 93. Thus I shall put a stop to old feelings and shall not arouse new feelings: thus as a sick man uses medicine, he uses [alms food, thinking]: “By use of this alms food I shall put a stop to the old feeling of hunger,

vsm1.1:93.2.verse: and I shall not arouse a new feeling by immoderate eating, like one of the [proverbial] brahmans, that is, one who eats till he has to be helped up by hand, or till his clothes will not meet, or till he rolls there [on the ground], or till crows can peck from his mouth, or until he vomits what he has eaten.

vsm1.1:93.3.verse: Or alternatively, there is that which is called ‘old feelings’ because, being conditioned by former kamma, it arises now in dependence on unsuitable immoderate eating

vsm1.1:93.4.verse: —I shall put a stop to that old feeling, forestalling its condition by suitable moderate eating.

vsm1.1:93.5.verse: And there is that which is called ‘new feeling’ because it will arise in the future in dependence on the accumulation of kamma consisting in making improper use [of the requisite of alms food] now

vsm1.1:93.6.verse: —I shall also not arouse that new feeling, avoiding by means of proper use the production of its root.” This is how the meaning should be understood here.

vsm1.1:93.7.verse: What has been shown so far can be understood to include proper use [of requisites], abandoning of devotion to self-mortification, and not giving up lawful bliss (pleasure).

vsm1.1:94.1.verse: 94. And I shall be healthy: “In this body, which exists in dependence on requisites, I shall, by moderate eating, have health called ‘long endurance’ since there will be no danger of severing the life faculty or interrupting the [continuity of the] postures.” [Reflecting] in this way, he makes use [of the alms food]

vsm1.1:94.2.verse: as a sufferer from a chronic disease does of his medicine.

vsm1.1:94.3.verse: And blameless and live in comfort (lit. “and have blamelessness and a comfortable abiding”): he makes use of them thinking: “I shall have blamelessness by avoiding improper search, acceptance and eating,

vsm1.1:94.4.verse: and I shall have a comfortable abiding by moderate eating.”

vsm1.1:94.5.verse: Or he does so thinking: “I shall have blamelessness due to absence of such faults as boredom, sloth, sleepiness, blame by the wise, etc., that have unseemly immoderate eating as their condition;

vsm1.1:94.6.verse: and I shall have a comfortable abiding by producing bodily strength that has seemly moderate eating as its condition.”

vsm1.1:94.7.verse: Or he does so thinking: “I shall have blamelessness by abandoning the pleasure of lying down, lolling and torpor, through refraining from eating as much as possible to stuff the belly;

vsm1.1:94.8.verse: and I shall have a comfortable abiding by controlling the four postures through eating four or five mouthfuls less than the maximum.”

vsm1.1:94.9.verse: For this is said: “With four or five lumps still to eat Let him then end by drinking water; For energetic bhikkhus’ needs This should suffice to live in comfort” (Th 983).

vsm1.1:94.10.verse: Now, what has been shown at this point can be understood as discernment of purpose and practice of the middle way.

vsm1.1:95.1.verse: 95. Resting place (senāsana): this is the bed (sena) and seat (āsana).

vsm1.1:95.2.verse: For wherever one sleeps (seti), whether in a monastery or in a lean-to, etc., that is the bed (sena);

vsm1.1:95.3.verse: wherever one seats oneself (āsati), sits (nisīdati), that is the seat (āsana).

vsm1.1:95.5.verse: For the purpose of warding off the perils of climate and enjoying retreat: the climate itself in the sense of imperilling (parisahana) is “perils of climate” (utu-parissaya).

vsm1.1:95.6.verse: Unsuitable climatic conditions that cause mental distraction due to bodily affliction can be warded off by making use of the resting place;

vsm1.1:95.7.verse: it is for the purpose of warding off these and for the purpose of the pleasure of solitude, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:95.8.verse: Of course, the warding off of the perils of climate is stated by [the phrase] “protection from cold,” etc., too;

vsm1.1:95.9.verse: but, just as in the case of making use of the robes the concealment of the private parts is stated as an invariable purpose while the others are periodical [purposes],

vsm1.1:95.10.verse: so here also this [last] should be understood as mentioned with reference to the invariable warding off of the perils of climate.

vsm1.1:95.11.verse: Or alternatively, this “climate” of the kind stated is just climate;

vsm1.1:95.12.verse: but “perils” are of two kinds: evident perils and concealed perils (see Nidd I 12).

vsm1.1:95.13.verse: Herein, evident perils are lions, tigers, etc.,

vsm1.1:95.14.verse: while concealed perils are greed, hate, and so on.

vsm1.1:95.15.verse: When a bhikkhu knows and reflects thus in making use of the kind of resting place where these [perils] do not, owing to unguarded doors and sight of unsuitable visible objects, etc., cause affliction,

vsm1.1:95.16.verse: he can be understood as one who “reflecting wisely makes use of the resting place for the purpose of warding off the perils of climate.”

vsm1.1:96.1.verse: 96. The requisite of medicine as cure for the sick: here “cure” (paccaya = going against) is in the sense of going against (pati-ayana) illness;

vsm1.1:96.2.verse: in the sense of countering, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:96.3.verse: This is a term for any suitable remedy.

vsm1.1:96.4.verse: It is the medical man’s work (bhisakkassa kammaṃ) because it is permitted by him, thus it is medicine (bhesajja).

vsm1.1:96.5.verse: Or the cure for the sick itself as medicine is “medicine as cure for the sick.”

vsm1.1:96.6.verse: Any work of a medical man such as oil, honey, ghee, etc., that is suitable for one who is sick, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:96.7.verse: A “requisite” (parikkhāra), however, in such passages as “It is well supplied with the requisites of a city” (A IV 106) is equipment;

vsm1.1:96.8.verse: in such passages as “The chariot has the requisite of virtue, the axle of jhāna, the wheel of energy” (S V 6) it is an ornament;

vsm1.1:96.9.verse: in such passages as “The requisites for the life of one who has gone into homelessness that should be available” (M I 104), it is an accessory.

vsm1.1:96.10.verse: But here both equipment and accessory are applicable.

vsm1.1:96.11.verse: For that medicine as a cure for the sick is equipment for maintaining life

vsm1.1:96.12.verse: because it protects by preventing the arising of affliction destructive to life; and it is an accessory too because it is an instrument for prolonging life.

vsm1.1:96.13.verse: That is why it is called “requisite.”

vsm1.1:96.14.verse: So it is medicine as cure for the sick and that is a requisite, thus it is a “requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.”

vsm1.1:96.15.verse: [He makes use of] that requisite of medicine as cure for the sick;

vsm1.1:96.16.verse: any requisite for life consisting of oil, honey, molasses, ghee, etc., that is allowed by a medical man as suitable for the sick, is what is meant.

vsm1.1:97.1.verse: 97. From arisen: from born, become, produced.

vsm1.1:97.2.verse: Hurtful: here “hurt (affliction)” is a disturbance of elements,

vsm1.1:97.3.verse: and it is the leprosy, tumours, boils, etc., originated by that disturbance.

vsm1.1:97.4.verse: Hurtful (veyyābādhika) because arisen in the form of hurt (byābādha).

vsm1.1:97.5.verse: Feelings: painful feelings, feelings resulting from unprofitable kamma

vsm1.1:97.7.verse: For complete immunity from affliction: for complete freedom from pain;

vsm1.1:97.8.verse: so that all that is painful is abandoned, is the meaning.

vsm1.1:97.9.verse: This is how this virtue concerning requisites should be understood. In brief its characteristic is the use of requisites after wise reflection.

vsm1.1:97.10.verse: The word-meaning here is this: because breathing things go (ayanti), move, proceed, using [what they use] in dependence on these robes, etc., these robes, etc., are therefore called requisites (paccaya = ger. of paṭi + ayati);

vsm1.1:98.0.verse: [The Method of Achieving the Fourfold Purification]

vsm1.1:98.1.verse: 98. (a) So, in this fourfold virtue, Pātimokkha restraint has to be undertaken by means of faith.

vsm1.1:98.2.verse: For that is accomplished by faith, since the announcing of training precepts is outside the disciples’ province;

vsm1.1:98.3.verse: and the evidence here is the refusal of the request to [allow disciples to] announce training precepts (see Vin III 9–10).

vsm1.1:98.4.verse: Having therefore undertaken through faith the training precepts without exception as announced, one should completely perfect them without regard for life.

vsm1.1:98.5.verse: For this is said: “As a hen guards her eggs, Or as a yak her tail, Or like a darling child, Or like an only eye— So you who are engaged Your virtue to protect, Be prudent at all times And ever scrupulous.” (Source untraced)

vsm1.1:98.6.verse: Also it is said further: “So too, sire, when a training precept for disciples is announced by me,

vsm1.1:98.7.verse: my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of life” (A IV 201).

vsm1.1:99.1.verse: 99. And the story of the elders bound by robbers in the forest should be understood in this sense.

vsm1.1:99.2.verse: It seems that robbers in the Mahāvaṭṭanī Forest bound an elder with black creepers and made him lie down.

vsm1.1:99.3.verse: While he lay there for seven days he augmented his insight, and after reaching the fruition of non-return, he died there and was reborn in the Brahmā-world.

vsm1.1:99.4.verse: Also they bound another elder in Tambapaṇṇi Island (Sri Lanka) with string creepers and made him lie down.

vsm1.1:99.5.verse: When a forest fire came and the creepers were not cut, he established insight and attained Nibbāna simultaneously with his death.

vsm1.1:99.6.verse: When the Elder Abhaya, a preacher of the Dīgha Nikāya, passed by with five hundred bhikkhus, he saw [what had happened] and he had the elder’s body cremated and a shrine built.

vsm1.1:99.7.verse: Therefore let other clansmen also: Maintain the rules of conduct pure, Renouncing life if there be need, Rather than break virtue’s restraint By the World’s Saviour decreed.

vsm1.1:100.1.verse: 100. (b) And as Pātimokkha restraint is undertaken out of faith,

vsm1.1:100.2.verse: so restraint of the sense faculties should be undertaken with mindfulness.

vsm1.1:100.3.verse: For that is accomplished by mindfulness,

vsm1.1:100.4.verse: because when the sense faculties’ functions are founded on mindfulness, there is no liability to invasion by covetousness and the rest.

vsm1.1:100.5.verse: So, recollecting the Fire Discourse, which begins thus, “Better, bhikkhus, the extirpation of the eye faculty by a red-hot burning blazing glowing iron spike than the apprehension of signs in the particulars of visible objects cognizable by the eye” (S IV 168),

vsm1.1:100.6.verse: this [restraint] should be properly undertaken by preventing with unremitting mindfulness any apprehension, in the objective fields consisting of visible data, etc., of any signs, etc., likely to encourage covetousness, etc., to invade consciousness occurring in connection with the eye door, and so on.

vsm1.1:101.1.verse: 101. When not undertaken thus, virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is unenduring: it does not last,

vsm1.1:101.2.verse: like a crop not fenced in with branches.

vsm1.1:101.3.verse: And it is raided by the robber defilements as a village with open gates is by thieves.

vsm1.1:101.4.verse: And lust leaks into his mind as rain does into a badly-roofed house.

vsm1.1:101.5.verse: For this is said: “Among the visible objects, sounds, and smells, And tastes, and tangibles, guard the faculties; For when these doors are open and unguarded, Then thieves will come and raid as ’twere a village (?). And just as with an ill-roofed house The rain comes leaking in, so too Will lust come leaking in for sure Upon an undeveloped mind” (Dhp 13).

vsm1.1:102.1.verse: 102. When it is undertaken thus, virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is enduring: it lasts, like a crop well fenced in with branches.

vsm1.1:102.2.verse: And it is not raided by the robber defilements, as a village with well-guarded gates is not by thieves.

vsm1.1:102.3.verse: And lust does not leak into his mind, as rain does not into a well-roofed house.

vsm1.1:102.4.verse: For this is said: “Among the visible objects, sounds and smells, And tastes and tangibles, guard the faculties; For when these doors are closed and truly guarded, Thieves will not come and raid as ’twere a village (?). “And just as with a well-roofed house No rain comes leaking in, so too No lust comes leaking in for sure Upon a well-developed mind” (Dhp 14).

vsm1.1:103.1.verse: 103. This, however, is the teaching at its very highest.

vsm1.1:103.2.verse: This mind is called “quickly transformed” (A I 10),

vsm1.1:103.3.verse: so restraint of the faculties should be undertaken by removing arisen lust with the contemplation of foulness, as was done by the Elder Vaṅgīsa soon after he had gone forth.

vsm1.1:103.4.verse: As the elder was wandering for alms, it seems, soon after going forth, lust arose in him on seeing a woman.

vsm1.1:103.5.verse: Thereupon he said to the venerable Ānanda: “I am afire with sensual lust. And burning flames consume my mind; In pity tell me, Gotama, How to extinguish it for good” (S I 188).

vsm1.1:103.6.verse: The elder said: “You do perceive mistakenly, That burning flames consume your mind. Look for no sign of beauty there, For that it is which leads to lust. See foulness there and keep your mind Harmoniously concentrated; Formations see as alien, As ill, not self, so this great lust May be extinguished, and no more Take fire thus ever and again” (S I 188).

vsm1.1:103.7.verse: The elder expelled his lust and then went on with his alms round.

vsm1.1:104.1.verse: 104. Moreover, a bhikkhu who is fulfilling restraint of the faculties should be like the Elder Cittagutta resident in the Great Cave at Kuraṇḍaka, and like the Elder Mahā Mitta resident at the Great Monastery of Coraka.

vsm1.1:105.1.verse: 105. In the Great Cave of Kuraṇḍaka, it seems, there was a lovely painting of the Renunciation of the Seven Buddhas.

vsm1.1:105.2.verse: A number of bhikkhus wandering about among the dwellings saw the painting and said, “What a lovely painting, venerable sir!”

vsm1.1:105.3.verse: The elder said: “For more than sixty years, friends, I have lived in the cave, and I did not know whether there was any painting there or not.

vsm1.1:105.4.verse: Now, today, I know it through those who have eyes.”

vsm1.1:105.5.verse: The elder, it seems, though he had lived there for so long, had never raised his eyes and looked up at the cave.

vsm1.1:105.6.verse: And at the door of his cave there was a great ironwood tree.

vsm1.1:105.7.verse: And the elder had never looked up at that either.

vsm1.1:105.8.verse: He knew it was in flower when he saw its petals on the ground each year.

vsm1.1:106.1.verse: 106. The king heard of the elder’s great virtues, and he sent for him three times, desiring to pay homage to him. When the elder did not go,

vsm1.1:106.2.verse: he had the breasts of all the women with infants in the town bound and sealed off, [saying] “As long as the elder does not come let the children go without milk,”

vsm1.1:106.3.verse: Out of compassion for the children the elder went to Mahāgāma.

vsm1.1:106.4.verse: When the king heard [that he had come, he said] “Go and bring the elder in. I shall take the precepts.” Having had him brought up into the inner palace, he paid homage to him and provided him with a meal.

vsm1.1:106.5.verse: Then, saying, “Today, venerable sir, there is no opportunity. I shall take the precepts tomorrow,” he took the elder’s bowl.

vsm1.1:106.6.verse: After following him for a little, he paid homage with the queen and turned back.

vsm1.1:106.7.verse: As seven days went by thus, whether it was the king who paid homage or whether it was the queen,

vsm1.1:106.8.verse: the elder said, “May the king be happy.”

vsm1.1:107.1.verse: 107. Bhikkhus asked: “Why is it, venerable sir,

vsm1.1:107.2.verse: that whether it is the king who pays the homage or the queen you say ‘May the king be happy’?”

vsm1.1:107.3.verse: The elder replied: “Friends, I do not notice whether it is the king or the queen.”

vsm1.1:107.4.verse: At the end of seven days [when it was found that] the elder was not happy living there, he was dismissed by the king. He went back to the Great Cave at Kuraṇḍaka. When it was night he went out onto his walk.

vsm1.1:107.5.verse: A deity who dwelt in the ironwood tree stood by with a torch of sticks.

vsm1.1:107.6.verse: Then his meditation subject became quite clear and plain.

vsm1.1:107.7.verse: The elder, [thinking] “How clear my meditation subject is today!” was glad, and immediately after the middle watch he reached Arahantship, making the whole rock resound.

vsm1.1:108.1.verse: 108. So when another clansman seeks his own good: Let him not be hungry-eyed, Like a monkey in the groves, Like a wild deer in the woods, Like a nervous little child. Let him go with eyes downcast Seeing a plough yoke’s length before, That he fall not in the power Of the forest-monkey mind.

vsm1.1:109.1.verse: 109. The Elder Mahā Mitta’s mother was sick with a poisoned tumour.

vsm1.1:109.2.verse: She told her daughter, who as a bhikkhunī had also gone forth,

vsm1.1:109.3.verse: “Lady, go to your brother. Tell him my trouble and bring back some medicine.”

vsm1.1:109.5.verse: The elder said: “I do not know how to gather root medicines and such things and concoct a medicine from them. But rather I will tell you a medicine:

vsm1.1:109.6.verse: since I went forth I have not broken [my virtue of restraint of] the sense faculties by looking at the bodily form of the opposite sex with a lustful mind.

vsm1.1:109.7.verse: By this declaration of truth may my mother get well. Go and tell the lay devotee and rub her body.”

vsm1.1:109.8.verse: She went and told her what had happened and then did as she had been instructed.

vsm1.1:109.9.verse: At that very moment the lay devotee’s tumour vanished, shrinking away like a lump of froth.

vsm1.1:109.10.verse: She got up and uttered a cry of joy: “If the Fully Enlightened One were still alive, why should he not stroke with his netadorned hand the head of a bhikkhu like my son?”

vsm1.1:110.1.verse: 110. Let another noble clansman Gone forth in the Dispensation Keep, as did the Elder Mitta, Perfect faculty restraint.

vsm1.1:111.1.verse: 111. (c) As restraint of the faculties is to be undertaken by means of mindfulness,

vsm1.1:111.2.verse: so livelihood purification is to be undertaken by means of energy.

vsm1.1:111.3.verse: For that is accomplished by energy, because the abandoning of wrong livelihood is effected in one who has rightly applied energy.

vsm1.1:111.4.verse: Abandoning, therefore, unbefitting wrong search, this should be undertaken with energy by means of the right kind of search consisting in going on alms round, etc.,

vsm1.1:111.5.verse: avoiding what is of impure origin as though it were a poisonous snake, and using only requisites of pure origin.

vsm1.1:112.1.verse: 112. Herein, for one who has not taken up the ascetic practices, any requisites obtained from the Community, from a group of bhikkhus,

vsm1.1:112.2.verse: or from laymen who have confidence in his special qualities of teaching the Dhamma, etc., are called “of pure origin.”

vsm1.1:112.3.verse: But those obtained on alms round, etc., are of extremely pure origin.

vsm1.1:112.4.verse: For one who has taken up the ascetic practices, those obtained on alms round, etc., and—as long as this is in accordance with the rules of the ascetic practices—from people who have confidence in his special qualities of asceticism, are called “of pure origin.”

vsm1.1:112.5.verse: And if he has got putrid urine with mixed gall nuts and “four-sweets” for the purpose of curing a certain affliction, and he eats only the broken gall nuts, thinking, “Other companions in the life of purity will eat the ‘four-sweets’,” his undertaking of the ascetic practices is befitting,

vsm1.1:112.6.verse: for he is then called a bhikkhu who is supreme in the Noble Ones’ heritages (A II 28).

vsm1.1:113.1.verse: 113. As to the robe and the other requisites,

vsm1.1:113.2.verse: no hint, indication, roundabout talk, or intimation about robes and alms food is allowable for a bhikkhu who is purifying his livelihood.

vsm1.1:113.3.verse: But a hint, indication, or roundabout talk about a resting place is allowable for one who has not taken up the ascetic practices.

vsm1.1:114.1.verse: 114. Herein, a “hint” is when one who is getting the preparing of the ground, etc., done for the purpose of [making] a resting place is asked, “What is being done, venerable sir? Who is having it done?” and he replies, “No one”;

vsm1.1:114.2.verse: or any other such giving of hints.

vsm1.1:114.3.verse: An “indication” is saying, “Lay follower, where do you live?”—”In a mansion, venerable sir”—

vsm1.1:114.4.verse: ”But, lay follower, a mansion is not allowed for bhikkhus.” Or any other such giving of indication.

vsm1.1:114.5.verse: “Roundabout talk” is saying, “The resting place for the Community of Bhikkhus is crowded”; or any other such oblique talk.

vsm1.1:115.1.verse: 115. All, however, is allowed in the case of medicine.

vsm1.1:115.2.verse: But when the disease is cured, is it or is it not allowed to use the medicine obtained in this way?

vsm1.1:115.3.verse: Herein, the Vinaya specialists say that the opening has been given by the Blessed One, therefore it is allowable.

vsm1.1:115.4.verse: But the Suttanta specialists say that though there is no offence,

vsm1.1:115.5.verse: nevertheless the livelihood is sullied, therefore it is not allowable.

vsm1.1:116.1.verse: 116. But one who does not use hints, indications, roundabout talk, or intimation, though these are permitted by the Blessed One, and who depends only on the special qualities of fewness of wishes, etc., and makes use only of requisites obtained otherwise than by indication, etc., even when he thus risks his life,

vsm1.1:116.2.verse: is called supreme in living in effacement,

vsm1.1:117.1.verse: 117. It seems that the venerable one was cultivating seclusion at one time, living in a certain forest with the Elder Mahā Moggallāna.

vsm1.1:117.2.verse: One day an affliction of colic arose in him, causing him great pain.

vsm1.1:117.3.verse: In the evening the Elder Mahā Moggallāna went to attend upon him. Seeing him lying down, he asked what the reason was.

vsm1.1:117.4.verse: And then he asked, “What used to make you better formerly, friend?”

vsm1.1:117.5.verse: The elder said, “When I was a layman, friend, my mother used to mix ghee, honey, sugar and so on, and give me rice gruel with pure milk. That used to make me better.”

vsm1.1:117.6.verse: Then the other said, “So be it, friend. If either you or I have merit, perhaps tomorrow we shall get some.”

vsm1.1:118.1.verse: 118. Now, a deity who dwelt in a tree at the end of the walk overheard their conversation. [Thinking] “I will find rice gruel for the lord tomorrow,”

vsm1.1:118.2.verse: he went meanwhile to the family who was supporting the elder and entered into the body of the eldest son, causing him discomfort.

vsm1.1:118.3.verse: Then he told the assembled relatives the price of the cure: “If you prepare rice gruel of such a kind tomorrow for the elder, I will set this one free.”

vsm1.1:118.4.verse: They said: “Even without being told by you we regularly supply the elder’s needs,” and on the following day they prepared rice gruel of the kind needed.

vsm1.1:119.1.verse: 119. The Elder Mahā Moggallāna came in the morning and said, “Stay here, friend, till I come back from the alms round.” Then he went into the village.

vsm1.1:119.2.verse: Those people met him. They took his bowl, filled it with the stipulated kind of rice gruel, and gave it back to him.

vsm1.1:119.3.verse: The elder made as though to go,

vsm1.1:119.4.verse: but they said, “Eat, venerable sir, we shall give you more.” When the elder had eaten, they gave him another bowlful.

vsm1.1:119.5.verse: The elder left. Bringing the alms food to the venerable Sāriputta, he said, “Here, friend Sāriputta, eat.”

vsm1.1:119.6.verse: When the elder saw it, he thought, “The gruel is very nice. How was it got?”

vsm1.1:119.7.verse: and seeing how it had been obtained, he said, “Friend, the alms food cannot be used.”

vsm1.1:120.1.verse: 120. Instead of thinking, “He does not eat alms food brought by the likes of me,” the other at once took the bowl by the rim and turned it over on one side.

vsm1.1:120.2.verse: As the rice gruel fell on the ground the elder’s affliction vanished.

vsm1.1:120.3.verse: From then on it did not appear again during forty-five years.

vsm1.1:121.1.verse: 121. Then he said to the venerable Mahā Moggallāna, “Friend, even if one’s bowels come out and trail on the ground, it is not fitting to eat gruel got by verbal intimation,”

vsm1.1:121.2.verse: and he uttered this exclamation: My livelihood might well be blamed If I were to consent to eat The honey and the gruel obtained By influence of verbal hints. And even if my bowels obtrude And trail outside, and even though My life is to be jeopardized, I will not blot my livelihood (Mil 370). For I will satisfy my heart By shunning all wrong kinds of search; And never will I undertake The search the Buddhas have condemned.

vsm1.1:122.1.verse: 122. And here too should be told the story of the Elder Mahā Tissa the Mango-eater who lived at Cīragumba (see §132 below).

vsm1.1:122.2.verse: So in all respects: A man who has gone forth in faith Should purify his livelihood And, seeing clearly, give no thought To any search that is not good.

vsm1.1:123.1.verse: 123. (d) And as livelihood purification is to be undertaken by means of energy,

vsm1.1:123.2.verse: so virtue dependent on requisites is to be undertaken by means of understanding.

vsm1.1:123.3.verse: For that is accomplished by understanding,

vsm1.1:123.4.verse: because one who possesses understanding is able to see the advantages and the dangers in requisites.

vsm1.1:123.5.verse: So one should abandon greed for requisites and undertake that virtue by using requisites obtained lawfully and properly, after reviewing them with understanding in the way aforesaid.

vsm1.1:124.1.verse: 124. Herein, reviewing is of two kinds: at the time of receiving requisites and at the time of using them.

vsm1.1:124.2.verse: For use (paribhoga) is blameless in one who at the time of receiving robes, etc., reviews them either as [mere] elements or as repulsive, and puts them aside for later use, and in one who reviews them thus at the time of using them.

vsm1.1:125.1.verse: Here is an explanation to settle the matter.

vsm1.1:125.2.verse: There are four kinds of use: use as theft, use as a debt?, use as an inheritance, use as a master.

vsm1.1:125.3.verse: Herein, use by one who is unvirtuous and makes use [of requisites], even sitting in the midst of the Community, is called “use as theft.”

vsm1.1:125.4.verse: Use without reviewing by one who is virtuous is “use as a debt”;

vsm1.1:125.5.verse: therefore the robe should be reviewed every time it is used, and the alms food lump by lump.

vsm1.1:125.6.verse: One who cannot do this [should review it] before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, in the middle watch, and in the last watch.

vsm1.1:125.7.verse: If dawn breaks on him without his having reviewed it, he finds himself in the position of one who has used it as a debt.

vsm1.1:125.8.verse: Also the resting place should be reviewed each time it is used.

vsm1.1:125.9.verse: Recourse to mindfulness both in the accepting and the use of medicine is proper;

vsm1.1:125.10.verse: but while this is so, though there is an offence for one who uses it without mindfulness after mindful acceptance,

vsm1.1:125.11.verse: there is no offence for one who is mindful in using after accepting without mindfulness.

vsm1.1:126.1.verse: 126. Purification is of four kinds: purification by the Teaching,

vsm1.1:126.2.verse: purification by restraint, purification by search, and purification by reviewing.

vsm1.1:126.3.verse: Herein, virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is called “purification by the Teaching”;

vsm1.1:126.4.verse: for that is so called because it purifies by means of teaching.

vsm1.1:126.5.verse: Virtue of restraint of faculties is called “purification by restraint”;

vsm1.1:126.6.verse: for that is so called because it purifies by means of the restraint in the mental resolution, “I shall not do so again.”

vsm1.1:126.7.verse: Virtue of livelihood purification is called “purification by search”;

vsm1.1:126.8.verse: for that is so called because search is purified in one who abandons wrong search and gets requisites lawfully and properly.

vsm1.1:126.9.verse: Virtue dependent on requisites is called “purification by reviewing”;

vsm1.1:126.10.verse: for that is so called because it purifies by the reviewing of the kind already described.

vsm1.1:126.11.verse: Hence it was said above (§125): “There is no offence for one who is mindful in using after accepting without mindfulness.”

vsm1.1:127.1.verse: 127. Use of the requisites by the seven kinds of trainers is called “use as an inheritance”;

vsm1.1:127.2.verse: for they are the Buddha’s sons, therefore they make use of the requisites as the heirs of requisites belonging to their father.

vsm1.1:127.3.verse: But how then, is it the Blessed One’s requisites or the laity’s requisites that are used?

vsm1.1:127.4.verse: Although given by the laity, they actually belong to the Blessed One, because it is by the Blessed One that they are permitted.

vsm1.1:127.5.verse: That is why it should be understood that the Blessed One’s requisites are used.

vsm1.1:127.6.verse: The confirmation here is in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta (MN 3).

vsm1.1:127.7.verse: Use by those whose cankers are destroyed is called “use as a master”;

vsm1.1:127.8.verse: for they make use of them as masters because they have escaped the slavery of craving.

vsm1.1:128.1.verse: 128. As regards these kinds of use, use as a master and use as an inheritance are allowable for all.

vsm1.1:128.2.verse: Use as a debt is not allowable,

vsm1.1:128.3.verse: to say nothing of use as theft.

vsm1.1:128.4.verse: But this use of what is reviewed by one who is virtuous

vsm1.1:128.5.verse: is use freed from debt because it is the opposite of use as a debt or is included in use as an inheritance too.

vsm1.1:128.6.verse: For one possessed of virtue is called a trainer too because of possessing this training.

vsm1.1:129.1.verse: 129. As regards these three kinds of use, since use as a master is best, when a bhikkhu undertakes virtue dependent on requisites, he should aspire to that and use them after reviewing them in the way described.

vsm1.1:129.2.verse: And this is said: “The truly wise disciple Who listens to the Dhamma As taught by the Sublime One Makes use, after reviewing, Of alms food, and of dwelling, And of a resting place, And also of the water For washing dirt from robes” (Sn 391). “So like a drop of water Lying on leaves of lotus, A bhikkhu is unsullied By any of these matters, By alms food, [and by dwelling,] And by a resting place, And also by the water For washing dirt from robes” (Sn 392).

vsm1.1:129.3.verse: “Since aid it is and timely Procured from another The right amount he reckons, Mindful without remitting In chewing and in eating, In tasting food besides: He treats it as an ointment Applied upon a wound.” (Source untraced)

vsm1.1:129.4.verse: “So like the child’s flesh in the desert Like the greasing for the axle, He should eat without delusion Nutriment to keep alive.” (Source untraced)

vsm1.1:130.1.verse: 130. And in connection with the fulfilling of this virtue dependent on requisites there should be told the story of the novice Saṅgharakkhita the Nephew.

vsm1.1:130.2.verse: For he made use of requisites after reviewing,

vsm1.1:130.3.verse: according as it is said: “Seeing me eat a dish of rice Quite cold, my preceptor observed: ‘Novice, if you are not restrained, Be careful not to burn your tongue.’

vsm1.1:130.4.verse: On hearing my Preceptor’s words, I then and there felt urged to act And, sitting in a single session, I reached the goal of Arahantship.

vsm1.1:130.5.verse: Since I am now waxed full in thought Like the full moon of the fifteenth (M III 277), And all my cankers are destroyed, There is no more becoming now.”

vsm1.1:130.6.verse: And so should any other man Aspiring to end suffering Make use of all the requisites Wisely after reviewing them.

vsm1.1:130.7.verse: So virtue is of four kinds as “virtue of Pātimokkha restraint,” and so on.

vsm1.1:131.1.verse: 131. In the first pentad in the fivefold section the meaning should be understood in accordance with the virtue of those not fully admitted to the Order, and so on.

vsm1.1:131.2.verse: For this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “(a) What is virtue consisting in limited purification? That of the training precepts for those not fully admitted to the Order:

vsm1.1:131.3.verse: such is virtue consisting in limited purification.

vsm1.1:131.4.verse: (b) What is virtue consisting in unlimited purification? That of the training precepts for those fully admitted to the Order:

vsm1.1:131.5.verse: such is virtue consisting in unlimited purification.

vsm1.1:131.6.verse: (c) What is virtue consisting in fulfilled purification? That of magnanimous ordinary men devoted to profitable things, who are perfecting [the course] that ends in trainership, regardless of the physical body and life, having given up [attachment to] life:

vsm1.1:131.7.verse: such is virtue of fulfilled purification,

vsm1.1:131.8.verse: (d) What is virtue consisting in purification not adhered to? That of the seven kinds of trainer:

vsm1.1:131.9.verse: such is virtue consisting in purification not adhered to.

vsm1.1:131.10.verse: (e) What is virtue consisting in tranquillized purification? That of the Perfect One’s disciples with cankers destroyed, of the Paccekabuddhas, of the Perfect Ones, accomplished and fully enlightened:

vsm1.1:131.11.verse: such is virtue consisting in tranquillized purification” (Paṭis I 42–43).

vsm1.1:132.1.verse: 132. (a) Herein, the virtue of those not fully admitted to the Order should be understood as virtue consisting in limited purification, because it is limited by the number [of training precepts, that is, five or eight or ten].

vsm1.1:132.2.verse: (b) That of those fully admitted to the Order is [describable] thus: Nine thousand millions, and a hundred And eighty millions then as well, And fifty plus a hundred thousand, And thirty-six again to swell. The total restraint disciplines: These rules the Enlightened One explains Told under heads for filling out, Which the Discipline restraint contains.

vsm1.1:132.3.verse: So although limited in number, it should yet be understood as virtue consisting in unlimited purification, since it is undertaken without reserve and has no obvious limit such as gain, fame, relatives, limbs or life.

vsm1.1:132.4.verse: Like the virtue of the Elder Mahā Tissa the Mango-eater who lived at Cīragumba (see §122 above).

vsm1.1:133.1.verse: 133. For that venerable one never abandoned the following good man’s recollection: “Wealth for a sound limb’s sake should be renounced, And one who guards his life gives up his limbs; And wealth and limbs and life, each one of these, A man gives up who practices the Dhamma.”

vsm1.1:133.2.verse: And he never transgressed a training precept

vsm1.1:133.3.verse: even when his life was in the balance, and in this way he reached Arahantship with that same virtue of unlimited purification as his support while he was being carried on a lay devotee’s back.

vsm1.1:133.4.verse: According to as it is said: “Nor your mother nor your father Nor your relatives and kin Have done as much as this for you Because you are possessed of virtue.” So, stirred with urgency, and wisely Comprehending with insight, While carried on his helper’s back He reached the goal of Arahantship.

vsm1.1:134.1.verse: 134. (c) The magnanimous ordinary man’s virtue, which from the time of admission to the Order is devoid even of the stain of a [wrong] thought because of its extreme purity, like a gem of purest water, like well-refined gold, becomes the proximate cause for Arahantship itself,

vsm1.1:134.2.verse: which is why it is called consisting of fulfilled purification;

vsm1.1:134.3.verse: like that of the elders Saṅgharakkhita the Great and Saṅgharakkhita the Nephew.

vsm1.1:135.1.verse: 135. The Elder Saṅgharakkhita the Great (Mahā Saṅgharakkhita), aged over sixty, was lying, it seems, on his deathbed. The Order of Bhikkhus questioned him about attainment of the supramundane state.

vsm1.1:135.2.verse: The elder said: “I have no supramundane state.”

vsm1.1:135.3.verse: Then the young bhikkhu who was attending on him said: “Venerable sir, people have come as much as twelve leagues, thinking that you have reached Nibbāna.

vsm1.1:135.4.verse: It will be a disappointment for many if you die as an ordinary man.”

vsm1.1:135.5.verse: —“Friend, thinking to see the Blessed One Metteyya, I did not try for insight. So help me to sit up and give me the chance.”

vsm1.1:135.6.verse: He helped the elder to sit up and went out.

vsm1.1:135.7.verse: As he went out the elder reached Arahantship and he gave a sign by snapping his fingers.

vsm1.1:135.8.verse: The Order assembled and said to him: “Venerable sir, you have done a difficult thing in achieving the supramundane state in the hour of death.”

vsm1.1:135.10.verse: But rather I will tell you what is difficult. Friends, I see no action done [by me] without mindfulness and unknowingly since the time I went forth.”

vsm1.1:135.11.verse: His nephew also reached Arahantship in the same way at the age of fifty years.

vsm1.1:136.1.verse: 136. “Now, if a man has little learning And he is careless of his virtue, They censure him on both accounts For lack of virtue and of learning.

vsm1.1:136.2.verse: “But if he is of little learning Yet he is careful of his virtue, They praise him for his virtue, so It is as though he too had learning.

vsm1.1:136.3.verse: “And if he is of ample learning Yet he is careless of his virtue, They blame him for his virtue, so It is as though he had no learning.

vsm1.1:136.4.verse: “But if he is of ample learning And he is careful of his virtue, They give him praise on both accounts For virtue and as well for learning.

vsm1.1:136.5.verse: “The Buddha’s pupil of much learning Who keeps the Law with understanding— A jewel of Jambu River gold Who is here fit to censure him? Deities praise him [constantly], By Brahmā also is he praised” (A II 7).

vsm1.1:137.1.verse: 137. (d) What should be understood as virtue consisting in purification not adhered to is trainers’ virtue, because it is not adhered to by [false] view,

vsm1.1:137.2.verse: and ordinary men’s virtue when not adhered to by greed. Like the virtue of the Elder Tissa the Landowner’s Son (Kuṭumbiyaputta-Tissa-thera).

vsm1.1:137.3.verse: Wanting to become established in Arahantship in dependence on such virtue, this venerable one told his enemies: I broke the bones of both my legs To give the pledge you asked from me. I am revolted and ashamed At death accompanied by greed.

vsm1.1:137.4.verse: “And after I had thought on this, And wisely then applied insight, When the sun rose and shone on me, I had become an Arahant” (M-a I 233).

vsm1.1:138.1.verse: 138. Also there was a certain senior elder who was very ill and unable to eat with his own hand.

vsm1.1:138.2.verse: He was writhing smeared with his own urine and excrement.

vsm1.1:138.3.verse: Seeing him, a certain young bhikkhu said, “Oh, what a painful process life is!”

vsm1.1:138.4.verse: The senior elder told him: “If I were to die now, friend, I should obtain the bliss of heaven; I have no doubt of that.

vsm1.1:138.5.verse: But the bliss obtained by breaking this virtue would be like the lay state obtained by disavowing the training,”

vsm1.1:138.6.verse: and he added: “I shall die together with my virtue.” As he lay there, he comprehended that same illness [with insight], and he reached Arahantship. Having done so, he pronounced these verses to the Order of Bhikkhus:

vsm1.1:138.7.verse: “I am victim of a sickening disease That racks me with its burden of cruel pain; As flowers in the dust burnt by the sun, So this my corpse will soon have withered up.

vsm1.1:138.8.verse: “Unbeautiful called beautiful, Unclean while reckoned as if clean, Though full of ordure seeming fair To him that cannot see it clear.

vsm1.1:138.9.verse: “So out upon this ailing rotting body, Fetid and filthy, punished with affliction, Doting on which this silly generation Has lost the way to be reborn in heaven!” (J-a II 437)

vsm1.1:139.1.verse: 139. (e) It is the virtue of the Arahants, etc., that should be understood as tranquillized purification, because of tranquillization of all disturbance and because of purifiedness.

vsm1.1:139.2.verse: So it is of five kinds as “consisting in limited purification,” and so on.

vsm1.1:140.1.verse: In the second pentad the meaning should be understood as the abandoning, etc., of killing living things, etc.;

vsm1.1:140.2.verse: for this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: "Five kinds of virtue: (1) In the case of killing living things, (a) abandoning is virtue, (b) abstention is virtue, (c) volition is virtue, (d) restraint is virtue, (e) non-transgression is virtue. (2) In the case of taking what is not given … (3) In the case of sexual misconduct … (4) In the case of false speech … (5) In the case of malicious speech … (6) In the case of harsh speech … (7) In the case of gossip … (8) In the case of covetousness … (9) In the case of ill will … (10) In the case of wrong view … (11) "Through renunciation in the case of lust, (a) abandoning is virtue … (12) Through non-ill-will in the case of ill-will … (13) Through perception of light in the case of stiffness-and-torpor … (14) Through non-distraction … agitation … (15) Through definition of states (dhamma) … uncertainty … (16) Through knowledge … ignorance … (17) Through gladdening in the case of boredom … (18) "Through the first jhāna in the case of the hindrances, (a) abandoning is virtue … (19) Through the second jhāna … applied and sustained thought … (20) Through the third jhāna … happiness … (21) Through the fourth jhāna in the case of pleasure and pain, (a) abandoning is virtue … (22) Through the attainment of the base consisting of boundless space in the case of perceptions of matter, perceptions of resistance, and perceptions of variety, (a) abandoning is virtue … (23) Through the attainment of the base consisting of boundless consciousness in the case of the perception of the base consisting of boundless space … (24) Through the attainment of the base consisting of nothingness in the case of the perception of the base consisting of boundless consciousness … (25) Through the attainment of the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception in the case of the perception of the base consisting of nothingness … (26) "Through the contemplation of impermanence in the case of the perception of permanence, (a) abandoning is virtue … (27) Through the contemplation of pain in the case of the perception of pleasure … (28) Through the contemplation of not-self in the case of the perception of self … (29) Through the contemplation of dispassion in the case of the perception of delighting … (30) Through the contemplation of fading away in the case of greed … (31) Through the contemplation of cessation in the case of originating … (32) Through the contemplation of relinquishment in the case of grasping … (33) "Through the contemplation of destruction in the case of the perception of compactness, (a) abandoning is virtue … (34) Through the contemplation of fall [of formations] in the case of accumulating [kamma] … (35) Through the contemplation of change in the case of the perception of lastingness … (36) Through the contemplation of the signless in the case of a sign … (37) Through the contemplation of the desireless in the case of desire … (38) Through the contemplation of voidness in the case of misinterpreting (insistence) … (39) Through insight into states that is higher understanding in the case of misinterpreting (insistence) due to grasping … (40) Through correct knowledge and vision in the case of misinterpreting (insistence) due to confusion … (41) Through the contemplation of danger in the case of misinterpreting (insistence) due to reliance [on formations] … (42) Through reflection in the case of non-reflection … (43) Through the contemplation of turning away in the case of misinterpreting (insistence) due to bondage … (44) "Through the path of stream-entry in the case of defilements coefficient with [false] view, (a) abandoning is virtue … (45) Through the path of once-return in the case of gross defilements … (46) Through the path of non-return in the case of residual defilements … (47) Through the path of Arahantship in the case of all defilements, (a) abandoning is virtue, (b) abstention is virtue, (c) volition is virtue, (d) restraint is virtue, (e) non-transgression is virtue. "Such virtues lead to non-remorse in the mind, to gladdening, to happiness, to tranquillity, to joy, to repetition, to development, to cultivation, to embellishment, to the requisite [for concentration], to the equipment [of concentration], to fulfilment, to complete dispassion, to fading away, to cessation, to peace, to direct-knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna."[^38] (Paṭis I 46–47)

vsm1.1:141.1.verse: And here there is no state called abandoning other than the mere non-arising of the killing of living things, etc., as stated.

vsm1.1:141.2.verse: But the abandoning of a given [unprofitable state] upholds a given profitable state in the sense of providing a foundation for it,

vsm1.1:141.3.verse: and concentrates it by preventing wavering,

vsm1.1:141.4.verse: so it is called "virtue" (sīla) in the sense of composing (sīlana), reckoned as upholding and concentrating as stated earlier (§19).

vsm1.1:141.5.verse: The other four things mentioned refer to the presence[^39] of occurrence of will as abstention from such and such, as restraint of such and such,

vsm1.1:141.6.verse: as the volition associated with both of these, and as non-transgression in one who does not transgress such and such.

vsm1.1:141.7.verse: But their meaning of virtue has been explained already.

vsm1.1:141.8.verse: So it is of five kinds as "virtue consisting in abandoning" and so on.

vsm1.1:142.1.verse: At this point the answers to the questions, "What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What are the benefits of virtue? How many kinds of virtue are there?"

vsm1.1:143.0.verse: [(vi) The Defiling and the Cleansing of Virtue]

vsm1.1:143.1.verse: However, it was also asked (vi) WHAT IS THE DEFILING OF IT? and WHAT IS THE CLEANSING OF IT?

vsm1.1:143.2.verse: We answer that virtue’s tornness, etc., is its defiling, and that its untornness, etc., is its cleansing.

vsm1.1:143.3.verse: Now, that tornness, etc., are comprised under the breach that has gain, fame, etc., as its cause, and under the seven bonds of sexuality.

vsm1.1:143.4.verse: When a man has broken the training course at the beginning or at the end in any instance of the seven classes of offences,[^40]

vsm1.1:143.5.verse: his virtue is called torn, like a cloth that is cut at the edge.

vsm1.1:143.6.verse: But when he has broken it in the middle, it is called rent, like a cloth that is rent in the middle.

vsm1.1:143.7.verse: When he has broken it twice or thrice in succession,

vsm1.1:143.8.verse: it is called blotched, like a cow whose body is some such colour as black or red with a discrepant colour appearing on the back or the belly.

vsm1.1:143.9.verse: When he has broken it [all over] at intervals,

vsm1.1:143.10.verse: it is called mottled, like a cow speckled [all over] with discrepant-coloured spots at intervals.

vsm1.1:143.11.verse: This in the first place, is how there comes to be tornness with the breach that has gain, etc., as its cause.

vsm1.1:144.1.verse: And likewise with the seven bonds of sexuality; for this is said by the Blessed One:

vsm1.1:144.2.verse: “Here, brahman, some ascetic or brahman claims to lead the life of purity rightly; for he does not [52] enter into actual sexual intercourse with women. Yet he agrees to massage, manipulation, bathing and rubbing down by women. He enjoys it, desires it and takes satisfaction in it.

vsm1.1:144.3.verse: This is what is torn, rent, blotched and mottled in one who leads the life of purity.

vsm1.1:144.4.verse: This man is said to lead a life of purity that is unclean. As one who is bound by the bond of sexuality, he will not be released from birth, ageing and death …

vsm1.1:144.5.verse: he will not be released from suffering, I say.

vsm1.1:145.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], yet he jokes, plays and amuses himself with women …

vsm1.1:146.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], yet he gazes and stares at women eye to eye …

vsm1.1:147.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], yet he listens to the sound of women through a wall or through a fence as they laugh or talk or sing or weep …

vsm1.1:148.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], yet he recalls laughs and talks and games that he formerly had with women …

vsm1.1:149.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], [53] yet he sees a householder or a householder’s son possessed of, endowed with, and indulging in, the five cords of sense desire …

vsm1.1:150.1.verse: “Furthermore, brahman, … while he does not agree to [these things], yet he leads the life of purity aspiring to some order of deities, [thinking] ‘Through this rite (virtue) or this ritual (vow) or this asceticism I shall become a [great] deity or some [lesser] deity.’

vsm1.1:150.2.verse: He enjoys it, desires it, and takes satisfaction in it.

vsm1.1:150.3.verse: This, brahman, is what is torn, rent, blotched and mottled in one who leads the life of purity. This man … will not be released from suffering, I say” (A IV 54–56).

vsm1.1:150.4.verse: This is how tornness, etc., should be understood as included under the breach that has gain, etc., as its cause and under the seven bonds of sexuality.

vsm1.1:151.1.verse: Untornness, however, is accomplished by the complete non-breaking of the training precepts, by making amends for those broken for which amends should be made,

vsm1.1:151.2.verse: by the absence of the seven bonds of sexuality, and, as well, by the non-arising of such evil things as anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obduracy, presumption, pride (conceit), haughtiness, conceit (vanity), and negligence (MN 7),

vsm1.1:151.3.verse: and by the arising of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement (MN 24).

vsm1.1:152.1.verse: Virtues not broken for the purpose of gain, etc.,

vsm1.1:152.2.verse: and rectified by making amends after being broken by the faults of negligence, etc.,

vsm1.1:152.3.verse: and not damaged by the bonds of sexuality and by such evil things as anger and enmity, are called entirely untorn, unrent, unblotched, and unmottled.

vsm1.1:152.4.verse: And those same virtues are liberating since they bring about the state of a freeman, and praised by the wise since it is by the wise that they are praised,

vsm1.1:152.5.verse: and unadhered-to since they are not adhered to by means of craving and views, and conducive to concentration since they conduce to access concentration or to absorption concentration.

vsm1.1:152.6.verse: That is why their untornness, etc., should be understood as “cleansing” (see also VII.101f.).

vsm1.1:153.1.verse: This cleansing comes about in two ways: through seeing the danger of failure in virtue,

vsm1.1:153.2.verse: and through seeing the benefit of perfected virtue.

vsm1.1:153.3.verse: [54] Herein, the danger of failure in virtue can be seen in accordance with such suttas as that beginning, “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for the unvirtuous in the failure of virtue” (A III 252).

vsm1.1:154.1.verse: Furthermore, on account of his unvirtuousness an unvirtuous person is displeasing to deities and human beings, is uninstructable by his fellows in the life of purity,

vsm1.1:154.2.verse: suffers when unvirtuousness is censured, and is remorseful when the virtuous are praised. Owing to that unvirtuousness he is as ugly as hemp cloth.

vsm1.1:154.3.verse: Contact with him is painful because those who fall in with his views are brought to long-lasting suffering in the states of loss.

vsm1.1:154.4.verse: He is worthless because he causes no great fruit [to accrue] to those who give him gifts.

vsm1.1:154.5.verse: He is as hard to purify as a cesspit many years old.

vsm1.1:154.6.verse: He is like a log from a pyre (see It 99); for he is outside both [recluseship and the lay state].

vsm1.1:154.7.verse: Though claiming the bhikkhu state he is no bhikkhu, so he is like a donkey following a herd of cattle.

vsm1.1:154.8.verse: He is always nervous, like a man who is everyone’s enemy.

vsm1.1:154.9.verse: He is as unfit to live with as a dead carcase.

vsm1.1:154.10.verse: Though he may have the qualities of learning, etc., he is as unfit for the homage of his fellows in the life of purity as a charnel-ground fire is for that of brahmans.

vsm1.1:154.11.verse: He is as incapable of reaching the distinction of attainment as a blind man is of seeing a visible object.

vsm1.1:154.12.verse: He is as careless of the Good Law as a guttersnipe is of a kingdom.

vsm1.1:154.13.verse: Though he fancies he is happy, yet he suffers because he reaps suffering as told in the Discourse on the Mass of Fire (A IV 128–34).

vsm1.1:155.1.verse: Now, the Blessed One has shown that when the unvirtuous have their minds captured by pleasure and satisfaction in the indulgence of the five cords of sense desires, in [receiving] salutation, in being honoured, etc., the result of that kamma, directly visible in all ways, is very violent pain, with that [kamma] as its condition, capable of producing a gush of hot blood by causing agony of heart with the mere recollection of it. Here is the text:

vsm1.1:155.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing?— Yes, venerable sir.—

vsm1.1:155.3.verse: What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one [gone forth] should sit down or lie down embracing that mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing, or that he should sit down or lie down embracing a warrior-noble maiden or a brahman maiden or a maiden of householder family, with soft, delicate hands and feet?—

vsm1.1:155.4.verse: It would be better, venerable sir, that he should sit down or lie down embracing a warrior-noble maiden … [55]

vsm1.1:155.5.verse: It would be painful, venerable sir, if he sat down or lay down embracing that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing.

vsm1.1:156.1.verse: “I say to you, bhikkhus, I declare to you, bhikkhus, that it would be better for one [gone forth] who is unvirtuous, who is evil-natured, of unclean and suspect habits, secretive of his acts, who is not an ascetic and claims to be one, who does not lead the life of purity and claims to do so, who is rotten within, lecherous, and full of corruption, to sit down or lie down embracing that great mass of fire burning, blazing and glowing.

vsm1.1:156.2.verse: Why is that? By his doing so, bhikkhus, he might come to death or deadly suffering, yet he would not on that account, on the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in states of loss, in an unhappy destiny, in perdition, in hell. But if one who is unvirtuous, evil-natured … and full of corruption, should sit down or lie down embracing a warrior-noble maiden … that would be long for his harm and suffering: on the break-up of the body, after death, he would reappear in states of loss, in an unhappy destiny, in perdition, in hell” (A IV 128–29).

vsm1.1:157.1.verse: Having thus shown by means of the analogy of the mass of fire the suffering that is bound up with women and has as its condition the indulgence of the five cords of sense desires [by the unvirtuous], to the same intent he showed, by the following similes of the horse-hair rope, the sharp spear, the iron sheet, the iron ball, the iron bed, the iron chair, and the iron cauldron, the pain that has as its condition [acceptance of] homage and reverential salutation, and the use of robes, alms food, bed and chair, and dwelling [by unvirtuous bhikkhus]:

vsm1.1:157.2.verse: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong horse-hair rope twisted round both legs by a strong man and tightened so that it cut through the outer skin, and having cut through the outer skin it cut through the inner skin, and having cut through the inner skin it cut through the flesh,

vsm1.1:157.3.verse: and having cut through the flesh it cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews it cut through the bones, and having cut through the bones it remained crushing the bone marrow—

vsm1.1:157.4.verse: or that he should consent to the homage of great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 129).

vsm1.1:157.5.verse: And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong man wound one’s breast with a sharp spear tempered in oil—

vsm1.1:157.6.verse: or that he should consent to the reverential salutation of great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 130).

vsm1.1:157.7.verse: [56] And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one’s body should be wrapped by a strong man in a red-hot iron sheet burning, blazing and glowing—

vsm1.1:157.8.verse: or that he should use robes given out of faith by great warrior-nobles, great brahmans, great householders?” (A IV 130–31).

vsm1.1:157.9.verse: And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one’s mouth should be prised open by a strong man with red-hot iron tongs burning, blazing and glowing, and that into his mouth should be put a red-hot iron ball burning, blazing and glowing,

vsm1.1:157.10.verse: which burns his lips and burns his mouth and tongue and throat and belly and passes out below carrying with it his bowels and entrails—

vsm1.1:157.11.verse: or that he should use alms food given out of faith by great warrior-nobles …?” (A IV 131–32).

vsm1.1:157.12.verse: And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong man seize him by the head or seize him by the shoulders and seat him or lay him on a red-hot iron bed or iron chair, burning, blazing and glowing—

vsm1.1:157.13.verse: or that he should use a bed or chair given out of faith by great warrior-nobles … ?” (A IV 132–33).

vsm1.1:157.14.verse: And: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is better, that one should have a strong man take him feet up and head down and plunge him into a red-hot metal cauldron burning, blazing and glowing, to be boiled there in a swirl of froth,

vsm1.1:157.15.verse: and as he boils in the swirl of froth to be swept now up, now down, and now across—or that he should use a dwelling given out of faith by great warrior-nobles … ?” (A IV 133–34).

vsm1.1:157.16.verse: Thus, by these similes of the horse-hair rope, the sharp spear, the iron sheet, the iron ball, the iron bed and chair, and the iron cauldron, he showed the pain that has as its condition the use of homage, reverential salutation, robes, alms food, bed and chair, and dwelling.

vsm1.1:158.1.verse:
What pleasure has a man of broken virtue
Forsaking not sense pleasures, which bear fruit
Of pain more violent even than the pain
In the embracing of a mass of fire?

vsm1.1:158.2.verse:
What pleasure has he in accepting homage
Who, having failed in virtue, must partake
Of pain that will excel in agony
The crushing of his legs with horse-hair ropes? [57]

vsm1.1:158.3.verse:
What pleasure has a man devoid of virtue
Accepting salutations of the faithful,
Which is the cause of pain acuter still
Than pain produced by stabbing with a spear?

vsm1.1:158.4.verse:
What is the pleasure in the use of garments
For one without restraint, whereby in hell
He will for long be forced to undergo
The contact of the blazing iron sheet?

vsm1.1:158.5.verse:
Although to him his alms food may seem tasty,
Who has no virtue, it is direst poison,
Because of which he surely will be made
For long to swallow burning iron balls.

vsm1.1:158.6.verse:
And when the virtueless make use of couches
And chairs, though reckoned pleasing, it is pain
Because they will be tortured long indeed
On red-hot blazing iron beds and chairs.

vsm1.1:158.7.verse:
Then what delight is there for one unvirtuous
Inhabiting a dwelling given in faith,
Since for that reason he will have to dwell
Shut up inside a blazing iron pan?

vsm1.1:158.8.verse:
The Teacher of the world, in him condemning,
Described him in these terms: “Of suspect habits,
Full of corruption, lecherous as well,
By nature evil, rotten too within.”

vsm1.1:158.9.verse:
So out upon the life of him abiding
Without restraint, of him that wears the guise
Of the ascetic that he will not be,
And damages and undermines himself!

vsm1.1:158.10.verse:
What is the life he leads, since any person,
No matter who, with virtue to his credit
Avoids it here, as those that would look well
Keep far away from dung or from a corpse?

vsm1.1:158.11.verse:
He is not free from any sort of terror,
Though free enough from pleasure of attainment;
While heaven’s door is bolted fast against him,
He is well set upon the road to hell.

vsm1.1:158.12.verse:
Who else if not one destitute of virtue
More fit to be the object of compassion?
Many indeed and grave are the defects
That brand a man neglectful of his virtue.

vsm1.1:158.13.verse: Seeing danger in the failure of virtue should be understood as reviewing in such ways as these. And seeing benefits in perfected virtue should be understood in the opposite sense. Furthermore:

vsm1.1:159.1.verse:
His virtue is immaculate,
His wearing of the bowl and robes
Gives pleasure and inspires trust,
His going forth will bear its fruit.

vsm1.1:159.2.verse:
A bhikkhu in his virtue pure
Has never fear that self-reproach
Will enter in his heart: indeed
There is no darkness in the sun.

vsm1.1:159.3.verse:
A bhikkhu in his virtue bright
Shines forth in the Ascetics’ Wood[^41]
As by the brightness of his beams
The moon lights up the firmament.

vsm1.1:159.4.verse:
Now, if the bodily perfume
Of virtuous bhikkhus can succeed
In pleasing even deities,
What of the perfume of his virtue?

vsm1.1:159.5.verse:
It is more perfect far than all
The other perfumes in the world,
Because the perfume virtue gives
Is borne unchecked in all directions.

vsm1.1:159.6.verse:
The deeds done for a virtuous man,
Though they be few, will bear much fruit,
And so the virtuous man becomes
A vessel of honour and renown.

vsm1.1:159.7.verse:
There are no cankers here and now
To plague the virtuous man at all;
The virtuous man digs out the root
Of suffering in lives to come.

vsm1.1:159.8.verse:
Perfection among human kind
And even among deities.
If wished for, is not hard to gain
For him whose virtue is perfected;

vsm1.1:159.9.verse:
But once his virtue is perfected,
His mind then seeks no other kind
han the perfection of Nibbāna,
The state where utter peace prevails.

vsm1.1:159.10.verse:
Such is the blessed fruit of virtue,
Showing full many a varied form,
So let a wise man know it well
This root of all perfection’s branches.

vsm1.1:160.1.verse: The mind of one who understands thus, shudders at failure in virtue and reaches out towards the perfecting of virtue.

vsm1.1:160.2.verse: So virtue should be cleansed with all care, seeing this danger of failure in virtue and this benefit of the perfection of virtue in the way stated.

vsm1.1:161.1.verse: And at this point in the Path of Purification, which is shown under the headings of virtue, concentration and understanding by the stanza, “When a wise man, established well in virtue” (§1), virtue, firstly, has been fully illustrated.

vsm1.1:161.2.verse: The first chapter called “The Description of Virtue” in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

vsm1.2:1.1.verse: Now, while a meditator is engaged in the pursuit of virtue, he should set about undertaking the ascetic practices in order to perfect those special qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment, etc., by which the virtue of the kind already described, is cleansed.

vsm1.2:1.2.verse: For when his virtue is thus washed clean of stains by the waters of such special qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, dispersal, energy, and modest needs, it will become quite purified;

vsm1.2:1.3.verse: and his vows will succeed as well.

vsm1.2:1.4.verse: And so, when his whole behaviour has been purified by the special quality of blameless virtue and vows and he has become established in the [first] three of the ancient Noble Ones’ heritages, he may become worthy to attain to the fourth called “delight in development” (A II 27).

vsm1.2:1.5.verse: We shall therefore begin the explanation of the ascetic practices.

vsm1.2:2.1.verse: Thirteen kinds of ascetic practices have been allowed by the Blessed One to clansmen who have given up the things of the flesh and, regardless of body and life, are desirous of undertaking a practice in conformity [with their aim].

vsm1.2:2.2.verse: They are: i. the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice, ii. the triple-robe-wearer’s practice, iii. the alms-food-eater’s practice, iv. the house-to-house-seeker’s practice, v. the one-sessioner’s practice,

vsm1.2:2.3.verse: vi. the bowl-food-eater’s practice, vii. the later-food-refuser’s practice, viii. the forest-dweller’s practice, ix. the tree-root-dweller’s practice,

vsm1.2:2.4.verse: x. the open-air-dweller’s practice, xi. the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice, xii. the any-bed-user’s practice, xiii. the sitter’s practice.

vsm1.2:3.1.verse:
Herein:
(1) As to meaning, (2) characteristic, et cetera,
(3) The undertaking and directions,
And then the grade, and breach as well,
And benefits of each besides,
(4) As to the profitable triad,
(5) “Ascetic” and so on distinguished,
(6) And as to groups, and also (7) singly,
The exposition should be known.

vsm1.2:4.1.verse: Herein, as to meaning, in the first place. i. It is “refuse” (paṃsukūla) since, owing to its being found on refuse in any such place as a street, a charnel ground, or a midden, it belongs, as it were, to the refuse in the sense of being dumped in anyone of these places.

vsm1.2:4.2.verse: Or alternatively: like refuse it gets to a vile state (PAṂSU viya KUcchitabhāvaṃ ULAti), thus it is “refuse” (paṃsukūla); it goes to a vile state, is what is meant.

vsm1.2:4.3.verse: The wearing of a refuse-[rag], which has acquired its derivative name[^1] in this way, is “refuse-[rag-wearing]” (paṃsukūla). That is his habit, thus he is a “refuse-[rag-wear-]er” (paṃsukūlika). The practice (aṅga) of the refuse-[rag-wear-]er is the “refuse-[rag-wear-]er’s practice” (paṃsukūlikaṅga).

vsm1.2:4.4.verse: It is the action that is called the “practice.” Therefore it should be understood as a term for that by undertaking which one becomes a refuse-[rag-wear-]er.

vsm1.2:4.5.verse: ii. In the same way, he has the habit of [wearing] the triple robe (ti-cīvara)—in other words, the cloak of patches, the upper garment, and the inner clothing— thus he is a “triple-robe-[wear-]er” (tecīvarika).

vsm1.2:4.6.verse: His practice is called the “triple-robe-wearer’s practice.”

vsm1.2:5.1.verse: iii. The dropping (pāta) of the lumps (piṇḍa) of material sustenance (āmisa) called alms (bhikkhā) is “alms food” (piṇḍapāta);

vsm1.2:5.2.verse: the falling (nipatana) into the bowl of lumps (piṇḍa) given by others, is what is meant.

vsm1.2:5.3.verse: He gleans that alms food (that falling of lumps), he seeks it by approaching such and such a family, thus he is called an “alms-food [eat-]er” (piṇḍapātika).

vsm1.2:5.4.verse: Or his vow is to gather (patituṃ)[^2] the lump (piṇḍa), thus he is a “lump-gatherer” (piṇḍapātin). To “gather” is to wander for. A “lump-gatherer” (piṇḍapātin) is the same as an “alms-food-eater” (piṇḍapātika). The practice of the alms-food-eater is the “alms-food-eater’s practice.”

vsm1.2:6.1.verse: iv. It is a hiatus (avakhaṇḍana) that is called a “gap” (dāna).[^3]

vsm1.2:6.2.verse: It is removed (apeta) from a gap, thus it is called “gapless” (apadāna); the meaning is, it is without hiatus.

vsm1.2:6.3.verse: It is together with (saha) what is gapless (apadāna), thus it is “with the gapless” (sapadāna); devoid of hiatus—from house to house—is what is meant.

vsm1.2:6.4.verse: His habit is to wander on what-is-with-the-gapless, thus he is a “gapless wanderer” (sapadāna-cārin). A gapless wanderer is the same as a “house-to-house-seeker” (sapadāna-cārika). His practice is the “house-to-house-seeker’s practice.”

vsm1.2:7.1.verse: v. Eating in one session is “one-session.”

vsm1.2:7.2.verse: He has that habit, thus he is a “one-sessioner.” His practice is the “one-sessioner’s practice.”

vsm1.2:7.3.verse: vi. Alms (piṇḍa) in one bowl (patta) only because of refusing a second vessel, is “bowl-alms” (patta-piṇḍa).

vsm1.2:7.4.verse: Now, making “bowl alms” (patta-piṇḍa) the name for the taking of alms food in the bowl: bowl-alms-food is his habit, thus he is a “bowl-food-eater” (pattapiṇḍika). His practice is the “bowl-food-eater’s practice.”

vsm1.2:8.1.verse: vii. “No” (khalu) is a particle in the sense of refusing.

vsm1.2:8.2.verse: Food (bhatta) obtained later by one who has shown that he is satisfied is called “later-food” (pacchā-bhatta). The eating of that later food is “later-food-eating.” Making “later-food” (pacchā-bhatta) the name for that later-food-eating: later-food is his habit, thus he is a “later-food-[eat-]er” (pacchābhattika).

vsm1.2:8.3.verse: Not a later-food-eater is a “no-later-food-[eat-]er” (khalu-pacchābhattika), [that is, a “later-food-refuser”]. This is the name for one who as an undertaking refuses extra food.

vsm1.2:8.4.verse: But it is said in the commentary[^4] “Khalu is a certain kind of bird. When it has taken a fruit into its beak and that drops, it does not eat any more.

vsm1.2:8.5.verse: This [bhikkhu] is like that.” Thus he is “a later-food-refuser” (khalu-pacchā-bhattika). His practice is the “later-food-refuser’s practice.”

vsm1.2:9.1.verse: viii. His habit is dwelling in the forest, thus he is a “forest-dweller.” His practice is the “forest-dweller’s practice.”

vsm1.2:9.2.verse: ix. Dwelling at the root of a tree is “tree-root-dwelling.”

vsm1.2:9.3.verse: He has that habit, thus he is a “tree-root-dweller.” The practice of the tree-root-dweller is the “tree-root-dweller’s practice.” x., xi. Likewise with the open-air-dweller and the charnel-ground-dweller.

vsm1.2:10.1.verse: xii. Only what has been distributed (yad eva santhata) is “as distributed” (yathāsanthata).

vsm1.2:10.2.verse: This is a term for the resting place first allotted thus “This one falls to you.” He has the habit of dwelling in that as distributed, thus he is an “as-distributed-user” (yathāsanthatika), [that is, an “any-bed-user”]. His practice is the “any-bed-user’s practice.”

vsm1.2:10.3.verse: xiii. He has the habit of keeping to the sitting [posture when resting], refusing to lie down, thus he is a “sitter.” His practice is the “sitter’s practice.”

vsm1.2:11.1.verse: All these, however, are the practices (aṅga) of a bhikkhu who is ascetic (dhuta) because he has shaken off (dhuta) defilement by undertaking one or other of them. Or the knowledge that has got the name “ascetic” (dhuta) because it shakes off (dhunana) defilement is a practice (aṅga) belonging to these, thus they are “ascetic practices” (dhutaṅga).

vsm1.2:11.2.verse: Or alternatively, they are ascetic (dhuta) because they shake off (niddhunana) opposition, and they are practices (aṅga) because they are a way (paṭipatti). This, firstly, is how the exposition should be known here as to meaning.

vsm1.2:12.1.verse: All of them have as their characteristic the volition of undertaking.

vsm1.2:12.2.verse: For this is said [in the commentary]: “He who does the undertaking is a person. That whereby he does the undertaking is states of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants. The volition of the act of undertaking is the ascetic practice. What it rejects is the instance.”

vsm1.2:12.3.verse: All have the function of eliminating cupidity,

vsm1.2:12.4.verse: and they manifest themselves with the production of non-cupidity. For their proximate cause they have the noble states consisting of fewness of wishes, and so on. This is how the exposition should be known as to characteristic, etc., here.

vsm1.2:13.1.verse: As regards the five beginning with the undertaking and directions: during the Blessed One’s lifetime all ascetic practices should be undertaken in the Blessed One’s presence.

vsm1.2:13.2.verse: After his attainment of Nibbāna this should be done in the presence of a principal disciple.

vsm1.2:13.3.verse: When he is not available it should be done in the presence of one whose cankers are destroyed, of a non-returner, of a once-returner, of a stream-enterer,
