vsm1.3:130.3.verse: and a teacher who has not can know it by putting such questions to him as:

vsm1.3:130.5.verse: or “What states are usually present in you?”

vsm1.3:130.6.verse: or “What do you like bringing to mind?”

vsm1.3:130.7.verse: or “What meditation subject does your mind favour?”

vsm1.3:130.8.verse: When he knows, he can expound a meditation subject suitable to that temperament.

vsm1.3:130.9.verse: And in doing so, he can expound it in three ways:

vsm1.3:130.10.verse: it can be expounded to one who has already learnt the meditation subject by having him recite it at one or two sessions;

vsm1.3:130.11.verse: it can be expounded to one who lives in the same place each time he comes;

vsm1.3:130.12.verse: and to one who wants to learn it and then go elsewhere

vsm1.3:130.13.verse: it can be expounded in such a manner that it is neither too brief nor too long.

vsm1.3:131.1.verse: Herein, when first he is explaining the earth kasiṇa, there are nine aspects that he should explain. They are

vsm1.3:131.2.verse: the four faults of the kasiṇa,

vsm1.3:131.4.verse: the method of development for one who has made it,

vsm1.3:131.7.verse: the seven kinds of suitable and unsuitable,

vsm1.3:131.8.verse: the ten kinds of skill in absorption,

vsm1.3:131.11.verse: In the case of the other meditation subjects, each should be expounded in the way appropriate to it.

vsm1.3:131.12.verse: All this will be made clear in the directions for development.

vsm1.3:131.13.verse: But when the meditation subject is being expounded in this way, the meditator must apprehend the sign as he listens.

vsm1.3:132.1.verse: Apprehend the sign means that he must connect each aspect thus:

vsm1.3:132.7.verse: When he listens attentively, apprehending the sign in this way, his meditation subject is well apprehended.

vsm1.3:132.8.verse: Then, and because of that, he successfully attains distinction, but not otherwise.

vsm1.3:132.9.verse: This clarifies the meaning of the words “and he must apprehend.”

vsm1.3:133.2.verse: approach the good friend, the giver of a meditation subject,

vsm1.3:133.3.verse: and he should apprehend from among the forty meditation subjects one that suits his own temperament (§28)

vsm1.3:133.4.verse: have been expounded in detail in all their aspects.

vsm1.3:133.5.verse: The third chapter called “The Description of Taking a Meditation Subject” in the Treatise on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

vsm1.4:1.2.verse: After that he should avoid a monastery unfavourable to the development of concentration

vsm1.4:1.3.verse: and go to live in one that is favourable (III.28).

vsm1.4:1.4.verse: In the first place one who finds it convenient to live with the teacher in the same monastery

vsm1.4:1.5.verse: can live there while he is making certain of the meditation subject.

vsm1.4:1.6.verse: If it is inconvenient there, he can live in another monastery—a suitable one—a quarter or a half or even a whole league distant.

vsm1.4:1.7.verse: In that case, when he finds he is in doubt about, or has forgotten, some passage in the meditation subject,

vsm1.4:1.8.verse: then he should do the duties in the monastery in good time and set out afterwards,

vsm1.4:1.9.verse: going for alms on the way

vsm1.4:1.10.verse: and arriving at the teacher’s dwelling place after his meal.

vsm1.4:1.11.verse: He should make certain about the meditation subject that day in the teacher’s presence.

vsm1.4:1.12.verse: Next day, after paying homage to the teacher,

vsm1.4:1.13.verse: he should go for alms on his way back

vsm1.4:1.14.verse: and so he can return to his own dwelling place without fatigue.

vsm1.4:1.15.verse: But one who finds no convenient place within even a league

vsm1.4:1.16.verse: should clarify all difficulties about the meditation subject

vsm1.4:1.17.verse: and make quite sure it has been properly attended to.

vsm1.4:1.18.verse: Then he can even go far away and,

vsm1.4:1.19.verse: avoiding a monastery unfavourable to development of concentration,

vsm1.4:1.20.verse: live in one that is favourable.

vsm1.4:2.1.verse: Herein, one that is unfavourable has anyone of eighteen faults.

vsm1.4:2.2.verse: These are: (1) largeness, (2) newness, (3) dilapidatedness, (4) a nearby road,

vsm1.4:2.3.verse: (5) a pond, (6) [edible] leaves, (7) flowers, (8) fruits, (9) famousness,

vsm1.4:2.4.verse: (10) a nearby city, (11) nearby timber trees, (12) nearby arable fields, (13) presence of incompatible persons,

vsm1.4:2.5.verse: (14) a nearby port of entry, (15) nearness to the border countries, (16) nearness to the frontier of a kingdom,

vsm1.4:2.7.verse: [119] One with any of these faults is not favourable.

vsm1.4:3.1.verse: Firstly, people with varying aims collect in a large monastery.

vsm1.4:3.2.verse: They conflict with each other and so neglect the duties.

vsm1.4:3.3.verse: The Enlightenment-tree terrace, etc., remain unswept, the water for drinking and washing is not set out.

vsm1.4:3.4.verse: So if he thinks, “I shall go to the alms-resort village for alms” and takes his bowl and robe and sets out,

vsm1.4:3.5.verse: perhaps he sees that the duties have not been done or that a drinking-water pot is empty,

vsm1.4:3.6.verse: and so the duty has to be done by him unexpectedly.

vsm1.4:3.8.verse: By not doing it he would commit a wrongdoing in the breach of a duty.

vsm1.4:3.9.verse: But if he does it, he loses time.

vsm1.4:3.10.verse: He arrives too late at the village and gets nothing because the alms giving is finished.

vsm1.4:3.11.verse: Also, when he goes into retreat,

vsm1.4:3.12.verse: he is distracted by the loud noises of novices and young bhikkhus,

vsm1.4:3.13.verse: and by acts of the Community [being carried out].

vsm1.4:3.14.verse: However, he can live in a large monastery where all the duties are done and where there are none of the other disturbances.

vsm1.4:4.1.verse: In a new monastery there is much new building activity.

vsm1.4:4.2.verse: People criticize someone who takes no part in it.

vsm1.4:4.3.verse: But he can live in such a monastery where the bhikkhus say,

vsm1.4:4.4.verse: “Let the venerable one do the ascetic’s duties as much as he likes.

vsm1.4:4.5.verse: We shall see to the building work.”

vsm1.4:5.1.verse: In a dilapidated monastery there is much that needs repair.

vsm1.4:5.2.verse: People criticize someone who does not see about the repairing of at least his own lodging.

vsm1.4:5.3.verse: When he sees to the repairs, his meditation subject suffers.

vsm1.4:6.1.verse: In a monastery with a nearby road, by a main street, visitors keep arriving night and day.

vsm1.4:6.2.verse: He has to give up his own lodging to those who come late, and he has to go and live at the root of a tree or on top of a rock.

vsm1.4:6.3.verse: And next day it is the same. So there is no opportunity [to practice] his meditation subject.

vsm1.4:6.4.verse: But he can live in one where there is no such disturbance by visitors.

vsm1.4:7.1.verse: A pond is a rock pool.

vsm1.4:7.2.verse: Numbers of people come there for drinking water.

vsm1.4:7.3.verse: Pupils of city-dwelling elders supported by the royal family come to do dyeing work.

vsm1.4:7.4.verse: When they ask for vessels, wood, tubs, etc., [120] they must be shown where these things are.

vsm1.4:7.5.verse: So he is kept all the time on the alert.

vsm1.4:8.1.verse: If he goes with his meditation subject to sit by day where there are many sorts of edible leaves,

vsm1.4:8.2.verse: then women vegetable-gatherers, singing as they pick leaves nearby,

vsm1.4:8.3.verse: endanger his meditation subject by disturbing it with sounds of the opposite sex.

vsm1.4:8.4.verse: And where there are many sorts of flowering shrubs in bloom there is the same danger too.

vsm1.4:9.1.verse: Where there are many sorts of fruits such as mangoes, rose-apples and jak-fruits,

vsm1.4:9.2.verse: people who want fruits come and ask for them,

vsm1.4:9.3.verse: and they get angry if he does not give them any,

vsm1.4:9.4.verse: or they take them by force.

vsm1.4:9.5.verse: When walking in the monastery in the evening he sees them and asks,

vsm1.4:9.6.verse: “Why do you do so, lay followers?”

vsm1.4:9.7.verse: they abuse him as they please

vsm1.4:9.8.verse: and even try to evict him.

vsm1.4:10.1.verse: When he lives in a monastery that is famous and renowned in the world, like Dakkhiṇagiri[^1] Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri or Cittalapabbata,

vsm1.4:10.2.verse: there are always people coming who want to pay homage to him, supposing that he is an Arahant,

vsm1.4:10.4.verse: But if it suits him, he can live there at night and go elsewhere by day.

vsm1.4:11.1.verse: In one with a nearby city objects of the opposite sex come into focus.

vsm1.4:11.2.verse: Women-pot carriers go by bumping into him with their jars and giving no room to pass.

vsm1.4:11.3.verse: Also important people spread out carpets in the middle of the monastery and sit down.

vsm1.4:12.1.verse: One with nearby timber trees where there are timber trees and osiers useful for making framework

vsm1.4:12.2.verse: is inconvenient because of the wood-gatherers there, like the gatherers of branches and fruits already mentioned.

vsm1.4:12.3.verse: If there are trees in a monastery, people come and cut them down to build houses with.

vsm1.4:12.4.verse: When he has come out of his meditation room in the evening

vsm1.4:12.5.verse: and is walking up and down in the monastery, if he sees them

vsm1.4:12.6.verse: and asks, “Why do you do so, lay followers?”

vsm1.4:12.7.verse: they abuse him as they please

vsm1.4:12.8.verse: and even try to evict him.

vsm1.4:13.1.verse: People make use of one with nearby arable fields, quite surrounded by fields.

vsm1.4:13.2.verse: They make a threshing floor in the middle of the monastery itself. They thresh corn there,

vsm1.4:13.5.verse: And where there is extensive property belonging to the Community,

vsm1.4:13.6.verse: the monastery attendants impound cattle belonging to families

vsm1.4:13.7.verse: and deny the water supply [to their crops].

vsm1.4:13.8.verse: [121] Then people bring an ear of paddy and show it to the Community saying “Look at your monastery attendants’ work.”

vsm1.4:13.9.verse: For one reason or another he has to go to the portals of the king or the king’s ministers.

vsm1.4:13.10.verse: This [matter of property belonging to the Community] is included by [a monastery that is] near arable fields.

vsm1.4:14.1.verse: Presence of incompatible persons: where there are bhikkhus living who are incompatible and mutually hostile,

vsm1.4:14.2.verse: when they clash and it is protested,

vsm1.4:14.4.verse: they exclaim, “We no longer count now that this refuse-rag wearer has come.”

vsm1.4:15.1.verse: One with a nearby water port of entry or land port of entry[^3]

vsm1.4:15.2.verse: is made inconvenient by people constantly arriving respectively by ship or by caravan

vsm1.4:15.3.verse: and crowding round, asking for space or for drinking water or salt.

vsm1.4:16.1.verse: In the case of one near the border countries, people have no trust in the Buddha, etc., there.

vsm1.4:16.2.verse: In one near the frontier of a kingdom there is fear of kings.

vsm1.4:16.3.verse: For perhaps one king attacks that place, thinking, “It does not submit to my rule,”

vsm1.4:16.4.verse: and the other does likewise, thinking, “It does not submit to my rule.”

vsm1.4:16.5.verse: A bhikkhu lives there when it is conquered by one king and when it is conquered by the other.

vsm1.4:16.6.verse: Then they suspect him of spying, and they bring about his undoing.

vsm1.4:17.1.verse: Unsuitability is that due to the risk of encountering visible data, etc., of the opposite sex as objects

vsm1.4:17.2.verse: or to haunting by non-human beings.

vsm1.4:17.4.verse: An elder lived in a forest, it seems.

vsm1.4:17.5.verse: Then an ogress stood in the door of his leaf hut and sang.

vsm1.4:17.6.verse: The elder came out and stood in the door.

vsm1.4:17.7.verse: She went to the end of the walk and sang.

vsm1.4:17.8.verse: The elder went to the end of the walk.

vsm1.4:17.9.verse: She stood in a chasm a hundred fathoms deep and sang.

vsm1.4:17.11.verse: Then she suddenly grabbed him saying, “Venerable sir, it is not just one or two of the likes of you I have eaten.”

vsm1.4:18.2.verse: where it is not possible to find a good friend as a teacher or the equivalent of a teacher

vsm1.4:18.3.verse: or a preceptor or the equivalent of a preceptor,

vsm1.4:18.4.verse: the lack of good friends there is a serious fault.

vsm1.4:18.5.verse: One that has any of those eighteen faults should be understood as unfavourable.

vsm1.4:18.6.verse: And this is said in the commentaries:

vsm1.4:18.7.verse:
A large abode, a new abode,
One tumbling down, one near a road,

vsm1.4:18.8.verse:
One with a pond, or leaves, or flowers,
Or fruits, or one that people seek; [122]

vsm1.4:18.9.verse:
In cities, among timber, fields,
Where people quarrel, in a port,

vsm1.4:18.10.verse:
In border lands, on frontiers,
Unsuitableness, and no good friend—

vsm1.4:18.11.verse:
These are the eighteen instances
A wise man needs to recognize
And give them full as wide a berth
As any footpad-hunted road.

vsm1.4:19.0.verse: [The Five Factors of the Resting Place]

vsm1.4:19.1.verse: One that has the five factors beginning with “not too far from and not too near to” the alms resort is called favourable.

vsm1.4:19.2.verse: For this is said by the Blessed One: “And how has a lodging five factors, bhikkhus?

vsm1.4:19.3.verse: Here, bhikkhus, (1) a lodging is not too far, not too near, and has a path for going and coming.

vsm1.4:19.4.verse: (2) It is little frequented by day with little sound and few voices by night.

vsm1.4:19.5.verse: (3) There is little contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning [sun] and creeping things.

vsm1.4:19.6.verse: (4) One who lives in that lodging easily obtains robes, alms food, lodging, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.

vsm1.4:19.7.verse: (5) In that lodging there are elder bhikkhus living who are learned, versed in the scriptures,

vsm1.4:19.8.verse: observers of the Dhamma, observers of the Vinaya, observers of the Codes,

vsm1.4:19.9.verse: and when from time to time one asks them questions, ‘How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?’

vsm1.4:19.10.verse: then those venerable ones reveal the unrevealed,

vsm1.4:19.12.verse: and remove doubt about the many things that raise doubts.

vsm1.4:19.13.verse: This, bhikkhus, is how a lodging has five factors” (A V 15).

vsm1.4:19.14.verse: These are the details for the clause, “After that he should avoid a monastery unfavourable to the development of concentration

vsm1.4:19.15.verse: and go to live in one that is favourable” (III.28).

vsm1.4:20.1.verse: Then he should sever the lesser impediments (III.28):

vsm1.4:20.2.verse: one living in such a favourable monastery

vsm1.4:20.3.verse: should sever any minor impediments that he may still have,

vsm1.4:20.4.verse: that is to say, long head hair, nails, and body hair should be cut,

vsm1.4:20.5.verse: mending and patching of old robes should be done,

vsm1.4:20.6.verse: or those that are soiled should be dyed.

vsm1.4:20.7.verse: If there is a stain on the bowl, the bowl should be baked.

vsm1.4:20.8.verse: The bed, chair, etc., should be cleaned up.

vsm1.4:20.9.verse: These are the details for the clause, “Then he should sever the lesser impediments.”

vsm1.4:21.1.verse: Now, with the clause, And not overlook any of the directions for development (III.28),

vsm1.4:21.2.verse: the time has come for the detailed exposition of all meditation subjects, starting with the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.4:22.1.verse: [123] When a bhikkhu has thus severed the lesser impediments,

vsm1.4:22.2.verse: then, on his return from his alms round after his meal

vsm1.4:22.3.verse: and after he has got rid of drowsiness due to the meal,

vsm1.4:22.4.verse: he should sit down comfortably in a secluded place

vsm1.4:22.5.verse: and apprehend the sign in earth that is either made up or not made up.

vsm1.4:22.7.verse: “One who is learning the earth kasiṇa apprehends the sign in earth that is either made up or not made up;

vsm1.4:22.10.verse: with a periphery, not without a periphery;

vsm1.4:22.12.verse: either the size of a bushel (suppa) or the size of a saucer (sarāva).

vsm1.4:22.13.verse: He sees to it that that sign is well apprehended, well attended to, well defined.

vsm1.4:22.16.verse: and perceiving it as a treasure,

vsm1.4:22.19.verse: he anchors his mind to that object,

vsm1.4:22.20.verse: thinking, ‘Surely in this way I shall be freed from aging and death.’

vsm1.4:22.21.verse: Secluded from sense desires … he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna …”

vsm1.4:23.1.verse: Herein, when in a previous becoming a man has gone forth into homelessness in the Dispensation or [outside it] with the rishis’ going forth

vsm1.4:23.2.verse: and has already produced the jhāna tetrad or pentad on the earth kasiṇa,

vsm1.4:23.3.verse: and so has such merit and the support [of past practice of jhāna] as well,

vsm1.4:23.4.verse: then the sign arises in him on earth that is not made up, that is to say, on a ploughed area or on a threshing floor,

vsm1.4:23.5.verse: as in the Elder Mallaka’s case.

vsm1.4:23.6.verse: It seems that while that venerable one was looking at a ploughed area the sign arose in him the size of that area.

vsm1.4:23.7.verse: He extended it and attained the jhāna pentad.

vsm1.4:23.8.verse: Then by establishing insight with the jhāna as the basis for it,

vsm1.4:24.1.verse: But when a man has had no such previous practice,

vsm1.4:24.2.verse: he should make a kasiṇa, guarding against the four faults of a kasiṇa and not overlooking any of the directions for the meditation subject learnt from the teacher.

vsm1.4:24.3.verse: Now, the four faults of the earth kasiṇa are due to the intrusion of blue, yellow, red or white.

vsm1.4:24.4.verse: So instead of using clay of such colours,

vsm1.4:24.5.verse: he should make the kasiṇa of clay like that in the stream of the Gangā,[^5] which is the colour of the dawn.

vsm1.4:24.6.verse: [124] And he should make it not in the middle of the monastery in a place where novices, etc., are about

vsm1.4:24.7.verse: but on the confines of the monastery in a screened place, either under an overhanging rock or in a leaf hut.

vsm1.4:24.8.verse: He can make it either portable or as a fixture.

vsm1.4:25.1.verse: Of these, a portable one should be made by tying rags of leather or matting onto four sticks

vsm1.4:25.2.verse: and smearing thereon a disk of the size already mentioned, using clay picked clean of grass, roots, gravel, and sand, and well kneaded.

vsm1.4:25.3.verse: At the time of the preliminary work it should be laid on the ground and looked at.

vsm1.4:25.4.verse: A fixture should be made by knocking stakes into the ground in the form of a lotus calyx, lacing them over with creepers.

vsm1.4:25.6.verse: then other clay should be put underneath

vsm1.4:25.7.verse: and a disk a span and four fingers across made on top of that with the quite pure dawn-coloured clay.

vsm1.4:25.8.verse: For it was with reference only to measurement that it was said above either the size of a bushel or the size of a saucer (§22).

vsm1.4:25.9.verse: But that is bounded, not unbounded was said to show its delimitedness.

vsm1.4:26.1.verse: So, having thus made it delimited and of the size prescribed,

vsm1.4:26.2.verse: he should scrape it down with a stone trowel—a wooden trowel turns it a bad colour, so that should not be employed—

vsm1.4:26.3.verse: and make it as even as the surface of a drum.

vsm1.4:26.4.verse: Then he should sweep the place out and have a bath.

vsm1.4:26.5.verse: On his return he should seat himself on a well-covered chair with legs a span and four fingers high, prepared in a place that is two and a half cubits [that is, two and a half times elbow to finger-tip] from the kasiṇa disk.

vsm1.4:26.6.verse: For the kasiṇa does not appear plainly to him if he sits further off than that;

vsm1.4:26.7.verse: and if he sits nearer than that, faults in the kasiṇa appear.

vsm1.4:26.8.verse: If he sits higher up, he has to look at it with his neck bent; and if he sits lower down, his knees ache.

vsm1.4:27.1.verse: So, after seating himself in the way stated,

vsm1.4:27.2.verse: he should review the dangers in sense desires in the way beginning, “Sense desires give little enjoyment” (M I 91)

vsm1.4:27.3.verse: and arouse longing for the escape from sense desires, for the renunciation that is the means to the surmounting of all suffering.

vsm1.4:27.4.verse: He should next arouse joy of happiness by recollecting the special qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha;

vsm1.4:27.5.verse: then awe by thinking, “Now, this is the way of renunciation entered upon by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples”;

vsm1.4:27.6.verse: and then eagerness by thinking, “In this way I shall surely come to know the taste of the bliss of seclusion.”

vsm1.4:27.7.verse: [125] After that he should open his eyes moderately, apprehend the sign, and so proceed to develop it.[^6]

vsm1.4:28.1.verse: If he opens his eyes too wide, they get fatigued

vsm1.4:28.2.verse: and the disk becomes too obvious,

vsm1.4:28.3.verse: which prevents the sign becoming apparent to him.

vsm1.4:28.4.verse: If he opens them too little, the disk is not obvious enough,

vsm1.4:28.6.verse: which also prevents the sign becoming apparent to him.

vsm1.4:28.7.verse: So he should develop it by apprehending the sign (nimitta), keeping his eyes open moderately, as if he were seeing the reflection of his face (mukha-nimitta) on the surface of a looking-glass.[^7]

vsm1.4:29.1.verse: The colour should not be reviewed.

vsm1.4:29.2.verse: The characteristic should not be given attention.[^8]

vsm1.4:29.3.verse: But rather, while not ignoring the colour,

vsm1.4:29.4.verse: attention should be given by setting the mind on the [name] concept as the most outstanding mental datum, relegating the colour to the position of a property of its physical support.

vsm1.4:29.5.verse: That [conceptual state] can be called by anyone he likes among the names for earth (pathavī) such as “earth” (pathavī), “the Great One” (mahī), “the Friendly One” (medinī),

vsm1.4:29.6.verse: “ground” (bhūmi), “the Provider of Wealth” (vasudhā), “the Bearer of Wealth” (vasudharā), etc.,

vsm1.4:29.7.verse: whichever suits his manner of perception.

vsm1.4:29.8.verse: Still “earth” is also a name that is obvious, so it can be developed with the obvious one by saying “earth, earth.”

vsm1.4:29.9.verse: It should be adverted to now with eyes open, now with eyes shut.

vsm1.4:29.10.verse: And he should go on developing it in this way a hundred times, a thousand times, and even more than that, until the learning sign arises.

vsm1.4:30.1.verse: When, while he is developing it in this way,

vsm1.4:30.2.verse: it comes into focus[^9] as he adverts with his eyes shut exactly as it does with his eyes open,

vsm1.4:30.3.verse: then the learning sign is said to have been produced.

vsm1.4:30.4.verse: After its production he should no longer sit in that place;[^10]

vsm1.4:30.5.verse: he should return to his own quarters and go on developing it sitting there.

vsm1.4:30.6.verse: But in order to avoid the delay of foot washing, a pair of single-soled sandals and a walking stick are desirable.

vsm1.4:30.7.verse: Then if the new concentration vanishes through some unsuitable encounter,

vsm1.4:30.8.verse: he can put his sandals on, take his walking stick,

vsm1.4:30.9.verse: and go back to the place to re-apprehend the sign there.

vsm1.4:30.10.verse: When he returns he should seat himself comfortably

vsm1.4:30.11.verse: and develop it by reiterated reaction to it and by striking at it with thought and applied thought.

vsm1.4:31.1.verse: As he does so, the hindrances eventually become suppressed,

vsm1.4:31.3.verse: the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration,

vsm1.4:31.5.verse: The difference between the earlier learning sign and the counterpart sign is this.

vsm1.4:31.6.verse: In the learning sign any fault in the kasiṇa is apparent.

vsm1.4:31.7.verse: But the counterpart sign [126] appears as if breaking out from the learning sign, and a hundred times, a thousand times more purified, like a looking-glass disk drawn from its case, like a mother-of-pearl dish well washed, like the moon’s disk coming out from behind a cloud, like cranes against a thunder cloud.

vsm1.4:31.8.verse: But it has neither colour nor shape;

vsm1.4:31.10.verse: it would be cognizable by the eye, gross, susceptible of comprehension [by insight—(see XX.2f.)] and stamped with the three characteristics.[^11]

vsm1.4:31.11.verse: But it is not like that.

vsm1.4:31.12.verse: For it is born only of perception in one who has obtained concentration, being a mere mode of appearance.[^12]

vsm1.4:31.13.verse: But as soon as it arises the hindrances are quite suppressed,

vsm1.4:31.15.verse: and the mind becomes concentrated in access concentration.

vsm1.4:32.1.verse: Now, concentration is of two kinds, that is to say, access concentration and absorption concentration:

vsm1.4:32.2.verse: the mind becomes concentrated in two ways, that is, on the plane of access and on the plane of obtainment.

vsm1.4:32.3.verse: Herein, the mind becomes concentrated on the plane of access by the abandonment of the hindrances,

vsm1.4:32.4.verse: and on the plane of obtainment by the manifestation of the jhāna factors.

vsm1.4:33.1.verse: The difference between the two kinds of concentration is this.

vsm1.4:33.2.verse: The factors are not strong in access.

vsm1.4:33.3.verse: It is because they are not strong that when access has arisen, the mind now makes the sign its object and now re-enters the life-continuum,[^13] just as when a young child is lifted up and stood on its feet, it repeatedly falls down on the ground.

vsm1.4:33.4.verse: But the factors are strong in absorption.

vsm1.4:33.5.verse: It is because they are strong that when absorption concentration has arisen, the mind, having once interrupted the flow of the life-continuum, carries on with a stream of profitable impulsion for a whole night and for a whole day, just as a healthy man, after rising from his seat, could stand for a whole day.

vsm1.4:34.1.verse: The arousing of the counterpart sign, which arises together with access concentration, is very difficult.

vsm1.4:34.2.verse: Therefore if he is able to arrive at absorption in that same session by extending the sign, it is good.

vsm1.4:34.3.verse: If not, then he must guard the sign diligently as if it were the foetus of a Wheel-turning Monarch (World-ruler).

vsm1.4:34.4.verse:
So guard the sign, nor count the cost,
And what is gained will not be lost;

vsm1.4:34.5.verse:
Who fails to have this guard maintained
Will lose each time what he has gained. [127]

vsm1.4:35.1.verse: Herein, the way of guarding it is this:

vsm1.4:35.2.verse:
(1) Abode, (2) resort, (3) and speech, (4) and person,
(5) The food, (6) the climate, (7) and the posture—

vsm1.4:35.3.verse:
Eschew these seven different kinds
Whenever found unsuitable.

vsm1.4:35.4.verse:
But cultivate the suitable;
For one perchance so doing finds
He need not wait too long until
Absorption shall his wish fulfil.

vsm1.4:36.1.verse: Herein, an abode is unsuitable if, while he lives in it,

vsm1.4:36.2.verse: the unarisen sign does not arise in him

vsm1.4:36.3.verse: or is lost when it arises,

vsm1.4:36.4.verse: and where unestablished mindfulness fails to become established

vsm1.4:36.5.verse: and the unconcentrated mind fails to become concentrated.

vsm1.4:36.6.verse: That is suitable in which the sign arises and becomes confirmed,

vsm1.4:36.9.verse: as in the Elder Padhāniya-Tissa, resident at Nāgapabbata.

vsm1.4:36.10.verse: So if a monastery has many abodes he can try them one by one,

vsm1.4:36.11.verse: living in each for three days,

vsm1.4:36.12.verse: and stay on where his mind becomes unified.

vsm1.4:36.13.verse: For it was due to suitability of abode that

vsm1.4:36.14.verse: five hundred bhikkhus reached Arahantship while still dwelling in the Lesser Nāga Cave (Cūḷa-nāga-leṇa) in Tambapaṇṇi Island (Sri Lanka) after apprehending their meditation subject there.

vsm1.4:36.15.verse: There is no counting the stream-enterers who have reached Arahantship there after reaching the noble plane elsewhere;

vsm1.4:36.16.verse: so too in the monastery of Cittalapabbata, and others.

vsm1.4:37.1.verse: An alms-resort village lying to the north or south of the lodging,

vsm1.4:37.2.verse: not too far, within one kosa and a half,

vsm1.4:37.3.verse: and where alms food is easily obtained, is suitable.

vsm1.4:38.1.verse: Speech: that included in the thirty-two kinds of aimless talk is unsuitable; for it leads to the disappearance of the sign.

vsm1.4:38.2.verse: But talk based on the ten examples of talk is suitable, though even that should be discussed with moderation.[^15]

vsm1.4:39.1.verse: Person: one not given to aimless talk, who has the special qualities of virtue, etc.,

vsm1.4:39.2.verse: by acquaintanceship with whom the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated,

vsm1.4:39.3.verse: or the concentrated mind becomes more so,

vsm1.4:39.5.verse: One who is much concerned with his body,[^16] who is addicted to aimless talk, is unsuitable;

vsm1.4:39.6.verse: for he only creates disturbances, like muddy water added to clear water.

vsm1.4:39.7.verse: And it was owing to one such as this that

vsm1.4:39.8.verse: the attainments of the young bhikkhu who lived at Koṭapabbata vanished,

vsm1.4:40.1.verse: Food: Sweet food suits one, sour food another.

vsm1.4:40.2.verse: Climate: a cool climate suits one, a warm one another.

vsm1.4:40.3.verse: So when he finds that by using certain food or by living in a certain climate he is comfortable,

vsm1.4:40.4.verse: or his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated,

vsm1.4:40.5.verse: or his concentrated mind becomes more so,

vsm1.4:40.6.verse: then that food or that climate is suitable.

vsm1.4:40.7.verse: Any other food or climate is unsuitable.

vsm1.4:41.1.verse: Postures: walking suits one; standing or sitting or lying down suits another.

vsm1.4:41.2.verse: So he should try them, like the abode, for three days each,

vsm1.4:41.3.verse: and that posture is suitable in which his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated

vsm1.4:41.4.verse: or his concentrated mind becomes more so.

vsm1.4:41.5.verse: Any other should be understood as unsuitable.

vsm1.4:41.6.verse: So he should avoid the seven unsuitable kinds and cultivate the suitable.

vsm1.4:41.7.verse: For when he practices in this way,

vsm1.4:41.9.verse: then, “he need not wait too long until absorption shall his wish fulfil.”

vsm1.4:42.0.verse: [The Ten Kinds of Skill in Absorption]

vsm1.4:42.1.verse: However, if this does not happen while he is practicing in this way,

vsm1.4:42.2.verse: then he should have recourse to the ten kinds of skill in absorption.

vsm1.4:42.4.verse: Skill in absorption needs [to be dealt with in] ten aspects:

vsm1.4:42.8.verse: (4) he exerts the mind on an occasion when it should be exerted,

vsm1.4:42.9.verse: (5) he restrains the mind on an occasion when it should be restrained,

vsm1.4:42.10.verse: (6) he encourages the mind on an occasion when it should be encouraged,

vsm1.4:42.11.verse: (7) he looks on at the mind with equanimity when it should be looked on at with equanimity,

vsm1.4:42.12.verse: (8) avoidance of unconcentrated persons, (9) cultivation of concentrated persons, (10) resoluteness upon that (concentration).

vsm1.4:43.1.verse: Herein, making the basis clean is cleansing the internal and the external basis.

vsm1.4:43.2.verse: For when his head hair, nails and body hair are long,

vsm1.4:43.3.verse: or when the body is soaked with sweat,

vsm1.4:43.4.verse: then the internal basis is unclean and unpurified.

vsm1.4:43.5.verse: But when an old dirty smelly robe is worn or when the lodging is dirty, then the external basis is unclean and unpurified.

vsm1.4:43.6.verse: [129] When the internal and external bases are unclean,

vsm1.4:43.7.verse: then the knowledge in the consciousness and consciousness-concomitants that arise is unpurified,

vsm1.4:43.8.verse: like the light of a lamp’s flame that arises with an unpurified lamp-bowl, wick and oil as its support;

vsm1.4:43.9.verse: formations do not become evident to one who tries to comprehend them with unpurified knowledge,

vsm1.4:43.10.verse: and when he devotes himself to his meditation subject,

vsm1.4:43.11.verse: it does not come to growth, increase and fulfilment.

vsm1.4:44.1.verse: But when the internal and external bases are clean,

vsm1.4:44.2.verse: then the knowledge in the consciousness and consciousness-concomitants that arise is clean and purified,

vsm1.4:44.3.verse: like the light of a lamp’s flame that arises with a purified lamp bowl, wick and oil as its support;

vsm1.4:44.4.verse: formations become evident to one who tries to comprehend them with purified knowledge,

vsm1.4:44.5.verse: and as he devotes himself to his meditation subject,

vsm1.4:44.6.verse: it comes to growth, increase and fulfilment.

vsm1.4:45.1.verse: Maintaining balanced faculties is equalizing the [five] faculties of faith and the rest.

vsm1.4:45.2.verse: For if his faith faculty is strong and the others weak,

vsm1.4:45.3.verse: then the energy faculty cannot perform its function of exerting,

vsm1.4:45.4.verse: the mindfulness faculty its function of establishing,

vsm1.4:45.5.verse: the concentration faculty its function of not distracting,

vsm1.4:45.6.verse: and the understanding faculty its function of seeing.

vsm1.4:45.7.verse: So in that case the faith faculty should be modified either by reviewing the individual essences of the states [concerned, that is, the objects of attention]

vsm1.4:45.8.verse: or by not giving [them] attention in the way in which the faith faculty became too strong.

vsm1.4:45.9.verse: And this is illustrated by the story of the Elder Vakkali (S III 119).

vsm1.4:46.1.verse: Then if the energy faculty is too strong,

vsm1.4:46.2.verse: the faith faculty cannot perform its function of resolving,

vsm1.4:46.3.verse: nor can the rest of the faculties perform their several functions.

vsm1.4:46.4.verse: So in that case the energy faculty should be modified by developing tranquillity, and so on.

vsm1.4:46.5.verse: And this should be illustrated by the story of the Elder Soṇa (Vin I 179–85; A III 374–76).

vsm1.4:46.6.verse: So too with the rest; for it should be understood that when anyone of them is too strong

vsm1.4:46.7.verse: the others cannot perform their several functions.

vsm1.4:47.1.verse: However, what is particularly recommended is balancing faith with understanding, and concentration with energy.

vsm1.4:47.2.verse: For one strong in faith and weak in understanding has confidence uncritically and groundlessly.

vsm1.4:47.3.verse: One strong in understanding and weak in faith

vsm1.4:47.4.verse: errs on the side of cunning

vsm1.4:47.5.verse: and is as hard to cure as one sick of a disease caused by medicine.

vsm1.4:47.6.verse: With the balancing of the two a man has confidence only when there are grounds for it.

vsm1.4:47.7.verse: Then idleness overpowers one strong in concentration and weak in energy, since concentration favours idleness.

vsm1.4:47.8.verse: [130] Agitation overpowers one strong in energy and weak in concentration, since energy favours agitation.

vsm1.4:47.9.verse: But concentration coupled with energy cannot lapse into idleness,

vsm1.4:47.10.verse: and energy coupled with concentration cannot lapse into agitation.

vsm1.4:47.11.verse: So these two should be balanced;

vsm1.4:47.12.verse: for absorption comes with the balancing of the two.

vsm1.4:48.1.verse: Again, [concentration and faith should be balanced]. One working on concentration needs strong faith,

vsm1.4:48.2.verse: since it is with such faith and confidence that he reaches absorption.

vsm1.4:48.3.verse: Then there is [balancing of] concentration and understanding. One working on concentration needs strong unification,

vsm1.4:48.4.verse: since that is how he reaches absorption;

vsm1.4:48.5.verse: and one working on insight needs strong understanding,

vsm1.4:48.6.verse: since that is how he reaches penetration of characteristics;

vsm1.4:48.7.verse: but with the balancing of the two he reaches absorption as well.

vsm1.4:49.1.verse: Strong mindfulness, however, is needed in all instances;

vsm1.4:49.2.verse: for mindfulness protects the mind from lapsing into agitation through faith, energy and understanding, which favour agitation,

vsm1.4:49.3.verse: and from lapsing into idleness through concentration, which favours idleness.

vsm1.4:49.4.verse: So it is as desirable in all instances as a seasoning of salt in all sauces, as a prime minister in all the king’s business.

vsm1.4:49.5.verse: Hence it is said [in the commentaries (D-a 788, M-a I 292, etc)]:

vsm1.4:49.6.verse: “And mindfulness has been called universal by the Blessed One.

vsm1.4:49.8.verse: Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge,

vsm1.4:49.9.verse: and mindfulness is manifested as protection,

vsm1.4:49.10.verse: and there is no exertion and restraint of the mind without mindfulness.”

vsm1.4:50.1.verse: Skill in the sign is skill in producing the as yet unproduced sign of unification of mind through the earth kasiṇa, etc.;

vsm1.4:50.2.verse: and it is skill in developing [the sign] when produced,

vsm1.4:50.3.verse: and skill in protecting [the sign] when obtained by development.

vsm1.4:50.4.verse: The last is what is intended here.

vsm1.4:51.1.verse: How does he exert the mind on an occasion when it should be exerted?

vsm1.4:51.2.verse: When his mind is slack with over-laxness of energy, etc.,

vsm1.4:51.3.verse: then, instead of developing the three enlightenment factors beginning with tranquillity,

vsm1.4:51.4.verse: he should develop those beginning with investigation-of-states.

vsm1.4:51.5.verse: For this is said by the Blessed One:

vsm1.4:51.6.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man wanted to make a small fire burn up,

vsm1.4:51.7.verse: and he put wet grass on it,

vsm1.4:51.12.verse: would that man be able to make the small fire burn up?” [131]

vsm1.4:51.14.verse: —“So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is slack,

vsm1.4:51.15.verse: that is not the time to develop the tranquillity enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:51.18.verse: Why is that? Because a slack mind cannot well be roused by those states.

vsm1.4:51.20.verse: that is the time to develop the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:51.23.verse: Why is that? Because a slack mind can well be roused by those states.”

vsm1.4:51.24.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man wanted to make a small fire burn up,

vsm1.4:51.25.verse: and he put dry grass on it,

vsm1.4:51.28.verse: blew on it with his mouth,

vsm1.4:51.29.verse: and did not scatter dust on it,

vsm1.4:51.30.verse: would that man be able to make that small fire burn up?”

vsm1.4:52.1.verse: And here the development of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, etc., should be understood as the nutriment for each one respectively,

vsm1.4:52.3.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are profitable and unprofitable states,

vsm1.4:52.6.verse: dark and bright states the counterpart of each other.

vsm1.4:52.8.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:52.9.verse: or leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor.”

vsm1.4:52.10.verse: Likewise: “Bhikkhus there is the element of initiative, the element of launching, and the element of persistence.

vsm1.4:52.12.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen energy enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:52.13.verse: or leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen energy enlightenment factors.”

vsm1.4:52.14.verse: Likewise: “Bhikkhus, there are states productive of the happiness enlightenment factor.

vsm1.4:52.16.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen happiness enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:52.17.verse: or leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen happiness enlightenment factor” (S V 104). [132]

vsm1.4:53.1.verse: Herein, wise attention given to the profitable, etc., is attention occurring in penetration of individual essences and of [the three] general characteristics.

vsm1.4:53.2.verse: Wise attention given to the element of initiative, etc., is attention occurring in the arousing of the element of initiative, and so on.

vsm1.4:53.3.verse: Herein, initial energy is called the element of initiative.

vsm1.4:53.4.verse: The element of launching is stronger than that because it launches out from idleness.

vsm1.4:53.5.verse: The element of persistence is still stronger than that because it goes on persisting in successive later stages.

vsm1.4:53.6.verse: States productive of the happiness enlightenment factor is a name for happiness itself;

vsm1.4:53.7.verse: and attention that arouses that is wise attention.

vsm1.4:54.1.verse: There are, besides, seven things that lead to the arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:54.7.verse: (vi) reviewing the field for the exercise of profound knowledge,

vsm1.4:55.1.verse: Eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:55.2.verse: (i) reviewing the fearfulness of the states of loss such as the hell realms, etc.,

vsm1.4:55.3.verse: (ii) seeing benefit in obtaining the mundane and supramundane distinctions dependent on energy,

vsm1.4:55.4.verse: (iii) reviewing the course of the journey [to be travelled] thus: “The path taken by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the great disciples has to be taken by me, and it cannot be taken by an idler,”

vsm1.4:55.5.verse: (iv) being a credit to the alms food by producing great fruit for the givers,

vsm1.4:55.6.verse: (v) reviewing the greatness of the Master thus: “My Master praises the energetic, and this unsurpassable Dispensation that is so helpful to us is honoured in the practice, not otherwise,”

vsm1.4:55.7.verse: (vi) reviewing the greatness of the heritage thus: “It is the great heritage called the Good Dhamma that is to be acquired by me, and it cannot be acquired by an idler,”

vsm1.4:55.8.verse: (vii) removing stiffness and torpor by attention to perception of light, change of postures, frequenting the open air, etc.,

vsm1.4:56.1.verse: Eleven things lead to the arising of the happiness enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:56.2.verse: the recollections (i) of the Buddha, (ii) of the Dhamma, (iii) of the Sangha, (iv) of virtue, (v) of generosity, and (vi) of deities,

vsm1.4:56.6.verse: (x) reviewing encouraging discourses, (xi) resoluteness upon that [happiness].

vsm1.4:56.7.verse: So by arousing these things in these ways he develops the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, and the others.

vsm1.4:56.8.verse: This is how he exerts the mind on an occasion when it should be exerted.

vsm1.4:57.1.verse: How does he restrain the mind on an occasion when it should be restrained?

vsm1.4:57.2.verse: When his mind is agitated through over-energeticness, etc.,

vsm1.4:57.3.verse: then, instead of developing the three enlightenment factors beginning with investigation-of-states,

vsm1.4:57.4.verse: he should develop those beginning with tranquillity;

vsm1.4:57.5.verse: for this is said by the Blessed One:

vsm1.4:57.6.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire,

vsm1.4:57.7.verse: and he put dry grass on it …

vsm1.4:57.8.verse: and did not scatter dust on it,

vsm1.4:57.9.verse: would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?”

vsm1.4:57.11.verse: —“So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is agitated,

vsm1.4:57.12.verse: that is not the time to develop the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:57.15.verse: Why is that? Because an agitated mind cannot well be quieted by those states.

vsm1.4:57.17.verse: that is the time to develop the tranquillity enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:57.20.verse: Why is that? Because an agitated mind can well be quieted by those states.”

vsm1.4:57.21.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire,

vsm1.4:57.22.verse: and he put wet grass on it …

vsm1.4:57.24.verse: would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?”

vsm1.4:58.1.verse: And here the development of the tranquillity enlightenment factor, etc., should be understood as the nutriment for each one respectively,

vsm1.4:58.3.verse: “Bhikkhus, there is bodily tranquillity and mental tranquillity. [134]

vsm1.4:58.5.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquillity enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:58.6.verse: or leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen tranquillity enlightenment factor.”

vsm1.4:58.7.verse: Likewise: “Bhikkhus, there is the sign of serenity, the sign of non-diversion.

vsm1.4:58.9.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen concentration enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:58.10.verse: or it leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen concentration enlightenment factor.”

vsm1.4:58.11.verse: Likewise: “Bhikkhus, there are states productive of the equanimity enlightenment factor.

vsm1.4:58.13.verse: is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor,

vsm1.4:58.14.verse: or it leads to the growth, fulfilment, development and perfection of the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor” (S V 104).

vsm1.4:59.1.verse: Herein wise attention given to the three instances is attention occurring in arousing tranquillity, etc., by observing the way in which they arose in him earlier.

vsm1.4:59.2.verse: The sign of serenity is a term for serenity itself,

vsm1.4:59.3.verse: and non-diversion is a term for that too in the sense of non-distraction.

vsm1.4:60.1.verse: There are, besides, seven things that lead to the arising of the tranquillity enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:60.7.verse: (vi) cultivation of persons tranquil in body,

vsm1.4:61.1.verse: Eleven things lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:61.7.verse: (vi) encouraging the listless mind by means of faith and a sense of urgency,

vsm1.4:61.8.verse: (vii) looking on with equanimity at what is occurring rightly,

vsm1.4:61.11.verse: (x) reviewing of the jhānas and liberations,

vsm1.4:62.1.verse: Five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor:

vsm1.4:62.2.verse: (i) maintenance of neutrality towards living beings;

vsm1.4:62.3.verse: (ii) maintenance of neutrality towards formations (inanimate things);

vsm1.4:62.4.verse: (iii) avoidance of persons who show favouritism towards beings and formations;

vsm1.4:62.5.verse: (iv) cultivation of persons who maintain neutrality towards beings and formations; (v) resoluteness upon that [equanimity].

vsm1.4:62.6.verse: [135] So by arousing these things in these ways he develops the tranquillity enlightenment factor, as well as the others.

vsm1.4:62.7.verse: This is how he restrains the mind on an occasion when it should be restrained.

vsm1.4:63.1.verse: How does he encourage the mind on an occasion when it should be encouraged?

vsm1.4:63.2.verse: When his mind is listless owing to sluggishness in the exercise of understanding or to failure to attain the bliss of peace,

vsm1.4:63.3.verse: then he should stimulate it by reviewing the eight grounds for a sense of urgency.

vsm1.4:63.4.verse: These are the four, namely, birth, aging, sickness, and death,

vsm1.4:63.5.verse: with the suffering of the states of loss as the fifth,

vsm1.4:63.6.verse: and also the suffering in the past rooted in the round [of rebirths],

vsm1.4:63.7.verse: the suffering in the future rooted in the round [of rebirths],

vsm1.4:63.8.verse: and the suffering in the present rooted in the search for nutriment.

vsm1.4:63.9.verse: And he creates confidence by recollecting the special qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.

vsm1.4:63.10.verse: This is how he encourages the mind on an occasion when it should be encouraged.

vsm1.4:64.1.verse: How does he look on at the mind with equanimity on an occasion when it should be looked on at with equanimity?

vsm1.4:64.2.verse: When he is practicing in this way and his mind follows the road of serenity, occurs evenly on the object, and is unidle, unagitated and not listless,

vsm1.4:64.3.verse: then he is not interested to exert or restrain or encourage it;

vsm1.4:64.4.verse: he is like a charioteer when the horses are progressing evenly.

vsm1.4:64.5.verse: This is how he looks on at the mind with equanimity on an occasion when it should be looked on at with equanimity.

vsm1.4:65.1.verse: Avoidance of unconcentrated persons is keeping far away from persons

vsm1.4:65.2.verse: who have never trodden the way of renunciation,

vsm1.4:65.3.verse: who are busy with many affairs,

vsm1.4:65.5.verse: Cultivation of concentrated persons is approaching periodically

vsm1.4:65.6.verse: persons who have trodden the way of renunciation and obtained concentration.

vsm1.4:65.7.verse: Resoluteness upon that is the state of being resolute upon concentration;

vsm1.4:65.8.verse: the meaning is, giving concentration importance, tending, leaning and inclining to concentration.

vsm1.4:65.9.verse: This is how the tenfold skill in concentration should be undertaken.

vsm1.4:66.1.verse:
Any man who acquires this sign,
This tenfold skill will need to heed
In order for absorption to gain
Thus achieving his bolder goal.

vsm1.4:66.2.verse:
But if in spite of his efforts
No result comes that might requite
His work, still a wise wight persists,
Never this task relinquishing, [136]

vsm1.4:66.3.verse:
Since a tiro, if he gives up,
Thinking not to continue in
The task, never gains distinction
Here no matter how small at all.

vsm1.4:66.4.verse:
A man wise in temperament[^17]
Notices how his mind inclines:
Energy and serenity
Always he couples each to each.

vsm1.4:66.5.verse:
Now, his mind, seeing that it holds back,
He prods, now the restraining rein
Tightening, seeing it pull too hard;
Guiding with even pace the race.

vsm1.4:66.6.verse:
Well-controlled bees get the pollen;
Well-balanced efforts meet to treat
Leaves, thread, and ships, and oil-tubes too,
Gain thus, not otherwise, the prize.

vsm1.4:66.7.verse:
Let him set aside this lax
Also this agitated state,
Steering here his mind at the sign
As the bee and the rest suggest.

vsm1.4:67.1.verse: Here is the explanation of the meaning.

vsm1.4:67.2.verse: When a too clever bee learns that a flower on a tree is blooming,

vsm1.4:67.5.verse: and arrives when the pollen is finished;

vsm1.4:67.6.verse: and another, not clever enough bee, who sets out with too slow a speed, arrives when the pollen is finished too;

vsm1.4:67.7.verse: but a clever bee sets out with balanced speed,

vsm1.4:67.8.verse: arrives with ease at the cluster of flowers,

vsm1.4:67.9.verse: takes as much pollen as it pleases

vsm1.4:68.1.verse: Again, when a surgeon’s pupils are being trained in the use of the scalpel on a lotus leaf in a dish of water,

vsm1.4:68.2.verse: one who is too clever applies the scalpel hurriedly

vsm1.4:68.3.verse: and either cuts the lotus leaf in two

vsm1.4:68.4.verse: or pushes it under the water,

vsm1.4:68.5.verse: and another who is not clever enough

vsm1.4:68.6.verse: does not even dare to touch it with the scalpel for fear of cutting it in two or pushing it under;

vsm1.4:68.7.verse: but one who is clever shows the scalpel stroke on it by means of a balanced effort,

vsm1.4:68.8.verse: and being good at his craft

vsm1.4:68.9.verse: he is rewarded on such occasions.

vsm1.4:69.1.verse: Again when the king announces, “Anyone who can draw out a spider’s thread four fathoms long shall receive four thousand,”

vsm1.4:69.2.verse: one man who is too clever breaks the spider’s thread here and there by pulling it hurriedly,

vsm1.4:69.3.verse: and another who is not clever enough does not dare to touch it with his hand for fear of breaking it,

vsm1.4:69.4.verse: but a clever man pulls it out starting from the end with a balanced effort, winds it on a stick, and so wins the prize.

vsm1.4:70.1.verse: Again, a too clever [137] skipper hoists full sails in a high wind and sends his ship adrift,

vsm1.4:70.2.verse: and another, not clever enough skipper, lowers his sails in a light wind and remains where he is,

vsm1.4:70.3.verse: but a clever skipper hoists full sails in a light wind,

vsm1.4:70.4.verse: takes in half his sails in a high wind,

vsm1.4:70.5.verse: and so arrives safely at his desired destination.

vsm1.4:71.1.verse: Again, when a teacher says, “Anyone who fills the oil-tube without spilling any oil will win a prize,”

vsm1.4:71.2.verse: one who is too clever fills it hurriedly out of greed for the prize, and he spills the oil,

vsm1.4:71.3.verse: and another who is not clever enough does not dare to pour the oil at all for fear of spilling it,

vsm1.4:71.4.verse: but one who is clever fills it with a balanced effort and wins the prize.

vsm1.4:72.1.verse: Just as in these five similes, so too when the sign arises,

vsm1.4:72.2.verse: one bhikkhu forces his energy, thinking “I shall soon reach absorption.”

vsm1.4:72.3.verse: Then his mind lapses into agitation because of his mind’s over-exerted energy and he is prevented from reaching absorption.

vsm1.4:72.4.verse: Another who sees the defect in over-exertion slacks off his energy, thinking, “What is absorption to me now?”

vsm1.4:72.5.verse: Then his mind lapses into idleness because of his mind’s too lax energy and he too is prevented from reaching absorption.

vsm1.4:72.6.verse: Yet another who frees his mind from idleness even when it is only slightly idle

vsm1.4:72.7.verse: and from agitation when only slightly agitated,

vsm1.4:72.8.verse: confronting the sign with balanced effort,

vsm1.4:72.10.verse: One should be like the last-named.

vsm1.4:73.1.verse: It was with reference to this meaning that it was said above:

vsm1.4:73.2.verse:
“Well-controlled bees get the pollen;
Well-balanced efforts meet to treat
Leaves, thread, and ships, and oil-tubes too,
Gain thus, not otherwise, the prize.

vsm1.4:73.3.verse:
Let him set aside then this lax
Also this agitated state,
Steering here his mind at the sign
As the bee and the rest suggest”.

vsm1.4:74.1.verse: So, while he is guiding his mind in this way, confronting the sign,

vsm1.4:74.3.verse: there arises in him mind-door adverting with that same earth kasiṇa as its object, interrupting the [occurrence of consciousness as] life-continuum, and evoked by the constant repeating of “earth, earth.”

vsm1.4:74.4.verse: After that, either four or five impulsions impel on that same object, the last one of which is an impulsion of the fine-material sphere.

vsm1.4:74.5.verse: The rest are of the sense sphere, but they have stronger applied thought, sustained thought, happiness, bliss, and unification of mind than the normal ones.

vsm1.4:74.6.verse: They are called “preliminary work” [consciousnesses] because they are the preliminary work for absorption; and they are also called “access” [consciousnesses] because of their nearness to absorption because they happen in its neighbourhood, just as the words “village access” and “city access” are used for a place near to a village, etc.; and they are also called “conformity” [consciousnesses] because they conform to those that precede the “preliminary work” [consciousnesses] and to the absorption that follows.

vsm1.4:74.7.verse: And the last of these is also called “change-of-lineage” because it transcends the limited [sense-sphere] lineage

vsm1.4:74.8.verse: and brings into being the exalted [fine-material-sphere] lineage.

vsm1.4:75.1.verse: But omitting repetitions, then either the first is the “preliminary work,”

vsm1.4:75.8.verse: Then either the fourth [in the latter case] or the fifth [in the former case] is the absorption consciousness.

vsm1.4:75.9.verse: For it is only either the fourth or the fifth that fixes in absorption.

vsm1.4:75.10.verse: And that is according as there is swift or sluggish direct-knowledge.

vsm1.4:76.1.verse: But the Abhidhamma scholar, the Elder Godatta, quoted this text: “Preceding profitable states are a condition, as repetition condition, for succeeding profitable states” (Paṭṭh I 5).

vsm1.4:76.2.verse: Adding, “It is owing to the repetition condition that each succeeding state is strong, so there is absorption also in the sixth and seventh.”

vsm1.4:77.1.verse: That is rejected by the commentaries with the remark that it is merely that elder’s opinion,

vsm1.4:77.2.verse: adding that, “It is only either in the fourth or the fifth that there is absorption.

vsm1.4:77.3.verse: Beyond that, impulsion lapses. It is said to do so because of nearness of the life-continuum.”

vsm1.4:77.4.verse: And that has been stated in this way after consideration, so it cannot be rejected.

vsm1.4:77.5.verse: For just as a man who is running towards a precipice and wants to stop cannot do so when he has his foot on the edge but falls over it,

vsm1.4:77.6.verse: so there can be no fixing in absorption in the sixth or the seventh because of the nearness to the life-continuum.

vsm1.4:77.7.verse: That is why it should be understood that there is absorption only in the fourth or the fifth.

vsm1.4:78.1.verse: But that absorption is only of a single conscious moment.

vsm1.4:78.2.verse: For there are seven instances in which the normal extent [of the cognitive series] does not apply.

vsm1.4:78.3.verse: They are in the cases of the first absorption,

vsm1.4:78.7.verse: life-continuum jhāna in the fine-material and immaterial kinds of becoming,

vsm1.4:78.8.verse: the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception as condition for cessation [of perception and feeling],

vsm1.4:78.9.verse: and the fruition attainment in one emerging from cessation.

vsm1.4:78.10.verse: Here the fruition next after the path does not exceed three [consciousnesses in number];

vsm1.4:78.11.verse: the [consciousnesses] of the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception as condition for cessation

vsm1.4:78.13.verse: there is no measure of the [number of consciousnesses in the] life-continuum in the fine-material and immaterial [kinds of becoming].

vsm1.4:78.14.verse: In the remaining instances [the number of consciousnesses is] one only.

vsm1.4:78.15.verse: So absorption is of a single consciousness moment.

vsm1.4:78.16.verse: After that, it lapses into the life-continuum.

vsm1.4:78.17.verse: Then the life-continuum is interrupted by adverting for the purpose of reviewing the jhāna,

vsm1.4:78.18.verse: next to which comes the reviewing of the jhāna.

vsm1.4:79.1.verse: [The First Jhāna] At this point, “Quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things

vsm1.4:79.2.verse: he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought with happiness and bliss born of seclusion” (Vibh 245),

vsm1.4:79.3.verse: and so he has attained the first jhāna, which abandons five factors, possesses five factors,

vsm1.4:79.4.verse: is good in three ways, possesses ten characteristics, and is of the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.4:80.1.verse: Herein, quite secluded from sense desires means having secluded himself from,

vsm1.4:80.3.verse: having gone away from, sense desires.

vsm1.4:80.4.verse: Now, this word quite (eva) should be understood to have the meaning of absoluteness.

vsm1.4:80.5.verse: Precisely because it has the meaning of absoluteness it shows how, on the actual occasion of entering upon and dwelling in the first jhāna,

vsm1.4:80.6.verse: sense desires as well as being non-existent then are the first jhāna’s contrary opposite,

vsm1.4:80.7.verse: and it also shows that the arrival takes place only (eva) through the letting go of sense desires.

vsm1.4:81.1.verse: When absoluteness is introduced thus, “quite secluded from sense desires,” what is expressed is this:

vsm1.4:81.2.verse: sense desires are certainly incompatible with this jhāna; when they exist, it does not occur,

vsm1.4:81.3.verse: just as when there is darkness, there is no lamplight;

vsm1.4:81.4.verse: and it is only by letting go of them that it is reached, just as the further bank is reached only by letting go of the near bank.

vsm1.4:81.5.verse: That is why absoluteness is introduced.

vsm1.4:82.1.verse: Here it might be asked: But why is this [word “quite”] mentioned only in the first phrase and not in the second?

vsm1.4:82.2.verse: How is this, might he enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna even when not secluded from unprofitable things?

vsm1.4:82.3.verse: It should not be regarded in that way.

vsm1.4:82.4.verse: It is mentioned in the first phrase as the escape from them;

vsm1.4:82.5.verse: for this jhāna is the escape from sense desires since it surmounts the sense-desire element and since it is incompatible with greed for sense desires,

vsm1.4:82.6.verse: according as it is said: “The escape from sense desires is this, that is to say, renunciation” (D III 275).

vsm1.4:82.7.verse: But in the second phrase the word eva should be adduced and taken as said, as in the passage, “Bhikkhus, only (eva) here is there an ascetic, here a second ascetic” (M I 63).

vsm1.4:82.8.verse: For it is impossible to enter upon and dwell in jhāna unsecluded also from unprofitable things, in other words, the hindrances other than that [sense desire].

vsm1.4:82.9.verse: So this word must be read in both phrases thus: “Quite secluded from sense desires, quite secluded from unprofitable things.”

vsm1.4:82.10.verse: And although the word “secluded” as a general term

vsm1.4:82.11.verse: includes all kinds of seclusion, that is to say, seclusion by substitution of opposites, etc., and bodily seclusion, etc.,

vsm1.4:82.12.verse: still only the three, namely, bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression (suspension) should be regarded here.

vsm1.4:83.1.verse: But this term “sense desires” should be regarded as including all kinds, that is to say, sense desires as object as given in the Niddesa in the passage beginning, “What are sense desires as object? They are agreeable visible objects …” (Nidd I 1),

vsm1.4:83.2.verse: and the sense desires as defilement given there too and in the Vibhaṅga thus: “Zeal as sense desire (kāma), greed as sense desire, zeal and greed as sense desire, thinking as sense desire, greed as sense desire, thinking and greed as sense desire” (Nidd I 2; Vibh 256).

vsm1.4:83.3.verse: That being so, the words “quite secluded from sense desires” properly mean “quite secluded from sense desires as object,”

vsm1.4:83.5.verse: while the words “secluded from unprofitable things” properly mean “secluded from sense desires as defilement or from all unprofitable things,”

vsm1.4:83.7.verse: And in this case giving up of pleasure in sense desires is indicated by the first since it only expresses seclusion from sense desires as object,

vsm1.4:83.8.verse: while acquisition of pleasure in renunciation is indicated by the second since it expresses seclusion from sense desire as defilement.

vsm1.4:84.1.verse: And with sense desires as object and sense desires as defilement expressed in this way, it should also be recognized that the abandoning of the objective basis for defilement is indicated by the first of these two phrases

vsm1.4:84.2.verse: and the abandoning of the [subjective] defilement by the second;

vsm1.4:84.3.verse: also that the giving up of the cause of cupidity is indicated by the first

vsm1.4:84.4.verse: and [the giving up of the cause] of stupidity by the second;

vsm1.4:84.5.verse: also that the purification of one’s occupation is indicated by the first and the educating of one’s inclination by the second.

vsm1.4:84.6.verse: This, firstly, is the method here when the words from sense desires are treated as referring to sense desires as object.

vsm1.4:85.1.verse: But if they are treated as referring to sense desires as defilement, then it is simply just zeal for sense desires (kāmacchanda) in the various forms of zeal (chanda), greed (rāga), etc.,

vsm1.4:85.2.verse: that is intended as “sense desires” (kāma) (§83, 2nd quotation).

vsm1.4:85.3.verse: And although that [lust] is also included by [the word] “unprofitable,”

vsm1.4:85.4.verse: it is nevertheless stated separately in the Vibhaṅga in the way beginning, “Herein, what are sense desires? Zeal as sense desire …” (Vibh 256) because of its incompatibility with jhāna.

vsm1.4:85.5.verse: Or, alternatively, it is mentioned in the first phrase because it is sense desire as defilement

vsm1.4:85.6.verse: and in the second phrase because it is included in the “unprofitable.”

vsm1.4:85.7.verse: And because this [lust] has various forms, therefore “from sense desires” is said instead of “from sense desire.”

vsm1.4:86.1.verse: And although there may be unprofitableness in other states as well,

vsm1.4:86.2.verse: nevertheless only the hindrances are mentioned subsequently in the Vibhaṅga thus, “Herein, what states are unprofitable? Lust …” (Vibh 256), etc., in order to show their opposition to, and incompatibility with, the jhāna factors.

vsm1.4:86.3.verse: For the hindrances are the contrary opposites of the jhāna factors:

vsm1.4:86.4.verse: what is meant is that the jhāna factors are incompatible with them, eliminate them, abolish them.

vsm1.4:86.5.verse: And it is said accordingly in the Peṭaka (Peṭakopadesa): “Concentration is incompatible with lust,

vsm1.4:86.7.verse: applied thought with stiffness and torpor,

vsm1.4:86.9.verse: and sustained thought with uncertainty” (not in Peṭakopadesa).

vsm1.4:87.1.verse: So in this case it should be understood that seclusion by suppression (suspension) of lust is indicated by the phrase quite secluded from sense desires,

vsm1.4:87.2.verse: and seclusion by suppression (suspension) of [all] five hindrances

vsm1.4:87.3.verse: by the phrase secluded from unprofitable things. But omitting repetitions, that of lust is indicated by the first and that of the remaining hindrances by the second.

vsm1.4:87.4.verse: Similarly with the three unprofitable roots, that of greed, which has the five cords of sense desire (M I 85) as its province, is indicated by the first,

vsm1.4:87.5.verse: and that of hate and delusion, which have as their respective provinces the various grounds for annoyance (A IV 408; V 150), etc., by the second.

vsm1.4:87.6.verse: Or with the states consisting of the floods, etc., that of the flood of sense desires, of the bond of sense desires, of the canker of sense desires, of sense-desire clinging, of the bodily tie of covetousness, and of the fetter of greed for sense desires, is indicated by the first,

vsm1.4:87.7.verse: and that of the remaining floods, bonds, cankers, clingings, ties, and fetters, is indicated by the second.

vsm1.4:87.8.verse: Again, that of craving and of what is associated with craving is indicated by the first,

vsm1.4:87.9.verse: and that of ignorance and of what is associated with ignorance is indicated by the second.

vsm1.4:87.10.verse: Furthermore, that of the eight thought-arisings associated with greed (XIV.90) is indicated by the first,

vsm1.4:87.11.verse: and that of the remaining kinds of unprofitable thought-arisings is indicated by the second.

vsm1.4:87.12.verse: This, in the first place, is the explanation of the meaning of the words “quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things.”

vsm1.4:88.1.verse: So far the factors abandoned by the jhāna have been shown.

vsm1.4:88.2.verse: And now, in order to show the factors associated with it, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought is said.

vsm1.4:88.3.verse: Herein, applied thinking (vitakkana) is applied thought (vitakka); hitting upon, is what is meant.

vsm1.4:88.4.verse: It has the characteristic of directing the mind on to an object (mounting the mind on its object).

vsm1.4:88.5.verse: Its function is to strike at and thresh—

vsm1.4:88.6.verse: for the meditator is said, in virtue of it, to have the object struck at by applied thought, threshed by applied thought.

vsm1.4:88.7.verse: It is manifested as the leading of the mind onto an object.

vsm1.4:88.8.verse: Sustained thinking (vicaraṇa) is sustained thought (vicāra); continued sustainment (anusañcaraṇa), is what is meant.

vsm1.4:88.9.verse: It has the characteristic of continued pressure on (occupation with) the object.

vsm1.4:88.10.verse: Its function is to keep conascent [mental] states [occupied] with that.

vsm1.4:88.11.verse: It is manifested as keeping consciousness anchored [on that object].

vsm1.4:89.2.verse: applied thought is the first impact of the mind in the sense that it is both gross and inceptive, like the striking of a bell.

vsm1.4:89.3.verse: Sustained thought is the act of keeping the mind anchored, in the sense that it is subtle with the individual essence of continued pressure,

vsm1.4:89.4.verse: like the ringing of the bell.

vsm1.4:89.5.verse: Applied thought intervenes, being the interference of consciousness at the time of first arousing [thought],

vsm1.4:89.6.verse: like a bird’s spreading out its wings when about to soar into the air,

vsm1.4:89.7.verse: and like a bee’s diving towards a lotus when it is minded to follow up the scent of it.

vsm1.4:89.8.verse: The behaviour of sustained thought is quiet, being the near non-interference of consciousness,

vsm1.4:89.9.verse: like the bird’s planing with outspread wings after soaring into the air,

vsm1.4:89.10.verse: and like the bee’s buzzing above the lotus after it has dived towards it.

vsm1.4:90.1.verse: In the commentary to the Book of Twos this is said: “Applied thought occurs as a state of directing the mind onto an object, like the movement of a large bird taking off into the air by engaging the air with both wings

vsm1.4:90.2.verse: and forcing them downwards. For it causes absorption by being unified.

vsm1.4:90.3.verse: Sustained thought occurs with the individual essence of continued pressure, like the bird’s movement when it is using (activating) its wings for the purpose of keeping hold on the air. For it keeps pressing the object”.

vsm1.4:90.4.verse: That fits in with the latter’s occurrence as anchoring.

vsm1.4:90.5.verse: This difference of theirs becomes evident in the first and second jhānas [in the fivefold reckoning].

vsm1.4:91.1.verse: Furthermore, applied thought is like the hand that grips firmly and sustained thought is like the hand that rubs, when one grips a tarnished metal dish firmly with one hand and rubs it with powder and oil and a woollen pad with the other hand.

vsm1.4:91.2.verse: Likewise, when a potter has spun his wheel with a stroke on the stick and is making a dish,

vsm1.4:91.3.verse: his supporting hand is like applied thought and his hand that moves back and forth is like sustained thought.

vsm1.4:91.4.verse: Likewise, when one is drawing a circle,

vsm1.4:91.5.verse: the pin that stays fixed down in the centre is like applied thought, which directs onto the object, and the pin that revolves round it is like sustained thought, which continuously presses.

vsm1.4:92.1.verse: So this jhāna occurs together with this applied thought and this sustained thought

vsm1.4:92.2.verse: and it is called, “accompanied by applied and sustained thought” as a tree is called “accompanied by flowers and fruits.”

vsm1.4:92.4.verse: the teaching is given in terms of a person in the way beginning, “He is possessed, fully possessed, of this applied thought and this sustained thought” (Vibh 257).

vsm1.4:92.5.verse: The meaning should be regarded in the same way there too.

vsm1.4:93.1.verse: Born of seclusion: here secludedness (vivitti) is seclusion (viveka); the meaning is, disappearance of hindrances.

vsm1.4:93.2.verse: Or alternatively, it is secluded (vivitta), thus it is seclusion;

vsm1.4:93.3.verse: the meaning is, the collection of states associated with the jhāna is secluded from hindrances.

vsm1.4:93.4.verse: “Born of seclusion” is born of or in that kind of seclusion.

vsm1.4:94.1.verse: Happiness and bliss: it refreshes (pīnayati), thus it is happiness (pīti).

vsm1.4:94.2.verse: It has the characteristic of endearing (sampiyāyanā).

vsm1.4:94.3.verse: Its function is to refresh the body and the mind;

vsm1.4:94.4.verse: or its function is to pervade (thrill with rapture). It is manifested as elation.

vsm1.4:94.5.verse: But it is of five kinds as minor happiness,

vsm1.4:94.9.verse: Herein, minor happiness is only able to raise the hairs on the body.

vsm1.4:94.10.verse: Momentary happiness is like flashes of lightning at different moments.

vsm1.4:94.11.verse: Showering happiness breaks over the body again and again like waves on the sea shore.

vsm1.4:95.1.verse: Uplifting happiness can be powerful enough to levitate the body and make it spring up into the air.

vsm1.4:95.2.verse: For this was what happened to the Elder Mahā-Tissa, resident at Puṇṇavallika. He went to the shrine terrace on the evening of the full-moon day.

vsm1.4:95.3.verse: Seeing the moonlight, he faced in the direction of the Great Shrine [at Anurādhapura],

vsm1.4:95.4.verse: thinking, “At this very hour the four assemblies are worshipping at the Great Shrine!”

vsm1.4:95.5.verse: By means of objects formerly seen [there] he aroused uplifting happiness with the Enlightened One as object,

vsm1.4:95.6.verse: and he rose into the air like a painted ball bounced off a plastered floor and alighted on the terrace of the Great Shrine.

vsm1.4:96.1.verse: And this was what happened to the daughter of a clan in the village of Vattakālaka

vsm1.4:96.2.verse: near the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery when she sprang up into the air owing to strong uplifting happiness with the Enlightened One as object.

vsm1.4:96.3.verse: As her parents were about to go to the monastery in the evening, it seems, in order to hear the Dhamma,

vsm1.4:96.4.verse: they told her: “My dear, you are expecting a child; you cannot go out at an unsuitable time. We shall hear the Dhamma and gain merit for you.” So they went out.

vsm1.4:96.5.verse: And though she wanted to go too, she could not well object to what they said. She stepped out of the house onto a balcony

vsm1.4:96.6.verse: and stood looking at the Ākāsacetiya Shrine at Girikaṇḍaka lit by the moon. She saw the offering of lamps at the shrine,

vsm1.4:96.7.verse: and the four communities as they circumambulated it to the right after making their offerings of flowers and perfumes;

vsm1.4:96.8.verse: and she heard the sound of the massed recital by the Community of Bhikkhus.

vsm1.4:96.9.verse: Then she thought: “How lucky they are to be able to go to the monastery and wander round such a shrine terrace and listen to such sweet preaching of Dhamma!”

vsm1.4:96.10.verse: Seeing the shrine as a mound of pearls and arousing uplifting happiness,

vsm1.4:96.11.verse: she sprang up into the air, and before her parents arrived

vsm1.4:96.12.verse: she came down from the air into the shrine terrace, where she paid homage and stood listening to the Dhamma.

vsm1.4:97.1.verse: When her parents arrived, they asked her, “What road did you come by?”

vsm1.4:97.2.verse: She said, “I came through the air, not by the road,”

vsm1.4:97.3.verse: and when they told her, “My dear, those whose cankers are destroyed come through the air. But how did you come?” she replied:

vsm1.4:97.4.verse: “As I was standing looking at the shrine in the moonlight a strong sense of happiness arose in me with the Enlightened One as its object.

vsm1.4:97.5.verse: Then I knew no more whether I was standing or sitting, but only that I was springing up into the air with the sign that I had grasped, and I came to rest on this shrine terrace.”

vsm1.4:97.6.verse: So uplifting happiness can be powerful enough to levitate the body, make it spring up into the air.

vsm1.4:98.1.verse: But when pervading (rapturous) happiness arises, the whole body is completely pervaded,

vsm1.4:98.2.verse: like a filled bladder, like a rock cavern invaded by a huge inundation.

vsm1.4:99.1.verse: Now, this fivefold happiness, when conceived and matured, perfects the twofold tranquillity,

vsm1.4:99.2.verse: that is, bodily and mental tranquillity.

vsm1.4:99.3.verse: When tranquillity is conceived and matured, it perfects the twofold bliss, that is, bodily and mental bliss.

vsm1.4:99.4.verse: When bliss is conceived and matured, it perfects the threefold concentration,

vsm1.4:99.5.verse: that is, momentary concentration, access concentration, and absorption concentration.

vsm1.4:99.6.verse: Of these, what is intended in this context by happiness is pervading happiness, which is the root of absorption and comes by growth into association with absorption.

vsm1.4:100.1.verse: But as to the other word: pleasing (sukhana) is bliss (sukha).

vsm1.4:100.2.verse: Or alternatively: it thoroughly (suṭṭhu) devours (khādati), consumes (khaṇati), bodily and mental affliction, thus it is bliss (sukha).

vsm1.4:100.3.verse: It has gratifying as its characteristic.

vsm1.4:100.4.verse: Its function is to intensify associated states. It is manifested as aid.

vsm1.4:100.5.verse: And wherever the two are associated, happiness is the contentedness at getting a desirable object,

vsm1.4:100.6.verse: and bliss is the actual experiencing of it when got.

vsm1.4:100.7.verse: Where there is happiness there is bliss (pleasure);

vsm1.4:100.8.verse: but where there is bliss there is not necessarily happiness.

vsm1.4:100.9.verse: Happiness is included in the formations aggregate;

vsm1.4:100.10.verse: bliss is included in the feeling aggregate.

vsm1.4:100.11.verse: If a man, exhausted in a desert, saw or heard about a pond on the edge of a wood, he would have happiness;

vsm1.4:100.12.verse: if he went into the wood’s shade and used the water, he would have bliss.

vsm1.4:100.13.verse: And it should be understood that this is said because they are obvious on such occasions.

vsm1.4:101.1.verse: Accordingly, (a) this happiness and this bliss are of this jhāna,

vsm1.4:101.2.verse: or in this jhāna; so in this way this jhāna is qualified by the words with happiness and bliss [and also born of seclusion].

vsm1.4:101.3.verse: Or alternatively: (b) the words happiness and bliss (pītisukhaṃ) can be taken as “the happiness and the bliss” independently,

vsm1.4:101.5.verse: and so then it can be taken as seclusion-born happiness-and-bliss of this jhāna,

vsm1.4:101.6.verse: or in this jhāna; so in this way it is the happiness and bliss [rather than the jhāna] that are born of seclusion.

vsm1.4:101.7.verse: For just as the words “born of seclusion” can [as at (a)] be taken as qualifying the word “jhāna,”

vsm1.4:101.8.verse: so too they can be taken here [as at (b)] as qualifying the expression “happiness and bliss,”

vsm1.4:101.9.verse: and then that [total expression] is predicated of this [jhāna]. So it is also correct to call “happiness-and-bliss born-of-seclusion” a single expression.

vsm1.4:101.10.verse: In the Vibhaṅga it is stated in the way beginning, “This bliss accompanied by this happiness” (Vibh 257).

vsm1.4:101.11.verse: The meaning should be regarded in the same way there too.
