vsm1.4:102.1.verse: First jhāna: this will be explained below (§119).

vsm1.4:102.2.verse: Enters upon (upasampajja): arrives at; reaches, is what is meant;

vsm1.4:102.3.verse: or else, taking it as “makes enter” (upasampādayitvā), then producing, is what is meant.

vsm1.4:102.4.verse: In the Vibhaṅga this is said:

vsm1.4:102.5.verse: “‘Enters upon’: the gaining, the regaining, the reaching, the arrival at, the touching, the realizing of, the entering upon (upasampadā, the first jhāna” (Vibh 257),

vsm1.4:102.6.verse: the meaning of which should be regarded in the same way.

vsm1.4:103.2.verse: by becoming possessed of jhāna of the kind described above through dwelling in a posture favourable to that [jhāna], he produces a posture, a procedure, a keeping, an enduring, a lasting, a behaviour, a dwelling, of the person.

vsm1.4:103.3.verse: For this is said in the Vibhaṅga:

vsm1.4:103.4.verse: “‘Dwells in’: poses, proceeds, keeps, endures, lasts, behaves, dwells; hence ‘dwells’ is said” (Vibh 252).

vsm1.4:104.1.verse: Now, it was also said above which abandons five factors, possesses five factors (§79; cf. M I 294).

vsm1.4:104.2.verse: Herein, the abandoning of the five factors should be understood as the abandoning of these five hindrances, namely, lust,

vsm1.4:104.6.verse: for no jhāna arises until these have been abandoned,

vsm1.4:104.7.verse: and so they are called the factors of abandoning.

vsm1.4:104.8.verse: For although other unprofitable things too are abandoned at the moment of jhāna,

vsm1.4:104.9.verse: still only these are specifically obstructive to jhāna.

vsm1.4:105.1.verse: The mind affected through lust by greed for varied objective fields

vsm1.4:105.2.verse: does not become concentrated on an object consisting in unity,

vsm1.4:105.3.verse: or being overwhelmed by lust, it does not enter on the way to abandoning the sense-desire element.

vsm1.4:105.4.verse: When pestered by ill will towards an object, it does not occur uninterruptedly.

vsm1.4:105.5.verse: When overcome by stiffness and torpor, it is unwieldy.

vsm1.4:105.6.verse: When seized by agitation and worry, it is unquiet and buzzes about.

vsm1.4:105.7.verse: When stricken by uncertainty, it fails to mount the way to accomplish the attainment of jhāna.

vsm1.4:105.8.verse: So it is these only that are called factors of abandoning because they are specifically obstructive to jhāna.

vsm1.4:106.1.verse: But applied thought directs the mind onto the object; sustained thought keeps it anchored there.

vsm1.4:106.2.verse: Happiness produced by the success of the effort refreshes the mind whose effort has succeeded through not being distracted by those hindrances;

vsm1.4:106.3.verse: and bliss intensifies it for the same reason.

vsm1.4:106.4.verse: Then unification aided by this directing onto, this anchoring, this refreshing and this intensifying,

vsm1.4:106.5.verse: evenly and rightly centres (III.3) the mind with its remaining associated states on the object consisting in unity.

vsm1.4:106.6.verse: Consequently, possession of five factors should be understood as the arising of these five, namely, applied thought, sustained thought, happiness, bliss and unification of mind.

vsm1.4:107.1.verse: For it is when these are arisen that jhāna is said to be arisen,

vsm1.4:107.2.verse: which is why they are called the five factors of possession.

vsm1.4:107.3.verse: Therefore it should not be assumed that the jhāna is something other which possesses them.

vsm1.4:107.4.verse: But just as “The army with the four factors” (Vin IV 104) and

vsm1.4:107.5.verse: “Music with the five factors” (M-a II 300) and

vsm1.4:107.6.verse: “The path with the eight factors (eightfold path)” are stated simply in terms of their factors,

vsm1.4:107.7.verse: so this too [147] should be understood as stated simply in terms of its factors,

vsm1.4:107.8.verse: when it is said to “have five factors” or “possess five factors.”

vsm1.4:108.1.verse: And while these five factors are present also at the moment of access and are stronger in access than in normal consciousness,

vsm1.4:108.2.verse: they are still stronger here than in access and acquire the characteristic of the fine-material sphere.

vsm1.4:108.3.verse: For applied thought arises here directing the mind on to the object in an extremely lucid manner,

vsm1.4:108.4.verse: and sustained thought does so pressing the object very hard,

vsm1.4:108.5.verse: and the happiness and bliss pervade the entire body.

vsm1.4:108.6.verse: Hence it is said: “And there is nothing of his whole body not permeated by the happiness and bliss born of seclusion” (D I 73).

vsm1.4:108.7.verse: And unification too arises in the complete contact with the object that the surface of a box’s lid has with the surface of its base.

vsm1.4:108.8.verse: This is how they differ from the others.

vsm1.4:109.1.verse: Although unification of mind is not actually listed among these factors in the [summary] version [beginning]

vsm1.4:109.2.verse: “which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought” (Vibh 245),

vsm1.4:109.3.verse: nevertheless it is mentioned [later] in the Vibhaṅga as follows:

vsm1.4:109.4.verse: “‘Jhāna’: it is applied thought, sustained thought, happiness, bliss, unification”(Vibh 257), and so it is a factor too;

vsm1.4:109.5.verse: for the intention with which the Blessed One gave the summary

vsm1.4:109.6.verse: is the same as that with which he gave the exposition that follows it.

vsm1.4:110.1.verse: Is good in three ways, possesses ten characteristics (§79): the goodness in three ways is in the beginning, middle, and end.

vsm1.4:110.2.verse: The possession of the ten characteristics should be understood as the characteristics of the beginning, middle, and end, too.

vsm1.4:111.1.verse: “Of the first jhāna, purification of the way is the beginning,

vsm1.4:111.2.verse: intensification of equanimity is the middle, and satisfaction is the end.

vsm1.4:111.3.verse: “‘Of the first jhāna, purification of the way is the beginning’: how many characteristics has the beginning?

vsm1.4:111.4.verse: The beginning has three characteristics: the mind is purified of obstructions to that [jhāna];

vsm1.4:111.5.verse: because it is purified the mind makes way for the central [state of equilibrium, which is the] sign of serenity;

vsm1.4:111.6.verse: because it has made way the mind enters into that state.

vsm1.4:111.7.verse: And it is since the mind becomes purified of obstructions

vsm1.4:111.8.verse: and, through being purified, makes way for the central [state of equilibrium, which is the] sign of serenity

vsm1.4:111.9.verse: and, having made way, enters into that state,

vsm1.4:111.10.verse: that the purification of the way is the beginning of the first jhāna. These are the three characteristics of the beginning.

vsm1.4:111.11.verse: Hence it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in the beginning which possesses three characteristics.’ [148]

vsm1.4:112.1.verse: “‘Of the first jhāna intensification of equanimity is the middle’: how many characteristics has the middle?

vsm1.4:112.2.verse: The middle has three characteristics. He [now] looks on with equanimity at the mind that is purified;

vsm1.4:112.3.verse: he looks on with equanimity at it as having made way for serenity;

vsm1.4:112.4.verse: he looks on with equanimity at the appearance of unity.

vsm1.4:112.5.verse: And in that he [now] looks on with equanimity at the mind that is purified

vsm1.4:112.6.verse: and looks on with equanimity at it as having made way for serenity

vsm1.4:112.7.verse: and looks on with equanimity at the appearance of unity,

vsm1.4:112.8.verse: that intensification of equanimity is the middle of the first jhāna. These are the three characteristics of the middle.

vsm1.4:112.9.verse: Hence it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in the middle which possesses three characteristics.’

vsm1.4:113.1.verse: “‘Of the first jhāna satisfaction is the end’: how many characteristics has the end?

vsm1.4:113.2.verse: The end has four characteristics. The satisfaction in the sense that there was non-excess of any of the states arisen therein,

vsm1.4:113.3.verse: and the satisfaction in the sense that the faculties had a single function,

vsm1.4:113.4.verse: and the satisfaction in the sense that the appropriate energy was effective,

vsm1.4:113.5.verse: and the satisfaction in the sense of repetition,

vsm1.4:113.6.verse: are the satisfaction in the end of the first jhāna. These are the four characteristics of the end.

vsm1.4:113.7.verse: Hence it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in the end which possesses four characteristics’“ (Paṭis I 167–68).

vsm1.4:114.1.verse: Herein, purification of the way is access together with its concomitants.

vsm1.4:114.3.verse: Satisfaction is reviewing. So some comment.

vsm1.4:114.4.verse: But it is said in the text, “The mind arrived at unity enters into purification of the way,

vsm1.4:114.5.verse: is intensified in equanimity, and is satisfied by knowledge” (Paṭis I 167),

vsm1.4:114.6.verse: and therefore it is from the standpoint within actual absorption that purification of the way firstly should be understood as the approach,

vsm1.4:114.7.verse: with intensification of equanimity as the function of equanimity consisting in specific neutrality,

vsm1.4:114.8.verse: and satisfaction as the manifestation of clarifying knowledge’s function in accomplishing non-excess of states.

vsm1.4:115.1.verse: Firstly, in a cycle [of consciousness] in which absorption arises

vsm1.4:115.2.verse: the mind becomes purified from the group of defilements called hindrances that are an obstruction to jhāna.

vsm1.4:115.3.verse: Being devoid of obstruction because it has been purified,

vsm1.4:115.4.verse: it makes way for the central [state of equilibrium, which is the] sign of serenity.

vsm1.4:115.5.verse: Now, it is the absorption concentration itself occurring evenly that is called the sign of serenity.

vsm1.4:115.6.verse: But the consciousness immediately before that [149] reaches that state by way of change in a single continuity (cf. XXII.1–6),

vsm1.4:115.7.verse: and so it is said that it makes way for the central [state of equilibrium, which is the] sign of serenity. And it is said that it enters into that state by approaching it through having made way for it.

vsm1.4:115.8.verse: That is why in the first place purification of the way, while referring to aspects existing in the preceding consciousness,

vsm1.4:115.9.verse: should nevertheless be understood as the approach at the moment of the first jhāna’s actual arising.

vsm1.4:116.1.verse: Secondly, when he has more interest in purifying, since there is no need to re-purify what has already been purified thus,

vsm1.4:116.2.verse: it is said that he looks on with equanimity at the mind that is purified.

vsm1.4:116.3.verse: And when he has no more interest in concentrating again what has already made way for serenity by arriving at the state of serenity,

vsm1.4:116.4.verse: it is said that he looks on with equanimity at it as having made way for serenity.

vsm1.4:116.5.verse: And when he has no more interest in again causing appearance of unity in what has already appeared as unity through abandonment of its association with defilement in making way for serenity,

vsm1.4:116.6.verse: it is said that he looks on with equanimity at the appearance of unity.

vsm1.4:116.7.verse: That is why intensification of equanimity should be understood as the function of equanimity that consists in specific neutrality.

vsm1.4:117.1.verse: And lastly, when equanimity was thus intensified,

vsm1.4:117.2.verse: the states called concentration and understanding produced there, occurred coupled together without either one exceeding the other.

vsm1.4:117.3.verse: And also the [five] faculties beginning with faith occurred with the single function (taste) of deliverance

vsm1.4:117.4.verse: owing to deliverance from the various defilements.

vsm1.4:117.5.verse: And also the energy appropriate to that, which was favourable to their state of non-excess and single function, was effective.

vsm1.4:117.6.verse: And also its repetition occurs at that moment.

vsm1.4:117.7.verse: Now, all these [four] aspects are only produced because it is after seeing with knowledge the various dangers in defilement and advantages in cleansing

vsm1.4:117.8.verse: that satisfiedness, purifiedness and clarifiedness ensue accordingly.

vsm1.4:117.9.verse: That is the reason why it was said that satisfaction should be understood as the manifestation of clarifying knowledge’s function

vsm1.4:117.10.verse: in accomplishing non-excess, etc., of states (§114).

vsm1.4:118.1.verse: Herein, satisfaction as a function of knowledge is called “the end” since the knowledge is evident as due to onlooking equanimity,

vsm1.4:118.2.verse: according as it is said: “He looks on with complete equanimity at the mind thus exerted;

vsm1.4:118.3.verse: then the understanding faculty is outstanding as understanding due to equanimity.

vsm1.4:118.4.verse: Owing to equanimity the mind is liberated from the many sorts of defilements;

vsm1.4:118.5.verse: then the understanding faculty is outstanding as understanding due to liberation.

vsm1.4:118.6.verse: Because of being liberated these states come to have a single function;

vsm1.4:118.7.verse: then [the understanding faculty is outstanding as understanding due to] development in the sense of the single function” (Paṭis II 25).

vsm1.4:118.8.verse: That is why satisfaction, being a function of knowledge, is called the end.

vsm1.4:119.1.verse: Now, as to the words and so he has attained the first jhāna … of the earth kasiṇa (§79):

vsm1.4:119.2.verse: Here it is first because it starts a numerical series; [150] also it is first because it arises first.

vsm1.4:119.3.verse: It is called jhāna because of lighting (upanijjhāna) the object and because of burning up (jhāpana) opposition (Paṭis I 49).

vsm1.4:119.4.verse: The disk of earth is called earth kasiṇa (paṭhavīkasiṇa—lit. “earth universal”) in the sense of entirety,

vsm1.4:119.5.verse: and the sign acquired with that as its support and also the jhāna acquired in the earth-kasiṇa sign are so called too.

vsm1.4:119.6.verse: So that jhāna should be understood as of the earth kasiṇa in this sense,

vsm1.4:119.7.verse: with reference to which it was said above “and so he has attained to the first jhāna … of the earth kasiṇa.”

vsm1.4:120.1.verse: When it has been attained in this way, the mode of its attainment must be discerned by the meditator as if he were a hair-splitter or

vsm1.4:120.3.verse: For when a very skilful archer, who is working to split a hair, actually splits the hair on one occasion,

vsm1.4:120.4.verse: he discerns the modes of the position of his feet, the bow, the bowstring, and the arrow thus:

vsm1.4:120.5.verse: “I split the hair as I stood thus, with the bow thus, the bowstring thus, the arrow thus.”

vsm1.4:120.6.verse: From then on he recaptures those same modes and repeats the splitting of the hair without fail.

vsm1.4:120.7.verse: So too the meditator must discern such modes as that of suitable food, etc., thus: “I attained this after eating this food, attending on such a person,

vsm1.4:120.9.verse: in this posture at this time.”

vsm1.4:120.10.verse: In this way, when that [absorption] is lost, he will be able to recapture those modes and renew the absorption,

vsm1.4:120.11.verse: or while familiarizing himself with it he will be able to repeat that absorption again and again.

vsm1.4:121.1.verse: And just as when a skilled cook is serving his employer, he notices whatever he chooses to eat

vsm1.4:121.2.verse: and from then on brings only that sort and so obtains a reward,

vsm1.4:121.3.verse: so too this meditator discerns such modes as that of the food, etc., at the time of the attaining,

vsm1.4:121.4.verse: and he recaptures them and re-obtains absorption each time it is lost.

vsm1.4:121.5.verse: So he must discern the modes as a hair-splitter or a cook does.

vsm1.4:121.6.verse: And this has been said by the Blessed One:

vsm1.4:122.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a wise, clever, skilful cook set various kinds of sauces before a king or a king’s minister, such as sour, bitter, sharp, [151] sweet, peppery and unpeppery, salty and unsalty sauces;

vsm1.4:122.2.verse: then the wise, clever, skilful cook learned his master’s sign thus ‘today this sauce pleased my master’ or ‘he held out his hand for this one’ or ‘he took a lot of this one’ or ‘he praised this one’ or ‘today the sour kind pleased my master’ or ‘he held out his hand for the sour kind’ or ‘he took a lot of the sour kind’ or ‘he praised the sour kind’ … or ‘he praised the unsalty kind’;

vsm1.4:122.3.verse: then the wise, clever, skilful cook is rewarded with clothing and wages and presents.

vsm1.4:122.4.verse: Why is that? Because that wise, clever, skilful cook learned his master’s sign in this way.

vsm1.4:122.5.verse: So too, bhikkhus, here a wise, clever, skilful bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body … He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings … consciousness as consciousness … mental objects as mental objects, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. As he dwells contemplating mental objects as mental objects, his mind becomes concentrated, his defilements are abandoned.

vsm1.4:122.6.verse: He learns the sign of that.

vsm1.4:122.7.verse: Then that wise, clever, skilful bhikkhu is rewarded with a happy abiding here and now, he is rewarded with mindfulness and full awareness.

vsm1.4:122.8.verse: Why is that? Because that wise, clever, skilful bhikkhu learned his consciousness’s sign” (S V 151–52).

vsm1.4:123.1.verse: And when he recaptures those modes by apprehending the sign, he just succeeds in reaching absorption, but not in making it last.

vsm1.4:123.2.verse: It lasts when it is absolutely purified from states that obstruct concentration.

vsm1.4:124.1.verse: When a bhikkhu enters upon a jhāna without [first] completely suppressing lust by reviewing the dangers in sense desires, etc.,

vsm1.4:124.2.verse: and without [first] completely tranquillizing bodily irritability by tranquillizing the body,

vsm1.4:124.3.verse: and without [first] completely removing stiffness and torpor by bringing to mind the elements of initiative, etc., (§55),

vsm1.4:124.4.verse: and without [first] completely abolishing agitation and worry by bringing to mind the sign of serenity, etc., [152]

vsm1.4:124.5.verse: and without [first] completely purifying his mind of other states that obstruct concentration, then that bhikkhu

vsm1.4:124.6.verse: soon comes out of that jhāna again, like a bee that has gone into an unpurified hive, like a king who has gone into an unclean park.

vsm1.4:125.1.verse: But when he enters upon a jhāna after [first] completely purifying his mind of states that obstruct concentration,

vsm1.4:125.2.verse: then he remains in the attainment even for a whole day, like a bee that has gone into a completely purified hive, like a king who has gone into a perfectly clean park.

vsm1.4:125.4.verse: “So let him dispel any sensual lust, and resentment, Agitation as well, and then torpor, and doubt as the fifth;

vsm1.4:125.5.verse: There let him find joy with a heart that is glad in seclusion, Like a king in a garden where all and each corner is clean.”

vsm1.4:126.1.verse: So if he wants to remain long in the jhāna, he must enter upon it after [first] purifying his mind from obstructive states.

vsm1.4:127.1.verse: In order to perfect the development of consciousness he should besides extend the counterpart sign according as acquired.

vsm1.4:127.2.verse: Now, there are two planes for extension, namely, access and absorption;

vsm1.4:127.3.verse: for it is possible to extend it on reaching access and on reaching absorption.

vsm1.4:127.4.verse: But the extending should be done consistently in one [or the other],

vsm1.4:127.5.verse: which is why it was said “he should besides extend the counterpart sign according as acquired.”

vsm1.4:127.6.verse: The way to extend it is this.

vsm1.4:127.7.verse: The meditator should not extend the sign as a clay bowl or a cake or boiled rice or a creeper or a piece of cloth is extended.

vsm1.4:127.8.verse: He should first delimit with his mind successive sizes for the sign, according as acquired, that is to say, one finger, two fingers, three fingers, four fingers, and then extend it by the amount delimited, just as a ploughman delimits with the plough the area to be ploughed and then ploughs within the area delimited, or just as bhikkhus fixing a boundary first observe the marks and then fix it.

vsm1.4:127.9.verse: He should not, in fact, extend it without having delimited [the amount it is to be extended by].

vsm1.4:127.10.verse: After that has been done, he can further extend it, doing so by delimiting successive boundaries of, say, a span, a ratana (=2 spans), the veranda, the surrounding space, the monastery,

vsm1.4:127.11.verse: and the boundaries of the village, the town, the district, the kingdom and the ocean, [153] making the extreme limit the world-sphere or even beyond.

vsm1.4:128.1.verse: Just as young swans first starting to use their wings soar a little distance at a time, and by gradually increasing it

vsm1.4:128.2.verse: eventually reach the presence of the moon and sun, so too when a bhikkhu extends the sign by successive delimitations in the way described, he can extend it up to the limit of the world-sphere or even beyond.

vsm1.4:129.1.verse: Then that sign [appears] to him like an ox hide stretched out with a hundred pegs over the earth’s ridges and hollows, river ravines, tracts of scrub and thorns, and rocky inequalities (see M III 105)

vsm1.4:129.2.verse: in any area to which it has been extended.

vsm1.4:129.3.verse: When a beginner has reached the first jhāna in this sign, he should enter upon it often without reviewing it much.

vsm1.4:129.4.verse: For the first jhāna factors occur crudely and weakly in one who reviews it much.

vsm1.4:129.5.verse: Then because of that they do not become conditions for higher endeavour.

vsm1.4:129.6.verse: While he is endeavouring for the unfamiliar [higher jhāna] he falls away from the first jhāna and fails to reach the second.

vsm1.4:130.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a foolish stupid mountain cow, with no knowledge of fields and no skill in walking on craggy mountains,

vsm1.4:130.3.verse: who thought: ‘What if I walked in a direction I never walked in before, ate grass I never ate before, drank water I never drank before?’

vsm1.4:130.4.verse: and without placing her forefoot properly she lifted up her hind foot;

vsm1.4:130.5.verse: then she would not walk in the direction she never walked in before or eat the grass she never ate before or drink the water she never drank before,

vsm1.4:130.6.verse: and also she would not get back safely to the place where she had thought, ‘What if I walked in a direction I never walked in before … drank water I never drank before?’

vsm1.4:130.7.verse: Why is that? Because that mountain cow was foolish and stupid with no knowledge of fields and no skill in walking on craggy mountains.

vsm1.4:130.8.verse: So too, bhikkhus, here is a certain foolish stupid bhikkhu with no knowledge of fields and no skill, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things, in entering upon and dwelling in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought with happiness and bliss born of seclusion;

vsm1.4:130.9.verse: he does not repeat, develop or cultivate that sign or properly establish it.

vsm1.4:130.10.verse: He thinks: ‘What if with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought I entered upon and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is … with happiness and bliss born of concentration?’ [154]

vsm1.4:130.11.verse: He is unable with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought to enter upon and dwell in the second jhāna, which is … with happiness and bliss born of concentration.

vsm1.4:130.12.verse: Then he thinks: ‘What if, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things, I entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is … with happiness and bliss born of seclusion?’

vsm1.4:130.13.verse: He is unable, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things, to enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna which is … with happiness and bliss born of seclusion. This bhikkhu is called one who has slipped between the two, who has fallen between the two, just like the foolish stupid mountain cow with no knowledge of fields and no skill in walking on craggy mountains …” (A IV 418–19).

vsm1.4:131.1.verse: Therefore he should acquire mastery in the five ways first of all with respect to the first jhāna.

vsm1.4:131.2.verse: Herein, these are the five kinds of mastery: mastery in adverting, mastery in attaining, mastery in resolving (steadying the duration),

vsm1.4:131.3.verse: mastery in emerging, and mastery in reviewing.

vsm1.4:131.4.verse: “He adverts to the first jhāna where, when, and for as long as, he wishes;

vsm1.4:131.5.verse: he has no difficulty in adverting; thus it is mastery in adverting.

vsm1.4:131.6.verse: He attains the first jhāna where … he has no difficulty in attaining; thus it is mastery in attaining” (Paṭis I 100),

vsm1.4:131.7.verse: and all the rest should be quoted in detail (XXIII.27).

vsm1.4:132.1.verse: The explanation of the meaning here is this. When he emerges from the first jhāna and first of all adverts to the applied thought, then, next to the adverting that arose interrupting the life-continuum,

vsm1.4:132.2.verse: either four or five impulsions impel with that applied thought as their object.

vsm1.4:132.3.verse: Then there are two life-continuum [consciousnesses]. Then there is adverting with the sustained thought as its object

vsm1.4:132.4.verse: and followed by impulsions in the way just stated. When he is able to prolong his conscious process uninterruptedly in this way with the five jhāna factors, then his mastery of adverting is successful.

vsm1.4:132.5.verse: But this mastery is found at its acme of perfection in the Blessed One’s Twin Marvel (Paṭis I 125),

vsm1.4:132.6.verse: or for others on the aforesaid occasions.

vsm1.4:132.7.verse: There is no quicker mastery in adverting than that.

vsm1.4:133.2.verse: ability to enter upon jhāna quickly, as in the taming of the royal nāga-serpent Nandopananda (XII.106f.),

vsm1.4:134.1.verse: Ability to remain in jhāna for a moment consisting in exactly a finger-snap or exactly ten finger-snaps

vsm1.4:134.2.verse: is called mastery in resolving (steadying the duration).

vsm1.4:134.3.verse: Ability to emerge quickly in the same way is called mastery in emerging.

vsm1.4:134.4.verse: The story of the Elder Buddharakkhita may be told in order to illustrate both these last.

vsm1.4:135.1.verse: [155] Eight years after his admission to the Community

vsm1.4:135.2.verse: that elder was sitting in the midst of thirty thousand bhikkhus possessed of supernormal powers who had gathered to attend upon the sickness of the Elder Mahā-Rohanagutta at Therambatthala.

vsm1.4:135.3.verse: He saw a royal supaṇṇa (bird) swooping down from the sky intending to seize an attendant royal nāga-serpent as he was getting rice-gruel accepted for the elder.

vsm1.4:135.4.verse: The Elder Buddharakkhita created a rock meanwhile, and seizing the royal nāga by the arm, he pushed him inside it.

vsm1.4:135.5.verse: The royal supaṇṇa gave the rock a blow and made off.

vsm1.4:135.6.verse: The senior elder remarked: “Friends, if Rakkhita had not been there, we should all have been put to shame.”

vsm1.4:136.1.verse: Mastery in reviewing is described in the same way as mastery in adverting;

vsm1.4:136.2.verse: for the reviewing impulsions are in fact those next to the adverting mentioned there (§132).

vsm1.4:137.1.verse: When he has once acquired mastery in these five ways, then on emerging from the now familiar first jhāna

vsm1.4:137.2.verse: he can regard the flaws in it in this way: “This attainment is threatened by the nearness of the hindrances, and its factors are weakened by the grossness of the applied and sustained thought.”

vsm1.4:137.3.verse: He can bring the second jhāna to mind as quieter and so end his attachment to the first jhāna

vsm1.4:137.4.verse: and set about doing what is needed for attaining the second.

vsm1.4:138.1.verse: When he has emerged from the first jhāna, applied and sustained thought appear gross to him as he reviews the jhāna factors with mindfulness and full awareness,

vsm1.4:138.2.verse: while happiness and bliss and unification of mind appear peaceful.

vsm1.4:138.3.verse: Then, as he brings that same sign to mind as “earth, earth” again and again with the purpose of abandoning the gross factors and obtaining the peaceful factors,

vsm1.4:138.5.verse: there arises in him mind-door adverting with that same earth kasiṇa as its object, interrupting the life-continuum.

vsm1.4:138.6.verse: After that, either four or five impulsions impel on that same object,

vsm1.4:138.7.verse: the last one of which is an impulsion of the fine-material sphere belonging to the second jhāna.

vsm1.4:138.8.verse: The rest are of the sense sphere of the kinds already stated (§74).

vsm1.4:139.1.verse: And at this point, “With the stilling of applied and sustained thought

vsm1.4:139.2.verse: he enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind without applied thought, without sustained thought, with happiness and bliss born of concentration” (Vibh 245),

vsm1.4:139.3.verse: and so he has attained the second jhāna, which abandons two factors, possesses three factors,

vsm1.4:139.4.verse: is good in three ways, possesses ten characteristics and is of the earth kasiṇa. [156]

vsm1.4:140.1.verse: Herein, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought: with the stilling, with the surmounting, of these two, namely, applied thought and sustained thought;

vsm1.4:140.2.verse: with their non-manifestation at the moment of the second jhāna, is what is meant.

vsm1.4:140.3.verse: Herein, although none of the states belonging to the first jhāna exist in the second jhāna—

vsm1.4:140.4.verse: for the contact, etc. (see M III 25), in the first jhāna are one and here they are another—

vsm1.4:140.5.verse: it should be understood all the same that the phrase “with the stilling of applied and sustained thought” is expressed in this way in order to indicate that the attaining of the other jhānas, beginning with that of the second from the first, is effected by the surmounting of the gross factor in each case.

vsm1.4:141.1.verse: Internal: here one’s own internal is intended;

vsm1.4:141.2.verse: but that much is actually stated in the Vibhaṅga too with the words “internally in oneself” (Vibh 258).

vsm1.4:141.3.verse: And since one’s own internal is intended, the meaning here is this: born in oneself, generated in one’s own continuity.

vsm1.4:142.1.verse: Confidence: it is faith that is called confidence.

vsm1.4:142.2.verse: The jhāna “has confidence” because it is associated with confidence

vsm1.4:142.3.verse: as a cloth “has blue colour” because it is associated with blue colour.

vsm1.4:142.4.verse: Or alternatively, that jhāna is stated to “have confidence” because it makes the mind confident with the confidence possessed by it

vsm1.4:142.5.verse: and by stilling the disturbance created by applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:142.6.verse: And with this conception of the meaning the word construction must be taken as “confidence of mind.”

vsm1.4:142.7.verse: But with the first-mentioned conception of the meaning the words “of mind” must be construed with “singleness.”

vsm1.4:143.1.verse: Here is the construction of the meaning in that case. Unique (eka) it comes up (udeti), thus it is single (ekodi);

vsm1.4:143.2.verse: the meaning is, it comes up as the superlative, the best, because it is not overtopped by applied and sustained thought,

vsm1.4:143.3.verse: for the best is called “unique” in the world.

vsm1.4:143.4.verse: Or it is permissible to say that when deprived of applied and sustained thought it is unique, without companion.

vsm1.4:143.5.verse: Or alternatively: it evokes (udāyati) associated states, thus it is an evoker (udi); the meaning is, it arouses.

vsm1.4:143.6.verse: And that is unique (eka) in the sense of best, and it is an evoker (udi), thus it is a unique evoker (ekodi = single).

vsm1.4:143.7.verse: This is a term for concentration.

vsm1.4:143.8.verse: Then, since the second jhāna gives existingness to (bhāveti), augments, this single [thing], it “gives singleness” (ekodibhāva).

vsm1.4:143.9.verse: But as this single [thing] is a mind’s, not a being’s or a soul’s, so singleness of mind is said.

vsm1.4:144.1.verse: It might be asked: But does not this faith exist in the first jhāna too, and also this concentration with the name of the “single [thing]?”

vsm1.4:144.2.verse: Then why is only this second jhāna said to have confidence and singleness of mind?

vsm1.4:144.3.verse: It may be replied as follows: It is because that first jhāna [157] is not fully confident owing to the disturbance created by applied and sustained thought, like water ruffled by ripples and wavelets.

vsm1.4:144.4.verse: That is why, although faith does exist in it, it is not called “confidence.”

vsm1.4:144.5.verse: And there too concentration is not fully evident because of the lack of full confidence.

vsm1.4:144.6.verse: That is why it is not called “singleness” there.

vsm1.4:144.7.verse: But in this second jhāna faith is strong,

vsm1.4:144.8.verse: having got a footing in the absence of the impediments of applied and sustained thought; and concentration is also evident through having strong faith as its companion.

vsm1.4:144.9.verse: That may be understood as the reason why only this jhāna is described in this way.

vsm1.4:145.1.verse: But that much is actually stated in the Vibhaṅga too with the words: “‘Confidence’ is faith, having faith, trust, full confidence.

vsm1.4:145.2.verse: ‘Singleness of mind’ is steadiness of consciousness … right concentration” (Vibh 258).

vsm1.4:145.3.verse: And this commentary on the meaning should not be so understood as to conflict with the meaning stated in that way,

vsm1.4:145.4.verse: but on the contrary so as to agree and concur with it.

vsm1.4:146.1.verse: Without applied thought, without sustained thought: since it has been abandoned by development,

vsm1.4:146.2.verse: there is no applied thought in this, or of this, [jhāna], thus it is without applied thought.

vsm1.4:146.3.verse: The same explanation applies to sustained thought.

vsm1.4:146.4.verse: Also it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “So this applied thought and this sustained thought are quieted, quietened, stilled,

vsm1.4:146.5.verse: set at rest, set quite at rest,

vsm1.4:146.6.verse: done away with, quite done away with,

vsm1.4:146.7.verse: dried up, quite dried up, made an end of; hence it is said: without applied thought, without sustained thought” (Vibh 258).

vsm1.4:146.8.verse: Here it may be asked: Has not this meaning already been established

vsm1.4:146.9.verse: by the words “with the stilling of applied and sustained thought?” So why is it said again “without applied thought, without sustained thoughts?”

vsm1.4:146.10.verse: It may be replied: Yes, that meaning has already been established. But this does not indicate that meaning.

vsm1.4:146.11.verse: Did we not say earlier: “The phrase ‘with the stilling of applied and sustained thought’ is expressed in this way in order to indicate that the act of attaining the other jhānas, beginning with that of the second from the first, is effected by the surmounting of the gross factor in each case?” (§140).

vsm1.4:147.1.verse: Besides, this confidence comes about with the act of stilling, not the darkness of defilement, but the applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:147.2.verse: And the singleness comes about, not as in access jhāna with the abandoning of the hindrances, nor as in the first jhāna with the manifestation of the factors, but with the act of stilling the applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:147.3.verse: So that [first] clause indicates the cause of the confidence and singleness.

vsm1.4:147.4.verse: In the same way this jhāna is without applied thought and without sustained thought, not as in the third and fourth jhānas or as in eye-consciousness, etc., with just absence, but with the actual act of stilling the applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:147.5.verse: So that [first clause] also indicates the cause of the state without applied and sustained thought; it does not indicate the bare absence of applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:147.6.verse: [158] The bare absence of applied and sustained thought is indicated by this [second] clause,

vsm1.4:147.7.verse: namely, “without applied thought, without sustained thought.”

vsm1.4:147.8.verse: Consequently it needs to be stated notwithstanding that the first has already been stated.

vsm1.4:148.1.verse: Born of concentration: born of the first-jhāna concentration, or born of associated concentration, is the meaning.

vsm1.4:148.2.verse: Herein, although the first was born of associated concentration too,

vsm1.4:148.3.verse: still it is only this concentration that is quite worthy to be called “concentration” because of its complete confidence and extreme immobility due to absence of disturbance by applied and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:148.4.verse: So only this [jhāna] is called “born of concentration,” and that is in order to recommend it.

vsm1.4:148.5.verse: With happiness and bliss is as already explained.

vsm1.4:148.7.verse: Also second because entered upon second.

vsm1.4:149.1.verse: Then it was also said above which abandons two factors, possesses three factors (§139).

vsm1.4:149.2.verse: Herein, the abandoning of two factors should be understood as the abandoning of applied thought and sustained thought.

vsm1.4:149.3.verse: But while the hindrances are abandoned at the moment of the access of the first jhāna,

vsm1.4:149.4.verse: in the case of this jhāna the applied thought and sustained thought are not abandoned at the moment of its access.

vsm1.4:149.5.verse: It is only at the moment of actual absorption that the jhāna arises without them.

vsm1.4:149.6.verse: Hence they are called its factors of abandoning.

vsm1.4:150.1.verse: Its possession of three factors should be understood as the arising of the three, that is, happiness, bliss, and unification of mind.

vsm1.4:150.2.verse: So when it is said in the Vibhaṅga, “‘Jhāna’: confidence, happiness, bliss, unification of mind” (Vibh 258),

vsm1.4:150.3.verse: this is said figuratively in order to show that jhāna with its equipment.

vsm1.4:150.4.verse: But, excepting the confidence, this jhāna has literally

vsm1.4:150.5.verse: three factors qua factors that have attained to the characteristic of lighting (see §119),

vsm1.4:150.6.verse: according as it is said: “What is jhāna of three factors on that occasion?

vsm1.4:150.7.verse: It is happiness, bliss, unification of mind” (Vibh 263).

vsm1.4:150.8.verse: The rest is as in the case of the first jhāna.

vsm1.4:180.1.verse: Once this has been obtained in this way, and once he has mastery in the five ways already described, then on emerging from the now familiar third jhāna,

vsm1.4:180.2.verse: he can regard the flaws in it thus: “This attainment is threatened by the nearness of happiness; ‘Whatever there is in it of mental concern about bliss proclaims its grossness’ (D I 37; see Ch. IX, n. 20),

vsm1.4:180.3.verse: and its factors are weakened by the grossness of the bliss so expressed.”

vsm1.4:180.4.verse: He can bring the fourth jhāna to mind as quieter

vsm1.4:180.5.verse: and so end his attachment to the third jhāna and set about doing what is needed for attaining the fourth.

vsm1.4:181.1.verse: When he has emerged from the third jhāna, the bliss, in other words, the mental joy, appears gross to him as he reviews the jhāna factors with mindfulness and full awareness,

vsm1.4:181.2.verse: while the equanimity as feeling and the unification of mind appear peaceful. Then, as he brings that same sign to mind as “earth, earth” again and again with the purpose of abandoning the gross factor and obtaining the peaceful factors,

vsm1.4:181.4.verse: there arises in him mind-door adverting with that same earth kasiṇa as its object, interrupting the life-continuum.

vsm1.4:181.5.verse: After that either four or five impulsions impel on that same object, [165]

vsm1.4:181.6.verse: the last one of which is an impulsion of the fine-material sphere belonging to the fourth jhāna.

vsm1.4:181.7.verse: The rest are of the kinds already stated (§74).

vsm1.4:182.1.verse: But there is this difference: blissful (pleasant) feeling is not a condition, as repetition condition, for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,

vsm1.4:182.2.verse: and [the preliminary work] must be aroused in the case of the fourth jhāna with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

vsm1.4:182.3.verse: consequently these [consciousnesses of the preliminary work] are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,

vsm1.4:182.4.verse: and here happiness vanishes simply owing to their association with equanimity.

vsm1.4:183.1.verse: And at this point, “With the abandoning of pleasure and pain

vsm1.4:183.2.verse: and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief

vsm1.4:183.3.verse: he enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity” (Vibh 245),

vsm1.4:183.4.verse: and so he has attained the fourth jhāna, which abandons one factor, possesses two factors,

vsm1.4:183.5.verse: is good in three ways, possesses ten characteristics, and is of the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.4:184.1.verse: Herein, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain: with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain.

vsm1.4:184.2.verse: With the previous: which took place before, not in the moment of the fourth jhāna.

vsm1.4:184.3.verse: Disappearance of joy and grief: with the previous disappearance of the two, that is, mental bliss (pleasure) and mental pain;

vsm1.4:184.4.verse: with the abandoning, is what is meant.

vsm1.4:185.1.verse: But when does the abandoning of these take place?

vsm1.4:185.2.verse: At the moment of access of the four jhānas.

vsm1.4:185.3.verse: For [mental] joy is only abandoned at the moment of the fourth-jhāna access,

vsm1.4:185.4.verse: while [bodily] pain, [mental] grief, and [bodily] bliss (pleasure) are abandoned respectively at the moments of access of the first, second, and third jhānas.

vsm1.4:185.5.verse: So although the order in which they are abandoned is not actually mentioned,

vsm1.4:185.6.verse: nevertheless the abandoning of the pleasure, pain, joy, and grief, is stated here according to the order in which the faculties are summarized in the Indriya Vibhaṅga (Vibh 122).

vsm1.4:186.1.verse: But if these are only abandoned at the moments of access of the several jhānas,

vsm1.4:186.2.verse: why is their cessation said to. take place in the jhāna itself in the following passage: “And where does the arisen pain faculty cease without remainder?

vsm1.4:186.3.verse: Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things, a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is … born of seclusion.

vsm1.4:186.4.verse: It is here that the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder …

vsm1.4:186.5.verse: Where does the arisen grief faculty [cease without remainder? … in the second jhāna] … Where does the arisen pleasure faculty [cease without remainder? … in the third jhāna] … Where does the arisen joy faculty cease without remainder? [166]

vsm1.4:186.6.verse: Here, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain [and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief] a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which … has mindfulness purified by equanimity.

vsm1.4:186.7.verse: It is here that the arisen joy faculty ceases without remainder” (S V 213–15) evaṃ jhānesveva nirodho vutto?

vsm1.4:186.8.verse: It is said in that way there referring to reinforced cessation.

vsm1.4:186.9.verse: For in the first jhāna, etc., it is their reinforced cessation, not just their cessation, that takes place.

vsm1.4:186.10.verse: At the moment of access it is just their cessation, not their reinforced cessation, that takes place.

vsm1.4:187.1.verse: For accordingly, during the first jhāna access, which has multiple adverting,

vsm1.4:187.2.verse: there could be rearising of the [bodily] pain faculty[^49] due to contact with gadflies, flies, etc.

vsm1.4:187.3.verse: or the discomfort of an uneven seat, though that pain faculty had already ceased, but not so during absorption.

vsm1.4:187.4.verse: Or else, though it has ceased during access, it has not absolutely ceased there since it is not quite beaten out by opposition.

vsm1.4:187.5.verse: But during absorption the whole body is showered with bliss owing to pervasion by happiness.

vsm1.4:187.6.verse: And the pain faculty has absolutely ceased in one whose body is showered with bliss, since it is beaten out then by opposition.

vsm1.4:188.1.verse: And during the second-jhāna access too, which has multiple advertings, there could be rearising of the [mental] grief faculty, although it had already ceased there,

vsm1.4:188.2.verse: because it arises when there is bodily weariness and mental vexation, which have applied thought and sustained thought as their condition,

vsm1.4:188.3.verse: but it does not arise when applied and sustained thought are absent.

vsm1.4:188.4.verse: When it arises, it does so in the presence of applied and sustained thought, and they are not abandoned in the second-jhāna access;

vsm1.4:188.5.verse: but this is not so in the second jhāna itself because its conditions are abandoned there.

vsm1.4:189.1.verse: Likewise in the third-jhāna access there could be rearising of the abandoned [bodily] pleasure faculty

vsm1.4:189.2.verse: in one whose body was pervaded by the superior materiality originated by the [consciousness associated with the] happiness.

vsm1.4:189.3.verse: But not so in the third jhāna itself.

vsm1.4:189.4.verse: For in the third jhāna the happiness that is a condition for the [bodily] bliss (pleasure) has ceased entirely.

vsm1.4:189.5.verse: Likewise in the fourth-jhāna access there could be re-arising of the abandoned [mental] joy faculty

vsm1.4:189.6.verse: because of its nearness and because it has not been properly surmounted owing to the absence of equanimity brought to absorption strength.

vsm1.4:189.7.verse: But not so in the fourth jhāna itself.

vsm1.4:189.8.verse: And that is why in each case (§186) the words “without remainder” are included thus:

vsm1.4:189.9.verse: “It is here that the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder.”

vsm1.4:190.1.verse: Here it may be asked: Then if these kinds of feeling are abandoned in the access in this way, why are they brought in here?

vsm1.4:190.2.verse: It is done so that they can be readily grasped.

vsm1.4:190.3.verse: For the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling described here by the words “which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure” is subtle,

vsm1.4:190.4.verse: hard to recognize and not readily grasped.

vsm1.4:190.5.verse: So just as, when a cattle-herd[^50] wants to catch a refractory ox that cannot be caught at all by approaching it,

vsm1.4:190.6.verse: he collects all the cattle into one pen [167]

vsm1.4:190.7.verse: and lets them out one by one,

vsm1.4:190.8.verse: and then [he says] “That is it; catch it,” and so it gets caught as well, so too the Blessed One has collected all these [five kinds of feeling] together so that they can be grasped readily;

vsm1.4:190.9.verse: for when they are shown collected together in this way, then what is not [bodily] pleasure (bliss) or [bodily] pain or [mental] joy or [mental] grief

vsm1.4:190.10.verse: can still be grasped in this way: “This is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

vsm1.4:191.1.verse: Besides, this may be understood as said in order to show the condition for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant mind-deliverance.

vsm1.4:191.2.verse: For the abandoning of [bodily] pain, etc., are conditions for that,

vsm1.4:191.3.verse: according as it is said: “There are four conditions, friend, for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant mind-deliverance.

vsm1.4:191.4.verse: Here, friend, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna … equanimity.

vsm1.4:191.5.verse: These are the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant mind-deliverance” (M I 296).

vsm1.4:192.1.verse: Or alternatively, just as, although mistaken view of individuality, etc., have already been abandoned in the earlier paths, they are nevertheless mentioned as abandoned in the description of the third path for the purpose of recommending it (cf. §155),

vsm1.4:192.2.verse: so too these kinds of feeling can be understood as mentioned here for the purpose of recommending this jhāna.

vsm1.4:192.3.verse: Or alternatively, they can be understood as mentioned for the purpose of showing that greed and hate are very far away

vsm1.4:192.4.verse: owing to the removal of their conditions;

vsm1.4:192.5.verse: for of these, pleasure (bliss) is a condition for joy, and joy for greed;

vsm1.4:192.6.verse: pain is a condition for grief and grief for hate.

vsm1.4:192.7.verse: So with the removal of pleasure (bliss), etc., greed and hate are very far away since they are removed along with their conditions.

vsm1.4:193.1.verse: Which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure: no pain owing to absence of pain; no pleasure owing to absence of pleasure (bliss).

vsm1.4:193.2.verse: By this he indicates the third kind of feeling

vsm1.4:193.3.verse: that is in opposition both to pain and to pleasure, not the mere absence of pain and pleasure.

vsm1.4:193.4.verse: This third kind of feeling named neither-pain-nor-pleasure is also called “equanimity.”

vsm1.4:193.5.verse: It has the characteristic of experiencing what is contrary to both the desirable and the undesirable.

vsm1.4:193.8.verse: Its proximate cause should be understood as the cessation of pleasure (bliss).

vsm1.4:194.1.verse: And has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity: has purity of mindfulness brought about by equanimity.

vsm1.4:194.2.verse: For the mindfulness in this jhāna is quite purified, and its purification is effected by equanimity, not by anything else.

vsm1.4:194.3.verse: That is why it is said to have purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

vsm1.4:194.4.verse: Also it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “This mindfulness is cleared, purified, clarified, by equanimity;

vsm1.4:194.5.verse: hence it is said to have purity of mindfulness due to equanimity” (Vibh 261).

vsm1.4:194.6.verse: And the equanimity due to which there comes to be this purity of mindfulness should be understood as specific neutrality in meaning.

vsm1.4:194.7.verse: And not only mindfulness is purified by it here, but also all associated states.

vsm1.4:194.8.verse: However, the teaching is given under the heading of mindfulness.

vsm1.4:195.1.verse: Herein, this equanimity exists in the three lower jhānas too;

vsm1.4:195.2.verse: but just as, although a crescent moon exists by day but is not purified or clear since it is outshone by the sun’s radiance in the daytime or since it is deprived of the night, which is its ally owing to gentleness and owing to helpfulness to it,

vsm1.4:195.3.verse: so too, this crescent moon of equanimity consisting in specific neutrality exists in the first jhāna, etc., but it is not purified since it is outshone by the glare of the opposing states consisting in applied thought, etc., and since it is deprived of the night of equanimity-as-feeling for its ally.

vsm1.4:195.4.verse: And because it is not purified,

vsm1.4:195.5.verse: the conascent mindfulness and other states are not purified either, like the unpurified crescent moon’s radiance by day.

vsm1.4:195.6.verse: That is why no one among these [first three jhānas] is said to have purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

vsm1.4:195.7.verse: But here this crescent moon consisting in specific neutrality is utterly pure because it is not outshone by the glare of the opposing states consisting in applied thought, etc., and because it has the night of equanimity-as-feeling for its ally.

vsm1.4:195.9.verse: the conascent mindfulness and other states are purified and clear also, like the purified crescent moon’s radiance.

vsm1.4:195.10.verse: That, it should be understood, is why only this jhāna is said to have purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

vsm1.4:196.1.verse: Fourth: it is fourth in numerical series;

vsm1.4:196.2.verse: and it is fourth because it is entered upon fourth.

vsm1.4:197.1.verse: Then it was said, which abandons one factor, possesses two factors (§183);

vsm1.4:197.2.verse: here the abandoning of the one factor should be understood as the abandoning of joy.

vsm1.4:197.3.verse: But that joy is actually abandoned in the first impulsions of the same cognitive series (cf. §185).

vsm1.4:197.4.verse: Hence it is called its factor of abandoning.

vsm1.4:197.5.verse: The possession of the two factors should be understood as the arising of the two, namely, equanimity as feeling and unification of mind.

vsm1.4:197.6.verse: The rest is as stated in the case of the first jhāna.

vsm1.4:197.7.verse: This, in the first place, is according to the fourfold reckoning of jhāna.

vsm1.4:198.1.verse: When, however, he is developing fivefold jhāna, then, on emerging from the now familiar first jhāna,

vsm1.4:198.2.verse: he can regard the flaws in it in this way: “This attainment is threatened by the nearness of the hindrances, and its factors are weakened by the grossness of applied thought.” [169]

vsm1.4:198.3.verse: He can bring the second jhāna to mind as quieter

vsm1.4:198.4.verse: and so end his attachment to the first jhāna and set about doing what is needed for attaining the second.

vsm1.4:199.1.verse: Now, he emerges from the first jhāna mindfully and fully aware;

vsm1.4:199.2.verse: and only applied thought appears gross to him as he reviews the jhāna factors, while the sustained thought, etc., appear peaceful.

vsm1.4:199.3.verse: Then, as he brings that same sign to mind as “earth, earth” again and again with the purpose of abandoning the gross factor and obtaining the peaceful factors,

vsm1.4:199.4.verse: the second jhāna arises in him in the way already described.

vsm1.4:199.5.verse: Its factor of abandoning is applied thought only.

vsm1.4:199.6.verse: The four beginning with sustained thought are the factors that it possesses.

vsm1.4:199.7.verse: The rest is as already stated.

vsm1.4:200.1.verse: When this has been obtained in this way, and once he has mastery in the five ways already described, then on emerging from the now familiar second jhāna

vsm1.4:200.2.verse: he can regard the flaws in it in this way: “This attainment is threatened by the nearness of applied thought, and its factors are weakened by the grossness of sustained thought.”

vsm1.4:200.3.verse: He can bring the third jhāna to mind as quieter

vsm1.4:200.4.verse: and so end his attachment to the second jhāna and set about doing what is needed for attaining the third.

vsm1.4:201.1.verse: Now, he emerges from the second jhāna mindfully and fully aware;

vsm1.4:201.2.verse: only sustained thought appears gross to him as he reviews the jhāna factors, while happiness, etc., appear peaceful.

vsm1.4:201.3.verse: Then, as he brings that same sign to mind as “earth, earth” again and again with the purpose of abandoning the gross factor and obtaining the peaceful factors,

vsm1.4:201.4.verse: the third jhāna arises in him in the way already described.

vsm1.4:201.5.verse: Its factor of abandoning is sustained thought only.

vsm1.4:201.6.verse: The three beginning with happiness, as in the second jhāna in the fourfold reckoning, are the factors that it possesses.

vsm1.4:201.7.verse: The rest is as already stated.

vsm1.4:202.1.verse: So that which is the second in the fourfold reckoning

vsm1.4:202.2.verse: becomes the second and third in the fivefold reckoning by being divided into two.

vsm1.4:202.3.verse: And those which are the third and fourth in the former reckoning become the fourth and fifth in this reckoning.

vsm1.4:202.4.verse: The first remains the first in each case.

vsm1.4:202.5.verse: The fourth chapter called “The Description of the Earth Kasiṇa” in the Treatise on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

vsm1.5:1.1.verse: Now, the water kasiṇa comes next after the earth kasiṇa (III.105).

vsm1.5:1.3.verse: One who wants to develop the water kasiṇa should, as in the case of the earth kasiṇa,

vsm1.5:1.4.verse: seat himself comfortably and apprehend the sign in water that “is either made up or not made up,” etc.;

vsm1.5:1.5.verse: and so all the rest should be repeated in detail (IV.22).

vsm1.5:1.6.verse: And as in this case, so with all those that follow [in this chapter].

vsm1.5:1.7.verse: We shall in fact not repeat even this much and shall only point out what is different.

vsm1.5:2.1.verse: Here too, when someone has had practice in previous [lives],

vsm1.5:2.2.verse: the sign arises for him in water that is not made up, such as a pool, a lake, a lagoon, or the ocean

vsm1.5:2.3.verse: as in the case of the Elder Cūḷa-Sīva.

vsm1.5:2.4.verse: The venerable one, it seems, thought to abandon gain and honour and live a secluded life.

vsm1.5:2.5.verse: He boarded a ship at Mahātittha (Mannar) and sailed to Jambudīpa (India).

vsm1.5:2.6.verse: As he gazed at the ocean meanwhile, the kasiṇa sign, the counterpart of that ocean, arose in him.

vsm1.5:3.1.verse: Someone with no such previous practice should guard against the four faults of a kasiṇa (IV.24)

vsm1.5:3.2.verse: and not apprehend the water as one of the colours, blue, yellow, red or white.

vsm1.5:3.3.verse: He should fill a bowl or a four-footed water pot to the brim with water uncontaminated by soil, taken in the open through a clean cloth [strainer], or with any other clear unturbid water.

vsm1.5:3.4.verse: He should put it in a screened place on the outskirts of the monastery as already described and seat himself comfortably.

vsm1.5:3.5.verse: He should neither review its colour

vsm1.5:3.6.verse: nor bring its characteristic to mind.

vsm1.5:3.7.verse: Apprehending the colour as belonging to its physical support,

vsm1.5:3.8.verse: he should set his mind on the [name] concept as the most outstanding mental datum,

vsm1.5:3.9.verse: and using any among the [various] names for water (āpo) such as “rain” (ambu), “liquid” (udaka), “dew” (vāri), “fluid” (salila),

vsm1.5:3.10.verse: he should develop [the kasiṇa] by using [preferably] the obvious “water, water.”

vsm1.5:4.1.verse: As he develops it in this way, the two signs eventually arise in him in the way already described.

vsm1.5:4.2.verse: Here, however, the learning sign has the appearance of moving.

vsm1.5:4.3.verse: If the water has bubbles of froth mixed with it,

vsm1.5:4.4.verse: the learning sign has the same appearance,

vsm1.5:4.5.verse: and it is evident as a fault in the kasiṇa.

vsm1.5:4.6.verse: But the counterpart sign appears inactive, like a crystal fan set in space, like the disk of a looking-glass made of crystal.

vsm1.5:4.7.verse: With the appearance of that sign he reaches access jhāna and the jhāna tetrad and pentad in the way already described.

vsm1.5:5.1.verse: Anyone who wants to develop the fire kasiṇa should apprehend the sign in fire.

vsm1.5:5.2.verse: Herein, when someone with merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:5.3.verse: is apprehending the sign, it arises in him in any sort of fire, not made up, as he looks at the fiery combustion in a lamp’s flame or in a furnace or in a place for baking bowls or in a forest conflagration,

vsm1.5:5.4.verse: as in the Elder Cittagutta’s case.

vsm1.5:5.5.verse: The sign arose in that elder as he was looking at a lamp’s flame while he was in the Uposatha house on the day of preaching the Dhamma.

vsm1.5:6.1.verse: Anyone else should make one up.

vsm1.5:6.2.verse: Here are the directions for making it.

vsm1.5:6.3.verse: He should split up some damp heartwood, dry it, and break it up into short lengths.

vsm1.5:6.4.verse: He should go to a suitable tree root or to a shed and there make a pile in the way done for baking bowls, and have it lit.

vsm1.5:6.5.verse: He should make a hole a span and four fingers wide in a rush mat or a piece of leather or a cloth,

vsm1.5:6.6.verse: and after hanging it in front of the fire, he should sit down in the way already described.

vsm1.5:6.7.verse: Instead of giving attention to the grass and sticks below or the smoke above,

vsm1.5:6.8.verse: he should apprehend the sign in the dense combustion in the middle.

vsm1.5:7.1.verse: He should not review the colour as blue or yellow, etc.,

vsm1.5:7.2.verse: or give attention to its characteristic as heat, etc.,

vsm1.5:7.3.verse: but taking the colour as belonging to its physical support,

vsm1.5:7.4.verse: and setting his mind on the [name] concept as the most outstanding mental datum,

vsm1.5:7.5.verse: and using any among the names for fire (tejo) such as “the Bright One” (pāvaka), “the Leaver of the Black Trail” (kaṇhavattani), “the Knower of Creatures” (jātaveda), “the Altar of Sacrifice” (hutāsana), etc.,

vsm1.5:7.6.verse: he should develop [the kasiṇa] by using [preferably] the obvious “fire, fire.”

vsm1.5:8.1.verse: As he develops it in this way the two signs eventually arise in him as already described.

vsm1.5:8.2.verse: Herein, the learning sign appears like [the fire to keep] sinking down as the flame keeps detaching itself.

vsm1.5:8.3.verse: But when someone apprehends it in a kasiṇa that is not made up, any fault in the kasiṇa is evident [in the learning sign],

vsm1.5:8.4.verse: and any firebrand, or pile of embers or ashes, or smoke appears in it.

vsm1.5:8.5.verse: The counterpart sign appears motionless like a piece of red cloth set in space, like a gold fan, like a gold column.

vsm1.5:8.6.verse: With its appearance he reaches access jhāna and the jhāna tetrad and pentad in the way already described.

vsm1.5:9.1.verse: Anyone who wants to develop the air kasiṇa should apprehend the sign in air.

vsm1.5:9.2.verse: And that is done either by sight or by touch.

vsm1.5:9.3.verse: For this is said in the Commentaries:

vsm1.5:9.4.verse: “One who is learning the air kasiṇa apprehends the sign in air.

vsm1.5:9.5.verse: He notices the tops of [growing] sugarcane moving to and fro;

vsm1.5:9.6.verse: or he notices the tops of bamboos, or the tops of trees, or the ends of the hair, moving to and fro;

vsm1.5:9.7.verse: or he notices the touch of it on the body.”

vsm1.5:10.1.verse: So when he sees sugarcanes with dense foliage standing with tops level or bamboos or trees,

vsm1.5:10.2.verse: or else hair four fingers long on a man’s head,

vsm1.5:10.4.verse: he should establish mindfulness in this way: “This wind is striking on this place.”

vsm1.5:10.5.verse: Or he can establish mindfulness where the wind strikes a part of his body after entering by a window opening or by a crack in a wall,

vsm1.5:10.6.verse: and using any among the names for wind (vāta) beginning with “wind” (vāta), “breeze” (māluta), “blowing” (anila),

vsm1.5:10.7.verse: he should develop [the kasiṇa] by using [preferably] the obvious “air, air.”

vsm1.5:11.1.verse: Here the learning sign appears to move like the swirl of hot [steam] on rice gruel just withdrawn from an oven.

vsm1.5:11.2.verse: The counterpart sign is quiet and motionless.

vsm1.5:11.3.verse: The rest should be understood in the way already described.

vsm1.5:12.1.verse: Next it is said [in the Commentaries]: “One who is learning the blue kasiṇa apprehends the sign in blue,

vsm1.5:12.2.verse: whether in a flower or in a cloth or in a colour element.”

vsm1.5:12.3.verse: Firstly, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:12.4.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees a bush with blue flowers, or such flowers spread out on a place of offering, or any blue cloth or gem.

vsm1.5:13.1.verse: But anyone else should take flowers such as blue lotuses, girikaṇṇikā (morning glory) flowers, etc.,

vsm1.5:13.2.verse: and spread them out to fill a tray or a flat basket completely so that no stamen or stalk shows or with only their petals.

vsm1.5:13.3.verse: Or he can fill it with blue cloth bunched up together;

vsm1.5:13.4.verse: or he can fasten the cloth over the rim of the tray or basket like the covering of a drum.

vsm1.5:13.5.verse: Or he can make a kasiṇa disk, either portable as described under the earth kasiṇa or on a wall, with one of the colour elements such as bronze-green, leaf-green, añjana-ointment black,

vsm1.5:13.6.verse: surrounding it with a different colour.

vsm1.5:13.7.verse: After that, he should bring it to mind as “blue, blue” in the way already described under the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.5:14.1.verse: And here too any fault in the kasiṇa is evident in the learning sign;

vsm1.5:14.2.verse: the stamens and stalks and the gaps between the petals, etc., are apparent.

vsm1.5:14.3.verse: The counterpart sign appears like a crystal fan in space, free from the kasiṇa disk.

vsm1.5:14.4.verse: The rest should be understood as already described.

vsm1.5:15.2.verse: for this is said: “One who is learning the yellow kasiṇa apprehends the sign in yellow,

vsm1.5:15.3.verse: either in a flower or in a cloth or in a colour element.”

vsm1.5:15.4.verse: Therefore here too, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:15.5.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees a flowering bush or flowers spread out, or yellow cloth or colour element,

vsm1.5:15.6.verse: as in the case of the Elder Cittagutta.

vsm1.5:15.7.verse: That venerable one, it seems, saw an offering being made on the flower altar, with pattaṅga flowers at Cittalapabbata,

vsm1.5:15.8.verse: and as soon as he saw it the sign arose in him the size of the flower altar.

vsm1.5:16.1.verse: Anyone else should make a kasiṇa, in the way described for the blue kasiṇa, with kaṇikāra flowers, etc., or with yellow cloth or with a colour element.

vsm1.5:16.2.verse: He should bring it to mind as “yellow, yellow.”

vsm1.5:17.2.verse: for this is said: “One who is learning the red kasiṇa apprehends the sign in red,

vsm1.5:17.3.verse: either in a flower or in a cloth or in a colour element.”

vsm1.5:17.4.verse: Therefore here too, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:17.5.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees a bandhujīvaka (hibiscus) bush, etc., in flower, or such flowers spread out, or a red cloth or gem or colour element.

vsm1.5:18.1.verse: But anyone else should make a kasiṇa, in the way already described for the blue kasiṇa, with jayasumana flowers or bandhujīvaka or red koraṇḍaka flowers, etc., or with red cloth or with a colour element.

vsm1.5:18.2.verse: He should bring it to mind as “red, red.”

vsm1.5:19.1.verse: Of the white kasiṇa it is said: “One who is learning the white kasiṇa apprehends the sign in white,

vsm1.5:19.2.verse: either in a flower or in a cloth or in a colour element.”

vsm1.5:19.3.verse: So firstly, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:19.4.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees a flowering bush of such a kind or vassikasumana (jasmine) flowers, etc., spread out, or a heap of white lotuses or lilies, white cloth or colour element;

vsm1.5:19.5.verse: and it also arises in a tin disk, a silver disk, and the moon’s disk.

vsm1.5:20.1.verse: Anyone else should make a kasiṇa, in the way already described for the blue kasiṇa, with the white flowers already mentioned, or with cloth or colour element.

vsm1.5:20.2.verse: He should bring it to mind as “white, white.”

vsm1.5:21.1.verse: Of the light kasiṇa it is said: “One who is learning the light kasiṇa apprehends the sign in light

vsm1.5:21.2.verse: in a hole in a wall, or in a keyhole, or in a window opening.”

vsm1.5:21.3.verse: So firstly, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:21.4.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees the circle thrown on a wall or a floor by sunlight or moonlight entering through a hole in a wall, etc.,

vsm1.5:21.5.verse: or when he sees a circle thrown on the ground by sunlight or moonlight coming through a gap in the branches of a dense-leaved tree or through a gap in a hut made of closely packed branches.

vsm1.5:22.1.verse: Anyone else should use that same kind of circle of luminosity just described,

vsm1.5:22.2.verse: developing it as “luminosity, luminosity” or “light, light.”

vsm1.5:22.3.verse: If he cannot do so, he can light a lamp inside a pot,

vsm1.5:22.4.verse: close the pot’s mouth, make a hole in it and place it with the hole facing a wall.

vsm1.5:22.5.verse: The lamplight coming out of the hole throws a circle on the wall.

vsm1.5:22.6.verse: He should develop that as “light, light.”

vsm1.5:22.7.verse: This lasts longer than the other kinds.

vsm1.5:23.1.verse: Here the learning sign is like the circle thrown on the wall or the ground.

vsm1.5:23.2.verse: The counterpart sign is like a compact bright cluster of lights.

vsm1.5:24.1.verse: Of the limited-space kasiṇa it is said: “One who is learning the space kasiṇa apprehends the sign

vsm1.5:24.2.verse: in a hole in a wall, or in a keyhole, or in a window opening.”

vsm1.5:24.3.verse: So firstly, when someone has merit, having had previous practice,

vsm1.5:24.4.verse: the sign arises in him when he sees any [such gap as a] hole in a wall.

vsm1.5:25.1.verse: Anyone else should make a hole a span and four fingers broad in a well-thatched hut, or in a piece of leather, or in a rush mat, and so on.

vsm1.5:25.2.verse: He should develop one of these, or a hole such as a hole in a wall, as “space, space.”

vsm1.5:26.1.verse: Here the learning sign resembles the hole together with the wall, etc., that surrounds it.

vsm1.5:26.3.verse: The counterpart sign appears only as a circle of space.

vsm1.5:26.5.verse: The rest should be understood as described under the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.5:27.1.verse:
He with Ten Powers, who all things did see,
Tells ten kasiṇas, each of which can be
The cause of fourfold and of fivefold jhāna,
The fine-material sphere’s own master key.

vsm1.5:27.2.verse:
Now, knowing their descriptions and the way
To tackle each and how they are developed,
There are some further points that will repay
Study, each with its special part to play.

vsm1.5:28.1.verse: Of these, the earth kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as the state described as “Having been one, he becomes many” (D I 78), etc.,

vsm1.5:28.2.verse: and stepping or standing or sitting on space or on water by creating earth,

vsm1.5:28.3.verse: and the acquisition of the bases of mastery (M II 13) by the limited and measureless method.

vsm1.5:29.1.verse: The water kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as diving in and out of the earth (D I 78),

vsm1.5:29.2.verse: causing rain, storms, creating rivers and seas,

vsm1.5:29.3.verse: making the earth and rocks and palaces quake (M I 253).

vsm1.5:30.1.verse: The fire kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as smoking, flaming, causing showers of sparks,

vsm1.5:30.2.verse: countering fire with fire, ability to burn only what one wants to burn (S IV 290),

vsm1.5:30.3.verse: causing light for the purpose of seeing visible objects with the divine eye,

vsm1.5:30.4.verse: burning up the body by means of the fire element at the time of attaining Nibbāna (M-a IV 196).

vsm1.5:31.1.verse: The air kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as going with the speed of the wind, causing wind storms.

vsm1.5:32.1.verse: The blue kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as creating black forms, causing darkness,

vsm1.5:32.2.verse: acquisition of the bases of mastery by the method of fairness and ugliness,

vsm1.5:32.3.verse: and attainment of the liberation by the beautiful (see M II 12)

vsm1.5:33.1.verse: The yellow kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as creating yellow forms, resolving that something shall be gold (S I 116),

vsm1.5:33.2.verse: acquisition of the bases of mastery in the way stated,

vsm1.5:33.3.verse: and attainment of the liberation by the beautiful.

vsm1.5:34.1.verse: The red kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as creating red forms,

vsm1.5:34.2.verse: acquisition of the bases of mastery in the way stated,

vsm1.5:34.3.verse: and attainment of the liberation by the beautiful.

vsm1.5:35.1.verse: The white kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as creating white forms,

vsm1.5:35.2.verse: banishing stiffness and torpor, dispelling darkness,

vsm1.5:35.3.verse: causing light for the purpose of seeing visible objects with the divine eye.

vsm1.5:36.1.verse: The light kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as creating luminous forms,

vsm1.5:36.2.verse: banishing stiffness and torpor, dispelling darkness,

vsm1.5:36.3.verse: causing light for the purpose of seeing visible objects with the divine eye.

vsm1.5:37.1.verse: The space kasiṇa is the basis for such powers as revealing the hidden,

vsm1.5:37.2.verse: maintaining postures inside the earth and rocks by creating space inside them,

vsm1.5:37.3.verse: travelling unobstructed through walls, and so on.

vsm1.5:38.1.verse: The classification “above, below, around, exclusive, measureless” applies to all kasiṇas;

vsm1.5:38.2.verse: for this is said: “He perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, around, exclusive, measureless” (M II 14), and so on.

vsm1.5:39.1.verse: Herein, above is upwards towards the sky’s level.

vsm1.5:39.2.verse: Below is downwards towards the earth’s level.

vsm1.5:39.3.verse: Around is marked off all around like the perimeter of a field.

vsm1.5:39.4.verse: For one extends a kasiṇa upwards only, another downwards, another all round;

vsm1.5:39.5.verse: or for some reason another projects it thus

vsm1.5:39.6.verse: as one who wants to see visible objects with the divine eye projects light.

vsm1.5:39.8.verse: The word exclusive, however, shows that anyone such state has nothing to do with any other.

vsm1.5:39.9.verse: Just as there is water and nothing else in all directions for one who is actually in water,

vsm1.5:39.10.verse: so too, the earth kasiṇa is the earth kasiṇa only;

vsm1.5:39.11.verse: it has nothing in common with any other kasiṇa.

vsm1.5:39.14.verse: He is intent upon the entirety with his mind,

vsm1.5:39.15.verse: taking no measurements in this way: “This is its beginning, this is its middle.”

vsm1.5:40.1.verse: No kasiṇa can be developed by any living being described as follows: “Beings hindered by kamma, by defilement or by kamma-result,

vsm1.5:40.2.verse: who lack faith, zeal and understanding,

vsm1.5:40.3.verse: will be incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness in profitable states” (Vibh 341).

vsm1.5:41.1.verse: Herein, the words hindered by kamma refer to those who possess bad kamma entailing immediate effect [on rebirth].

vsm1.5:41.2.verse: By defilement: who have fixed wrong view or are hermaphrodites or eunuchs.

vsm1.5:41.3.verse: By kamma-result: who have had a rebirth-linking with no [profitable] root-cause or with only two [profitable] root-causes.

vsm1.5:41.4.verse: Lack faith: are destitute of faith in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.

vsm1.5:41.5.verse: Zeal: are destitute of zeal for the unopposed way.

vsm1.5:41.6.verse: Understanding: are destitute of mundane and supramundane right view.

vsm1.5:41.7.verse: Will be incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness in profitable states

vsm1.5:41.8.verse: means that they are incapable of entering into the noble path called “certainty” and “rightness in profitable states.”

vsm1.5:42.1.verse: And this does not apply only to kasiṇas; for none of them will succeed in developing any meditation subject at all.

vsm1.5:42.2.verse: So the task of devotion to a meditation subject must be undertaken by a clansman who has no hindrance by kamma-result,

vsm1.5:42.3.verse: who shuns hindrance by kamma and by defilement,

vsm1.5:42.4.verse: and who fosters faith, zeal and understanding by listening to the Dhamma, frequenting good men, and so on.

vsm1.5:42.5.verse: The fifth chapter called “The Description of the Remaining Kasiṇas” in the Treatise on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

vsm1.6:1.1.verse: Now, ten kinds of foulness, [as corpses] without consciousness, were listed next after the kasiṇas thus:

vsm1.6:1.2.verse: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut up, the gnawed,

vsm1.6:1.3.verse: the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm infested, a skeleton (III.105).

vsm1.6:1.4.verse: *The bloated*: it is bloated (*uddhumāta*) because bloated by gradual dilation and swelling after (*uddhaṃ*) the close of life, as a bellows is with wind.

vsm1.6:1.5.verse: What is bloated (*uddhumāta*) is the same as “the bloated” (*uddhumātaka*).

vsm1.6:1.6.verse: Or alternatively, what is bloated (*uddhumāta*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the bloated” (*uddhumātaka*).

vsm1.6:1.7.verse: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.

vsm1.6:2.1.verse: *The livid*: what has patchy discolouration is called livid (*vinīla*).

vsm1.6:2.2.verse: What is livid is the same as “the livid” (*vinīlaka*).

vsm1.6:2.3.verse: Or alternatively, what is livid (*vinīla*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the livid” (*vinīlaka*).[^1]

vsm1.6:2.4.verse: This is a term for a corpse that is reddish-coloured in places where flesh is prominent,

vsm1.6:2.5.verse: whitish-coloured in places where pus has collected,

vsm1.6:2.7.verse: as if draped with blue-black cloth in the blue-black places.

vsm1.6:3.1.verse: *The festering*: what is trickling with pus in broken places is festering (*vipubba*).

vsm1.6:3.2.verse: What is festering is the same as “the festering” (*vipubbaka*).

vsm1.6:3.3.verse: Or alternatively, what is festering (*vipubba*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the festering” (*vipubbaka*).

vsm1.6:3.4.verse: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.

vsm1.6:4.1.verse: *The cut up*: what has been opened up[^2] by cutting it in two is called cut up (*vicchidda*).

vsm1.6:4.2.verse: What is cut up is the same as “the cut up” (*vicchiddaka*).

vsm1.6:4.3.verse: Or alternatively, what is cut up (*vicchidda*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the cut up” (*vicchiddaka*).

vsm1.6:4.4.verse: This is a term for a corpse cut in the middle.

vsm1.6:5.1.verse: *The gnawed*: what has been chewed here and there in various ways by dogs, jackals, etc., is what is gnawed (*vikkhāyita*).

vsm1.6:5.2.verse: What is gnawed is the same as “the gnawed” (*vikkhāyitaka*).

vsm1.6:5.3.verse: Or alternatively, what is gnawed (*vikkhāyita*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the gnawed” (*vikkhāyitaka*).

vsm1.6:5.4.verse: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.
