vsm1.6:6.1.verse: *The scattered*: what is strewed about (*vividhaṃ khittaṃ*) is scattered (*vikkhittaṃ*).

vsm1.6:6.2.verse: What is scattered is the same as “the scattered” (*vikkhittaka*).

vsm1.6:6.3.verse: Or alternatively, what is scattered (*vikkhitta*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the scattered” (*vikkhittaka*).

vsm1.6:6.4.verse: This is a term for a corpse that is strewed here and there in this way: “Here a hand, there a foot, there the head” (cf. M I 58).

vsm1.6:7.1.verse: *The hacked and scattered*: it is hacked, and it is scattered in the way just described, thus it is “hacked and scattered” (*hata-vikkhittaka*).

vsm1.6:7.2.verse: This is a term for a corpse scattered in the way just described after it has been hacked with a knife in a crow’s-foot pattern on every limb.

vsm1.6:8.1.verse: *The bleeding*: it sprinkles (*kirati*), scatters, blood (*lohita*), and it trickles here and there, thus it is “the bleeding” (*lohitaka*).

vsm1.6:8.2.verse: This is a term for a corpse smeared with trickling blood.

vsm1.6:9.1.verse: *The worm-infested*: it is maggots that are called worms (*puḷuva*); it sprinkles worms (*puḷuve kirati*), thus it is worm-infested (*puḷuvaka*).

vsm1.6:9.2.verse: This is a term for a corpse full of maggots.

vsm1.6:10.1.verse: *A skeleton*: bone (*aṭṭhi*) is the same as skeleton (*aṭṭhika*).

vsm1.6:10.2.verse: Or alternatively, bone (*aṭṭhi*) is vile (*kucchita*) because of repulsiveness, thus it is a skeleton (*aṭṭhika*).

vsm1.6:10.3.verse: This is a term both for a single bone and for a framework of bones.

vsm1.6:11.1.verse: These names are also used both for the signs that arise with the bloated, etc., as their support,

vsm1.6:11.2.verse: and for the jhānas obtained in the signs.

vsm1.6:12.1.verse: Herein, when a meditator wants to develop the jhāna called “of the bloated” by arousing the sign of the bloated on a bloated body,

vsm1.6:12.2.verse: he should in the way already described approach a teacher of the kind mentioned under the earth kasiṇa

vsm1.6:12.3.verse: and learn the meditation subject from him.

vsm1.6:12.4.verse: In explaining the meditation subject to him, the teacher should explain it all, that is,

vsm1.6:12.5.verse: the directions for going with the aim of acquiring the sign of foulness,

vsm1.6:12.6.verse: the characterizing of the surrounding signs,

vsm1.6:12.7.verse: the eleven ways of apprehending the sign,

vsm1.6:12.8.verse: the reviewing of the path gone by and come by,

vsm1.6:12.9.verse: concluding with the directions for absorption.

vsm1.6:12.10.verse: And when the meditator has learnt it all well,

vsm1.6:12.11.verse: he should go to an abode of the kind already described

vsm1.6:12.12.verse: and live there while seeking the sign of the bloated.

vsm1.6:13.1.verse: Meanwhile, when he hears people saying that at some village gate or on some road or at some forest’s edge or

vsm1.6:13.2.verse: at the base of some rock or at the root of some tree or on some charnel ground a bloated corpse is lying,

vsm1.6:13.3.verse: he should not go there at once, like one who plunges into a river where there is no ford.

vsm1.6:14.2.verse: Because this foulness is beset by wild beasts and non-human beings,

vsm1.6:14.3.verse: and he might risk his life there.

vsm1.6:14.4.verse: Or perhaps the way to it goes by a village gate or a bathing place or an irrigated field,

vsm1.6:14.5.verse: and there a visible object of the opposite sex might come into focus.

vsm1.6:14.6.verse: Or perhaps the body is of the opposite sex;

vsm1.6:14.7.verse: for a female body is unsuitable for a man, and a male body for a woman.

vsm1.6:14.8.verse: If only recently dead, it may even look beautiful;

vsm1.6:14.9.verse: hence there might be danger to the life of purity.

vsm1.6:14.10.verse: But if he judges himself thus, “This is not difficult for one like me,” then he can go there.

vsm1.6:15.1.verse: And when he goes, he should do so only after he has spoken to the senior elder of the Community or to some well-known bhikkhu.

vsm1.6:16.2.verse: Because if all his limbs are seized with shuddering at the charnel ground, or if his gorge rises when he is confronted with disagreeable objects such as the visible forms and sounds of non-human beings, lions, tigers, etc.,

vsm1.6:16.4.verse: then he whom he told will have his bowl and robe well looked after in the monastery,

vsm1.6:16.5.verse: or he will care for him by sending young bhikkhus or novices to him.

vsm1.6:17.1.verse: Besides, robbers may meet there thinking a charnel ground a safe place for them whether or not they have done anything wrong.

vsm1.6:17.2.verse: And when men chase them, they drop their goods near the bhikkhu and run away.

vsm1.6:17.3.verse: Perhaps the men seize the bhikkhu, saying “We have found the thief with the goods,” and bully him.

vsm1.6:17.4.verse: Then he whom he told will explain to the men “Do not bully him; he went to do this special work after telling me,”

vsm1.6:17.6.verse: This is the advantage of going only after informing someone.

vsm1.6:18.1.verse: Therefore he should inform a bhikkhu of the kind described

vsm1.6:18.2.verse: and then set out eager to see the sign,

vsm1.6:18.3.verse: and as happy and joyful as a warrior-noble (*khattiya*) on his way to the scene of anointing,

vsm1.6:18.4.verse: as one going to offer libations at the hall of sacrifice,

vsm1.6:18.5.verse: or as a pauper on his way to unearth a hidden treasure.

vsm1.6:18.6.verse: And he should go there in the way advised by the Commentaries.

vsm1.6:19.2.verse: “One who is learning the bloated sign of foulness

vsm1.6:19.5.verse: with his sense faculties turned inwards,

vsm1.6:19.6.verse: with his mind not turned outwards,

vsm1.6:19.7.verse: reviewing the path gone by and come by.

vsm1.6:19.8.verse: In the place where the bloated sign of foulness has been left

vsm1.6:19.9.verse: he notes any stone or termite-mound or tree or bush or creeper there each with its particular sign

vsm1.6:19.10.verse: and in relation to the object.

vsm1.6:19.12.verse: he characterizes the bloated sign of foulness by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence. (see §84)

vsm1.6:19.13.verse: Then he sees that the sign is properly apprehended, that it is properly remembered, that it is properly defined, by its colour, by its mark, by its shape, by its direction, by its location, by its delimitation, by its joints, by its openings, by its concavities, by its convexities, and all round.

vsm1.6:20.1.verse: “When he has properly apprehended the sign, properly remembered it, properly defined it,

vsm1.6:20.2.verse: he goes alone with no companion,

vsm1.6:20.4.verse: with his sense faculties turned inwards,

vsm1.6:20.5.verse: with his mind not turned outwards,

vsm1.6:20.6.verse: reviewing the path gone by and come by.

vsm1.6:20.7.verse: When he walks, he resolves that his walk is oriented towards it;

vsm1.6:20.8.verse: when he sits, he prepares a seat that is oriented towards it.

vsm1.6:21.1.verse: “What is the purpose, what is the advantage of characterizing the surrounding signs?

vsm1.6:21.2.verse: Characterizing the surrounding signs has non-delusion for its purpose, it has non-delusion for its advantage.

vsm1.6:21.3.verse: What is the purpose, what is the advantage of apprehending the sign in the [other] eleven ways?

vsm1.6:21.4.verse: Apprehending the sign in the [other] eleven ways has anchoring [the mind] for its purpose, it has anchoring [the mind] for its advantage.

vsm1.6:21.5.verse: What is the purpose, what is the advantage of reviewing the path gone by and come by?

vsm1.6:21.6.verse: Reviewing the path gone by and come by has keeping [the mind] on the track for its purpose, it has keeping [the mind] on the track for its advantage.

vsm1.6:22.1.verse: “When he has established reverence for it by seeing its advantages and by perceiving it as a treasure and so come to love it,

vsm1.6:22.2.verse: he anchors his mind upon that object:

vsm1.6:22.3.verse: ‘Surely in this way I shall be liberated from ageing and death.’

vsm1.6:22.4.verse: Quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna … [seclusion].

vsm1.6:22.5.verse: He has arrived at the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere.

vsm1.6:22.6.verse: His is a heavenly abiding and an instance of the meritorious action consisting in [meditative] development.” (*Source untraced.*)

vsm1.6:23.1.verse: So if he goes to the charnel ground to test his control of mind, let him do so after striking the gong or summoning a chapter.

vsm1.6:23.2.verse: If he goes there mainly for [developing that] meditation subject,

vsm1.6:23.3.verse: let him go alone with no companion,

vsm1.6:23.4.verse: without renouncing his basic meditation subject and keeping it always in mind,

vsm1.6:23.5.verse: taking a walking stick or a staff to keep off attacks by dogs, etc.,

vsm1.6:23.6.verse: ensuring unremitting mindfulness by establishing it well,

vsm1.6:23.7.verse: with his mind not turned outwards because he has ensured that his faculties, of which his mind is the sixth, are turned inwards.

vsm1.6:24.1.verse: As he goes out of the monastery he should note the gate: “I have gone out in such a direction by such a gate.”

vsm1.6:24.2.verse: After that he should define the path by which he goes:

vsm1.6:24.3.verse: “This path goes in an easterly direction … westerly … northerly … southerly direction”

vsm1.6:24.4.verse: or “It goes in an intermediate direction”;

vsm1.6:24.5.verse: and “In this place it goes to the left, in this place to the right”;

vsm1.6:24.6.verse: and “In this place there is a stone, in this a termite-mound, in this a tree, in this a bush, in this a creeper.”

vsm1.6:24.7.verse: He should go to the place where the sign is, defining in this way the path by which he goes.

vsm1.6:25.1.verse: And he should not approach it upwind;

vsm1.6:25.2.verse: for if he did so and the smell of corpses assailed his nose,

vsm1.6:25.4.verse: or he might throw up his food,

vsm1.6:25.5.verse: or he might repent his coming, thinking “What a place of corpses I have come to!”

vsm1.6:25.6.verse: So instead of approaching it upwind, he should go downwind.

vsm1.6:25.7.verse: If he cannot go by a downwind path—

vsm1.6:25.8.verse: if there is a mountain or a ravine or a rock or a fence or a patch of thorns or water or a bog in the way—

vsm1.6:25.9.verse: then he should go stopping his nose with the corner of his robe.

vsm1.6:25.10.verse: These are the duties in going.

vsm1.6:26.1.verse: When he has gone there in this way, he should not at once look at the sign of foulness;

vsm1.6:26.2.verse: he should make sure of the direction.

vsm1.6:26.3.verse: For perhaps if he stands in a certain direction, the object does not appear clearly to him and his mind is not wieldy.

vsm1.6:26.4.verse: So rather than there he should stand where the object appears clearly and his mind is wieldy.

vsm1.6:26.5.verse: And he should avoid standing to leeward or to windward of it.

vsm1.6:26.6.verse: For if he stands to leeward he is bothered by the corpse smell and his mind strays;

vsm1.6:26.7.verse: and if he stands to windward and non-human beings are dwelling there, they may get annoyed and do him a mischief.

vsm1.6:26.8.verse: So he should move round a little and not stand too much to windward.

vsm1.6:27.1.verse: Then he should stand not too far off or too near, or too much towards the feet or the head.

vsm1.6:27.2.verse: For if he stands too far off, the object is not clear to him,

vsm1.6:27.3.verse: and if he stands too near, he may get frightened.

vsm1.6:27.4.verse: If he stands too much towards the feet or the head, not all the foulness becomes manifest to him equally.

vsm1.6:27.5.verse: So he should stand not too far off or too near, opposite the middle of the body, in a place convenient for him to look at it.

vsm1.6:28.1.verse: Then he should characterize the surrounding signs in the way stated thus: “In the place where the bloated sign of foulness has been left he notes any stone … or creeper there with its sign” (§19).

vsm1.6:29.1.verse: These are the directions for characterizing them.

vsm1.6:29.2.verse: If there is a rock in the eye’s focus near the sign,

vsm1.6:29.3.verse: he should define it in this way: “This rock is high or low, small or large, brown or black or white, long or round,”

vsm1.6:29.4.verse: after which he should observe [the relative positions] thus: “In this place, this is a rock, this is the sign of foulness;

vsm1.6:29.5.verse: this is the sign of foulness, this is a rock.”

vsm1.6:30.2.verse: he should define it in this way: “This is high or low, small or large, brown or black or white, long or round,”

vsm1.6:30.3.verse: after which he should observe [the relative positions] thus: “In this place, this is a termite-mound, this is the sign of foulness.”

vsm1.6:31.2.verse: he should define it in this way: “This is a pipal fig tree or a banyan fig tree or a *kacchaka* fig tree or a *kapittha* fig tree;

vsm1.6:31.3.verse: it is tall or short, small or large, black or white,”

vsm1.6:31.4.verse: after which he should observe [the relative positions] thus: “In this place, this is a tree, this is the sign of foulness.”

vsm1.6:32.2.verse: he should define it in this way: “This is a *sindi* bush or a *karamanda* bush or a *kaṇavīra* bush or a *koraṇḍaka* bush;

vsm1.6:32.3.verse: it is tall or short, small or large,”

vsm1.6:32.4.verse: after which he should observe [the relative positions] thus: “In this place, this is a bush, this is the sign of foulness.”

vsm1.6:33.2.verse: he should define it in this way: “This is a pumpkin creeper or a gourd creeper or a brown creeper or a black creeper or a stinking creeper,”

vsm1.6:33.3.verse: after which he should observe [the relative positions] thus: “In this place, this is a creeper, this is the sign of foulness;

vsm1.6:33.4.verse: this is the sign of foulness, this is a creeper.”

vsm1.6:34.1.verse: Also *with its particular sign and in relation to the object* was said (§19); but that is included by what has just been said;

vsm1.6:34.2.verse: for he “characterizes it with its particular sign” when he defines it again and again,

vsm1.6:34.3.verse: and he “characterizes it in relation to the object” when he defines it by combining it each time in pairs thus: “This is a rock, this is the sign of foulness;

vsm1.6:34.4.verse: this is the sign of foulness, this is a rock.”

vsm1.6:35.2.verse: again he should bring to mind the fact that it has an individual essence, its own state of being bloated, which is not common to anything else, since it was said that he defines[^4] it *by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence*.

vsm1.6:35.3.verse: The meaning is that it should be defined according to individual essence, according to its own nature, as “the inflated,[^5] the bloated.”

vsm1.6:35.4.verse: Having defined it in this way,

vsm1.6:35.5.verse: he should apprehend the sign in the following six ways, that is to say, (1) by its colour, (2) by its mark, (3) by its shape,

vsm1.6:35.6.verse: (4) by its direction, (5) by its location, (6) by its delimitation.

vsm1.6:36.1.verse: (1) The meditator should define it *by its colour* thus: “This is the body of one who is black or white or yellow-skinned.”

vsm1.6:37.1.verse: (2) Instead of defining it by the female mark or the male mark, he should define it *by its mark* thus:

vsm1.6:37.2.verse: “This is the body of one who was in the first phase of life, in the middle phase, in the last phase.”

vsm1.6:38.1.verse: (3) *By its shape*: he should define it only by the shape of the bloated thus:

vsm1.6:38.2.verse: “This is the shape of its head, this is the shape of its neck, this is the shape of its hand,

vsm1.6:38.3.verse: this is the shape of its chest, this is the shape of its belly, this is the shape of its navel,

vsm1.6:38.4.verse: this is the shape of its hips, this is the shape of its thigh, this is the shape of its calf, this is the shape of its foot.”

vsm1.6:39.1.verse: (4) He should define it *by its direction* thus:

vsm1.6:39.2.verse: “There are two directions in this body, that is, down from the navel as the lower direction,

vsm1.6:39.3.verse: and up from it as the upper direction.”

vsm1.6:39.4.verse: Or alternatively, he can define it thus: “I am standing in this direction; the sign of foulness is in that direction.”

vsm1.6:40.1.verse: (5) He should define it *by its location* thus:

vsm1.6:40.2.verse: “The hand is in this location, the foot in this, the head in this, the middle of the body in this.”

vsm1.6:40.3.verse: Or alternatively, he can define it thus: “I am in this location; the sign of foulness is in that.”

vsm1.6:41.1.verse: (6) He should define it *by its delimitation* thus:

vsm1.6:41.2.verse: “This body is delimited below by the soles of the feet, above by the tips of the hair, all round by the skin;

vsm1.6:41.3.verse: the space so delimited is filled up with thirty-two pieces of corpse.”

vsm1.6:41.4.verse: Or alternatively, he can define it thus:

vsm1.6:41.5.verse: “This is the delimitation of its hand, this is the delimitation of its foot,

vsm1.6:41.6.verse: this is the delimitation of its head, this is the delimitation of the middle part of its body.”

vsm1.6:41.7.verse: Or alternatively, he can delimit as much of it as he has apprehended thus: “Just this much of the bloated is like this.”

vsm1.6:42.1.verse: However, a female body is not appropriate for a man or a male one for a woman;

vsm1.6:42.2.verse: for the object, [namely, the repulsive aspect], does not make its appearance in a body of the opposite sex,

vsm1.6:42.3.verse: which merely becomes a condition for the wrong kind of excitement.[^6]

vsm1.6:42.4.verse: To quote the Majjhima Commentary: “Even when decaying,[^7] a woman invades a man’s mind and stays there.”

vsm1.6:42.5.verse: That is why the sign should be apprehended in the six ways only in a body of the same sex.

vsm1.6:43.1.verse: But when a clansman has cultivated the meditation subject under former Enlightened Ones, kept the ascetic practices,

vsm1.6:43.2.verse: threshed out the great primary elements, discerned formations, defined mentality-materiality,

vsm1.6:43.3.verse: eliminated the perception of a being, done the ascetic’s duties, lived the moral life, and developed the development,

vsm1.6:43.4.verse: when he contains the seed [of turning away from formations], and has mature knowledge and little defilement,

vsm1.6:43.5.verse: then the counterpart sign appears to him in the place while he keeps looking.

vsm1.6:43.6.verse: If it does not appear in that way, then it appears to him as he is apprehending the sign in the six ways.

vsm1.6:44.1.verse: But if it does not appear to him even then,

vsm1.6:44.2.verse: he should apprehend the sign again in five more ways: (7) by its joints, (8) by its openings, (9) by its concavities, (10) by its convexities, and (11) all round.

vsm1.6:45.1.verse: Herein, (7) *by its joints* is [properly] by its hundred and eighty joints.

vsm1.6:45.2.verse: But how can he define the hundred and eighty joints in the bloated?

vsm1.6:45.3.verse: Consequently he can define it by its fourteen major joints thus: Three joints in the right arm, three in the left arm,

vsm1.6:45.4.verse: three in the right leg, three in the left leg,

vsm1.6:45.5.verse: one neck joint, one waist joint.

vsm1.6:46.2.verse: an “opening” is the hollow between the arm [and the side], the hollow between the legs, the hollow of the stomach, the hollow of the ear.

vsm1.6:46.3.verse: He should define it by its openings in this way.

vsm1.6:46.4.verse: Or alternatively, the opened or closed state of the eyes and the opened or closed state of the mouth can be defined.

vsm1.6:47.2.verse: he should define any concave place on the body such as the eye sockets or the inside of the mouth or the base of the neck.

vsm1.6:47.3.verse: Or he can define it thus: “I am standing in a concave place, the body is in a convex place.”

vsm1.6:48.1.verse: (10) *By its convexities*: he should define any raised place on the body such as the knee or the chest or the forehead.

vsm1.6:48.2.verse: Or he can define it thus: “I am standing in a convex place, the body is in a concave place.”

vsm1.6:49.1.verse: (11) *All round*: the whole body should be defined all round.

vsm1.6:49.2.verse: After working over the whole body with knowledge,

vsm1.6:49.3.verse: he should establish his mind thus, “The bloated, the bloated,” upon any part that appears clearly to him.

vsm1.6:49.4.verse: If it has not appeared even yet,

vsm1.6:49.5.verse: and if there is special intensity of the bloatedness in the belly,[^8]

vsm1.6:49.6.verse: he should establish his mind thus, “The bloated, the bloated,” on that.

vsm1.6:50.1.verse: Now, as to the words, *he sees that the sign is properly apprehended*, etc., the explanation is this.

vsm1.6:50.2.verse: The meditator should apprehend the sign thoroughly in that body in the way of apprehending the sign already described.

vsm1.6:50.3.verse: He should advert to it with well-established mindfulness.

vsm1.6:50.4.verse: He should see that it is properly remembered, properly defined, by doing that again and again.

vsm1.6:50.5.verse: Standing in a place not too far from and not too near to the body, he should open his eyes, look and apprehend the sign.

vsm1.6:50.6.verse: He should open his eyes and look a hundred times, a thousand times, [thinking], “Repulsiveness of the bloated, repulsiveness of the bloated,”

vsm1.6:50.7.verse: and he should close his eyes and advert to it.

vsm1.6:51.1.verse: As he does so again and again, the learning sign becomes properly apprehended by him.

vsm1.6:51.3.verse: When it comes into focus alike whether he opens his eyes and looks or closes his eyes and adverts,

vsm1.6:51.4.verse: then it is called properly apprehended.

vsm1.6:52.1.verse: When he has thus properly apprehended the sign, properly remembered it, and properly defined it,

vsm1.6:52.2.verse: then if he is unable to conclude his development on the spot,

vsm1.6:52.3.verse: he can go to his own lodging, alone, in the same way as described of his coming, with no companion,

vsm1.6:52.4.verse: keeping that same meditation subject in mind, with mindfulness well established,

vsm1.6:52.5.verse: and with his mind not turned outwards owing to his faculties being turned inwards.

vsm1.6:53.1.verse: As he leaves the charnel ground he should define the path he comes back by thus:

vsm1.6:53.2.verse: “The path by which I have left goes in an easterly direction, westerly … northerly … southerly direction,”

vsm1.6:53.3.verse: or “It goes in an intermediate direction”;

vsm1.6:53.4.verse: or “In this place it goes to the left, in this place to the right”;

vsm1.6:53.5.verse: and “In this place there is a stone, in this a termite-mound, in this a tree, in this a bush, in this a creeper.”

vsm1.6:54.1.verse: When he has defined the path he has come back by

vsm1.6:54.2.verse: and when, once back, he is walking up and down, he should see that his walk is oriented towards it too;

vsm1.6:54.3.verse: the meaning is that he should walk up and down on a piece of ground that faces in the direction of the sign of foulness.

vsm1.6:54.4.verse: And when he sits, he should prepare a seat oriented towards it too.

vsm1.6:55.1.verse: But if there is a bog or a ravine or a tree or a fence or a swamp in that direction,

vsm1.6:55.2.verse: if he cannot walk up and down on a piece of ground facing in that direction,

vsm1.6:55.3.verse: if he cannot prepare his seat thus because there is no room for it,

vsm1.6:55.4.verse: then he can both walk up and down and sit in a place where there is room, even though it does not face that way;

vsm1.6:55.5.verse: but he should turn his mind in that direction.

vsm1.6:56.1.verse: Now, as to the questions beginning with *what is the purpose … characterizing the surrounding signs*?

vsm1.6:56.2.verse: The intention of the answer that begins with the words, *has non-delusion for its purpose*, is this:

vsm1.6:56.3.verse: If someone goes at the wrong time to the place where the sign of the bloated is,

vsm1.6:56.4.verse: and opens his eyes for the purpose of apprehending the sign by characterizing the surrounding signs,

vsm1.6:56.5.verse: then as soon as he looks the dead body appears as if it were standing up

vsm1.6:56.7.verse: and when he sees the hideous and fearful object,

vsm1.6:56.8.verse: his mind reels, he is like one demented,

vsm1.6:56.9.verse: gripped by panic, fear and terror, and his hair stands on end.

vsm1.6:56.10.verse: For among the thirty-eight meditation subjects expounded in the texts no object is so frightening as this one.

vsm1.6:56.11.verse: There are some who lose jhāna in this meditation subject.

vsm1.6:57.1.verse: So the meditator must stand firm.

vsm1.6:57.2.verse: Establishing his mindfulness well, he should remove his fears in this way:

vsm1.6:57.3.verse: “No dead body gets up and pursues one.

vsm1.6:57.4.verse: If that stone or that creeper close to it were to come, the body might come too;

vsm1.6:57.5.verse: but since that stone or that creeper does not come, the body will not come either.

vsm1.6:57.6.verse: Its appearance to you in this way is born: of your perception, created by your perception.

vsm1.6:57.7.verse: Today your meditation subject has appeared to you.

vsm1.6:57.9.verse: He should laugh it off and direct his mind to the sign.

vsm1.6:57.10.verse: In that way he will arrive at distinction.

vsm1.6:57.11.verse: The words “Characterizing the surrounding signs has non-delusion for its purpose” are said on this account.

vsm1.6:58.1.verse: To succeed in apprehending the sign in the eleven ways is to anchor the meditation subject.

vsm1.6:58.2.verse: For the opening of his eyes and looking conditions the arising of the learning sign;

vsm1.6:58.3.verse: and as he exercises his mind on that the counterpart sign arises;

vsm1.6:58.4.verse: and as he exercises his mind on that he reaches absorption.

vsm1.6:58.5.verse: When he is sure of absorption, he works up insight and realizes Arahantship.

vsm1.6:58.6.verse: Hence it was said: *apprehending the sign in the* [*other*] *eleven ways has anchoring* [*the mind*] *for its purpose*.

vsm1.6:59.1.verse: *The reviewing of the path gone by and come by has keeping* [*the mind*] *on the track for its purpose*:

vsm1.6:59.2.verse: the meaning is that the reviewing of the path gone by and of the path come back by mentioned

vsm1.6:59.3.verse: is for the purpose of keeping properly to the track of the meditation subject.

vsm1.6:60.1.verse: For if this bhikkhu is going along with his meditation subject and people on the way

vsm1.6:60.2.verse: ask him about the day, “What is today, venerable sir?”

vsm1.6:60.3.verse: or they ask him some question [about Dhamma],

vsm1.6:60.5.verse: he ought not to go on in silence, thinking “I have a meditation subject.”

vsm1.6:60.6.verse: The day must be told, the question must be answered,

vsm1.6:60.7.verse: even by saying “I do not know” if he does not know,

vsm1.6:60.8.verse: a legitimate welcome must be responded to.

vsm1.6:60.9.verse: As he does so, the newly acquired sign vanishes.

vsm1.6:60.10.verse: But even if it does vanish, he should still tell the day when asked;

vsm1.6:60.11.verse: if he does not know the answer to the question, he should still say “I do not know,”

vsm1.6:60.12.verse: and if he does know it, he should explain it surely;[^10] and he must respond to a welcome.

vsm1.6:60.13.verse: Also reception of visitors must be attended to on seeing a visiting bhikkhu,

vsm1.6:60.14.verse: and all the remaining duties in the Khandhakas must be carried out too, that is, the duties of the shrine terrace, the duties of the Bodhi-tree terrace, the duties of the Uposatha house, the duties of the refectory and the bath house, and those to the teacher, the preceptor, visitors, departing bhikkhus, and the rest.

vsm1.6:61.1.verse: And the newly acquired sign vanishes while he is carrying out these too.

vsm1.6:61.2.verse: When he wants to go again, thinking “I shall go and take up the sign,”

vsm1.6:61.3.verse: he finds he cannot go to the charnel ground because it has been invaded by non-human beings or by wild beasts,

vsm1.6:61.5.verse: For a bloated corpse only lasts one or two days and then turns into a livid corpse.

vsm1.6:61.6.verse: Of all the meditation subjects there is none so hard to come by as this.

vsm1.6:62.1.verse: So when the sign has vanished in this way,

vsm1.6:62.2.verse: the bhikkhu should sit down in his night quarters or in his day quarters

vsm1.6:62.3.verse: and first of all review the path gone by and come by up to the place where he is actually sitting cross-legged, doing it in this way:

vsm1.6:62.4.verse: “I went out of the monastery by this gate,

vsm1.6:62.5.verse: I took a path leading in such and such a direction,

vsm1.6:62.6.verse: I turned left at such and such a place,

vsm1.6:62.7.verse: I turned right at such and such a place,

vsm1.6:62.8.verse: in one part of it there was a stone, in another a termite-mound or a tree or a bush or a creeper;

vsm1.6:62.9.verse: having gone by that path, I saw the foulness in such and such a place,

vsm1.6:62.10.verse: I stood there facing in such and such a direction

vsm1.6:62.11.verse: and observed such and such surrounding signs,

vsm1.6:62.12.verse: I apprehended the sign of foulness in this way;

vsm1.6:62.13.verse: I left the charnel ground in such and such a direction,

vsm1.6:62.14.verse: I came back by such and such a path doing this and this,

vsm1.6:62.15.verse: and I am now sitting here.”

vsm1.6:63.1.verse: As he reviews it in this way, the sign becomes evident and appears as if placed in front of him;

vsm1.6:63.2.verse: the meditation subject rides in its track as it did before.

vsm1.6:63.3.verse: Hence it was said: *the reviewing of the path gone by and come by has keeping* [*the mind*] *on the track for its purpose*.

vsm1.6:64.1.verse: Now, as to the words, *when he has established reverence for it by seeing its advantages and by perceiving it as a treasure and so come to love it, he anchors the mind on that object*:

vsm1.6:64.2.verse: here, having gained jhāna by exercising his mind on the repulsiveness in the bloated,

vsm1.6:64.3.verse: he should increase insight with the jhāna as its proximate cause,

vsm1.6:64.4.verse: and then he should see the advantages in this way: “Surely in this way I shall be liberated from ageing and death.”

vsm1.6:65.1.verse: Just as a pauper who acquired a treasure of gems

vsm1.6:65.2.verse: would guard and love it with great affection, feeling reverence for it as one who appreciates the value of it, “I have got what is hard indeed to get!”

vsm1.6:65.3.verse: so too [this bhikkhu] should guard the sign, loving it and feeling reverence for it as one who appreciates the value of it,

vsm1.6:65.4.verse: “I have got this meditation subject, which is indeed as hard to get as a very valuable treasure is for a pauper to get.

vsm1.6:65.5.verse: For one whose meditation subject is the four elements discerns the four primary elements in himself,

vsm1.6:65.6.verse: one whose meditation subject is breathing discerns the wind in his own nostrils,

vsm1.6:65.7.verse: and one whose meditation subject is a kasiṇa makes a kasiṇa and develops it at his ease,

vsm1.6:65.8.verse: so these other meditation subjects are easily got.

vsm1.6:65.9.verse: But this one lasts only one, or two days, after which it turns into a livid corpse.

vsm1.6:65.10.verse: There is none harder to get than this one.”

vsm1.6:65.11.verse: In his night quarters and in his day quarters

vsm1.6:65.12.verse: he should keep his mind anchored there thus, “Repulsiveness of the bloated, repulsiveness of the bloated.”

vsm1.6:65.13.verse: And he should advert to the sign, bring it to mind and strike at it with thought and applied thought over and over again.

vsm1.6:66.1.verse: As he does so, the counterpart sign arises.

vsm1.6:66.2.verse: Here is the difference between the two signs.

vsm1.6:66.3.verse: The learning sign appears as a hideous, dreadful and frightening sight;

vsm1.6:66.4.verse: but the counterpart sign appears like a man with big limbs lying down after eating his fill.

vsm1.6:67.1.verse: Simultaneously with his acquiring the counterpart sign,

vsm1.6:67.2.verse: his lust is abandoned by suppression owing to his giving no attention externally to sense desires [as object].

vsm1.6:67.3.verse: And owing to his abandoning of approval, ill will is abandoned too, as pus is with the abandoning of blood.

vsm1.6:67.4.verse: Likewise stiffness and torpor are abandoned through exertion of energy,

vsm1.6:67.5.verse: agitation and worry are abandoned through devotion to peaceful things that cause no remorse;

vsm1.6:67.6.verse: and uncertainty about the Master who teaches the way, about the way, and about the fruit of the way, is abandoned through the actual experience of the distinction attained.

vsm1.6:67.7.verse: So the five hindrances are abandoned.

vsm1.6:67.8.verse: And there are present applied thought with the characteristic of directing the mind on to that same sign,

vsm1.6:67.9.verse: and sustained thought accomplishing the function of pressing on the sign,

vsm1.6:67.10.verse: and happiness due to the acquisition of distinction,

vsm1.6:67.11.verse: and tranquillity due to the production of tranquillity in one whose mind is happy,

vsm1.6:67.12.verse: and bliss with that tranquillity as its sign,

vsm1.6:67.13.verse: and unification that has bliss as its sign due to the production of concentration in one whose mind is blissful.

vsm1.6:67.14.verse: So the jhāna factors become manifest.

vsm1.6:68.1.verse: Thus access, which is the obverse of the first jhāna, is produced in him too at that same moment.

vsm1.6:68.2.verse: All after that up to absorption in the first jhāna and mastery in it should be understood as described under the earth kasiṇa.

vsm1.6:69.1.verse: As regards the livid and the rest:

vsm1.6:69.2.verse: the characterizing already described, starting with the going in the way beginning “One who is learning the bloated sign of foulness goes alone with no companion, with unremitting mindfulness established” (§19),

vsm1.6:69.3.verse: should all be understood with its exposition and intention, substituting for the word “bloated” the appropriate word in each case thus: “One who is learning the livid sign of foulness …”, “One who is learning the festering sign of foulness …”

vsm1.6:69.4.verse: But the differences are as follows.

vsm1.6:70.1.verse: *The livid* should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the livid, repulsiveness of the livid.”

vsm1.6:70.2.verse: Here the learning sign appears blotchy-coloured;

vsm1.6:70.3.verse: but the counterpart sign’s appearance has the colour which is most prevalent.

vsm1.6:71.1.verse: *The festering* should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the festering, repulsiveness of the festering.”

vsm1.6:71.2.verse: Here the learning sign appears as though trickling;

vsm1.6:71.3.verse: but the counterpart sign appears motionless and quiet.

vsm1.6:72.1.verse: *The cut up* is found on a battlefield or in a robbers’ forest or on a charnel ground where kings have robbers cut up

vsm1.6:72.2.verse: or in the jungle in a place where men are torn up by lions and tigers.

vsm1.6:72.3.verse: So, if when he goes there, it comes into focus at one adverting although lying in different places, that is good.

vsm1.6:72.4.verse: If not, then he should not touch it with his own hand;

vsm1.6:72.5.verse: for by doing so he would become familiar with it.[^11]

vsm1.6:72.6.verse: He should get a monastery attendant or one studying to become an ascetic or someone else to put it together in one place.

vsm1.6:72.7.verse: If he cannot find anyone to do it,

vsm1.6:72.8.verse: he should put it together with a walking stick or a staff in such a way that there is only a finger’s breadth separating [the parts].

vsm1.6:72.9.verse: Having put it together thus, he should bring it to mind as “Repulsiveness of the cut up, repulsiveness of the cut up.”

vsm1.6:72.10.verse: Herein, the learning sign appears as though cut in the middle;

vsm1.6:72.11.verse: but the counterpart sign appears whole.

vsm1.6:73.1.verse: *The gnawed* should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the gnawed, repulsiveness of the gnawed.”

vsm1.6:73.2.verse: Here the learning sign appears as though gnawed here and there;

vsm1.6:73.3.verse: but the counterpart sign appears whole.

vsm1.6:74.1.verse: After getting *the scattered* put together or putting it together in the way described under the cut up so that there is only a finger’s breadth, separating [the pieces],

vsm1.6:74.2.verse: it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the scattered, repulsiveness of the scattered.”

vsm1.6:74.3.verse: Here the learning sign appears with the gaps evident;

vsm1.6:74.4.verse: but the counterpart sign appears whole.

vsm1.6:75.1.verse: *The hacked and scattered* is found in the same places as those described under the cut up.

vsm1.6:75.2.verse: Therefore, after going there and getting it put together or putting it together in the way described under the cut up so that there is only a finger’s breadth separating [the pieces],

vsm1.6:75.3.verse: it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the hacked and scattered, repulsiveness of the hacked and scattered.”

vsm1.6:75.4.verse: Here, when the learning sign becomes evident, it does so with the fissures of the wounds;

vsm1.6:75.5.verse: but the counterpart sign appears whole.

vsm1.6:76.1.verse: *The bleeding* is found at the time when [blood] is trickling from the openings of wounds received on battlefields, etc., or from the openings of burst boils and abscesses when the hands and feet have been cut off.

vsm1.6:76.2.verse: So on seeing that, it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the bleeding, repulsiveness of the bleeding.”

vsm1.6:76.3.verse: Here the learning sign appears to have the aspect of moving like a red banner struck by wind;

vsm1.6:76.4.verse: but the counterpart sign appears quiet.

vsm1.6:77.1.verse: There is a *worm-infested* corpse when at the end of two or three days a mass of maggots oozes out from the corpse’s nine orifices,

vsm1.6:77.2.verse: and the mass lies there like a heap of paddy or boiled rice as big as the body, whether the body is that of a dog, a jackal, a human being,[^12] an ox, a buffalo, an elephant, a horse, a python, or what you will.

vsm1.6:77.3.verse: It can be brought to mind with respect to anyone of these as “Repulsiveness of the worm-infested, repulsiveness of the worm-infested.”

vsm1.6:77.4.verse: For the sign arose for the Elder Cūḷa-Piṇḍapātika-Tissa in the corpse of an elephant’s carcass in the Kāḷadīghavāpi reservoir.

vsm1.6:77.5.verse: Here the learning sign appears as though moving;

vsm1.6:77.6.verse: but the counterpart sign appears quiet, like a ball of boiled rice.

vsm1.6:78.1.verse: *A skeleton* is described in various aspects in the way beginning “As though he were looking at a corpse thrown onto a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews” (D II 296).

vsm1.6:78.2.verse: So he should go in the way already described to where it has been put,

vsm1.6:78.3.verse: and noticing any stones, etc., with their surrounding signs and in relation, to the object,

vsm1.6:78.4.verse: he should characterize it *by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence* thus, “This is a skeleton,”

vsm1.6:78.5.verse: and he should apprehend the sign in the eleven ways by colour and the rest.

vsm1.6:78.3.verse: But if he looks at it, [apprehending it only] by its colour as white, it does not appear to him [with its individual essence as repulsive],

vsm1.6:78.4.verse: but only as a variant of the white kasiṇa.

vsm1.6:78.5.verse: Consequently he should only look at it as ‘a skeleton’ in the repulsive aspect.

vsm1.6:79.1.verse: “Mark” is a term for the hand, etc., here,

vsm1.6:79.2.verse: so he should define it *by its mark* according to hand, foot, head, chest, arm, waist, thigh, and shin.

vsm1.6:79.3.verse: He should define it *by its shape*, however, according as it is long, short, square, round, small or large.

vsm1.6:79.4.verse: *By its direction and by its location* are as already described (§39–40).

vsm1.6:79.5.verse: Having defined it *by its delimitation* according to the periphery of each bone,

vsm1.6:79.6.verse: he should reach absorption by apprehending whichever appears most evident to him.

vsm1.6:79.7.verse: But it can also be defined *by its concavities* and *by its convexities* according to the concave and convex places in each bone.

vsm1.6:79.8.verse: And it can also be defined by position thus:

vsm1.6:79.9.verse: “I am standing in a concave place, the skeleton is in a convex place;

vsm1.6:79.10.verse: or I am standing in a convex place, the skeleton is in a concave place.”

vsm1.6:79.11.verse: It should be defined *by its joints* according as any two bones are joined together.

vsm1.6:79.12.verse: It should be defined *by its openings* according to the gaps separating the bones.

vsm1.6:79.13.verse: It should be defined *all round* by directing knowledge to it comprehensively thus: “In this place there is this skeleton.”

vsm1.6:79.14.verse: If the sign does not arise even in this way, then the mind should be established on the frontal bone.

vsm1.6:79.16.verse: just as in the case of those that precede it beginning with the worm-infested, the apprehending of the sign should be observed in this elevenfold manner as appropriate.

vsm1.6:80.1.verse: This meditation subject is successful with a whole skeleton frame and even with a single bone as well.

vsm1.6:80.2.verse: So having learnt the sign in anyone of these in the eleven ways,

vsm1.6:80.3.verse: he should bring it to mind as “Repulsiveness of a skeleton, repulsiveness of a skeleton.”

vsm1.6:80.4.verse: Here the learning sign and the counterpart sign are alike, so it is said.

vsm1.6:80.5.verse: That is correct for a single bone.

vsm1.6:80.6.verse: But when the learning sign becomes manifest in a skeleton frame, what is correct [to say] is that there are gaps in the learning sign

vsm1.6:80.7.verse: while the counterpart sign appears whole.

vsm1.6:80.8.verse: And the learning sign even in a single bone should be dreadful and terrifying

vsm1.6:80.9.verse: but the counterpart sign produces happiness and joy because it brings access.

vsm1.6:81.1.verse: What is said in the Commentaries in this context allows that deduction.

vsm1.6:81.2.verse: For there, after saying this, “There is no counterpart sign in the four divine abidings and in the ten kinds of foulness;

vsm1.6:81.3.verse: for in the case of the divine abidings the sign is the breaking down of boundaries itself,

vsm1.6:81.4.verse: and in the case of the ten kinds of foulness the sign comes into being as soon as the repulsiveness is seen, without any thinking about it,”

vsm1.6:81.5.verse: it is again said, immediately next:

vsm1.6:81.6.verse: “Here the sign is twofold: the learning sign and the counterpart sign.

vsm1.6:81.7.verse: The learning sign appears hideous, dreadful and terrifying,” and so on.

vsm1.6:81.8.verse: So what we said was well considered.

vsm1.6:81.9.verse: And it is only this that is correct here.

vsm1.6:81.10.verse: Besides, the appearance of a woman’s whole body as a collection of bones to the Elder Mahā-Tissa through his merely looking at her teeth demonstrates this here (see I.55).

vsm1.6:82.1.verse:
The Divine Ruler with ten hundred eyes
Did him with the Ten Powers eulogize,
Who, fair in fame, made known as cause of jhāna
This foulness of ten species in such wise.

vsm1.6:82.2.verse:
Now, knowing their description and the way
To tackle each and how they are developed,
There are some further points that will repay
Study, each with its special part to play.

vsm1.6:83.1.verse: One who has reached jhāna in anyone of these

vsm1.6:83.2.verse: goes free from cupidity; he resembles [an Arahant] without greed because his greed has been well suppressed.

vsm1.6:83.4.verse: this classification of foulness should be understood as stated

vsm1.6:83.5.verse: in accordance with the particular individual essences successively reached by the [dead] body

vsm1.6:83.6.verse: and also in accordance with the particular subdivisions of the greedy temperament.

vsm1.6:84.1.verse: When a corpse has entered upon the repulsive state,

vsm1.6:84.2.verse: it may have reached the individual essence of the bloated

vsm1.6:84.3.verse: or anyone of the individual essences beginning with that of the livid.

vsm1.6:84.4.verse: So the sign should be apprehended as “Repulsiveness of the bloated,” “Repulsiveness of the livid,” according to whichever he has been able to find.

vsm1.6:84.5.verse: This, it should be understood, is how the classification of foulness comes to be tenfold with the body’s arrival at each particular individual essence.

vsm1.6:85.1.verse: And individually *the bloated* suits one who is greedy about shape since it makes evident the disfigurement of the body’s shape.

vsm1.6:85.2.verse: *The livid* suits one who is greedy about the body’s colour since it makes evident the disfigurement of the skin’s colour.

vsm1.6:85.3.verse: *The festering* suits one who is greedy about the smell of the body aroused by scents, perfumes, etc., since it makes evident the evil smells connected with this sore, the body.

vsm1.6:85.4.verse: *The cut up* suits one who is greedy about compactness in the body since it makes evident the hollowness inside it.

vsm1.6:85.5.verse: *The gnawed* suits one who is greedy about accumulation of flesh in such parts of the body as the breasts since it makes it evident how a fine accumulation of flesh comes to nothing.

vsm1.6:85.6.verse: *The scattered* suits one who is greedy about the grace of the limbs since it makes it evident how limbs can be scattered.

vsm1.6:85.7.verse: *The hacked* and scattered suits one who is greedy about a fine body as a whole since it makes evident the disintegration and alteration of the body as a whole.

vsm1.6:85.8.verse: *The bleeding* suits one who is greedy about elegance produced by ornaments since it makes evident its repulsiveness when smeared with blood.

vsm1.6:85.9.verse: *The worm-infested* suits one who is greedy about ownership of the body since it makes it evident how the body is shared with many families of worms.

vsm1.6:85.10.verse: *A skeleton* suits one who is greedy about fine teeth since it makes evident the repulsiveness of the bones in the body.

vsm1.6:85.11.verse: This, it should be understood, is how the classification of foulness comes to be tenfold according to the subdivisions of the greedy temperament.

vsm1.6:86.1.verse: But as regards the tenfold foulness,

vsm1.6:86.2.verse: just as it is only by virtue of its rudder that a boat keeps steady in a river with turbulent[^13] waters and a rapid current,

vsm1.6:86.3.verse: and it cannot be steadied without a rudder,

vsm1.6:86.4.verse: so too [here], owing to the weak hold on the object, consciousness when unified only keeps steady by virtue of applied thought,

vsm1.6:86.5.verse: and it cannot be steadied without applied thought,

vsm1.6:86.6.verse: which is why there is only the first jhāna here, not the second and the rest.

vsm1.6:87.1.verse: And repulsive as this object is,

vsm1.6:87.2.verse: still it arouses joy and happiness in him by his seeing its advantages thus, “*Surely in this way I shall be liberated from ageing and death*,”

vsm1.6:87.3.verse: and by his abandoning the hindrances’ oppression;

vsm1.6:87.4.verse: just as a garbage heap does in a flower-scavenger by his seeing the advantages thus, “Now I shall get a high wage,”

vsm1.6:87.5.verse: and as the workings of purges and emetics do in a man suffering the pains of sickness.

vsm1.6:88.1.verse: This foulness, while of ten kinds, has only one characteristic.

vsm1.6:88.2.verse: For though it is of ten kinds, nevertheless its characteristic is only its impure, stinking, disgusting and repulsive state (essence).

vsm1.6:88.3.verse: And foulness appears with this characteristic not only in a dead body

vsm1.6:88.4.verse: but also in a living one, as it did to the Elder Mahā-Tissa who lived at Cetiyapabbata (I.55),

vsm1.6:88.5.verse: and to the novice attendant on the Elder Saṅgharakkhita while he was watching the king riding an elephant.

vsm1.6:88.6.verse: For a living body is just as foul as a dead one,

vsm1.6:88.7.verse: only the characteristic of foulness is not evident in a living body, being hidden by adventitious embellishments.

vsm1.6:89.1.verse: This is the body’s nature: it is a collection of over three hundred bones, jointed by one hundred and eighty joints,

vsm1.6:89.2.verse: bound together by nine hundred sinews, plastered over with nine hundred pieces of flesh,

vsm1.6:89.3.verse: enveloped in the moist inner skin, enclosed in the outer cuticle, with orifices here and there,

vsm1.6:89.4.verse: constantly dribbling and trickling like a grease pot, inhabited by a community of worms,

vsm1.6:89.5.verse: the home of disease, the basis of painful states,

vsm1.6:89.6.verse: perpetually oozing from the nine orifices like a chronic open carbuncle,

vsm1.6:89.7.verse: from both of whose eyes eye-filth trickles, from whose ears comes ear-filth,

vsm1.6:89.8.verse: from whose nostrils snot, from whose mouth food and bile and phlegm and blood,

vsm1.6:89.9.verse: from whose lower outlets excrement and urine, and from whose ninety-nine thousand pores the broth of stale sweat seeps,

vsm1.6:89.10.verse: with bluebottles and their like buzzing round it,

vsm1.6:89.11.verse: which when untended with tooth sticks and mouth-washing and head-anointing and bathing and underclothing and dressing would,

vsm1.6:89.12.verse: judged by the universal repulsiveness of the body, make even a king, if he wandered from village to village with his hair in its natural wild disorder, no different from a flower-scavenger or an outcaste or what you will.

vsm1.6:89.13.verse: So there is no distinction between a king’s body and an outcaste’s in so far as its impure stinking nauseating repulsiveness is concerned.

vsm1.6:90.1.verse: But by rubbing out the stains on its teeth with tooth sticks and mouth-washing and all that,

vsm1.6:90.2.verse: by concealing its private parts under several cloths,

vsm1.6:90.3.verse: by daubing it with various scents and salves,

vsm1.6:90.4.verse: by pranking it with nosegays and such things,

vsm1.6:90.5.verse: it is worked up into a state that permits of its being taken as “I” and “mine.”

vsm1.6:90.6.verse: So men delight in women and women in men without perceiving the true nature of its characteristic foulness, now masked by this adventitious adornment.

vsm1.6:90.7.verse: But in the ultimate sense there is no place here even the size of an atom fit to lust after.

vsm1.6:91.1.verse: And then, when any such bits of it as head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, spittle, snot, excrement or urine have dropped off the body,

vsm1.6:91.3.verse: they are ashamed, humiliated and disgusted.

vsm1.6:91.4.verse: But as long as anyone of these things remains in it,

vsm1.6:91.5.verse: though it is just as repulsive,

vsm1.6:91.6.verse: they take it as agreeable, desirable, permanent, pleasant, self, because they are wrapped in the murk of ignorance and dyed with affection and greed for self.

vsm1.6:91.8.verse: they resemble the old jackal who saw a flower not yet fallen from a *kiṃsuka* tree in a forest and yearned after it, thinking, “This is a piece of meat, it is a piece of meat.”

vsm1.6:92.1.verse:
There was a jackal chanced to see
A flowering *kiṃsuka* in a wood;
In haste he went to where it stood:
“I have found a meat-bearing tree!”

vsm1.6:92.2.verse:
He chewed the blooms that fell, but could,
Of course, find nothing fit to eat;
He took it thus: “Unlike the meat
There on the tree, this is no good.”

vsm1.6:92.3.verse:
A wise man will not think to treat
As foul only the part that fell,
But treats as foul the part as well
That in the body has its seat.

vsm1.6:92.4.verse:
Fools cannot in their folly tell;
They take the body to be fair,
And soon get caught in Evil’s snare
Nor can escape its painful spell.

vsm1.6:92.5.verse:
But since the wise have thus laid bare
This filthy body’s nature, so,
Be it alive or dead, they know
There is no beauty lurking there.

vsm1.6:93.2.verse:
“This filthy body stinks outright
Like ordure, like a privy’s site;
This body men that have insight
Condemn, as object of a fool’s delight.

vsm1.6:93.3.verse:
“A tumour where nine holes abide
Wrapped in a coat of clammy hide
And trickling filth on every side,
Polluting the air with stenches far and wide.

vsm1.6:93.4.verse:
“If it perchance should come about
That what is inside it came out,
Surely a man would need a knout
With which to put the crows and dogs to rout.”

vsm1.6:94.1.verse: So a capable bhikkhu should apprehend the sign wherever the aspect of foulness is manifest, whether in a living body or in a dead one,

vsm1.6:94.2.verse: and he should make the meditation subject reach absorption.

vsm1.6:94.3.verse:
The sixth chapter called “The Description of Foulness as
a Meditation Subject” in the Treatise on the Development
of Concentration in the *Path of Purification* composed for
the purpose of gladdening good people.

vsm1.7:1.1.verse: [197] Now, ten recollections were listed next after the ten kinds of foulness (III.105).

vsm1.7:1.2.verse: As to these: Mindfulness (*sati*) itself is recollection (*anussati*) because it arises again and again;

vsm1.7:1.3.verse: or alternatively, the mindfulness (*sati*) that is proper (*anurūpa*) for a clansman gone forth out of faith, since it occurs only in those instances where it should occur, is “recollection” (*anussati*).

vsm1.7:1.4.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by the Enlightened One is the *recollection of the Buddha*.

vsm1.7:1.5.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the Enlightened One’s special qualities as its object.

vsm1.7:1.6.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by the Law is the *recollection of the Dhamma*.[^1]

vsm1.7:1.7.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the special qualities of the Law’s being well proclaimed, etc., as its object.

vsm1.7:1.8.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by the Community is the *recollection of the Saṅgha*.

vsm1.7:1.9.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the Community’s special qualities of being entered on the good way, etc., as its object.

vsm1.7:1.10.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by virtue is the *recollection of virtue*.

vsm1.7:1.11.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the special qualities of virtue’s untornness, etc., as its object.

vsm1.7:1.12.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by generosity is the *recollection of generosity*.

vsm1.7:1.13.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with generosity’s special qualities of free generosity, etc., as its object.

vsm1.7:1.14.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by deities is the *recollection of deities*.

vsm1.7:1.15.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the special qualities of one’s own faith, etc., as its object with deities standing as witnesses.

vsm1.7:1.16.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by death is the *recollection of death*.

vsm1.7:1.17.verse: This is a term for mindfulness with the termination of the life faculty as its object.

vsm1.7:1.18.verse: [*Mindfulness occupied with the body (kāya-gatā sati—*lit. “body-gone mindfulness”):] it is gone (*gata*) to the material body (*kāya*) that is analyzed into head hairs, etc., or it is gone into the body, thus it is “body-gone” (*kāya-gatā*).

vsm1.7:1.19.verse: It is body-gone (*kāya-gatā*) and it is mindfulness (*sati*), thus it is “body-gone-mindfulness” (*kāyagatasati—*single compound);

vsm1.7:1.20.verse: but instead of shortening [the vowel] thus in the usual way, “body-gone mindfulness” (*kāyagatā sati—* compound adj. + noun) is said.

vsm1.7:1.21.verse: This is a term for mindfulness that has as its object the sign of the bodily parts consisting of head hairs and the rest.

vsm1.7:1.22.verse: The mindfulness arisen inspired by breathing (*ānāpāna*) is *mindfulness of breathing*.

vsm1.7:1.23.verse: This is a term for mindfulness that has as its object the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths.

vsm1.7:1.24.verse: The recollection arisen inspired by peace is the *recollection of peace*.

vsm1.7:1.25.verse: This is a term that has as its object the stilling of all suffering.

vsm1.7:2.1.verse: [198] Now, a meditator with absolute confidence[^2] who wants to develop firstly the recollection of the Enlightened One among these ten

vsm1.7:2.2.verse: should go into solitary retreat in a favourable abode

vsm1.7:2.3.verse: and recollect the special qualities of the Enlightened One, the Blessed One, as follows: That Blessed One is such since he is accomplished, fully enlightened, endowed with [clear] vision and [virtuous] conduct, sublime, the knower of worlds, the incomparable leader of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and men, enlightened and blessed (M I 37; A III 285).

vsm1.7:3.1.verse: Here is the way he recollects:

vsm1.7:3.2.verse: “That Blessed One is such since he is accomplished, he is such since he is fully enlightened, … he is such since he is blessed”—

vsm1.7:3.3.verse: he is so for these several reasons, is what is meant.

vsm1.7:4.1.verse: Herein, what he recollects firstly is that the Blessed One is *accomplished* (*arahanta*) for the following reasons: (i) because of remoteness (*āraka*), and (ii) because of his enemies (*ari*) and (iii) the spokes (*ara*) having been destroyed (*hata*), and (iv) because of his worthiness (*araha*) of requisites, etc., and (v) because of absence of secret (*rahābhāva*) evil-doing.[^3]

vsm1.7:5.1.verse: (i) He stands utterly remote and far away from all defilements

vsm1.7:5.2.verse: because he has expunged all trace of defilement by means of the path—

vsm1.7:5.3.verse: because of such remoteness (*āraka*) he is accomplished (*arahanta*).

vsm1.7:5.4.verse:
A man remote (*āraka*) indeed we call
From something he has not at all;

vsm1.7:5.5.verse:
The Saviour too that has no stain
May well the name “accomplished” (*arahanta*) gain.

vsm1.7:6.1.verse: (ii) And these enemies (*ari*), these defilements, are destroyed (*hata*) by the path—because the enemies are thus destroyed he is accomplished (*arahanta*) also.

vsm1.7:6.2.verse:
The enemies (*ari*) that were deployed,
Greed and the rest, have been destroyed (*hata*)

vsm1.7:6.3.verse:
By his, the Helper’s, wisdom’s sword,
So he is “accomplished” (*arahanta*), all accord.

vsm1.7:7.1.verse: (iii) Now, this wheel of the round of rebirths with its hub made of ignorance and of craving for becoming, with its spokes consisting of formations of merit and the rest, with its rim of ageing and death,

vsm1.7:7.2.verse: which is joined to the chariot of the triple becoming by piercing it with the axle made of the origins of cankers (see M I 55),

vsm1.7:7.3.verse: has been revolving throughout time that has no beginning.

vsm1.7:7.4.verse: All of this wheel’s spokes (*ara*) were destroyed (*hata*) by him at the Place of Enlightenment, as he stood firm with the feet of energy on the ground of virtue, wielding with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that destroys kamma—

vsm1.7:7.5.verse: because the spokes are thus destroyed he is *accomplished* (*arahanta*) also.

vsm1.7:8.1.verse: Or alternatively, it is the beginningless round of rebirths that is called the “wheel of the round of rebirths.”

vsm1.7:8.2.verse: Ignorance is its hub because it is its root.

vsm1.7:8.3.verse: Ageing-and-death is its rim because it terminates it.

vsm1.7:8.4.verse: The remaining ten states [of the dependent origination] are its spokes because ignorance is their root and ageing-and-death their termination.

vsm1.7:9.1.verse: Herein, ignorance is unknowing about suffering and the rest.

vsm1.7:9.2.verse: And ignorance in sensual becoming [199] is a condition for formations in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:9.3.verse: Ignorance in fine-material becoming is a condition for formations in fine-material becoming.

vsm1.7:9.4.verse: Ignorance in immaterial becoming is a condition for formations in immaterial becoming.

vsm1.7:10.1.verse: Formations in sensual becoming are a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:11.1.verse: Rebirth-linking consciousness in sensual becoming is a condition for mentality-materiality in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:11.3.verse: In immaterial becoming it is a condition for mentality only.

vsm1.7:12.1.verse: Mentality-materiality in sensual becoming is a condition for the sixfold base in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:12.2.verse: Mentality-materiality in fine-material becoming is a condition for three bases in fine-material becoming.

vsm1.7:12.3.verse: Mentality in immaterial becoming is a condition for one base in immaterial becoming.

vsm1.7:13.1.verse: The sixfold base in sensual becoming is a condition for six kinds of contact in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:13.2.verse: Three bases in fine-material becoming are conditions for three kinds of contact in fine-material becoming.

vsm1.7:13.3.verse: The mind base alone in immaterial becoming is a condition for one kind of contact in immaterial becoming.

vsm1.7:14.1.verse: The six kinds of contact in sensual becoming are conditions for six kinds of feeling in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:14.2.verse: Three kinds of contact in fine-material becoming are conditions for three kinds of feeling there too.

vsm1.7:14.3.verse: One kind of contact in immaterial becoming is a condition for one kind of feeling there too.

vsm1.7:15.1.verse: The six kinds of feeling in sensual becoming are conditions for the six groups of craving in sensual becoming.

vsm1.7:15.2.verse: Three in the fine-material becoming are for three there too.

vsm1.7:15.3.verse: One kind of feeling in the immaterial becoming is a condition for one group of craving in the immaterial becoming.

vsm1.7:15.4.verse: The craving in the several kinds of becoming is a condition for the clinging there.

vsm1.7:16.1.verse: Clinging, etc., are the respective conditions for becoming and the rest.

vsm1.7:16.3.verse: Here someone thinks, “I shall enjoy sense desires,” and with sense-desire clinging as condition

vsm1.7:16.4.verse: he misconducts himself in body, speech, and mind.

vsm1.7:16.5.verse: Owing to the fulfilment of his misconduct he reappears in a state of loss (deprivation).

vsm1.7:16.6.verse: The kamma that is the cause of his reappearance there is kamma-process becoming,

vsm1.7:16.7.verse: the aggregates generated by the kamma are rebirth-process becoming,

vsm1.7:16.8.verse: the generating of the aggregates is birth,

vsm1.7:16.9.verse: their maturing is ageing, their dissolution is death.

vsm1.7:17.1.verse: Another thinks, “I shall enjoy the delights of heaven,” and in the parallel manner he conducts himself well.

vsm1.7:17.2.verse: Owing to the fulfilment of his good conduct he reappears in a [sensual-sphere] heaven.

vsm1.7:17.3.verse: The kamma that is the cause of his reappearance there is kamma-process becoming, and the rest as before.

vsm1.7:18.1.verse: Another thinks, “I shall enjoy the delights of the Brahmā-world,”

vsm1.7:18.2.verse: and with sense-desire clinging as condition he develops loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity.[^4] [200]

vsm1.7:18.3.verse: Owing to the fulfilment of the meditative development he is reborn in the Brahmā-world.

vsm1.7:18.4.verse: The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth there is kamma-process becoming, and the rest is as before.

vsm1.7:19.1.verse: Yet another thinks, “I shall enjoy the delights of immaterial becoming,”

vsm1.7:19.2.verse: and with the same condition he develops the attainments beginning with the base consisting of boundless space.

vsm1.7:19.3.verse: Owing to the fulfilment of the development he is reborn in one of these states.

vsm1.7:19.4.verse: The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth there is kamma-process becoming,

vsm1.7:19.5.verse: the aggregates generated by the kamma are rebirth-process becoming,

vsm1.7:19.6.verse: the generating of the aggregates is birth,

vsm1.7:19.7.verse: their maturing is ageing, their dissolution is death (see M II 263).

vsm1.7:19.8.verse: The remaining kinds of clinging are construable in the same way.

vsm1.7:20.1.verse: So, “Understanding of discernment of conditions thus, ‘Ignorance is a cause, formations are causally arisen, and both these states are causally arisen,’ is knowledge of the causal relationship of states.

vsm1.7:20.2.verse: Understanding of discernment of conditions thus, ‘In the past and in the future ignorance is a cause, formations are causally arisen, and both these states are causally arisen,’ is knowledge of the causal relationship of states” (Paṭis I 50),

vsm1.7:20.3.verse: and all the clauses should be given in detail in this way.

vsm1.7:21.1.verse: Herein, ignorance and formations are one summarization;

vsm1.7:21.2.verse: consciousness, mentality-materiality, the sixfold base, contact, and feeling are another;

vsm1.7:21.3.verse: craving, clinging, and becoming are another;

vsm1.7:21.4.verse: and birth and ageing-and-death are another.

vsm1.7:21.5.verse: Here the first summarization is past, the two middle ones are present, and birth and ageing-and-death are future.

vsm1.7:22.1.verse: Now, the Blessed One knew, saw, understood, and penetrated in all aspects this dependent origination with its four summarizations, its three times, its twenty aspects, and its three links.

vsm1.7:22.2.verse: “Knowledge is in the sense of that being known,[^5]

vsm1.7:22.3.verse: and understanding is in the sense of the act of understanding that.

vsm1.7:22.4.verse: Hence it was said: ‘Understanding of discernment of conditions is knowledge of the causal relationship of states’” (Paṭis I 52).

vsm1.7:22.5.verse: Thus when the Blessed One, by correctly knowing these states with knowledge of relations of states,

vsm1.7:22.6.verse: became dispassionate towards them, when his greed faded away, when he was liberated,

vsm1.7:22.7.verse: then he destroyed, quite destroyed, abolished, the spokes of this wheel of the round of rebirths of the kind just described.

vsm1.7:22.8.verse: Because the spokes are thus destroyed he is accomplished (*arahanta*) also.

vsm1.7:22.9.verse:
The spokes (*ara*) of rebirth’s wheel have been
Destroyed (*hata*) with wisdom’s weapon keen

vsm1.7:22.10.verse:
By him, the Helper of the World,
And so “accomplished” (*arahanta*) he is called.

vsm1.7:23.1.verse: (iv) And he is worthy (*arahati*) of the requisites of robes, etc., and of the distinction of being accorded homage because it is he who is most worthy of offerings.

vsm1.7:23.2.verse: For when a Perfect One has arisen, important deities and human beings pay homage to none else;

vsm1.7:23.3.verse: for Brahmā Sahampati paid homage to the Perfect One with a jewelled garland as big as Sineru,

vsm1.7:23.4.verse: and other deities did so according to their means, as well as human beings as King Bimbisāra [of Magadha] and the king of Kosala.

vsm1.7:23.5.verse: And after the Blessed One had finally attained Nibbāna,

vsm1.7:23.6.verse: King Asoka renounced wealth to the amount of ninety-six million for his sake

vsm1.7:23.7.verse: and founded eight-four thousand monasteries throughout all Jambudīpa (India).

vsm1.7:23.8.verse: And so, with all these, what need to speak of others? Because of worthiness of requisites he is accomplished (*arahanta*) also.

vsm1.7:23.9.verse:
So he is worthy, the Helper of the World,
Of homage paid with requisites;

vsm1.7:23.10.verse:
the word
“Accomplished” (*arahanta*) has this meaning in the world:
Hence the Victor is worthy of that word.

vsm1.7:24.1.verse: (v) And he does not act like those fools in the world who vaunt their cleverness and yet do evil, but in secret for fear of getting a bad name.

vsm1.7:24.2.verse: Because of absence of secret (*rahābhāva*) evil-doing he is accomplished (*arahanta*) also.

vsm1.7:24.3.verse:
No secret evil deed may claim
An author so august;

vsm1.7:24.4.verse:
the name
“Accomplished” (*arahanta*) is his deservedly
By absence of such secrecy (*rahābhāva*).

vsm1.7:25.2.verse:
The Sage of remoteness unalloyed,
Vanquished defiling foes deployed,

vsm1.7:25.3.verse:
The spokes of rebirth’s wheel destroyed,
Worthy of requisites employed,

vsm1.7:25.4.verse:
Secret evil he does avoid:
For these five reasons he may claim
This word “accomplished” for his name.

vsm1.7:26.1.verse: He is fully enlightened (*sammāsambuddha*) because he has discovered (*buddha*) all things rightly (*sammā*) and by himself (*sāmaṃ*).

vsm1.7:26.2.verse: In fact, all things were discovered by him rightly by himself in that he discovered,

vsm1.7:26.3.verse: of the things to be directly known, that they must be directly known (that is, learning about the four truths),

vsm1.7:26.4.verse: of the things to be fully understood that they must be fully understood (that is, penetration of suffering),

vsm1.7:26.5.verse: of the things to be abandoned that they must be abandoned (that is, penetration of the origin of suffering),

vsm1.7:26.6.verse: of the things to be realized that they must be realized (that is, penetration of the cessation of suffering),

vsm1.7:26.7.verse: and of the things to be developed that they must be developed (that is, penetration of the path).

vsm1.7:26.9.verse:
What must be directly known is directly known,
What has to be developed has been developed,

vsm1.7:26.10.verse:
What has to be abandoned has been abandoned;
And that, brahman, is why I am enlightened (Sn 558).

vsm1.7:36.1.verse: He is the *knower of worlds* because he has known the world in all ways.

vsm1.7:36.2.verse: For the Blessed One has experienced, known and penetrated the world in all ways to its individual essence, its arising, its cessation, and the means to its cessation,

vsm1.7:36.3.verse: according as it is said: “Friend, that there is a world’s end where one neither is born nor ages nor dies nor passes away nor reappears,

vsm1.7:36.4.verse: which is to be known or seen or reached by travel—that I do not say.

vsm1.7:36.5.verse: Yet I do not say that there is ending of suffering without reaching the world’s end.

vsm1.7:36.6.verse: Rather, it is in this fathom-long carcass with its perceptions and its consciousness

vsm1.7:36.7.verse: that I make known the world, the arising of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.

vsm1.7:36.8.verse:
“Tis utterly impossible
To reach by travel the world’s end;

vsm1.7:36.9.verse:
But there is no escape from pain
Until the world’s end has been reached.

vsm1.7:36.11.verse:
He is at peace who the world’s end has known
And hopes for neither this world nor the next” (S I 62).

vsm1.7:37.1.verse: Moreover, there are three worlds: the world of formations, the world of beings, and the world of location.

vsm1.7:37.2.verse: Herein, in the passage, “One world: all beings subsist by nutriment” (Paṭis I 122), [205]

vsm1.7:37.3.verse: the world of formations is to be understood.

vsm1.7:37.4.verse: In the passage, “‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal’” (M I 426) it is the world of beings.

vsm1.7:37.5.verse:
In the passage: “As far as moon and sun do circulate
Shining[^12] and lighting up the [four] directions,

vsm1.7:37.6.verse:
Over a thousand times as great a world
Your power holds unquestionable sway” (M I 328)—

vsm1.7:37.7.verse: it is the world of location.

vsm1.7:37.8.verse: The Blessed One has known that in all ways too.

vsm1.7:38.1.verse: Likewise, because of the words: “One world: all beings subsist by nutriment. Two worlds: mentality and materiality.

vsm1.7:38.2.verse: Three worlds: three kinds of feeling. Four worlds: four kinds of nutriment.

vsm1.7:38.3.verse: Five worlds: five aggregates as objects of clinging. Six worlds: six internal bases.

vsm1.7:38.4.verse: Seven worlds: seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: eight worldly states.

vsm1.7:38.5.verse: Nine worlds: nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: ten bases.

vsm1.7:38.6.verse: Twelve worlds: twelve bases. Eighteen worlds: eighteen elements” (Paṭis I 122),[^13]

vsm1.7:38.7.verse: this world of formations was known to him in all ways.

vsm1.7:39.1.verse: But he knows all beings’ habits, knows their inherent tendencies, knows their temperaments, knows their bents,

vsm1.7:39.2.verse: knows them as with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties,

vsm1.7:39.3.verse: with good behaviour and with bad behaviour, easy to teach and hard to teach, capable and incapable [of achievement] (cf. Paṭis I 121),

vsm1.7:39.4.verse: therefore this world of beings was known to him in all ways.

vsm1.7:40.1.verse: And as the world of beings so also the world of location.

vsm1.7:40.2.verse: For accordingly this [world measures as follows]: One world-sphere[^14] is twelve hundred thousand leagues and thirty-four hundred and fifty leagues (1,203,450) in breadth and width.

vsm1.7:40.4.verse:
[The measure of it] all around
Is six and thirty hundred thousand

vsm1.7:40.5.verse:
And then ten thousand in addition,
Four hundred too less half a hundred (3,610,350).

vsm1.7:41.2.verse:
Two times a hundred thousand leagues
And then four *nahutas* as well (240,000):

vsm1.7:41.3.verse:
This earth, this “Bearer of All Wealth,”
Has that much thickness, as they tell.

vsm1.7:41.5.verse:
Four times a hundred thousand leagues
And then eight *nahutas* as well (480,000):

vsm1.7:41.6.verse:
The water resting on the air
Has that much thickness, as they tell.

vsm1.7:41.8.verse:
Nine times a hundred thousand goes
The air out in the firmament

vsm1.7:41.9.verse:
And sixty thousand more besides (960,000)
So this much is the world’s extent.

vsm1.7:42.1.verse: Such is its extent. And these features are to be found in it:

vsm1.7:42.2.verse:
Sineru, tallest of all mountains, plunges down into the sea
Full four and eighty thousand leagues, and towers up in like degree

vsm1.7:42.3.verse:
Seven concentric mountain rings surround Sineru in suchwise
That each of them in depth and height is half its predecessor’s size:

vsm1.7:42.4.verse:
Vast ranges called Yugandhara, Ìsadhara, Karavīka,
Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa.

vsm1.7:42.5.verse:
Heavenly [breezes fan] their cliffs agleam with gems, and here reside
The Four Kings of the Cardinal Points, and other gods and sprites beside.[^15]

vsm1.7:42.6.verse: Himālaya’s lofty mountain mass rises in height five hundred leagues

vsm1.7:42.7.verse: And in its width and in its breadth it covers quite three thousand leagues,

vsm1.7:42.8.verse: And then it is bedecked besides with four and eighty thousand peaks.[^16]

vsm1.7:42.9.verse:
The Jambu Tree called Nāga lends the name, by its magnificence,
To Jambudīpa’s land; its trunk, thrice five leagues in circumference,
Soars fifty leagues, and bears all round branches of equal amplitude,
So that a hundred leagues define diameter and altitude.

vsm1.7:43.1.verse:
The World-sphere Mountains’ line of summits plunges down into the sea
Just two and eighty thousand leagues, and towers up in like degree,

vsm1.7:43.2.verse: Enringing one world-element all round in its entirety.

vsm1.7:43.3.verse: And the size of the Jambu (Rose-apple) Tree is the same as that of

vsm1.7:43.4.verse: the Citrapāṭaliya Tree of the Asura demons, the Simbali Tree of the Garuḷa demons,

vsm1.7:43.5.verse: the Kadamba Tree in [the western continent of] Aparagoyana, the Kappa Tree [in the northern continent] of the Uttarakurus,

vsm1.7:43.6.verse: the Sirīsa Tree in [the eastern continent of] Pubbavideha, and the Pāricchattaka Tree [in the heaven] of the Deities of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa).[^17]

vsm1.7:43.8.verse:
The Pāṭali, Simbali, and Jambu, the deities’ Pāricchattaka,
The Kadamba, the Kappa Tree and the Sirīsa as the seventh.

vsm1.7:44.1.verse: [207] Herein, the moon’s disk is forty-nine leagues [across]

vsm1.7:44.2.verse: and the sun’s disk is fifty leagues.

vsm1.7:44.3.verse: The realm of Tāvatiṃsa (the Thirty-three Gods) is ten thousand leagues.

vsm1.7:44.4.verse: Likewise the realm of the Asura demons, the great Avīci (unremitting) Hell, and Jambudīpa (India).

vsm1.7:44.8.verse: And herein, each great continent is surrounded by five hundred small islands.

vsm1.7:44.9.verse: And the whole of that constitutes a single world-sphere, a single world-element.

vsm1.7:44.10.verse: Between [this and the adjacent world-spheres] are the Lokantarika (world-interspace) hells.[^18]

vsm1.7:44.11.verse: So the world-spheres are infinite in number, the world-elements are infinite,

vsm1.7:44.12.verse: and the Blessed One has experienced, known and penetrated them with the infinite knowledge of the Enlightened Ones.

vsm1.7:45.1.verse: Therefore this world of location was known to him in all ways too.

vsm1.7:45.2.verse: So he is “knower of worlds” because he has seen the world in all ways.

vsm1.7:46.1.verse: In the absence of anyone more distinguished for special qualities than himself,

vsm1.7:46.2.verse: there is no one to compare with him, thus he is *incomparable*.

vsm1.7:46.3.verse: For in this way he surpasses the whole world in the special quality of virtue,

vsm1.7:46.4.verse: and also in the special qualities of concentration, understanding, deliverance, and knowledge and vision of deliverance.

vsm1.7:46.5.verse: In the special quality of virtue he is without equal, he is the equal only of those [other Enlightened Ones] without equal,

vsm1.7:46.6.verse: he is without like, without double, without counterpart; …

vsm1.7:46.7.verse: in the special quality of knowledge and vision of deliverance he is … without counterpart,

vsm1.7:46.8.verse: according as it is said: “I do not see in the world with its deities, its Māras and its Brahmās,

vsm1.7:46.9.verse: in this generation with its ascetics and brahmans, with its princes and men,[^19]

vsm1.7:46.10.verse: anyone more perfect in virtue than myself” (S I 139), with the rest in detail,

vsm1.7:46.11.verse: and likewise in the Aggappasāda Sutta (A II 34; It 87), and so on,

vsm1.7:46.12.verse: and in the stanzas beginning, “I have no teacher and my like does not exist in all the world” (M I 171), all of which should be taken in detail.

vsm1.7:47.1.verse: He guides (*sāreti*) men to be tamed (*purisa-damme*), thus he is *leader of men to be tamed* (*purisadammasārathī*);

vsm1.7:47.2.verse: he tames, he disciplines, is what is meant.

vsm1.7:47.3.verse: Herein, animal males (*purisā*) and human males, and non-human males that are not tamed but fit to be tamed (*dametuṃ yuttā*) are “men to be tamed” (*purisadammā*).

vsm1.7:47.4.verse: For the animal males, namely, the royal nāga (serpent) Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara,

vsm1.7:47.5.verse: Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, the royal nāga Āravāḷa, the elephant Dhanapālaka, and so on,

vsm1.7:47.6.verse: were tamed by the Blessed One, freed from the poison [of defilement] and established in the refuges and the precepts of virtue;

vsm1.7:47.7.verse: and also the human males, namely, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhas’ (Jains’) son, the brahman student Ambaṭṭha, [208] Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and so on;

vsm1.7:47.8.verse: and also the non-human males, namely, the spirits Āḷavaka, Sūciloma and Kharaloma, Sakka Ruler of Gods, etc.,[^20]
