vsm1.7:47.9.verse: were tamed and disciplined by various disciplinary means.

vsm1.7:47.10.verse: And the following sutta should be given in full here: “I discipline men to be tamed sometimes gently, Kesi, and I discipline them sometimes roughly, and I discipline them sometimes gently and roughly” (A II 112).

vsm1.7:48.1.verse: Then the Blessed One moreover further tames those already tamed, doing so by announcing the first jhāna, etc., respectively to those whose virtue is purified, etc., and also the way to the higher path to stream enterers, and so on.

vsm1.7:48.2.verse: Or alternatively, the words *incomparable leader of men* to be tamed can be taken together as one clause.

vsm1.7:48.3.verse: For the Blessed One so guides men to be tamed

vsm1.7:48.4.verse: that in a single session they may go in the eight directions [by the eight liberations] without hesitation.

vsm1.7:48.5.verse: Thus he is called the *incomparable leader of men to be tamed*.

vsm1.7:48.6.verse: And the following sutta passage should be given in full here: “Guided by the elephant-tamer, bhikkhus, the elephant to be tamed goes in one direction …” (M III 222).

vsm1.7:49.1.verse: He teaches (*anusāsati*) by means of the here and now, of the life to come, and of the ultimate goal, according as befits the case, thus he is the Teacher (*satthar*).

vsm1.7:49.2.verse: And furthermore this meaning should be understood according to the Niddesa thus: “‘Teacher (*satthar*)’: the Blessed One is a caravan leader (*satthar*) since he brings home caravans (*sattha*).

vsm1.7:49.3.verse: Just as one who brings a caravan home gets caravans across a wilderness, gets them across a robber-infested wilderness,

vsm1.7:49.4.verse: gets them across a wild-beast-infested wilderness, gets them across a foodless wilderness, gets them across a waterless wilderness,

vsm1.7:49.5.verse: gets them right across, gets them quite across, gets them properly across, gets them to reach a land of safety,

vsm1.7:49.6.verse: so too the Blessed One is a caravan leader, one who brings home the caravans, he gets them across a wilderness, gets them across the wilderness of birth” (Nidd I 446).

vsm1.7:50.1.verse: *Of gods and men: devamanussānaṃ* = *devānañ ca manussānañ ca* (resolution of compound).

vsm1.7:50.2.verse: This is said in order to denote those who are the best and also to denote those persons capable of progress.

vsm1.7:50.3.verse: For the Blessed One as a teacher bestowed his teaching upon animals as well.

vsm1.7:50.4.verse: For when animals can, through listening to the Blessed One’s Dhamma, acquire the benefit of a [suitable rebirth as] support [for progress],

vsm1.7:50.5.verse: and with the benefit of that same support they come, in their second or third rebirth, to partake of the path and its fruition.

vsm1.7:51.1.verse: *Maṇḍūka, the deity’s son*, and others illustrate this.

vsm1.7:51.2.verse: While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the inhabitants of the city of Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lake, it seems,

vsm1.7:51.3.verse: a frog (*maṇḍūka*) apprehended a sign in the Blessed One’s voice.

vsm1.7:51.4.verse: [209] A cowherd who was standing leaning on a stick put his stick on the frog’s head and crushed it.

vsm1.7:51.5.verse: He died and was straight away reborn in a gilded, divine palace, twelve leagues broad in the realm of the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*).

vsm1.7:51.6.verse: He found himself there, as if waking up from sleep, amidst a host of celestial nymphs,

vsm1.7:51.7.verse: and he exclaimed, “So I have actually been reborn here. What deed did I do?”

vsm1.7:51.8.verse: When he sought for the reason, he found it was none other than his apprehension of the sign in the Blessed One’s voice.

vsm1.7:51.9.verse: He went with his divine palace at once to the Blessed One and paid homage at his feet.

vsm1.7:51.10.verse: Though the Blessed One knew about it, he asked him:

vsm1.7:51.11.verse:
“Who now pays homage at my feet,
Shining with glory of success,
Illuminating all around
With beauty so outstanding?”

vsm1.7:51.12.verse:
“In my last life I was a frog,
The waters of a pond my home;

vsm1.7:51.13.verse:
A cowherd’s crook ended my life
While listening to your Dhamma” (Vv 49).

vsm1.7:51.14.verse: The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma.

vsm1.7:51.15.verse: Eighty-four thousand creatures gained penetration to the Dhamma.

vsm1.7:51.16.verse: As soon as the deity’s son became established in the fruition of stream-entry he smiled and then vanished.

vsm1.7:52.1.verse: He is *enlightened* (*buddha*) with the knowledge that belongs to the fruit of liberation, since everything that can be known has been discovered (*buddha*) by him.

vsm1.7:52.2.verse: Or alternatively, he discovered (*bujjhi*) the four truths by himself

vsm1.7:52.4.verse: thus and for other such reasons he is enlightened (*buddha*).

vsm1.7:52.5.verse: And in order to explain this meaning the whole passage in the Niddesa beginning thus: “He is the discoverer (*bujjhitar*) of the truths, thus he is enlightened (*buddha*).

vsm1.7:52.6.verse: He is the awakened (*bodhetar*) of the generation, thus he is enlightened (*buddha*)” (Nidd I 457),

vsm1.7:52.7.verse: or the same passage from the Paṭisambhidā (Paṭis I 174), should be quoted in detail.

vsm1.7:53.1.verse: *Blessed* (*bhagavant*) is a term signifying the respect and veneration accorded to him as the highest of all beings and distinguished by his special qualities.[^21]

vsm1.7:53.3.verse:
“Blessed” is the best of words,
“Blessed” is the finest word;
Deserving awe and veneration,
Blessed is the name therefore.

vsm1.7:54.1.verse: Or alternatively, names are of four kinds:

vsm1.7:54.2.verse: denoting a period of life, describing a particular mark, signifying a particular acquirement, and fortuitously arisen,[^22]

vsm1.7:54.3.verse: which last in the current usage of the world is called “capricious.”

vsm1.7:54.4.verse: Herein, [210] names denoting a period of life are those such as “yearling calf” (*vaccha*), “steer to be trained” (*damma*), “yoke ox” (*balivaddha*), and the like.

vsm1.7:54.5.verse: *Names describing a particular mark* are those such as “staff-bearer” (*daṇḍin*), “umbrella-bearer” (*chattin*), “topknot-wearer” (*sikhin*), “hand possessor” (*karin—*elephant), and the like.

vsm1.7:54.6.verse: *Names signifying a particular acquirement* are those such as “possessor of the threefold clear vision” (*tevijja*), “possessor of the six direct-knowledges” (*chaḷabhiñña*), and the like.

vsm1.7:54.7.verse: Such names are Sirivaḍḍhaka (“Augmenter of Lustre”), Dhanavaḍḍhaka (“Augmenter of Wealth”), etc.,

vsm1.7:54.8.verse: are *fortuitously arisen names*; they have no reference to the word-meanings.

vsm1.7:55.1.verse: This name, *Blessed*, is one signifying a particular acquirement;

vsm1.7:55.2.verse: it is not made by Mahā-Māyā, or by King Suddhodana, or by the eighty thousand kinsmen,

vsm1.7:55.3.verse: or by distinguished deities like Sakka, Santusita, and others.

vsm1.7:55.4.verse: And this is said by the General of the Law:[^23]

vsm1.7:55.5.verse: “‘Blessed’: this is not a name made by a mother …

vsm1.7:55.6.verse: This [name] ‘Buddha,’ which signifies final liberation, is a realistic description of Buddhas (Enlightened Ones), the Blessed Ones, together with their obtainment of omniscient knowledge at the root of an Enlightenment [Tree]” (Paṭis I 174; Nidd I 143).

vsm1.7:56.1.verse: Now, in order to explain also the special qualities signified by this name they cite the following stanza:

vsm1.7:56.2.verse:
*Bhagī bhajī bhāgī vibhattavā iti
Akāsi bhaggan ti garū ti bhāgyavā
Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano
Bhavantago so bhagavā ti vuccati.*

The reverend one (*garu*) has blessings (*bhagī*), is a frequenter (*bhajī*), a partaker (*bhāgī*), a possessor of what has been analyzed (*vibhattavā*); He has caused abolishing (*bhagga*), he is fortunate (*bhāgyavā*), He has fully developed himself (*subhāvitattano*) in many ways; He has gone to the end of becoming (*bhavantago*); thus is called “Blessed” (*bhagavā*).

vsm1.7:56.3.verse: The meaning of these words should be understood according to the method of explanation given in the Niddesa (Nidd I 142).[^24]

vsm1.7:57.1.verse: But there is this other way:

vsm1.7:57.2.verse:
*Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto bhagehi ca vibhattavā.
Bhattavā vanta-gamano bhavesu: bhagavā tato.*

He is fortunate (*bhāgyavā*), possessed of abolishment (*bhaggavā*), associated with blessings (*yutto bhagehi*), and a possessor of what has been analyzed (*vibhattavā*).

He has frequented (*bhattavā*), and he has rejected going in the kinds of becoming (*VAnta-GAmano BHAvesu*), thus he is Blessed (*Bhagavā*).

vsm1.7:58.1.verse: Herein, by using the characteristic of language beginning with “vowel augmentation of syllable, elision of syllable” (see *Kāśikā* VI.3.109),

vsm1.7:58.2.verse: or by using the characteristic of insertion beginning with [the example of] *pisodara*, etc. (see Pāṇini, *Gaṇapāṭha* 6, 3, 109),

vsm1.7:58.3.verse: it may be known that he [can also] be called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) when he can be called “fortunate” (*bhāgyavā*) owing to the fortunateness (*bhāgya*) to have reached the further shore [of the ocean of perfection] of giving, virtue, etc., which produce mundane and supramundane bliss (See Khp-a 108.).

vsm1.7:59.1.verse: [Similarly], he [can also] be called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) when he can be called “possessed of abolishment” (*bhaggavā*) owing to the following menaces having been abolished; for he has abolished (*abhañji*) all the hundred thousand kinds of trouble, anxiety and defilement classed as greed, as hate, as delusion, and as misdirected attention; as consciencelessness and shamelessness, as anger and enmity, as contempt and domineering, as envy and avarice, as deceit and fraud, as obduracy and presumption, as pride and haughtiness, as vanity and negligence, as craving and ignorance;

vsm1.7:59.2.verse: as the three roots of the unprofitable, kinds of misconduct, defilement, stains, [211] fictitious perceptions, applied thoughts, and diversifications; as the four perversenesses,

vsm1.7:59.3.verse: cankers, ties, floods, bonds, bad ways, cravings, and clingings; as the five wildernesses in the heart, shackles in the heart, hindrances, and kinds of delight;

vsm1.7:59.4.verse: as the six roots of discord, and groups of craving; as the seven inherent tendencies; as the eight wrongnesses; as the nine things rooted in craving; as the ten courses of unprofitable action; as the sixty-two kinds of [false] view;

vsm1.7:59.5.verse: as the hundred and eight ways of behaviour of craving[^25]—

vsm1.7:59.6.verse: or in brief, the five Māras, that is to say, the Māras of defilement, of the aggregates, and of kamma-formations, Māra as a deity, and Māra as death.

vsm1.7:59.7.verse: And in this context it is said:

vsm1.7:59.8.verse:
He has abolished (*bhagga*) greed and hate,
Delusion too, he is canker-free;

vsm1.7:59.9.verse:
Abolished every evil state,
“Blessed” his name may rightly be.

vsm1.7:60.1.verse: And by his fortunateness (*bhāgyavatā*) is indicated the excellence of his material body which bears a hundred characteristics of merit;

vsm1.7:60.2.verse: and by his having abolished defects (*bhaggadosatā*) is indicated the excellence of his Dhamma body.

vsm1.7:60.3.verse: Likewise, [by his fortunateness is indicated] the esteem of worldly [people; and by his having abolished defects, the esteem of] those who resemble him.

vsm1.7:60.4.verse: [And by his fortunateness it is indicated] that he is fit to be relied on[^26] by laymen; and [by his having abolished defects that he is fit to be relied on by] those gone forth into homelessness;

vsm1.7:60.5.verse: and when both have relied on him, they acquire relief from bodily and mental pain

vsm1.7:60.6.verse: as well as help with both material and Dhamma gifts,

vsm1.7:60.7.verse: and they are rendered capable of finding both mundane and supramundane bliss.

vsm1.7:61.1.verse: He is also called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) since he is “*associated with blessings*” (*bhagehi yuttattā*) such as those of the following kind,

vsm1.7:61.2.verse: in the sense that he “has those blessings” (*bhagā assa santi*).

vsm1.7:61.3.verse: Now, in the world the word “blessing” is used for six things, namely, lordship, Dhamma, fame, glory, wish, and endeavour.

vsm1.7:61.4.verse: He has supreme *lordship* over his own mind,

vsm1.7:61.5.verse: either of the kind reckoned as mundane and consisting in “minuteness, lightness,” etc.,[^27] or that complete in all aspects,

vsm1.7:61.7.verse: And he has exceedingly pure *fame*, spread through the three worlds, acquired though the special quality of veracity.

vsm1.7:61.8.verse: And he has *glory* of all limbs, perfect in every aspect, which is capable of comforting the eyes of people eager to see his material body.

vsm1.7:61.9.verse: And he has his *wish*, in other words, the production of what is wanted, since whatever is wanted and needed by him as beneficial to himself or others is then and there produced for him.

vsm1.7:61.10.verse: And he has the *endeavour*, in other words, the right effort, which is the reason why the whole world venerates him.

vsm1.7:62.1.verse: [He can also] be called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) when he can be called “*a possessor of what has been analyzed*” (*vibhattavā*) owing to his having analyzed [and clarified] all states into the [three] classes beginning with the profitable;

vsm1.7:62.2.verse: or profitable, etc., states into such classes as aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, etc.; [212]

vsm1.7:62.3.verse: or the noble truth of suffering into the senses of oppressing, being formed, burning, and changing;

vsm1.7:62.4.verse: and that of origin into the senses of accumulating, source, bond, and impediment;

vsm1.7:62.5.verse: and that of cessation into the senses of escape, seclusion, being unformed, and deathless;

vsm1.7:62.6.verse: and that of the path into the senses of outlet, cause, seeing, and predominance.

vsm1.7:62.7.verse: Having analyzed, having revealed, having shown them, is what is meant.

vsm1.7:63.1.verse: He [can also] be called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) when he can be called one who “*has frequented*” (*bhattavā*) owing to his having frequented (*bhaji*), cultivated, repeatedly practiced, such mundane and supramundane higher-than-human states as the heavenly, the divine, and the noble abidings,[^28]

vsm1.7:63.2.verse: as bodily, mental, and existential seclusion,

vsm1.7:63.3.verse: as the void, the desireless, and the signless liberations,

vsm1.7:64.1.verse: He [can also] be called “blessed” (*bhagavā*) when he can be called one who “*has rejected going in the kinds of becoming*” (*vantagamano bhavesu*) because in the three kinds of becoming (*bhava*), the going (*gamana*), in other words, craving, has been rejected (*vanta*) by him.

vsm1.7:64.2.verse: And the syllables *bha* from the word *bhava*, and *ga* from the word *gamana*, and *va* from the word *vanta* with the letter a lengthened, make the word *bhagavā*,

vsm1.7:64.3.verse: just as is done in the world [of the grammarians outside the Dispensation] with the word *mekhalā* (waist-girdle) since “garland for the private parts” (*MEhanassa KHAssa māLĀ*) can be said.

vsm1.7:65.1.verse: As long as [the meditator] recollects the special qualities of the Buddha in this way, “For this and this reason the Blessed One is accomplished, … for this and this reason he is blessed,”

vsm1.7:65.2.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:65.3.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion;

vsm1.7:65.4.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by the Perfect One” (A III 285).[^29]

vsm1.7:66.1.verse: So when he has thus suppressed the hindrances by preventing obsession by greed, etc.,

vsm1.7:66.2.verse: and his mind faces the meditation subject with rectitude,

vsm1.7:66.3.verse: then his applied thought and sustained thought occur with a tendency toward the Enlightened One’s special qualities.

vsm1.7:66.4.verse: As he continues to exercise applied thought and sustained thought upon the Enlightened One’s special qualities, happiness arises in him.

vsm1.7:66.5.verse: With his mind happy, with happiness as a proximate cause, his bodily and mental disturbances are tranquilized by tranquillity.

vsm1.7:66.6.verse: When the disturbances have been tranquilized, bodily and mental bliss arise in him.

vsm1.7:66.7.verse: When he is blissful, his mind, with the Enlightened One’s special qualities for its object, becomes concentrated,

vsm1.7:66.8.verse: and so the jhāna factors eventually arise in a single moment.

vsm1.7:66.9.verse: But owing to the profundity of the Enlightened One’s special qualities, or else owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:66.10.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:66.11.verse: And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of the Buddha” too, because it arises with the recollection of the Enlightened One’s special qualities as the means.

vsm1.7:67.1.verse: When a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of the Buddha, he is respectful and deferential towards the Master.

vsm1.7:67.2.verse: He attains fullness of faith, mindfulness, understanding and merit.

vsm1.7:67.3.verse: He has much happiness and gladness.

vsm1.7:67.5.verse: [213] He is able to endure pain.

vsm1.7:67.6.verse: He comes to feel as if he were living in the Master’s presence.

vsm1.7:67.7.verse: And his body, when the recollection of the Buddha’s special qualities dwells in it,

vsm1.7:67.8.verse: becomes as worthy of veneration as a shrine room.

vsm1.7:67.9.verse: His mind tends toward the plane of the Buddhas.

vsm1.7:67.10.verse: When he encounters an opportunity for transgression,

vsm1.7:67.11.verse: he has awareness of conscience and shame as vivid as though he were face to face with the Master.

vsm1.7:67.12.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:67.13.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be

vsm1.7:67.14.verse:
This recollection of the *Buddha*
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:67.15.verse: This, firstly, is the section dealing with the recollection of the Enlightened One in the detailed explanation.

vsm1.7:68.1.verse: One who wants to develop the recollection of the Dhamma (Law) should go into solitary retreat

vsm1.7:68.2.verse: and recollect the special qualities of both the Dhamma (Law) of the scriptures and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (state) as follows: “The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, not delayed (timeless), inviting of inspection, onward-leading, and directly experienceable by the wise” (M I 37; A III 285).

vsm1.7:69.1.verse: *Well proclaimed*: in this clause the Dhamma of the scriptures is included as well as the other;

vsm1.7:69.2.verse: in the rest of the clauses only the supramundane Dhamma is included.

vsm1.7:69.3.verse: Herein, the Dhamma of the scriptures is well proclaimed

vsm1.7:69.4.verse: because it is good in the beginning, the middle, and the end,

vsm1.7:69.5.verse: and because it announces the life of purity that is utterly perfect and pure with meaning and with detail (see M I 179).

vsm1.7:69.6.verse: Even a single stanza of the Blessed One’s teaching is good in the beginning with the first word,

vsm1.7:69.7.verse: good in the middle with the second, third, etc.,

vsm1.7:69.8.verse: and good in the end with the last word, because the Dhamma is altogether admirable.

vsm1.7:69.9.verse: A sutta with a single sequence of meaning[^30] is good in the beginning with the introduction,

vsm1.7:69.10.verse: good in the end with the conclusion,

vsm1.7:69.11.verse: and good in the middle with what is in between.

vsm1.7:69.12.verse: A sutta with several sequences of meaning is good in the beginning with the first sequence of meaning,

vsm1.7:69.13.verse: good in the end with the last sequence of meaning,

vsm1.7:69.14.verse: and good in the middle with the sequences of meaning in between.

vsm1.7:69.15.verse: Furthermore, it is good in the beginning with the introduction [giving the place of] and the origin [giving the reason for] its utterance.

vsm1.7:69.16.verse: It is good in the middle because it suits those susceptible of being taught since it is unequivocal in meaning and reasoned with cause and example.

vsm1.7:69.17.verse: It is good in the end with its conclusion that inspires faith in the hearers.

vsm1.7:70.1.verse: Also the entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is good in the beginning with virtue as one’s own well-being.

vsm1.7:70.2.verse: It is good in the middle with serenity and insight and with path and fruition.

vsm1.7:70.3.verse: It is good in the end with Nibbāna.

vsm1.7:70.4.verse: Or alternatively, it is good in the beginning with virtue and concentration. [214]

vsm1.7:70.5.verse: It is good in the middle with insight and the path.

vsm1.7:70.6.verse: It is good in the end with fruition and Nibbāna.

vsm1.7:70.7.verse: Or alternatively, it is good in the beginning because it is the good discovery made by the Buddha.

vsm1.7:70.8.verse: It is good in the middle because it is the well-regulatedness of the Dhamma.

vsm1.7:70.9.verse: It is good in the end because it is the good way entered upon by the Saṅgha.

vsm1.7:70.10.verse: Or alternatively, it is good in the beginning as the discovery of what can be attained by one who enters upon the way of practice in conformity after hearing about it.

vsm1.7:70.11.verse: It is good in the middle as the unproclaimed enlightenment [of Paccekabuddhas].

vsm1.7:70.12.verse: It is good in the end as the enlightenment of disciples.

vsm1.7:71.1.verse: And when listened to, it does good through hearing it because it suppresses the hindrances, thus it is good in the beginning.

vsm1.7:71.2.verse: And when made the way of practice it does good through the way being entered upon because it brings the bliss of serenity and insight,

vsm1.7:71.3.verse: thus it is good in the middle.

vsm1.7:71.4.verse: And when it has thus been made the way of practice and the fruit of the way is ready,

vsm1.7:71.5.verse: it does good through the fruit of the way because it brings [unshakable] equipoise,

vsm1.7:71.6.verse: thus it is good in the end.

vsm1.7:71.7.verse: So it is “well proclaimed” because of being good in the beginning, the middle and the end.

vsm1.7:72.1.verse: Now, the life of purity, that is to say, the life of purity of the Dispensation and the life of purity of the path, which the Blessed One announces, which he shows in various ways when he teaches the Dhamma,

vsm1.7:72.2.verse: is “with meaning” because of perfection of meaning,

vsm1.7:72.3.verse: and it is “with detail” because of perfection of detail, as it is proper that it should be.

vsm1.7:72.4.verse: It is “with meaning” because it conforms to the words declaring its meaning by pronouncing, clarifying, revealing, expounding, and explaining it.

vsm1.7:72.5.verse: It is “with detail” because it has perfection of syllables, words, details, style, language, and descriptions.

vsm1.7:72.6.verse: It is “with meaning” owing to profundity of meaning and profundity of penetration.

vsm1.7:72.7.verse: It is “with detail” owing to profundity of law and profundity of teaching.

vsm1.7:72.8.verse: It is “with meaning” because it is the province of the discriminations of meaning and of perspicuity.

vsm1.7:72.9.verse: It is “with detail” because it is the province of the discriminations of law and of language (see XIV.21).

vsm1.7:72.10.verse: It is “with meaning” since it inspires confidence in persons of discretion, being experienceable by the wise.

vsm1.7:72.11.verse: It is “with detail” since it inspires confidence in worldly persons, being a fit object of faith.

vsm1.7:72.12.verse: It is “with meaning” because its intention is profound.

vsm1.7:72.13.verse: It is “with detail” because its words are clear.

vsm1.7:72.14.verse: It is “utterly perfect” with the complete perfection due to absence of anything that can be added.

vsm1.7:72.15.verse: It is “pure” with the immaculateness due to absence of anything to be subtracted.

vsm1.7:73.1.verse: Furthermore, it is “with meaning” because it provides the particular distinction[^31] of achievement through practice of the way,

vsm1.7:73.2.verse: and it is “with detail” because it provides the particular distinction of learning through mastery of scripture.

vsm1.7:73.3.verse: It is “utterly perfect” because it is connected with the five aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue.[^32]

vsm1.7:73.4.verse: It is “pure” because it has no imperfection, because it exists for the purpose of crossing over [the round of rebirths’ flood (see M I 134)],

vsm1.7:73.5.verse: and because it is not concerned with worldly things.

vsm1.7:73.6.verse: So it is “well proclaimed” because it “announces the life of purity that is utterly perfect and pure with meaning and with detail.”

vsm1.7:73.7.verse: Or alternatively, it is *well proclaimed* since it has been properly proclaimed with no perversion of meaning.

vsm1.7:73.8.verse: For the meaning of other sectarians’ law suffers perversion

vsm1.7:73.9.verse: since there is actually no obstruction in the [215] things described there as obstructive

vsm1.7:73.10.verse: and actually no outlet in the things described there as outlets, which is why their law is ill-proclaimed;

vsm1.7:73.11.verse: but not so the Blessed One’s Law, whose meaning suffers no perversion

vsm1.7:73.12.verse: since the things described there as obstructions and the things described there as outlets are so in actual fact.

vsm1.7:73.13.verse: So, in the first place, the Dhamma of the scriptures is “well proclaimed.”

vsm1.7:74.1.verse: The supramundane Dhamma is *well proclaimed* since both the way that accords with Nibbāna and the Nibbāna that accords with the way have been proclaimed,

vsm1.7:74.2.verse: according as it is said: “The way leading to Nibbāna has been properly declared to the disciples by the Blessed One, and Nibbāna and the way meet.

vsm1.7:74.3.verse: Just as the water of the Ganges meets and joins with the water of the Yamunā,

vsm1.7:74.4.verse: so too the way leading to Nibbāna has been properly declared to the disciples by the Blessed One, and Nibbāna and the way meet” (D II 223).

vsm1.7:75.1.verse: And here the noble path, which is the middle way since it does not approach either extreme,

vsm1.7:75.2.verse: is *well proclaimed* in being proclaimed to be the middle way.

vsm1.7:75.3.verse: The fruits of asceticism, where defilements are tranquilized,

vsm1.7:75.4.verse: are *well proclaimed* too in being proclaimed to have tranquilized defilement.

vsm1.7:75.5.verse: Nibbāna, whose individual essence is eternal, deathless, the refuge, the shelter, etc.,

vsm1.7:75.6.verse: is *well proclaimed* too in being proclaimed to have an individual essence that is eternal, and so on.

vsm1.7:75.7.verse: So the supramundane Dhamma is also “well proclaimed.”

vsm1.7:76.1.verse: *Visible here and now*: firstly, the noble path is “visible here and now” since it can be seen by a noble person himself when he has done away with greed, etc., in his own continuity,

vsm1.7:76.2.verse: according as it is said: “When a man is dyed with greed, brahman, and is overwhelmed and his mind is obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:76.3.verse: then he thinks for his own affliction, he thinks for others’ affliction, he thinks for the affliction of both,

vsm1.7:76.4.verse: and he experiences mental suffering and grief.

vsm1.7:76.5.verse: When greed has been abandoned, he neither thinks for his own affliction, nor thinks for others’ affliction, nor thinks for the affliction of both,

vsm1.7:76.6.verse: and he does not experience mental suffering and grief.

vsm1.7:76.7.verse: This, brahman, is how the Dhamma is visible here and now” (A I 156). [216]

vsm1.7:77.1.verse: Furthermore, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is also *visible here and now*, since when anyone has attained it, it is visible to him through reviewing knowledge without his having to rely on faith in another.

vsm1.7:78.1.verse: Or alternatively, the view (*diṭṭhi*) that is recommended (*pasattha—*pp. of root *saṃs*) is “proper view” (*sandiṭṭhi*).

vsm1.7:78.2.verse: It conquers by means of proper view, thus it “has proper view” (*sandiṭṭhika—*“visible here and now”).

vsm1.7:78.3.verse: For in this way the noble path conquers defilements by means of the proper view associated with it,

vsm1.7:78.4.verse: and the noble fruition does so by means of the proper view that is its cause,

vsm1.7:78.5.verse: and Nibbāna does so by means of the proper view that has Nibbāna as its objective field.

vsm1.7:78.6.verse: So the ninefold supramundane Dhamma “has the proper view” (*sandiṭṭhika—*“is visible here and now”) since it conquers by means of proper view, just as a charioteer (*rathika*) is so called because he conquers by means of a chariot (*ratha*).

vsm1.7:80.1.verse: It has no delay (lit. “takes no time”—*kāla*) in the matter of giving its own fruit, thus it is “without delay” (*akāla*).

vsm1.7:80.2.verse: “Without delay” is the same as “not delayed” (*akālika*).

vsm1.7:80.3.verse: What is meant is that instead of giving its fruit after creating a delay (using up time), say, five days, seven days,

vsm1.7:80.4.verse: it gives its fruit immediately next to its own occurrence (see Sn 226).

vsm1.7:81.1.verse: Or alternatively, what is delayed (*kālika—*lit. “what takes time”) is what needs some distant[^34] time to be reached before it can give its fruit.

vsm1.7:81.3.verse: It is the mundane law of profitable [kamma].

vsm1.7:81.4.verse: This, however, is undelayed (*na kālika*) because its fruit comes immediately next to it, so it is “not delayed” (*akālika*).

vsm1.7:81.5.verse: This is said with reference to the path.

vsm1.7:82.1.verse: It is worthy of an invitation to inspect (*ehipassa-vidhi*) given thus: “Come and see this Dhamma” (*ehi passa imaṃ dhammaṃ*), thus it is “inviting of inspection” (*ehipassika*).

vsm1.7:82.2.verse: But why is it worthy of this invitation?

vsm1.7:82.3.verse: Because it is found and because of its purity.

vsm1.7:82.4.verse: For if a man has said that there is money or gold in an empty fist, he cannot say, “Come and see it.”

vsm1.7:82.7.verse: And on the other hand, while dung or urine may well be found,

vsm1.7:82.8.verse: a man cannot, for the purpose of cheering the mind by exhibiting beauty, say, “Come and see this;”

vsm1.7:82.9.verse: on the contrary, they have to be covered up with grass and leaves.

vsm1.7:82.12.verse: But this ninefold supramundane Dhamma is actually found as such in its individual essence,

vsm1.7:82.13.verse: and it is as pure as the full moon’s disk in a cloudless sky,

vsm1.7:82.14.verse: as a gem of pure water on bleached cloth. [217]

vsm1.7:82.15.verse: Consequently, it is worthy of the invitation to inspect since it is found and pure, thus it is “inviting of inspection.”

vsm1.7:83.1.verse: The word *opanayika* (“onward-leading”) is [equivalent to the gerund] *upanetabba* (“ought to—can—be induced”).

vsm1.7:83.2.verse: Here is an exposition. An inducing (*upanayana*) is an inducement (*upanaya*).

vsm1.7:83.3.verse: [As the four paths and four fruitions] this [Dhamma] is worth inducing (*upanayanaṃ arahati*) [that is, arousing] *in* one’s own mind [subjectively] by means of development, without any question of whether or not one’s clothing or one’s head is on fire (see A IV 320), thus it is “onward-leading” (*opanayika*).

vsm1.7:83.4.verse: This applies to the [above-mentioned eight] formed supramundane states (dhammas).

vsm1.7:83.5.verse: But the unformed [dhamma] is worth inducing *by* one’s own mind [to become the mind’s object], thus it is “onward-leading,” too;

vsm1.7:83.6.verse: the meaning is that it is worth treating as one’s shelter by realizing it.

vsm1.7:84.1.verse: Or alternatively, what induces (*upaneti*) [the noble person] onwards to Nibbāna is the noble path, which is thus inductive (*upaneyya*).

vsm1.7:84.2.verse: Again, what can (ought to) be induced (*upanetabba*) to realizability is the Dhamma consisting in fruition and Nibbāna, which is thus inductive (*upaneyya*), too.

vsm1.7:84.3.verse: The word *upaneyya* is the same as the word *opanayika*.[^35]

vsm1.7:85.2.verse: it can be experienced by all the kinds of wise men beginning with the “acutely wise” (see A II 135) each in himself thus:

vsm1.7:85.3.verse: “The path has been developed, fruition attained, and cessation realized, by me.”

vsm1.7:85.4.verse: For it does not happen that when a preceptor has developed the path his co-resident abandons his defilements,

vsm1.7:85.5.verse: nor does a co-resident dwell in comfort owing to the preceptor’s attainment of fruition,

vsm1.7:85.6.verse: nor does he realize the Nibbāna realized by the preceptor.

vsm1.7:85.7.verse: So this is not visible in the way that an ornament on another’s head is,

vsm1.7:85.8.verse: but rather it is visible only in one’s own mind.

vsm1.7:85.9.verse: What is meant is that it can be undergone by wise men,

vsm1.7:85.10.verse: but it is not the province of fools.

vsm1.7:86.1.verse: Now, in addition, this Dhamma is well proclaimed.

vsm1.7:86.3.verse: Because it is visible here and now.

vsm1.7:86.4.verse: It is visible here and now because it is not delayed.

vsm1.7:86.5.verse: It is not delayed because it invites inspection.

vsm1.7:86.6.verse: And what invites inspection is onward-leading.

vsm1.7:87.1.verse: As long as [the meditator] recollects the special qualities of the Dhamma in this way,

vsm1.7:87.2.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:87.3.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion;

vsm1.7:87.4.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by the Dhamma” (A III 285).

vsm1.7:87.5.verse: So when he has suppressed the hindrances in the way already described (§66),

vsm1.7:87.6.verse: the jhāna factors arise in a single conscious moment.

vsm1.7:87.7.verse: But owing to the profundity of the Dhamma’s special qualities, or else owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:87.8.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:87.9.verse: And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of the Dhamma” too because it arises with the recollection of the Dhamma’s special qualities as the means.

vsm1.7:88.1.verse: [218] When a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of the Dhamma, he thinks:

vsm1.7:88.2.verse: “I never in the past met a master who taught a law that led onward thus, who possessed this talent,

vsm1.7:88.3.verse: nor do I now see any such a master other than the Blessed One.”

vsm1.7:88.4.verse: Seeing the Dhamma’s special qualities in this way, he is respectful and deferential towards the Master.

vsm1.7:88.5.verse: He entertains great reverence for the Dhamma and attains fullness of faith, and so on.

vsm1.7:88.6.verse: He has much happiness and gladness.

vsm1.7:88.8.verse: He is able to endure pain.

vsm1.7:88.9.verse: He comes to feel as if he were living in the Dhamma’s presence.

vsm1.7:88.10.verse: And his body, when the recollection of the Dhamma’s special qualities dwells in it,

vsm1.7:88.11.verse: becomes as worthy of veneration as a shrine room.

vsm1.7:88.12.verse: His mind tends towards the realization of the peerless Dhamma.

vsm1.7:88.13.verse: When he encounters an opportunity for transgression,

vsm1.7:88.14.verse: he has vivid awareness of conscience and shame on recollecting the well-regulatedness of the Dhamma.

vsm1.7:88.15.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:88.16.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be

vsm1.7:88.17.verse:
This recollection of the *Dhamma*
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:88.18.verse: This is the section dealing with the recollection of the Dhamma in the detailed explanation.

vsm1.7:89.1.verse: One who wants to develop the recollection of the Community should go into solitary retreat

vsm1.7:89.2.verse: and recollect the special qualities of the community of Noble Ones as follows: “The community of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way,

vsm1.7:89.3.verse: the community of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the straight way,

vsm1.7:89.4.verse: the community of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the true way,

vsm1.7:89.5.verse: the community of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the proper way,

vsm1.7:89.6.verse: that is to say, the four pairs of men, the eight persons;

vsm1.7:89.7.verse: this community of the Blessed One’s disciples is fit for gifts, fit for hospitality, fit for offerings, fit for reverential salutation,

vsm1.7:89.8.verse: as an incomparable field of merit for the world” (A III 286).

vsm1.7:90.1.verse: Herein, *entered on the good way* (*supaṭipanna*) is thoroughly entered on the way (*suṭṭhu paṭipanna*).

vsm1.7:90.2.verse: What is meant is that it has entered on a way (*paṭipanna*) that is the right way (*sammā-paṭipadā*), the way that is irreversible, the way that is in conformity [with truth], the way that has no opposition, the way that is regulated by the Dhamma.

vsm1.7:90.3.verse: They hear (*suṇanti*) attentively the Blessed One’s instruction, thus they are his disciples (*sāvaka—*lit. “hearers”).

vsm1.7:90.4.verse: *The community of the disciples* is the community of those disciples.

vsm1.7:90.5.verse: The meaning is that the total of disciples forms a communality because it possesses in common both virtue and [right] view. [219]

vsm1.7:90.6.verse: That right way, being *straight*, unbent, uncrooked, unwarped,

vsm1.7:90.7.verse: is called noble and *true* and is known as *proper* owing to its becomingness,

vsm1.7:90.8.verse: therefore the noble community that has entered on that

vsm1.7:90.9.verse: is also said to have *entered on the straight way*, *entered on the true way*, and *entered on the proper way*.

vsm1.7:91.1.verse: Those who stand on the path can be understood to have *entered on the good way* since they possess the right way.

vsm1.7:91.2.verse: And those who stand in fruition can be understood to have *entered on the good way* with respect to the way that is now past since by means of the right way they have realized what should be realized.

vsm1.7:92.1.verse: Furthermore, the Community *has entered on the good way* because it has entered on the way according as instructed in the well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline (*dhamma-vinaya*),

vsm1.7:92.2.verse: and because it has entered on the immaculate way.

vsm1.7:92.3.verse: It *has entered on the straight way* because it has entered on the way avoiding the two extremes and taking the middle course,

vsm1.7:92.4.verse: and because it has entered on the way of the abandonment of the faults of bodily and verbal crookedness, tortuousness and warpedness.

vsm1.7:92.5.verse: It *has entered on the true way* because Nibbāna is what is called “true” and it has entered on the way with that as its aim.

vsm1.7:92.6.verse: It *has entered on the proper way* because it has entered on the way of those who are worthy of proper acts [of veneration].

vsm1.7:93.1.verse: The word *yadidaṃ* (“that is to say”) = *yāni imāni*.

vsm1.7:93.3.verse: taking them pairwise, the one who stands on the first path and the one who stands in the first fruition as one pair,

vsm1.7:93.4.verse: in this way there are four pairs.

vsm1.7:93.6.verse: taking them by persons, the one who stands on the first path as one and the one who stands in the first fruition as one,

vsm1.7:93.7.verse: in this way there are eight persons.

vsm1.7:93.8.verse: And there in the compound *purisa-puggala* (persons) the words *purisa* and *puggala* have the same meaning,

vsm1.7:93.9.verse: but it is expressed in this way to suit differing susceptibility to teaching.

vsm1.7:93.10.verse: *This community of the Blessed One’s disciples*:

vsm1.7:93.11.verse: this community of the Blessed One’s disciples taken by pairs as the four pairs of men (*purisa*)

vsm1.7:93.12.verse: and individually as the eight persons (*purisa-puggala*).

vsm1.7:94.2.verse: what should be brought (*ānetvā*) and given (*hunitabba*) is a gift (*āhuna—*lit. “sacrifice”);

vsm1.7:94.3.verse: the meaning is, what is to be brought even from far away and donated to the virtuous.

vsm1.7:94.4.verse: It is a term for the four requisites.

vsm1.7:94.5.verse: The Community is fit to receive that gift (sacrifice) because it makes it bear great fruit, thus it is “fit for gifts” (*āhuneyya*).

vsm1.7:95.1.verse: Or alternatively, all kinds of property, even when the bringer comes (*āgantvā*) from far away, can be given (*hunitabba*) here, thus the Community “can be given to” (*āhavanīya*);

vsm1.7:95.2.verse: or it is fit to be given to by Sakka and others, thus it “can be given to.”

vsm1.7:95.3.verse: And the brahmans’ fire is called “to be given (sacrificed) to” (*āhavanīya*),

vsm1.7:95.4.verse: for they believe that what is sacrificed to it brings great fruit. [220]

vsm1.7:95.5.verse: But if something is to be sacrificed to for the sake of the great fruit brought by what is sacrificed to it, then surely the Community should be sacrificed to;

vsm1.7:95.6.verse: for what is sacrificed (given) to the Community has great fruit,

vsm1.7:95.8.verse:
> “Were anyone to serve the fire
> Out in the woods a hundred years,

vsm1.7:95.9.verse:
> And pay one moment’s homage too
> To men of self-development,

vsm1.7:95.10.verse:
> His homage would by far excel
> His hundred years of sacrifice” (Dhp 107).

vsm1.7:95.11.verse: And the words *āhavanīya* (“to be sacrificed to”), which is used in the schools,[^36]

vsm1.7:95.12.verse: is the same in meaning as this word *āhuneyya* (“fit for gifts”) used here.

vsm1.7:95.13.verse: There is only the mere trifling difference of syllables.

vsm1.7:96.1.verse: *Fit for hospitality* (*pāhuneyya*): “hospitality” (*pāhuna*) is what a donation to visitors is called,

vsm1.7:96.2.verse: prepared with all honours for the sake of dear and beloved relatives and friends who have come from all quarters.

vsm1.7:96.3.verse: But even more than to such objects of hospitality, it is fitting that it should be given also to the Community;

vsm1.7:96.4.verse: for there is no object of hospitality so fit to receive hospitality as the Community

vsm1.7:96.5.verse: since it is encountered after an interval between Buddhas and possesses wholly endearing and lovable qualities.

vsm1.7:96.6.verse: So it is “fit for hospitality” since the hospitality is fit to be given to it and it is fit to receive it.

vsm1.7:96.7.verse: But those who take the text to be *pāhavanīya* (“fit to be given hospitality to”) have it that

vsm1.7:96.8.verse: the Community is worthy to be placed first

vsm1.7:96.9.verse: and so what is to be given should first of all be brought here and given (*sabba-Paṭhamaṃ Ānetvā ettha HUNitabbaṃ*), and for that reason it is “fit to be given hospitality to” (*pāhavanīya*)

vsm1.7:96.10.verse: or since it is worthy to be given to in all aspects (*sabba-Pakārena ĀHAVANAṃ arahati*), it is thus “fit to be given hospitality to” (*pāhavanīya*).

vsm1.7:96.11.verse: And here this is called *pāhuneyya* in the same sense.

vsm1.7:97.1.verse: ”Offering” (*dakkhiṇa*) is what a gift is called that is to be given out of faith in the world to come.

vsm1.7:97.2.verse: The Community is worthy of that offering,

vsm1.7:97.3.verse: or it is helpful to that offering because it purifies it by making it of great fruit,

vsm1.7:98.1.verse: It is worthy of being accorded by the whole world the reverential salutation (*añjali-kamma*) consisting in placing both hands [palms together] above the head, thus it is *fit for reverential salutation* (*añjalikaraṇīya*).

vsm1.7:98.2.verse: *As an incomparable field of merit for the world*: as a place without equal in the world for growing merit;

vsm1.7:98.3.verse: just as the place for growing the king’s or minister’s rice or corn

vsm1.7:98.4.verse: is the king’s rice-field or the king’s corn-field,

vsm1.7:98.5.verse: so the Community is the place for growing the whole world’s merit.

vsm1.7:98.6.verse: For the world’s various kinds of merit leading to welfare and happiness grow with the Community as their support.

vsm1.7:98.7.verse: Therefore the Community is “an incomparable field of merit for the world.”

vsm1.7:99.1.verse: As long as he recollects the special qualities of the Saṅgha in this way, classed as “having entered on the good way,” etc., [221]

vsm1.7:99.2.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:99.3.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion;

vsm1.7:99.4.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by the Saṅgha” (A III 286).

vsm1.7:99.5.verse: So when he has suppressed the hindrances in the way already described (§66),

vsm1.7:99.6.verse: the jhāna factors arise in a single conscious moment.

vsm1.7:99.7.verse: But owing to the profundity of the Community’s special qualities, or else owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:99.8.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:99.9.verse: And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of the Saṅgha” too because it arises with the recollection of the Community’s special qualities as the means.

vsm1.7:100.1.verse: When a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of the Community, he is respectful and deferential towards the Community.

vsm1.7:100.2.verse: He attains fullness of faith, and so on.

vsm1.7:100.3.verse: He has much happiness and bliss.

vsm1.7:100.5.verse: He is able to endure pain.

vsm1.7:100.6.verse: He comes to feel as if he were living in the Community’s presence.

vsm1.7:100.7.verse: And his body, when the recollection of the Sangha’s special qualities dwells in it,

vsm1.7:100.8.verse: becomes as worthy of veneration as an Uposatha house where the Community has met.

vsm1.7:100.9.verse: His mind tends towards the attainment of the Community’s special qualities.

vsm1.7:100.10.verse: When he encounters an opportunity for transgression,

vsm1.7:100.11.verse: he has awareness of conscience and shame as vividly as if he were face to face with the Community.

vsm1.7:100.12.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:100.13.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be

vsm1.7:100.14.verse:
This recollection of the *Saṅgha*
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:100.15.verse: This is the section dealing with the recollection of the Community in the detailed explanation.

vsm1.7:101.1.verse: One who wants to develop the recollection of virtue should go into solitary retreat

vsm1.7:101.2.verse: and recollect his own different kinds of virtue in their special qualities of being untorn, etc., as follows: Indeed, my various kinds of virtue are “untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled,

vsm1.7:101.3.verse: liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, and conducive to concentration” (A III 286).

vsm1.7:101.4.verse: And a layman should recollect them in the form of laymen’s virtue while one gone forth into homelessness should recollect them in the form of the virtue of those gone forth.

vsm1.7:102.1.verse: Whether they are the virtues of laymen or of those gone forth,

vsm1.7:102.2.verse: when no one of them is broken in the beginning or in the end,

vsm1.7:102.3.verse: not being torn like a cloth ragged at the ends, then they are *untorn*. [222]

vsm1.7:102.4.verse: When no one of them is broken in the middle, not being rent like a cloth that is punctured in the middle, then they are *unrent*.

vsm1.7:102.5.verse: When they are not broken twice or thrice in succession,

vsm1.7:102.6.verse: not being blotched like a cow whose body is some such colour as black or red with discrepant-coloured oblong or round patch appearing on her back or belly,

vsm1.7:102.8.verse: When they are not broken all over at intervals,

vsm1.7:102.9.verse: not being mottled like a cow speckled with discrepant-coloured spots, then they are *unmottled*.

vsm1.7:103.1.verse: Or in general they are *untorn*, *unrent*, *unblotched*, *unmottled* when they are undamaged by the seven bonds of sexuality (I.144) and by anger and enmity and the other evil things (see §59).

vsm1.7:104.1.verse: Those same virtues are *liberating* since they liberate by freeing from the slavery of craving.

vsm1.7:104.2.verse: They are *praised by the wise* because they are praised by such wise men as Enlightened Ones.

vsm1.7:104.3.verse: They are *not adhered to* (*aparāmaṭṭha*) since they are not adhered to (*aparāmaṭṭhattā*) with craving and [false] view,

vsm1.7:104.4.verse: or because of the impossibility of misapprehending (*parāmaṭṭhuṃ*) that “There is this flaw in your virtues.”

vsm1.7:104.5.verse: They are *conducive to concentration* since they conduce to access concentration and absorption concentration,

vsm1.7:104.6.verse: or to path concentration and fruition concentration.

vsm1.7:105.1.verse: As long as he recollects his own virtues in their special qualities of being untorn, etc., in this way,

vsm1.7:105.2.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:105.3.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion,

vsm1.7:105.4.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by virtue” (A III 286).

vsm1.7:105.5.verse: So when he has suppressed the hindrances in the way already described (§66),

vsm1.7:105.6.verse: the jhāna factors arise in a single conscious moment.

vsm1.7:105.7.verse: But owing to the profundity of the virtues’ special qualities, or owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:105.8.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:105.9.verse: And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of virtue” too because it arises with the virtues’ special qualities as the means.

vsm1.7:106.1.verse: And when a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of virtue, he has respect for the training.

vsm1.7:106.2.verse: He lives in communion [with his fellows in the life of purity].

vsm1.7:106.4.verse: He is devoid of the fear of self-reproach and so on.

vsm1.7:106.5.verse: He sees fear in the slightest fault.

vsm1.7:106.6.verse: He attains fullness of faith, and so on.

vsm1.7:106.7.verse: He has much happiness and gladness.

vsm1.7:106.8.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:106.9.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be
This recollection of his virtue
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:106.10.verse: This is the section dealing with the recollection of virtue in the detailed explanation. [223]

vsm1.7:107.1.verse: One who wants to develop the recollection of generosity

vsm1.7:107.2.verse: should be naturally devoted to generosity and the constant practice of giving and sharing.

vsm1.7:107.3.verse: Or alternatively, if he is one who is starting the development of it,

vsm1.7:107.4.verse: he should make the resolution: “From now on, when there is anyone present to receive, I shall not eat even a single mouthful without having given a gift.”

vsm1.7:107.5.verse: And that very day he should give a gift by sharing according to his means and his ability with those who have distinguished qualities.

vsm1.7:107.6.verse: When he has apprehended the sign in that,

vsm1.7:107.7.verse: he should go into solitary retreat and recollect his own generosity in its special qualities of being free from the stain of avarice, etc., as follows:

vsm1.7:107.8.verse: “It is gain for me, it is great gain for me,

vsm1.7:107.9.verse: that in a generation obsessed by the stain of avarice I abide with my heart free from stain by avarice,

vsm1.7:107.10.verse: and am freely generous and open-handed, that I delight in relinquishing, expect to be asked, and rejoice in giving and sharing” (A III 287).

vsm1.7:108.1.verse: Herein, *it is gain for me*: it is my gain, advantage.

vsm1.7:108.2.verse: The intention is: I surely partake of those kinds of gain for a giver that have been commended by the Blessed One as follows: “A man who gives life [by giving food] shall have life either divine or human” (A III 42),

vsm1.7:108.3.verse: and: “A giver is loved and frequented by many” (A III 40),

vsm1.7:108.4.verse: and: “One who gives is ever loved, according to the wise man’s law” (A III 41), and so on.

vsm1.7:109.1.verse: *It is great gain for me*: it is great gain for me that this Dispensation, or the human state, has been gained by me.

vsm1.7:109.3.verse: Because of the fact that “I abide *with my mind free from stain by avarice* … *and rejoice in giving and sharing*.”

vsm1.7:110.1.verse: Herein, *obsessed by the stain of avarice* is overwhelmed by the stain of avarice.

vsm1.7:110.2.verse: *Generation*: beings, so called owing to the fact of their being generated.

vsm1.7:110.3.verse: So the meaning here is this: among beings who are overwhelmed by the stain of avarice, which is one of the dark states that corrupt the [natural] transparency of consciousness (see A I 10) and which has the characteristic of inability to bear sharing one’s own good fortune with others.

vsm1.7:111.1.verse: *Free from stain by avarice* because of being both free from avarice and from the other stains, greed, hate, and the rest.

vsm1.7:111.2.verse: *I abide with my heart*: I abide with my consciousness of the kind already stated, is the meaning. [224]

vsm1.7:111.3.verse: But in the sutta, “I live the home life with my heart free” (A III 287; V 331), etc., is said because it was taught there as a [mental] abiding to depend on [constantly] to Mahānāma the Sakyan, who was a stream-enterer asking about an abiding to depend on.

vsm1.7:111.4.verse: There the meaning is “I live overcoming …”

vsm1.7:112.3.verse: What is meant is: with hands that are always washed in order to give gifts carefully with one’s own hands.

vsm1.7:112.4.verse: *That I delight in relinquishing*: the act of relinquishing (*vossajjana*) is relinquishing (*vossagga*); the meaning is, giving up.

vsm1.7:112.5.verse: To delight in relinquishing is to delight in constant devotion to that relinquishing.

vsm1.7:112.6.verse: *Expect to be asked* (*yācayoga*): accustomed to being asked (*yācana-yogga*) because of giving whatever others ask for, is the meaning.

vsm1.7:112.7.verse: *Yājayoga* is a reading, in which case the meaning is: devoted (*yutta*) to sacrifice (*yāja*), in other words, to sacrificing (*yajana*).

vsm1.7:112.9.verse: the meaning is, he recollects thus: “I give gifts and I share out what is to be used by myself, and I rejoice in both.”

vsm1.7:113.1.verse: As long as he recollects his own generosity in its special qualities of freedom from stain by avarice, etc., in this way,

vsm1.7:113.2.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:113.3.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion;

vsm1.7:113.4.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by generosity” (A III 287).

vsm1.7:113.5.verse: So when he has suppressed the hindrances in the way already described (§66),

vsm1.7:113.6.verse: the jhāna factors arise in a single conscious moment.

vsm1.7:113.7.verse: But owing to the profundity of the generosity’s special qualities, or owing to his being occupied in recollecting the generosity’s special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:113.8.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:113.9.verse: And that access jhāna is known as “recollection of generosity” too because it arises with the generosity’s special qualities as the means.

vsm1.7:114.1.verse: And when a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of generosity, he becomes ever more intent on generosity,

vsm1.7:114.3.verse: he acts in conformity with loving-kindness,

vsm1.7:114.5.verse: He has much happiness and gladness.

vsm1.7:114.6.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:114.7.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be
This recollection of his giving
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:114.8.verse: This is the section dealing with the recollection of generosity in the detailed explanation. [225]

vsm1.7:115.1.verse: One who wants to develop the recollection of deities

vsm1.7:115.2.verse: should possess the special qualities of faith, etc., evoked by means of the noble path,

vsm1.7:115.3.verse: and he should go into solitary retreat and recollect his own special qualities of faith, etc., with deities standing as witnesses, as follows:

vsm1.7:115.4.verse: “There are deities of the Realm of the Four Kings (*devā cātummahārājikā*), there are deities of the Realm of the Thirty-three (*devā tāvatiṃsā*), there are deities who are Gone to Divine Bliss (*yāmā*) … who are Contented (*tusitā*) … who Delight in Creating (*nimmānarati*) … who Wield Power Over Others’ Creations (*paranimmitavasavatti*),

vsm1.7:115.5.verse: there are deities of Brahmā’s Retinue (*brahmakāyikā*), there are deities higher than that.

vsm1.7:115.6.verse: And those deities were possessed of faith such that on dying here they were reborn there, and such faith is present in me too.

vsm1.7:115.7.verse: And those deities were possessed of virtue … of learning … of generosity …

vsm1.7:115.8.verse: of understanding such that when they died here they were reborn there, and such understanding is present in me too” (A III 287).

vsm1.7:116.1.verse: In the sutta, however, it is said: “On the occasion, Mahānāma, on which a noble disciple recollects the faith, the virtue, the learning, the generosity, and the understanding that are both his own and of those deities,”

vsm1.7:116.2.verse: on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed …” (A III 287).

vsm1.7:116.4.verse: it should nevertheless be understood as said for the purpose of showing that the special qualities of faith, etc., in oneself are those in the deities, making the deities stand as witnesses.

vsm1.7:116.5.verse: For it is said definitely in the Commentary: “He recollects his own special qualities, making the deities stand as witnesses.”

vsm1.7:117.1.verse: As long as in the prior stage he recollects the deities’ special qualities of faith, etc.,

vsm1.7:117.2.verse: and in the later stage he recollects the special qualities of faith, etc., existing in himself,

vsm1.7:117.3.verse: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,

vsm1.7:117.4.verse: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion,

vsm1.7:117.5.verse: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by deities” (A III 288).

vsm1.7:117.6.verse: So when he has suppressed the hindrances in the way already stated (§66), the jhāna factors arise in a single conscious moment.

vsm1.7:117.7.verse: But owing to the profundity of the special qualities of faith, etc., or owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,

vsm1.7:117.8.verse: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.

vsm1.7:117.9.verse: And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of deities” too because it arises with the deities special qualities as the means. [226]

vsm1.7:118.1.verse: And when a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of deities, he becomes dearly loved by deities.

vsm1.7:118.2.verse: He obtains even greater fullness of faith.

vsm1.7:118.3.verse: He has much happiness and gladness.

vsm1.7:118.4.verse: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.

vsm1.7:118.5.verse:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be
This recollection of deities
Blessed with such mighty potency.

vsm1.7:118.6.verse: This is the section dealing with the recollection of deities in the detailed explanation.

vsm1.7:119.1.verse: Now, in setting forth the detail of these recollections, after the words, “His mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by the Perfect One,”

vsm1.7:119.2.verse: it is added: “When a noble disciple’s mind has rectitude, Mahānāma, the meaning inspires him, the law inspires him,

vsm1.7:119.3.verse: and the application of the law makes him glad. When he is glad, happiness is born in him” (A III 285–88).

vsm1.7:119.4.verse: Herein, *the meaning inspires him* should be understood as said of contentment inspired by the meaning beginning, “This Blessed One is such since he is …” (§2).

vsm1.7:119.5.verse: *The law inspires him* is said of contentment inspired by the text.

vsm1.7:119.6.verse: The *application of the law makes him glad* is said of both (cf. M-a I 173).

vsm1.7:120.1.verse: And when in the case of the recollection of deities *inspired by deities* is said,

vsm1.7:120.2.verse: this should be understood as said either of the consciousness that occurs in the prior stage inspired by deities

vsm1.7:120.3.verse: or of the consciousness [that occurs in the later stage] inspired by the special qualities that are similar to those of the deities and are productive of the deities’ state (cf. §117).

vsm1.7:121.1.verse: These six recollections succeed only in noble disciples.

vsm1.7:121.2.verse: For the special qualities of the Enlightened One, the Law, and the Community, are evident to them;

vsm1.7:121.3.verse: and they possess the virtue with the special qualities of untornness, etc.,

vsm1.7:121.4.verse: the generosity that is free from stain by avarice,

vsm1.7:121.5.verse: and the special qualities of faith, etc., similar to those of deities.

vsm1.7:122.1.verse: And in the Mahānāma Sutta (A III 285 f.) they are expounded in detail by the Blessed One in order to show a stream-winner an abiding to depend upon when he asked for one.

vsm1.7:123.1.verse: Also in the Gedha Sutta they are expounded in order that a noble disciple should purify his consciousness by means of the recollections and so attain further purification in the ultimate sense thus:

vsm1.7:123.2.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the Perfect One in this way: That Blessed One is such since he is accomplished …

vsm1.7:123.3.verse: His mind has rectitude on that occasion. He has renounced, [227] got free from, emerged from cupidity.

vsm1.7:123.4.verse: Cupidity, bhikkhus, is a term for the five cords of sense desire.

vsm1.7:123.5.verse: Some beings gain purity here by making this [recollection] their prop” (A III 312).

vsm1.7:124.1.verse: And in the Sambādhokāsa Sutta taught by the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna they are expounded as the realization of the wide-open through the susceptibility of purification that exists in the ultimate sense only in a noble disciple thus:

vsm1.7:124.2.verse: “It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous

vsm1.7:124.3.verse: how the realization of the wide-open in the crowded [house life] has been discovered by the Blessed One who knows and sees, accomplished and fully enlightened, for the purification of beings, [for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way], for the realization of Nibbāna,

vsm1.7:124.4.verse: that is to say, the six stations of recollection. What six?

vsm1.7:124.5.verse: Here, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Perfect One … Some beings are susceptible to purification in this way” (A III 314–15).

vsm1.7:125.1.verse: Also in the Uposatha Sutta they are expounded in order to show the greatness of the fruit of the Uposatha, as a mind-purifying meditation subject for a noble disciple who is observing the Uposatha:

vsm1.7:125.2.verse: “And what is the Noble Ones’ Uposatha, Visākhā?

vsm1.7:125.3.verse: It is the gradual cleansing of the mind still sullied by imperfections.

vsm1.7:125.4.verse: And what is the gradual cleansing of the mind still sullied by imperfections?

vsm1.7:125.5.verse: Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Perfect One …” (A I 206–11).

vsm1.7:126.1.verse: And in the Book of Elevens, when a noble disciple has asked, “Venerable sir, in what way should we abide who abide in various ways?” (A V 328), they are expounded to him in order to show the way of abiding in this way:

vsm1.7:126.2.verse: “One who has faith is successful, Mahānāma, not one who has no faith.

vsm1.7:126.3.verse: One who is energetic … One whose mindfulness is established … One who is concentrated … One who has understanding is successful, Mahānāma, not one who has no understanding.

vsm1.7:126.4.verse: Having established yourself in these five things, Mahānāma, you should develop six things.

vsm1.7:126.5.verse: Here, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Perfect One: That Blessed One is such since …” (A V 329–32).

vsm1.7:127.1.verse: Still, though this is so, they can be brought to mind by an ordinary man too, if he possesses the special qualities of purified virtue, and the rest. [228]

vsm1.7:127.2.verse: For when he is recollecting the special qualities of the Buddha, etc., even only according to hearsay, his consciousness settles down,

vsm1.7:127.3.verse: by virtue of which the hindrances are suppressed.

vsm1.7:127.4.verse: In his supreme gladness he initiates insight,

vsm1.7:127.5.verse: and he even attains to Arahantship, like the Elder Phussadeva who dwelt at Kaṭakandhakāra.

vsm1.7:128.1.verse: That venerable one, it seems, saw a figure of the Enlightened One created by Māra.

vsm1.7:128.2.verse: He thought, “How good this appears despite its having greed, hate and delusion!

vsm1.7:128.3.verse: What can the Blessed One’s goodness have been like?

vsm1.7:128.4.verse: For he was quite without greed, hate and delusion!”

vsm1.7:128.5.verse: He acquired happiness with the Blessed One as object, and by augmenting his insight he reached Arahantship.

vsm1.7:128.6.verse:
The seventh chapter called “The Description of Six
Recollections” in the Treatise on the Development of
Concentration in the *Path of Purification* composed for the
purpose of gladdening good people.
